Summary verse (uddāna):
Kauṇḍinya, Nandīpāla, sweetmeats, and one should drink water.
Pūpaka was the son of Madhu and Vasiṣṭha, and he was foremost among those disciplined by calculation.
Karaka, Kalabhu, Viśvabhuj, and Vanaratha; Chattra, Kītaśiras, Maitrī, and likewise Ghaṇṭa proclaimed it.
When the Venerable Kauṇḍinya had realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements,
the Blessed One designated him as the foremost among those who carry the banner of the saṅghāṭī robe.
At that time, the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Kauṇḍinya, because of which he was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who carry the banner of the saṅghāṭī robe?
The Blessed One said:
"Karma was performed and accumulated by the monk Kauṇḍinya; its conditions have been gathered, its causes have matured, it has arrived like a rushing torrent, and it is inevitable."
Who else shall experience the actions performed and accumulated by Kauṇḍinya?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element,
nor in the wind element; rather, it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that deeds performed— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
The Story of Kauṇḍinya: Monks, formerly, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was one thousand years, a Samyaksaṃbuddha named Kāśyapa appeared in the world—
endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī on Mount Karakacchedaka.
Then, at another time, the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Vārāṇasī.
About five hundred members of the assembly were also departing;
those members of the assembly saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics.
Adorned with a fathom-wide aura of light,
possessing a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides.
Upon seeing him, they were filled with faith and began to converse:
"Sirs, we must go forth into the religious life in his presence.
Having thus made their agreement, some of them set out upon the great ocean.
Some have gone to other lands;
some have been joined with the law of time;
sixteen people remain.
Having gone to Mount Karakacchedaka, they went forth as monastics in the presence of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kāśyapa;
there they remained established in the practice of meditation and study.

Then, at another time, after the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa had completed all the work of a Buddha, he passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana—like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.
The deities announced this to them:
"Sirs, Kāśyapa has attained final nirvana."
"And since his parinirvāṇa seven days ago, his teaching has vanished; why do you stand here like those who have not yet obtained their fruit?
Upon hearing this, because they had not yet accomplished what was to be done, they were struck by great suffering.
Upon merely hearing this, five of them descended from Mount Karakacchedaka and entered Vārāṇasī;
by means of that very same spiritual urgency, those six exerted vigor and realized pratyekabodhi.
Afterwards, the other five descended and [proceeded] to enter Vārāṇasī.
They set out; meanwhile, a caravan of carts was departing. One cart-driver’s oxen were weak, so he struck them repeatedly with a goad-stick.
Because their vital strength was exhausted, they were unable to proceed;
that cart-driver was traveling at the head of that caravan of carts,
and he was addressed by those monks:
"O cartwright, these oxen of yours are weak;
why do you strike them again and again with the goad-stick?
If they are unable to go, [let them rest]."
"Follow behind me with a confident gait and movement," he said;
the other replied,
"If I go ahead of you, it will not be possible for me to travel together with this caravan of carts."

"If I follow behind, this caravan of carts will surely leave me abandoned"; thus, having conceived a sense of aversion toward the cart-driver due to improper conceptualizations, they said to one another:
"Sirs, since the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa has passed into parinirvāṇa, we have been delayed"—by this they made this reproach against us;
"What if we were now to exert ourselves?
Having understood this, they spoke this verse:
Even though the Dharma of the great sage Kāśyapa has disappeared,
we shall not slacken our vigor regarding that which was taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Even if our outflows (*āsrava*) do not reach total exhaustion,
we shall become the foremost disciples of the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas.
Having entered Vārāṇasī and wandered for alms, they returned once more to Mount Karakacchedaka and remained there established in the yoga of meditation and study.
Of them, four had passed away; one remained.
He, full of longing, uttered this inspired exclamation:

"This is that very Karakacchedaka mountain where I attended upon the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa; and there I saw one among his twenty thousand monks who was the sole bearer of the *saṅghāṭī*-banner throughout the entire Jambūdvīpa."
He began to make a formal vow:
"Although I have practiced the holy life for as long as my lifespan lasted under the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one, I have not attained any collection of qualities."
"By this root of merit, may I go forth in the teaching of that very Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Truly and Fully Awakened One, who prophesied of the young brahmin named Uttara:
'Young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Truly and Fully Awakened One, named Śākyamuni.
Having gone forth in his teaching, may I first of all realize Arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions."
"And may the Blessed One Śākyamuni designate me as the foremost among those who carry the banner of the saṅghāṭī robe.
What do you think, monks?

He who at that time, on that occasion, was among the twenty thousand monks of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, after he had passed into parinirvāṇa—[was it someone else? (SBV II 4)
In the entire Jambūdvīpa, there remains but one monk who bears the banner of the saṅghāṭī robe;
he is that very Kauṇḍinya monk by whom the vow was made on the mountain Karakacchedaka.
By the power of that vow, he has now been designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who carry the banner of the saṅghāṭī robe.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed; therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed,
you should apply yourselves only to actions that are exclusively white.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
When the Dharma that was to be done and not to be done had been taught by the Blessed One to the venerable Kauṇḍinya, [he asked:
'Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma?'"
"It is understood, Blessed One; is the Dharma understood by you, Kauṇḍinya? "It is understood, Sugata."
Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by Ājñātakauṇḍinya, such that the Dharma—both what is to be done and what is not to be done—was taught to him by the Blessed One, [and he replied]:
'Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma?'"
"It is understood, Blessed One; is the Dharma understood by you, Kauṇḍinya? "It is understood, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the monk Kauṇḍinya himself; their conditions have been met, and as before, they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings.
[This concludes] the story of Kāśisundaraka (the Preacher of Forbearance).
(Concerning a previous birth of Kauṇḍinya:

Once upon a time, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned; his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
At a later time, he played, enjoyed himself, and dallied with the queen;
while he was thus playing, enjoying himself, and dallying, the queen became pregnant;
and after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A son was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs;
having performed the birth ceremony upon his birth, his name was established.
"What shall be the name of the boy?
The ministers replied,
"Your Majesty, it is the custom in the Middle Country that one who is handsome and pleasing is called 'Sundara'."
"And this boy is handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing;
since he is the son of the King of Kāśi,
let the boy's name be Kāśisundara."
The name Kāśisundara was established for him;
the boy Kāśisundara was entrusted to eight nurses:
two to act as body-nurses, two to act as milk-nurses, and two—(A 426a) [to act as play-nurses and two to act as cleanliness-nurses].
He was raised by two nurses who attended to his needs and two nurses who played with him;
he was nourished by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various excellent provisions most refined, and he grew rapidly like a lotus in a pond.
Furthermore, while the king was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, the queen became pregnant;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth, and a boy was born.
On the very day that a great quarrel arose among the citizens and country-folk in Vārāṇasī, his birth festival was celebrated and his name was established;
they asked, "What shall be the name of this boy?"
The people of the inner apartments said: "Your Majesty, at the birth of this child, a great quarrel arose among the citizens and the people of the countryside in Vārāṇasī;
therefore, let the boy's name be Kalibhū."
King Brahmadatta ruled the kingdom with both righteousness and unrighteousness;
Prince Kāśisundara saw his father ruling the kingdom with both righteousness and unrighteousness,
and having seen this, it occurred to him:
"I too, upon the passing of my father, shall become king; I too, having ruled the kingdom through both righteousness and unrighteousness, shall be destined for hell;
what if I were to go forth from the home into the homeless state?"
He approached his father and, falling at his feet, said:
"Father, grant me your permission."
"I am going forth from the home to the homeless state";
he said,
"Son, for whose sake sacrifices are performed..."
Sacrifices are offered,
austerities are performed,
and that kingdom of yours has come into the palm of your hand.
"For whose sake do you cast [it] aside and go forth?
He spoke this verse:
"Better is it to dwell in the forest with beasts of prey, eating fruit and clothed in garments of bark."
"A wise person who fears the next world should not, for the sake of a kingdom, commit acts of killing, binding, or beating.
Thus he spoke. The king said:
"O Prince, you should know that you are our only son, dear and beloved, patient and not contrary to our will."
"By death alone shall we be separated from you against our will;
we will not abandon you while you are still living," said Prince Kāśisundara.
"Father, if you will grant me permission, that would be well;
but if you do not grant me permission, I shall not eat today."
"I shall not drink";
thereupon, the prince Kāśisundara missed one meal,
and two.
He fasted for three, up to six, meals;
then King Brahmadatta said this to Prince Kāśisundara: (SBV II 6)
Indeed, dear prince, you should know that the holy life is difficult to practice,
solitude is difficult to achieve, and dwelling alone is difficult to find pleasure in.
The forest retreats and wilderness dwellings are difficult to fully comprehend; it is hard to settle in remote lodgings,
and dwelling alone in the forest is painful.
For as long as you live, you must dwell with wild beasts;
for as long as you live, you must subsist on what is given by others;
for as long as you live, you must maintain a renunciation of human sensual pleasures.
"For as long as you live, you must renounce human pleasures and amusements;
come, my dear son, prince, remain right here and exercise the office of crown prince,
and enjoy sensual pleasures."
"Give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
When this was said, Prince Kāśisundara remained silent.
Then King Brahmadatta dispatched his harem, ministers, and domestic priests.
"Friends, please raise the prince.
"So be it, Your Majesty," replied the women of the inner apartments, the ministers, and the family priest, and they approached Prince Kāśisundara.
Having approached him, they said this to Prince Kāśisundara: "Indeed, [what you have said]..."
"Dear prince, you should know this: for you are delicate and a seeker of pleasure;
you do not understand suffering."
The holy life is difficult to practice;
seclusion is hard to achieve; solitude is difficult to find pleasure in.
The forest retreats and wilderness dwellings are difficult to fully comprehend; it is hard to settle in remote lodgings,
and dwelling alone in the forest is painful.
For as long as you live, you must dwell with wild beasts;
for as long as you live, you must subsist on what is given by others;
for as long as you live, you must maintain a renunciation of human sensual pleasures.
"For as long as you live, you must refrain from human pleasures and amusements;
come, dear prince, remain right here and exercise the office of crown prince,
and enjoy sensual pleasures."
Give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
When this had been said, Prince Kāśisundara remained silent.
Then King Brahmadatta dispatched the sons of the ministers, the sons of the family priests, and other princes to play with Prince Kāśisundara in the dust, saying:
"Come now, young princes, raise up Prince Kāśisundara!"
Then the sons of the ministers, the sons of the domestic priests, and the princes, having given their assent to King Brahmadatta,
approached Prince Kāśisundara;
having approached him, they said this to Prince Kāśisundara:
"Indeed, my dear boy, you should know this: for you are delicate and a seeker of pleasure; you do not know suffering, and the holy life (brahmacarya) is difficult to practice."
Solitude is difficult to practice;
delighting in solitude is hard to find;
the forest retreats and wilderness dwellings are difficult to fully comprehend.
To dwell in remote lodgings,
to live alone in the forest is difficult;
for as long as you live, you will be with fierce beasts.
You must dwell together with them;
for as long as you live, you must subsist on what is given by others;
for as long as you live, you must maintain restraint regarding human sensual pleasures.
"For as long as you live, you must refrain from human pleasures and amusements;
come, dear boy, remaining right here, exercise the office of crown prince and enjoy sensual delights."
Give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
When this had been said, Prince Kāśisundara remained silent.
Then the sons of the ministers and the sons of the domestic priests approached King Brahmadatta;
having approached, they said this to King Brahmadatta:
"Grant permission, O King, for the gentle Prince Kāśisundara;
for what will you do with one who is dead?
For the life of renunciation is praised by the wise."
If you take pleasure [in this],
you shall see him alive; if you do not take pleasure [in this], [you shall not].
For sages are indeed subject to rebirth;
what other refuge can a son have besides his mother and father?
King Brahmadatta said:
"Young men, if it is so,
let him be permitted."
Then the sons of the ministers, the sons of the family priests, and the princes approached Prince Kāśisundara; having approached, they said this to Prince Kāśisundara:
"Indeed, dear prince, you should know this:"
"You have been permitted by the king to go forth into homelessness; now do as you deem the time right.
Then Prince Kāśisundara, having performed the gradual rites of anointing, having generated physical stamina, strength, and vigor, departed from Vārāṇasī and went forth among the sages.
Therefore, by striving and exerting himself, having cultivated detachment from sensual pleasures, he attained loving-kindness.
He became exceedingly compassionate toward sentient beings;
by virtue of this disposition, even predatory wild animals placed their trust in his hermitage and did no harm.
He became known by the name Kṣāntivādī, "Proponent of Forbearance";
then, at a later time,
King Brahmadatta passed away.
Kālābhū was established in the kingdom;
he [ruled] the kingdom through both righteousness and unrighteousness.
He causes it to be done;
the seer Kṣāntivādī says: "Preceptor, I am deprived of food and drink."
"I am unable to subsist on wild forest herbs;
I shall go to the vicinity of a village," he said. [The other] replied: "Child, whether in the village or in the forest..."
"The sense faculties of a seer dwelling [in the forest] must indeed be guarded.
Go to the vicinity of Vārāṇasī;
having gone there, construct leaf-huts with branches and prepare a dwelling."
Having received permission from his preceptor, he went to Vārāṇasī and,
wandering here and there in search of a peaceful dwelling, eventually arrived at a park belonging to his father. While roaming about there, he saw a tranquil spot.

He remained there. Then, at another time, when the season of spring had arrived and the trees were in full bloom, and while the groves of the forest resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvañjīvaka birds, King Kalabhū went out to the pleasure gardens accompanied by his harem.
Having experienced pleasure there in the grove, he became weary and fell into a state of drowsiness;
meanwhile, the women, lusting after flowers and fruits, began to wander here and there in that grove,
until they saw the sage Kṣāntivādin sitting in a secluded spot with a tranquil deportment.
Having seen him, their mental continuums were suffused with reverence; they prostrated before the seer and stood surrounding him.
The seer Kṣāntivādī began to teach the Dharma to those women with an exceedingly peaceful deportment.
Meanwhile, King Kalabhū, having dispelled his fatigue from sleep, woke up and did not see the women of the inner apartments.
Taking his sword, he began to search for the young women;
when he saw them standing there surrounding the seer Kṣāntivādin,
his body became agitated by anger born of envy, and he approached that seer.
Seeing the woman standing in the presence of the king, she became terrified and fled;
the king, with great composure, said to Kṣāntivādin:
"O man, who are you?"
He replied:
"I am a proponent of patience.
King Kalabhū said:
"When I have become angry, do you still claim to be a teacher of patience? Now, are you truly a teacher of patience or not? Having said this, he cut off his hands;
then he asked him again.
"Who are you? he asked;
he replied, "I am Kṣāntivādī."
He cut off his feet;
as his limbs and members were being severed, he spoke this verse:
"Even if you were to cut my body into a hundred pieces and cast it upon the earth..."
I shall not abandon patience, even if my body were ground to pieces bit by bit as small as sesame seeds;

for that auspicious loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has been constantly cultivated in my mind, and I cannot bring myself to destroy that patience, just as a mother devoted to her child cannot bear to harm her son.

Having thus dispelled his pain with these verses and songs, he began to make this aspiration: "Just as this king, whose mind is obsessed by the afflictions, cuts off my limbs and members— both major and minor— for what should not be done,
so may I likewise be endowed with patience and gentleness."
"By means of this root of merit, having completely conquered the host of my own afflictions, may I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
then, with the weapon of wisdom, having first determined what is to be done and what is not to be done, may I utterly wither away those afflictions.
Then, the goddess who was devoted to Kṣāntivādin reflected:
"This seer has been rendered handless and footless by this King Kali, though he was innocent and had done him no harm;
what if I were now to exact my revenge upon him?
Having realized this, with intense [resolve]...
Driven by this obsession, he spoke this verse before Kṣāntivādin:
"Command that Kalabhu, along with his sons, wives, circle of kinsmen, and the people of the city and countryside—the entire world of living beings—be destroyed; I shall cause them to perish."
He too spoke this verse:

"I do not wish for even the slightest evil against him by whom my body was made mangled and distressed through the destruction of my hands and feet; how much less so against the world, which is entirely blameless?"
The deity who was there in Vārāṇasī was also dispatched hither and thither;
mice, locusts, and parrots became powerful.
The god did not send rain; the populace was dying;
the king summoned the diviners and questioned them.
"Sirs, for what reason does the Lord not send rain?
Mice, locusts, and parrots have become powerful,
and the populace is dying."
They said:
"Your Majesty, it is due to the wrath of a deity;
that deity who was well-disposed toward the seer Kṣāntivādin has become angry."
"This plague was created by her," they said.
The king asked, "Sirs, how should we proceed in this matter?"
The diviners said:
"Your Majesty, the deities are propitiated by offerings of oblations and garlands;
having made an offering of oblations and garlands, that seer must be asked for forgiveness."
Then the king had a proclamation made by the ringing of a bell in Vārāṇasī:
"Listen, you citizens residing in Vārāṇasī!
The deity dwelling in the park has conceived faith in the seer Kṣāntivādin."
By her, a plague was unleashed; because of it, the god did not rain,
and mice, locusts, and parrots became powerful.
"The populace is dying;
therefore, for the sake of pacifying this plague, you must go to the park tomorrow morning with offerings of food, garlands, and gifts, and perform worship to her.
That very night, the populace prepared offerings of food, garlands, and gifts, and went to that park.

The king, together with his harem, then gave gifts to the assembly of people— monks, brahmins, the poor, and beggars— and having performed a great worship at the shrine of the deity, he asked that deity for forgiveness.
Then the king went into the presence of the seer Kṣāntivādin, prostrated at his feet, and began to ask for forgiveness:
"Forgive me, Great Seer, for whatever offense I have committed against you while my mind was clouded by anger and my intellect was preoccupied with sense-objects.
The Proponent of Patience replied: "I have forgiven you, Great King."
How is this known?
He speaks this verse:
"Though you carry a weapon upon your limbs, I have loving-kindness toward all sentient beings."
"If you have any doubt in this matter, look at my blood, which is clear.
But that blood of his turned back;
even upon seeing such a miracle, that king, a doer of evil deeds, did not believe.
He spoke again:
"Forgive me, Great Seer";
"It is forgiven, Great King."
How is this known?
Then the Bodhisattva, having restored his severed limbs and members to their respective places, spoke this verse by means of a truthful invocation:
"O King, just as there was no pain for me while my limbs were being cut off by you..."
"May there not be even the slightest malice [toward me], and may my body become as it was before.
By virtue of his truthful prayer, his body was restored to its former state.
Then the king, his eyes wide with wonder, spoke this verse:
"Oh, this vow has been perfected! Oh, how well-practiced is your dharma, since you experience no agitation even while your limbs are being cut asunder!"
King Kalabhū, together with his harem, ministers, citizens, and countryfolk, having bowed his head at the feet of that seer, departed. What do you think, monks,
as to who he was at that time and on that occasion?
I myself was that seer who preached patience;
he who was King Kali is this very monk Kauṇḍinya.
Because I generated a mind of loving-kindness toward him and made a vow, [the result has come to pass].
"By this root of merit, may I cut away his defilements, both those that should be done and those that should not be done.
By the power of that aspiration, the Tathāgata has now taught him the Dharma regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done:
"For actions that are entirely black, the maturation is entirely black."
As before, up to: "In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.

When the Blessed One had gathered eighty thousand deities by means of the flavor of the Dharma and established them in the truths, the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable One, how eighty thousand deities have been gathered by the Blessed One through the flavor of the Dharma and established in the truths.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, I gathered these eighty thousand merchants with material gifts and established them in the five precepts."
Listen to that. Once upon a time, monks, there were two caravan leaders named Viśvabhuk and Suyātra.
Each one was accompanied by a retinue of forty thousand merchants;
among them, Suyātra delighted in renunciation,
and he went forth into homelessness in the midst of the ṛṣis.

Having exerted effort alone, without a teacher and without an instructor, he brought the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening into manifestation and realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
His caravan companions, not seeing their leader, began searching for him here and there; when they could not find him by any means, the caravan leader Viśvabhū departed without looking back.
"We have searched for him but have not found him; how should we proceed in this matter?
He replied, "Wait."
"Do not be despondent; let us search for the caravan leader.
Then the caravan leader Viśvabhuk, surrounded by eighty thousand merchants, began to search for the caravan leader Suyātra in gardens, dwellings, and ascetic groves.
He was seen by him and asked:
"Why have you gone forth, abandoning the caravan?
For those great-souled ones, the teaching of the Dharma is physical, not verbal.
By means of these miracles—of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning—that caravan leader, together with his retinue, was won over.
He then provided those eighty thousand merchants with material gifts and said to them:
"Perform services for him."
Services rendered to him invariably become fruit-bearing;
by means of those [services], many acts of service were performed for him.
What do you think, monks? That caravan leader Viśvabhū was none other than myself.
At that time, on that occasion,
those thousands of merchants were none other than these eighty thousand deities;
even then, having attracted them with material gifts, I established them in the five precepts.
Even now, having provided them with the essence of the True Dharma (*saddharma-rasa*), I have established them in the Truths.
Thus, monks, there is a mingling of entirely black deeds [with white ones]; in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.

When the Blessed One had drawn the five monks out from the wilderness of *saṃsāra* and shared with them the jewels of the faculties, the powers, and the factors of awakening, he satisfied them with the essence of the True Dharma.
Then the monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how the five monks have been rescued by the Blessed One from the wilderness of saṃsāra and satiated with the essence of the True Dharma."

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what is the wonder here that now, by me who am free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, and liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair?"

By the Omniscient One, the Knower of All Aspects, who has attained mastery over all knowledge and the objects of knowledge, the five monks were delivered from the wilderness of saṃsāra and satiated with the essence of the True Dharma;
whereas I, too, in past times, was possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, and was not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
When he was a caravan leader, five hundred [merchants] encountered hardship, peril, and distress on a desert path; being deprived of water, they were on the verge of losing their lives.
Having offered prayers to the deities, they were satiated by a rain of water sent by Mahendra.
Listen to that.
The Story of the Thirsty Caravan:

Once upon a time, monks, a merchant leader named Viśvabhuj was traveling for trade with five hundred merchants when he entered a desert path with little water. In due course, they reached the Vindhya forest, where all their water was completely exhausted.
A caravan of merchants set out on a journey because they were deprived of water;
however, five of the merchants, finding no water, became exceedingly distressed.
Seeing them in such a state, Viśvabhuk, the caravan leader, his heart trembling with compassion, turned his face upward and began to offer a prayer to the deities:

"Listen, O venerable gods, Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava, and the rest! By that truth, by that word of truth, through which my compassion is directed equally toward all, by this truth, by this word of truth, may the god Mahendra send rain!
Through the power of the Bodhisattva, the palace of Mahendra was shaken."
The knowledge and vision of Śakra, lord of the gods, operates below him; he perceives:
"By whom has the palace of Māhendra been shaken?"
He saw it through the power of the Bodhisattva;
he released such a rain from the realm of Indra that this caravan of merchants was fully satisfied and successfully traversed the path through the wilderness.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that caravan leader Viśvabhuj was none other than myself at that time and on that occasion;
those five merchants who became exceedingly distressed due to the lack of water were these very same five monks;
even then, having satisfied them with water, I delivered them from the path of the wilderness.
Even now, having satisfied them with the essence of the True Dharma, I have delivered them from the wilderness of saṃsāra.

When the Blessed One had delivered the five monks from the wilderness of saṃsāra and shared with them the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, the monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable One, how the Blessed One has rescued the five monks from the wilderness of saṃsāra and shared with them the jewels of the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
The Blessed One said: "What is there to see in this, monks?"

It is marvelous that now, having become free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion; being liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; having attained omniscience, the knowledge of all modes, and mastery over all knowledge and its objects—I have caused the five monks to cross over the wilderness of saṃsāra by means of the jewels of the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
They were shared out; and as for how, in the past, when I was still possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, and not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation,
pain, dejection, and despair, I— having become a caravan leader— rescued them from the great ocean by sacrificing my own life and shared the jewels with them.
Listen to that.
Long ago, there was this story concerning the merchant Dhanaratha.
Monks,
there was once a great caravan leader named Dhanaratha;
he set out for the great ocean together with five other caravan leaders.
Through their mutual conversation and friendly disposition, they became close friends with one another;
eventually, having reached the seashore in due course, each of them prepared his own ship.
At the time of disembarking, they addressed the caravan leader Dhanaratha.
"O caravan leader, we find no stability without you.
He replied,
"If that is so, mount right here and let the ships be released."
They had mounted it there when the wind arose;
as they were terrified, Dhanaratha said:
"Sirs, do not be afraid; when the ship meets with destruction, you must cling to my neck,
and I shall carry you across."
The Bodhisattvas became skilled in those various fields of arts and fields of labor;
therefore, highly precious jewels were fastened to their armpits.
The ship was wrecked;
they clung to the caravan leader,
and with their bodies exhausted and only a slight remnant of life remaining, they reached the shore of the ocean.
When they reached dry land, they set him down;
utterly disheartened, he passed away;
they then lifted him out of the water and onto the ground.
When they saw the precious jewels fastened to his armpits,
they took them and departed.
What do you think, monks?

He who was the caravan leader named Dhanaratha at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself; those five monks were also rescued by me from the great ocean at that time and shared in the jewels.
Even now, having been rescued by me from the wilderness of saṃsāra, they have been shared in the jewels of the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
When the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya sat at the head of the assembly, he sat there having formed a canopy over the congregation.
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the maturation of which causes him to sit with the assembly as if holding it over his head?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, actions were performed and accumulated by the monk Kauṇḍinya; having reached their requisite conditions, as previously stated, they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings."
The Story of the Householder Saṃdhāna (Concerning a Previous Birth of Kauṇḍinya)

Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī there lived a householder named Saṃdhana, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging possessions, and endowed with wealth equal to that of Vaiśravaṇa. At that time, a king named Brahmadatta reigned in Vārāṇasī, and his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people. Then, the fortune-tellers predicted a twelve-year drought.
King Brahmadatta caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout his realm:
"Listen, O citizens dwelling within my domain!
The astrologers have predicted a twelve-year drought."
Therefore, those among you who have food and drink sufficient for twelve years should dwell in my domain;
others must depart for various directions,
and upon the passing of twelve years, they should return.
Then the householder Saṃdhāna addressed the storekeeper:
"O man, is there twelve years' worth of food and drink in the storehouse?"
He replied, "Noble sir,
it will happen.
Then the householder Saṃdhāna sat down together with his retinue.
The multitude of people fled in all directions;
a great famine arose, a time of hardship and wilderness where alms were difficult for a beggar to obtain.

In the absence of the appearance of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world—those who have compassion for the lowly and the wretched, who delight in remote lodgings and seats, and who are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
At that time, not far from Vārāṇasī, five hundred pratyekabuddhas were dwelling in a certain hermitage.
When the populace, terrified by the fear of famine and death, had fled in all directions, their alms-food was cut off.
They all gathered together and approached the householder Sandhana, saying: "Householder,..."
"Provide sustenance for our five hundred renunciants with almsfood," he said;
he replied,
"First, let me look into the storehouse."
He addressed the steward:
"O man, is there in our storehouse enough food and drink for us and for these five hundred renunciants for twelve years?
He replied: "Noble sir, there will be."
Having heard that the householder Saṃdhāna had provided alms-food for five hundred renunciants, another five hundred pratyekabuddhas approached the householder Saṃdhāna;
having approached him, they said this to the householder Saṃdhāna:
"Householder, provide alms-food for our five hundred renunciants so that they may sustain their practice.
He replied, "Noble ones, you have already been given [this]; what more do you request?"
They said, "Householder, we are one thing and they are another.
He replied, "Noble sirs,
if that is so, let me first look after the steward of the storehouse."
He addressed the steward:
"O man, is there in our storehouse food and drink sufficient for ourselves and for this thousand renunciants for twelve years?
He replied:
"It will happen";
he said to those Pratyekabuddhas,
"Noble ones, stay!"
"Who among you is it whose time for food has come?
They replied,
"Householder, midday has not yet passed."
Then, by the householder Saṃdhāna, a hall for giving was constructed, a man was appointed as the overseer of the gifts, and a time-announcer was stationed;
they came every day and performed the meal service.

Among that assembly of a thousand Pratyekabuddhas, there was a senior elder (saṃghasthavira) who was exceedingly handsome; with a head shaped like a parasol, he stood there overshadowing that entire congregation.
The daughter of the householder Saṃdhāna, having seen the parasol-shaped head and the abundance of the elder of the Saṅgha’s complexion, became exceedingly devoted to him.
Then, at another time during the meal hour, it began to rain.
Then, that girl held a parasol over the head of the Elder of the Saṅgha; and when he had finished eating, she prostrated at his feet and made this aspiration:

"By this root of merit, may I become a possessor of such qualities as this noble one, and just as he sits in the assembly with a parasol held over him, so may I also [sit] with a parasol held over me."
"I shall sit in the assembly. What do you think, monks?
That daughter of the householder Saṃdhāna was none other than this very person.
As for the monk Kauṇḍinya:

when he was a young girl, having held a parasol over the elder of the community of pratyekabuddhas, she made this aspiration, "May I become a possessor of such qualities as these, and may I sit presiding over the assembly with a parasol held over me."
Thus, having now realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements, he stands with the assembly held as a parasol over him.

"For this reason, monks, the ripening of entirely black karmas is entirely black," and so on, as before, up to: "In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. When eighty thousand deities were satiated by the essence of the True Dharma through the Blessed One’s instruction of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the monks, filled with doubt, [approached] the one who cuts through all doubts...
They questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how eighty thousand deities have been satiated with the essence of the True Dharma by means of the Venerable Ājñāta-kaunḍinya.
The Blessed One said:
Monks, what is the wonder here that now, having become free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion;

being liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; being omniscient, possessing knowledge of all modes, and having attained mastery over all knowledge and the objects of knowledge—by relying on Ājñāta-kaundinya, eighty thousand deities [have been converted]?
Have they been fully satisfied by the flavor of the Dharma?

As for that which occurred in the past, when I was possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair,

with a body fallen into ruin and reborn in the animal realm as an eighty-thousand-fold swarm of insects while Kauṇḍinya had become a female insect— [have those beings been satisfied by the flavor of the Dharma?]
Having arrived, they were satiated with his own blood;
let that be heard.
The story of the tortoise.
Once upon a time, monks, concerning a former birth of Kauṇḍinya:
A bodhisattva situated in the indeterminate category was reborn among the tortoises in the great ocean and became their sovereign.
Eventually, five hundred merchants set out upon a ship for the great ocean and descended into the great ocean.
Then, having gathered various jewels, they set out;
however, their ship was brought to disaster by an unlawful sea-monster of the fish species,
and a great clamor arose there.
Upon hearing that sound, the tortoise emerged from the great ocean;
having approached them, he said:
"Enough of your despair! Climb onto my back and I will carry you across."
Having regained their lost lives, they all climbed onto the back of the tortoise;
taking them with him, he set out toward the shore of the ocean;
though oppressed by the extreme weight, he exerted his strength and did not fall into despair.
With his body exhausted, he stretched out his neck and fell asleep among those thickets.
Not far from him was an anthill inhabited by ants;
one ant, wandering about, caught the scent and approached him.
Then, seeing that great transformation of his body into such a massive form, a female ant who moved with swift gait went to the ant-city;
having awakened the ants by their own signals, she took eighty thousand ants and went to the side of the tortoise.
Thereupon, they began to devour him, who was as motionless as if dead, his life-breath having ceased.
When they devour his coarse flesh, he— exhausted by fatigue and firmly overcome by deep torpor— is not conscious of it;
but when they devour the flesh in the vital parts, then, having awakened, he sees his entire body covered with ants, and he reflects:
"If I move my body or turn it over, they will certainly kill me;
better to lose my life than to cause the obstruction of their lives."
Having understood this, as his vital organs were being cut and his joints were being severed, he began to make a formal aspiration:

"Just as these eighty thousand ants have been satiated by me with my own flesh and blood, so too, in a future time, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, may I satisfy them with the essence of the True Dharma."
What do you think, monks?
He who was that guide for the path of the ants is this very monk Kauṇḍinya;
and those eighty thousand ants who, by following him, were satiated with flesh and blood—[they are these monks here].
Those eighty thousand deities were then satiated by me with my own blood;
even now, they have been satiated by me with the essence of the True Dharma.
"Thus indeed, monks, regarding those who are entirely black... [and so on] ...in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.

When the Blessed One had satisfied the group of five monks with the essence of the True Dharma, delivered them from the wilderness of saṃsāra, and established them in the ultimate security of Nirvāṇa, the monks, overcome by doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Behold, Venerable One, how the Blessed One has satisfied the monks with the essence of the True Dharma, delivered them from the wilderness of saṃsāra, and established them in the ultimate security of nirvāṇa.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, what is the wonder here that now, by me who am free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion..."

By whom— liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; omniscient, possessing knowledge of all modes, and having attained mastery over all knowledge and its objects— were the five monks satiated with the essence of the true Dharma,
delivered from the wilderness of saṃsāra, and established in the ultimate, final security of nirvāṇa?

But listen to this: in the past, while I was still possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, and not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, I satisfied these beings with my own blood and established them in the five precepts.
Listen to that.
The Story of King Vajrabāhu.
Monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Vajrabāhu who ruled a kingdom that was prosperous, wealthy, and teeming with many people.

That king was faithful, noble, and of virtuous intent; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of everything, and one who gives without attachment.
And he abides in great renunciation;
by that, loving-kindness has been thoroughly practiced by him;
three times a day, he enters into the meditative attainment of loving-kindness.
As he was entering into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), beggars were being turned away;
therefore, he gave an order to his ministers:

"Sirs, having constructed almshouses at the four city gates of Vārāṇasī, provide whatever is required to whoever seeks it—whether they be ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, the needy, travelers, or beggars."

"So be it, Your Majesty," the ministers replied to King Vajrabāhu. Having thus assented, they constructed alms-halls at the four city gates of Vārāṇasī and established them with a vast collection of goods— food, drink, clothing, bedding, seats, gold, silver, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, native gold, silver, emerald, musāragalva, lohitikā, and right-spiraling conch—
to satisfy those who came as supplicants.
Then, at another time, King Vaiśravaṇa banished five yakṣas who were stealers of vitality from the capital city of Aḍakavatī;
wandering here and there, they eventually arrived at Vārāṇasī.
Seeing cowherds, shepherds, grass-gatherers, wood-gatherers, and people who subsist by the highway or by unlawful paths, they said:

"Sirs, are you not afraid of us? [They replied: "Sirs, why should we be afraid? For our king is one whose nature is loving-kindness and compassion, who, with the resolute intention to benefit all sentient beings, enters into the meditative attainment of loving-kindness three times each day."

Thus it was said; then, having transformed themselves into the guise of brahmins and inspected the halls of charity at the four gates of Vārāṇasī, and knowing that King Vajrabāhu had emerged from his state of loving-kindness, they approached the king while wearing modest attire.
Having approached and greeted the king with wishes for his victory and long life, they said:
"Your Majesty, we are hungry; please show us favor by granting us food.
The king summoned his ministers and spoke to them.
"Sirs, satisfy these brahmins with choice food";
they replied,
"We are eaters of flesh and blood."
The king addressed the ministers: "Sirs, if there is no availability of meat or blood, then provide blood obtained through the path of righteousness and justice."
They said:
"We are eaters of fresh blood and flesh;
show us favor with the flesh and blood of one recently slain."
The king reflected:
"How can there be the production of flesh and blood from one who has been killed on the spot without causing pain to another?
What if I were to give them my own blood?"
Then, having summoned the physicians, he said: "Sirs, perform a venesection on all my limbs;
I shall satisfy the people who come as supplicants."
The physicians said:
"We do not apply the surgical blade to the body of Your Majesty for the sake of ordinary men;
Bodhisattvas are indeed skilled in those various fields of arts and crafts."

He himself inflicted a wound with a weapon upon his five limbs; then, having satiated them with his own blood and delivered such a teaching on the Dharma that they heard, those yakṣas were established in the five precepts.
(What do you think, monks?)
He who was the king named Vajrabāhu at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself;
those five yakṣas who were takers of vital energy were these very same five monks; even then, having satisfied them with my own blood, they were established in the five bases of virtuous conduct.
Even now, having satisfied them with the essence of the True Dharma, I have delivered these from the wilderness of saṃsāra and established them in the ultimate security of nirvāṇa.
When the Blessed One had satisfied the group of five monks with the essence of the True Dharma, delivered them from the wilderness of saṃsāra,
and established them in the ultimate security of nirvāṇa, the monks, overcome by doubt, [approached] the one who cuts through all doubts.
They asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:

"Behold, Venerable Sir, how the five monks have been satiated by the Blessed One with the essence of the true Dharma, delivered from the wilderness of saṃsāra, and established in the ultimate security of nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what is the wonder here that now, by me who am free from passion and have attained mastery over all knowledge and its objects, the five monks have been satiated with the essence of the True Dharma, delivered from the wilderness of saṃsāra, and established in the ultimate security of liberation?"
They were established in nirvāṇa.

But as for how, in the past, when I was still subject to passion—as previously described—I satiated them with my own blood and established them in the five precepts amidst suffering, dejection, and despair;
listen to that.
The Story of Maitrabala:
"In the past, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Maitrabala who ruled over a kingdom that was prosperous and populous.
He was composed of loving-kindness, compassionate, magnanimous, and full of mercy toward all sentient beings."
Then, at another time, King Vaiśravaṇa banished five yakṣas who were takers of vital energy from the royal capital of Aḍakavatī for some offense.
Having wandered through that country, they arrived at Vārāṇasī;
yet no one there offered them any oblation, garland, or gift.
Having become enraged, they unleashed a pestilence;
a great multitude of people died in Vārāṇasī,
and the ministers informed King Maitrabala.
"Your Majesty, there is an exceedingly great number of people dead in Vārāṇasī.
The king gave them this command:
"Go to Vārāṇasī and cause a proclamation by bell to be made as follows:"
The Venerable King Maitrabala commands:
"With a mind solely intent on the altruistic resolve for the welfare of all sentient beings, I pass my days and nights;
therefore, you too should cultivate loving-kindness that extends to all sentient beings."
"In this way, peace shall come to you.
Those [monks] began to attend to loving-kindness (maitrī) that extends to all sentient beings;
meanwhile, the *yakṣas* who steal vitality (*ojas*) began to roam about the vicinity of Vārāṇasī.
They could not gain entrance;
being unable to enter, they saw cowherds, shepherds, grass-gatherers, wood-gatherers, and men who subsist by the highway or by off-the-road ways, and said to them:
"Sirs, are you not afraid of us?"
Thus they spoke: "We do not fear.
For what reason?"
For we think whatever King Maitrabala thinks;
what does King Maitrabala think?
He thinks of loving-kindness that extends to all sentient beings.
They reflected:
"This must be the reason why we do not find an opening now";
they [then entered] through the gate of Vārāṇasī.
They wandered about the gate, thinking,
"Perhaps we shall see King Maitrabala";
then, at another time, King Maitrabala set out for the pleasure garden outside.
Then, having transformed themselves into the guise of brahmins and approached the king with peaceful deportment, they greeted him with wishes for victory and long life and said:
"Your Majesty, we are hungry; please show us favor by granting us food."
The king summoned his ministers and said to them:
"Sirs, satisfy these brahmins with excellent food.
They replied:
"O King, we are eaters of flesh and blood.
The king addressed his ministers: "Sirs, if [there is no] meat..."
"There is a possibility of obtaining blood; provide meat and blood acquired through righteous means and according to the law.
[They replied: "Your Majesty, we consume the flesh and blood of those killed on the very spot; please favor us with meat from one recently slaughtered.
The king reflected:
"How can there be the production of flesh and blood from one recently killed without causing pain to another?
What if I were to give them my own blood?
Having thought this, he summoned the physicians and said:
"Gentlemen, perform a venesection on all my limbs so that I may satisfy the people who come as supplicants," he said.
The physicians replied,
"Your Majesty, we do not apply a surgical instrument to Your Majesty's body for the sake of ordinary men."
The Bodhisattvas were skilled in those various fields of arts and crafts;
therefore, he himself inflicted the blow of the weapon upon his own five limbs.
Then, having satisfied them with his own blood, he gave such a teaching of the Dharma that, upon hearing it, those yakṣas were established in the five precepts.
"What do you think, monks?
He who was that king named Maitrabala at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself;
and those five *yakṣas* who were the stealers of vital energy were [the others]."
These very ones are those five monks;
even then, having satisfied them with my own blood, I established them in the five bases of the vows;
and now as well, having satisfied them with the essence of the True Dharma, I have led them out from the wilderness of saṃsāra and established them in the ultimate, final security of nirvāṇa.
When the Blessed One had practiced austerities for six years,
attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
and gone to Vārāṇasī where he set the wheel of Dharma in motion;

When the group of five who had been disciplined, the group of fifty who were near the five, and the group of the sixty auspicious ones had been converted, and a great multitude of monks had arisen, the monks, overcome by doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable One, the karma performed by the Blessed One, the ripening of which resulted in his practicing austerities for six years.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births. [As stated] previously, they have reached their full measure and now bear fruit for embodied beings."
The story of Nandapāla the potter (*Ghaṭīkarasutta*, MN 81; cf. *Mahāvastu* I 319ff.):
"Once upon a time, monks, there was a village town named Vaibhiḍiṅgī, which was prosperous, flourishing, and populous.
In that village town of Vaibhiḍiṅgī, monks, there lived a wealthy brahmin householder named Nyagrodha."
He was wealthy, possessed of great riches and great enjoyments, and prosperous;
he enjoyed the Vaibhiḍiṅgī village, which was well-populated and provided with grass, wood, and water, having been granted as a *brahmadeya* by King Kṛkin.
Now, monks, the young brahmin student named Uttara was a pupil of the brahmin Mahāśāla of the Nyagrodha clan. He was endowed [with all the necessary qualities].
He is pure on both the mother’s and father’s side, unblemished by any reproach regarding birth or lineage, tracing back seven generations of maternal and paternal ancestors;

he is a teacher who has mastered the mantras, having reached the further shore of the three Vedas along with the Nighaṇṭus and Kaṭhas, including the phonetic analysis of syllables and the histories as the fifth, being a master of their exegesis.
He was handsome, pleasing to behold, and serene;
five hundred young brahmins were reciting the brahminical mantras under Nyagrodha, the great brahmin householder;
and in the village-town of Vaibhiḍiṅgī, monks, Nandīpāla the potter resided.
He has clear confidence in the Buddha, clear confidence in the Dharma, and clear confidence in the Saṅgha;

he has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dharma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; he is single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha, single-mindedly devoted to the Dharma, and single-mindedly devoted to the Saṅgha.
He is free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding the Buddha, free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha;

he is free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Having seen the truths, having realized the attainment of the fruit, he has laid aside the leaf-scraper and the pestle; he does not dig the earth with his own hand, nor does he cause it to be dug; he does nothing else [for this purpose].

Whatever there may be that is broken by water or scattered by mice, having gathered earth from that place with his body and soaked it with water free of living beings, he makes vessels, sets them aside in a secluded spot, and says:

"Come, noble ones; come, gentle-faced ones! Having set aside sesame seeds, or rice, or mung beans and the like, or black gram and the like, in a secluded spot, let whoever needs a particular vessel take it and depart."
He supported his blind parents from that [income] and provided food for the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa at the appropriate times.
Nandīpāla the potter, a friend, well-wisher, and companion of the young brahmin Uttara, approached the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there to one side...
The Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Nandīpāla the potter with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then Nandīpāla the potter, having bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, the young brahmin Uttara, having mounted a chariot drawn by mares that was entirely white, and holding a golden staff and water-pot, surrounded and preceded by a host of young brahmins, was departing from Vaibhiḍiṅgya;
desiring to have the brahmins outside Vaibhiḍiṅgya recite the mantras, the young brahmin Uttara saw Ghaṭīkāra Nandīpāla from afar.
Having seen him, he spoke thus:
"From where, dear Nandīpāla, do you come now?
"From here, dear sir, I have just now come from the north, after attending upon the Perfectly Awakened One, Kāśyapa."
"Come, dear Somya, let us go to the north;
we shall attend upon Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one.
Enough, dear Nandīpāla, with seeing Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one; enough with attending upon him."
For what reason?
From where could there be awakening in that shaven-headed ascetic?
For awakening is indeed extremely difficult to achieve.
"Do not speak thus, dear son, regarding that ascetic: 'How could there be awakening in that mendicant?
For awakening is indeed extremely difficult to achieve.'"
"Moreover, he is the Buddha, the Blessed One,
and all dharmas have been awakened to by him.
For a second time and for a third time, Nandīpāla the potter said this to the young man Uttara:
"Come, dear friend, let us go to the north;
we shall attend upon Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one.
For a second and even a third time, the young man Uttara said this to Nandīpāla the potter:
"Enough, dear Nandīpāla, with seeing the perfectly awakened Kāśyapa; enough with attending upon him.
For what reason?
How could there be awakening in that shaven-headed mendicant?"
"Awakening is indeed extremely difficult to achieve;
do not speak thus, gentle friend Uttara: 'How could there be awakening in that shaven-headed ascetic?
For awakening is indeed extremely difficult to achieve.'"
"Moreover, he is the Buddha,
the Blessed One, and by him all dharmas have been awakened to.
Then Nandīpāla the potter, having mounted the chariot of the young man Uttara, said this to the young man Uttara:
"Come, dear friend, let us go to the north;
we shall attend upon Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one.
Then this thought occurred to the young brahmin Uttara:
"Surely the Buddha will not be inferior, nor will his teaching of the Dharma be inferior,

since even Nandīpāla the potter— who for a long time has been free from anger, impetuosity, harshness, and recklessness— has now come to the point of seizing [the Buddha] by the hair. Having understood this, [he said] this to Nandīpāla the potter:
"Come, dear Nandīpāla, even further than this; come, dear Uttara, even further than this."
Even more so than that, my dear Nandīpāla; even more so than that,
my dear Uttara.
"In that case, dear Nandīpāla, let us go; we shall attend upon the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa."
Then the young brahmin Uttara and the potter Nandīpāla mounted their chariot and proceeded toward where the perfectly awakened Kāśyapa was.
Having gone by chariot as far as the ground would permit, they alighted from the vehicle and approached the perfectly awakened Kāśyapa.
Upon arrival, they bowed their heads at the feet of the perfectly awakened Kāśyapa and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Nandīpāla the potter said this to Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one:
"Venerable sir, this young man Uttara has no faith in the Buddha, nor does he have faith in the Dharma or the Saṅgha."
"It would be well if the Blessed One were to teach the Dharma to this Uttara Māṇava in such a way that he gains faith in the Buddha, gains faith in the Dharma, and gains faith in the Saṅgha.
The Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, consented and instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the young brahmin Uttara with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then the young man Uttara said this to Nandīpāla the potter:
"Why is it, dear Nandīpāla?"
"Having heard the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, do you not go forth from the home to the homeless state out of perfect faith?
My dear prince, do you not know that I support my blind parents?"
"I provide for the perfectly awakened Kāśyapa with almsfood from time to time;
you, gentle Nandīpāla, may either go forth or not;
as for me, I shall go forth."
Then Nandīpāla the potter said this to the Perfectly Awakened One, Kāśyapa:
"Venerable Sir, this young man Uttara desires the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
May the Blessed One, out of compassion, grant him the going-forth and the full ordination."
The Perfectly Awakened One, Kāśyapa, consented to Nandīpāla the potter by remaining silent.

Then, Nandīpāla the potter, understanding the consent of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa through his silence, bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa and rose from his seat.

Then, the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, knowing that Nandīpāla the potter had departed not long before, ordained and gave full ordination to the young brahmin Uttara; having stayed at Vaibhiḍiṅgī for as long as he pleased, he set out on a wandering tour toward Vārāṇasī, the market town of the Kāśīs.
Wandering on his journey by stages, he arrived at Vārāṇasī and stayed there in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
King Kṛkī of Kāśi heard that the Perfectly Awakened One, Kāśyapa, while wandering through the country of Kāśi, had reached Vārāṇasī and was staying there in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
Having heard this, he departed from Vārāṇasī and approached the place where Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, was staying.
Having approached and having paid homage with his head at the feet of Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, he sat down to one side.
To King Kṛkin, who was seated to one side, Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, taught, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, [the Blessed One] remained silent.
Then King Kṛkī rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, he said this to Kāśyapa:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow."
The Perfectly Awakened One, Kāśyapa, consented to King Kṛkin’s request by remaining silent.

Then King Kṛkin, understanding that the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa had consented through his silence, bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, rose from his seat, and departed.
That very night, King Kṛkin prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft; rising early in the morning, he arranged seats and set out water-jars.
He announced the time to the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa by messenger, saying:
"It is time, Venerable One; the meal is prepared; may the Blessed One do as he deems it the right time.

Then the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, went to where King Kṛkī’s meal-offering was being served.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared right in front of the community of monks.

Then King Kṛkī, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, in many ways; having thus personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, in many ways...

Having perceived that the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa had finished his meal, that he had washed his hands and set aside his bowl, he took a golden pitcher and stood before the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa, making this request:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept from me for three months the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick;
for the sake of the Blessed One, I shall cause five hundred monasteries to be built, and I shall have made five hundred sets of couches, stools, mats, woolen blankets, pillows, and square cushions."
"With such rice as this, covered with leaves, I shall attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks.
"Enough, Great King; let it be so, for your mind is already well-disposed.
A second and even a third time, King Kṛkī said this to the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kāśyapa:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept from me for three months the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick;
for the sake of the Blessed One, I shall have five hundred monasteries constructed, and I shall have five hundred sets of couches, stools, mattresses, pillows, bolsters, and square cushions made."
"By means of this very kind of rice, covered with leaves, I shall attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks.
A second and even a third time, Kāśyapa the Perfectly Enlightened One said this to King Kṛkī:
"Enough, Great King! Let it be as much as you have already done, namely, that your mind is full of serene faith."
Then King Kṛkī said this to the Perfectly Awakened One, Kāśyapa: "Is there, Blessed One, anyone else who could be such an attendant as I am now?
"There is, Great King; in your own realm there is a village-town named Vaibhiḍiṅgī."
There lived a potter named Nandīpāla;
he was devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dharma, and devoted to the Saṅgha;
he had gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dharma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.
He is resolutely devoted to the Buddha, resolutely devoted to the Dharma, and resolutely devoted to the Saṅgha.

He is free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; he is free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Having seen the Truths, having attained the fruit, and having realized it, he has laid aside the leaf and the pestle; he does not [use] his own hand...
He digs the earth himself but does not have it dug by others;

rather, whatever there may be that has been broken up by water or thrown up by mice, he gathers the clay from that with his own body, moistens it with water free of living beings, fashions vessels, and sets them aside in a secluded spot. Then he says, "O Noble Ones, O gentle-faced ones, having set aside sesame, rice, mung beans, or kidney beans in a secluded spot, whichever of you needs a particular vessel, let him take it."
Having taken [it], he departed;
from that time on, he supported his blind parents and provided me with almsfood from time to time.
“On one occasion, Great King, I was dwelling near the village-town of Vaibhiḍiṅgī.
Having dressed in the forenoon and taken my bowl and robe, I entered the village-town of Vaibhiḍiṅgī for alms.
While walking for alms in Vaibhiḍiṅgī with a steady gait, I approached the residence of Ghaṭīkāra.”
Having approached, I gently and very softly struck the bolt.
At that time, Nandīpāla the potter had gone out for some business,
and the blind parents of Nandīpāla the potter heard the sound of the bolt being struck.
Having heard this, they spoke thus:
"Who is this noble one? Who is this gentle-faced one who is knocking on the bolt so slowly and gently?
To them I said:
"I am Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, seeking alms-food. They both replied: "Enter, Noble One; enter, O Blessed One! Here are boiled grains in this pot and soup in this vessel."
"If you desire it, take it yourself and eat; your attendant has gone outside.
Thus, Great King, having empowered myself with the power of the Northern Kauravas, I took the boiled grain from the pot and the soup from the vessel myself and ate.
After that, Nandīpāla the potter arrived;
Nandīpāla the potter saw that the boiled grain was eaten from the bowl and the soup from the pot;
having seen this, he spoke thus to his blind parents:
"Mother, father, by whom have these boiled grains been eaten from the bowl, and the soup from the pot?
They replied thus:
In this matter, my dear Nandīpāla, you heard the sound of the bolt being struck shortly after you had gone out;
and having heard it, we spoke thus:
"Who is this noble one? Who is this gentle-faced one who strikes the bolt so slowly and very gently?"
He spoke thus: "I am Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, seeking alms.
We said to him:
"Enter, noble sir; enter, gentle-faced one."
"Here are boiled grains in the bowl and soup in the pot;
if you desire, take it yourself and eat.
Your attendant has gone outside."
"By that, you will have consumed the boiled grains from the pot and the soup from the saucepan.
Then, this thought occurred to Nandīpāla the potter:
"It is a great gain for me, a well-attained fortune for me, that the Perfectly Awakened Kāśyapa has placed such exceeding trust and confidence in my family."

Knowing that he had attained [this state], through that very joy and gladness he passes seven days in a single cross-legged posture, and for half a month his constant and continuous mindfulness does not leave his body;
it persists in the body without interruption.
For seven days, just as there was boiled grain for my parents from a pot and soup from a cooking vessel, so too was there rice from a jar and soup from a cooking vessel.
On one occasion, Great King, I entered the rains retreat residing near the village-town of Vaibhiḍiṅgī.
While that first rain fell upon me, my dwelling was drenched by the sky;
at that very time, the workshop of Nandīpāla the potter was covered with fresh grass.
I then addressed the monks who were my attendants:
"Go, monks, and having stripped away the fresh thatch from the workshop of Nandīpāla the potter, cover my vihāra.
Having assented to me with "So be it," they stripped away the fresh thatch from the workshop of Nandīpāla the potter.
Now at that time, Nandīpāla the potter had gone out on some business or other.
Nandīpāla’s blind parents heard the sound of the roof being covered in the workshop of the potter Ghaṭīkara;
having heard it, they spoke thus:
"Who is this noble one? Who is this gentle-faced one who is covering the workshop of Nandīpāla the potter, which was thatched with fresh grass?
They replied, "We are monks, attendants of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa.
The monastery of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa is being washed away by the rain falling for the first time since the season began."
"We shall cover the workshop of Nandīpāla the potter, which is thatched with fresh grass, and then cover the monastery of Kāśyapa the Perfectly Awakened One.
They both said, "Take it, noble ones! Take it, gentle sirs! Your attendant has gone outside.
Having covered that [workshop], they covered my monastery.
Later, Nandīpāla the potter returned and saw that the workshop was covered and concealed by fresh grass;
having seen this, he spoke thus to his blind parents:
"Mother, Father, by whom has this workshop been covered and concealed with fresh grass?"
They spoke thus:
"My dear Nandīpāla, not long after you had departed from here, we heard the sound of the roof-covering being laid upon the workshop shed that was covered with fresh grass.
Having heard it, we said: 'Who is this noble one? Who is this blessed-faced man who is covering the workshop shed covered with fresh grass?'"
They spoke thus: "O monks, we are the attendants of Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one.
When it rained for the first time upon the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa, his monastery was being washed away by the rain.
We, having covered the workshop of Nandīpāla the potter—which was thatched with fresh grass—covered the monastery of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa."
"We shall say this to them: 'Take it, noble sirs! Take it, gentle sirs! Your attendant has gone outside;
by him this workshop will be covered.
Then, this thought occurred to Nandīpāla the potter:"
"Great gain has been mine, well-attained by me, that the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kāśyapa, has placed such exceeding trust in my family and has become so confident," he thought.

Knowing this, through that very joy and gladness, he spent seven days in a single cross-legged posture; and for half a month, constant mindfulness did not leave his body, remaining uninterrupted within it.

For seven days during that very rainy season, Nandīpāla the potter’s workshop was not rained upon even by a single drop of water—this being due to the power of the Buddha and the power of the deities.

Now, Great King, might there be some change in your mind such that you think: "The perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa did not accept my offerings of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick for the three-month period"?
But there was no change in the mind of Nandīpāla the potter while his workshop, covered with fresh grass, remained uncovered.
"Venerable sir, great gain has been well-obtained by Nandīpāla the potter, in whose family the Blessed One has placed such extreme trust and confidence.
Then the Perfectly Awakened Kāśyapa expressed approval for King Kṛkin’s gift with this verse of appreciation:
The Agnihotra is the mouth of sacrifices; the Gāyatrī is the mouth of meters;
the king is the mouth of men; and the ocean is the mouth of rivers.
The moon is the face of the stars; the sun is the face of those that give heat.
As far as the movement of the world extends—above, across, and below—in all the worlds including the realms of the gods, the Perfectly Awakened One alone is the most worthy of worship.

Then the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Kṛkin with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed. Then King Kṛkin, not long after the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa had left, considering that everything subject to decay is subject to destruction, [dismissed] the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa.
Following closely behind him,
King Kṛkī followed right after the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa as far as he could;
then, having bowed his head at the feet of Kāśyapa and circumambulated the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa three times, he turned back from that very spot.

Then King Kṛkī, having learned that the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kāśyapa, had departed not long ago, addressed a certain man: "Come, my good man, fill five hundred carts with rice covered by leaves and go to where Nandīpāla the potter is; having approached him," [he said].
He said this to Ghaṭīkāra:
"My dear Nandīpāla, King Kṛkī has sent these five hundred carts filled with rice covered by leaves for you;
therefore, satisfy yourself well with happiness, as well as your blind parents."
"And provide for the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa with almsfood from time to time.
"So be it, Your Majesty," that man replied to King Kṛki. Having filled five hundred carts with rice hidden within leaves, he went to where Nandīpāla the potter was.
Having approached Nandīpāla the potter, he said this to him:

"Nandīpāla, my dear, King Kṛkī has sent these five hundred carts filled with śāli rice covered by leaves to you. With this, you should properly satisfy yourself with happiness, as well as your blind parents,
and from time to time provide alms-food to the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kāśyapa."
"O man, the king has many duties and much to do," he said, and did not consent.
What do you think, monks?
That young brahmin Uttara was none other than myself at that time and on that occasion.
Because of the harsh verbal action that I uttered toward the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa, saying:
"How could there be awakening in that shaven-headed mendicant?
For awakening is indeed extremely difficult to achieve."
"By the ripening of that karma, I have now practiced austerities for six years.
If, moreover, awakening had been disparaged by me, I would have again exhausted myself for three incalculable eons for the sake of my own awakening.
Therefore, monks, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black, as before; thus, one should apply oneself only to entirely white actions."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
On the very day the Bodhisattva went forth, on that same day Yaśodharā became pregnant with a child.
When the Bodhisattva practiced austerities, the women of the harem also began to practice austerities;
Yaśodharā’s fetus then perished.
When the Blessed One realized that such asceticism was fruitless, he breathed freely as he pleased.
He breathes out at ease;
he takes coarse food, such as boiled rice and sour gruel; he anoints his limbs with clarified butter and oil, and he bathes his body with warm water.
At that time, the women of the harem also breathed in and breathed out at ease,
