and they took substantial food, namely boiled rice and sour gruel.
She anoints her limbs with ghee and oil and bathes her body with warm water;
then that embryo again attains nourishment within her.
The signs of pregnancy appeared;
she was addressed with mockery by the Śākyas, saying:
"You have been unfaithful now that the Bodhisattva has gone to the forest of asceticism."
She said:
"May evil be averted;
I do not commit adultery."
How is this known?
I shall convince you:
until she has given birth.
A boy was born;
on the very day he was born, the moon was seized by Rāhu.
When he was born, they held a birth festival and established his name,
asking, "What shall be the name of this boy?"
His kinsmen said, "At the time of this child's birth, the moon was seized by Rāhu; therefore, let the boy's name be Rāhula.
When the prince was born, the Śākyas spoke even more extensively in this manner.
Having made a vow of truth, she placed Rāhulabhadra on the Bodhisattva’s exercise stone and immersed him in the pleasure pond, saying:
"If this child was born of the Bodhisattva, let him float!
He began to float.
She said:
"Let him come from the further shore to this shore";
he came from the further shore to this shore.
They were filled with wonder; Yaśodharā said:
"I shall demonstrate once more to you directly how this child was born by the Bodhisattva."
"I am not unfaithful.
When the Blessed One, having passed six years since his full awakening, arrived at Kapilavastu, he ate one day in the royal palace and one day in the inner apartments.
Then this thought occurred to Yaśodharā:
"What might be the means by which I could win the Blessed One over?
Now, in Kapilavastu, there was a certain female wanderer who was exceedingly skilled in the rites of subjugation and other such practices.
Yaśodharā gave her five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, saying,
"Noble lady, use these coins to perform a subjugation rite and send [the medicine] back";
she then sent a subjugation sweetmeat to Yaśodharā.
Yaśodharā placed [the jewel] in Rāhula’s hand and said,
"Son, give this to him who is your father.
At that moment, there is nothing whatsoever unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Blessed Buddhas.
The Blessed One reflected:
"An ill report concerning Yaśodharā has gone forth;
something must be done to remove it."
The Blessed One manifested five hundred Buddhas;
Rāhula, having observed all those Buddhas, offered [the bowl] to the Blessed One who was standing at the head of the assembly;
the Blessed One, having taken it, gave it back to him once again.
Rāhula had eaten it;
the Blessed One, having delivered his formal instruction, departed.
Prince Rāhulabhadra followed closely behind the Blessed One, and even though he was being turned back, he would not turn back.
"He wept. The Blessed One perceived:
"This being is in his final existence; it is not possible for him to dwell in the life of a householder."

Thus, when Rāhula was recognized by the Blessed One, King Śuddhodana, along with the women of his harem and the Śākyas, were struck with supreme amazement; and as for Yaśodharā, the calumny against her was completely and entirely cleared away. Then the Blessed One began to ordain the youth Rāhula.
King Śuddhodana heard this;
he approached the Blessed One, and having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One," he said.
"If Prince Rāhulabhadra is to be ordained, let him stay for this one day so that I may perform his consecration.
King Śuddhodana then held a great festival for Rāhula,
at which the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra.
"Śāriputra, ordain the young Rāhula."
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Śāriputra replied to the Blessed One, and the youth Rāhulabhadra was ordained.
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how the venerable Rāhula has made himself known to the Blessed One with a sweetmeat in the midst of a great multitude."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that I was recognized by this Rāhula through a garland; listen to how it was so in the past as well."
The Story of the Great Thief:
Once upon a time, monks, a householder lived in a certain mountain village;
he brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her;
while he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself,
a son was born.
He addressed his wife:
"My dear, one who takes away our wealth and one who takes away our debt has been born to us; I am going—I shall take my merchandise and embark upon the great ocean."
She said,
"Noble son, do exactly so";
taking his merchandise, he set out upon the great ocean.
He met his death right there;
then, after his wife had dispelled her grief, that boy was nourished, sustained, and raised by the strength of his own hands and the support of his kinsmen.
Not far from him lived a weaver, who was highly skilled in his own craft.
Everything was accomplished for him through his own craft;
seeing the abundance of enjoyments resulting from his own craft, she said to him: "The work of a weaver is better than embarking upon the ocean."
"When he has gone, they will fall into misfortune through misconduct";
thus she said to that weaver:
"Brother, teach this nephew of yours the craft of weaving as well."
He said: "Excellent; let it be so."
He began to teach him;
that man was quick in his movements,
and in a very short time he had learned the craft of weaving.
That weaver, having bathed well and being well-dressed, eats choice food;
the boy says:
"Uncle, you too perform that very same work."
"I am exactly like that;
so why is it that you, well-bathed and well-dressed, eat such excellent food, while for me it does not come to pass?"
He said: "Nephew, I perform two types of work: by day I am a weaver, and by night I am a thief."
He said: "Uncle, if that is so, I too shall commit theft. [The uncle replied:
"Nephew, will you be able to commit theft?"
"Uncle, I shall be able to do it.
He reflected:
"I will first test him."
Taking him, he went to the marketplace;
there, having bought a hare, he gave it to him, saying, "Nephew, prepare this meanwhile while I go and bathe";
he then returned after bathing.
Having prepared it very quickly indeed, he ate one leg;
the weaver returned after bathing and asked, "Nephew, has the hare been prepared?"
"Uncle, he has been captured; let me see him.
He was then handed over by him.
He saw three feet;
he asked, "Nephew, where has the fourth foot gone? He replied:
"The uncle of the hare has no fourth leg;
where will he go?
He reflected thus:
"I am but a thief, but this one is a great thief";
taking him along with the three-legged hare, he entered a tavern.
"Nephew, let us drink wine;
let us drink!
They both drank it.
The weaver said: "Nephew, let us deny the price of the liquor.
He replied:
"Uncle, let him who drank it deny it; I did not drink at all, so why should I deny it?"
That weaver reflected:
"This man is a great thief;
it is possible to commit theft together with him."
He began to commit theft together with him;
that weaver would thrust his head into the breach, whereupon he was told:
"Uncle, you do not even know how to commit a theft."
The feet should be cast in first, not the head;
for if the head is cut off and recognized, the entire family goes to destruction.
"Throw down your feet! He threw down his feet; then a clamor arose, "A thief! A thief!", and he was seized by the feet.
A great crowd of people clung to it; he was unable to pull it out alone,
so he cut off his head, took it with him, and departed.
The ministers informed the king:
"Your Majesty, a certain thief who had entered through a breach was captured; someone then cut off his head, took it, and departed."
The king said:
"Sirs, he who departed after cutting off his own head is a great thief."
"Go, place that headless trunk at the crossroads of the four great paths and remain in a concealed spot;
whoever seizes it and weeps must be a lone thief— seize him!"
Then those royal officers, having placed that headless trunk at the crossroads of the four great paths, stood in a concealed spot;
that lone thief reflected:
"Surely I must not weep while clutching my uncle by the neck."
Having made himself out to be in the guise of a madman, he began to seize women by the neck;
he also began to seize men, trees, horses, bulls, buffaloes, goats, and even dogs.
When the world recognized him as a madman, he took that headless trunk by the neck, wept as much as he wished, and departed;
the king’s men reported this to the king:
"Your Majesty, the madman took that headless trunk by the neck, wept as much as he wished, and has gone away."
The king said:
"Gentlemen, that is indeed that very same lone thief;
it was not well done that he was not captured."
"Now, take it!
A certain thief thought to himself:
"Should I not indeed show honor to my maternal uncle?"
Thus he said; then, having assumed the guise of a cartwright, he filled a wooden cart with wood and went to that place.
Having placed the wood-filled cart on top of him, he unyoked the oxen, set fire to the cart, and departed.
As it burned, that headless trunk was consumed by the flames.
The king's men informed the king:
"Your Majesty, that lone thief has been burned";
the king said:
"By whom? They related exactly what had occurred.
The king said:
"Gentlemen, that very cart-driver is this lone thief."
"It was not well done that he was not seized;
seize him!
Then that lone thief reflected:
"It was not indeed by me that the ancestral rites were performed for my maternal uncle in the cremation ground.
Having assumed the guise of a Brahmin, he wandered for alms in the city, cooked those alms in the cremation ground, offered the funeral cakes, and departed.
The king's men reported this to the king:
"Your Majesty, a brahmin, having wandered for alms in the city, gave five morsels of food at the place where that headless trunk was burned and then departed.
The king said, "Gentlemen, he is surely that very same lone thief!"
"It was not well done that it was not taken.
A certain thief reflected: "Is it not the case that I must cast my maternal uncle's bones into the Ganges?"
Thus he thought; having assumed the guise of a Kāpālika, he went to that place.
There, having smeared his body with ashes and filled a skull-bowl with bones and ashes, he threw it into the Gaṅgā and departed.
The king’s men reported to the king exactly what had occurred.
The king said:
"Gentlemen, this is that very same lone thief;
it was not well done that he was not apprehended."
"Stay all of you where you are;
I myself shall seize him. Thus, the king had a pleasure garden constructed on the Ganges by means of boats.
Guardmen were stationed on both banks;
the king’s daughter—beautiful, lovely, and graceful—was placed in that water-garden and told: "If anyone seizes you, you must cry out."
And an order was given to the guardsmen:
"When she cries out, you must go to the water-garden;
if there is any man there, he is to be seized and brought to me."
The thief thought to himself,
"I must certainly not enjoy myself with the princess";
he then stationed himself there in the Ganges, facing downstream.
He began to throw empty jars there; when one was thrown,
the guard-men, thinking he was a thief, ran toward him.
He was broken by their first blow; a second was hurled,
and he was broken by that as well.
The third was thrown;
that too was broken.
The guards, thinking, "These empty jars are being carried away," remained indifferent and stood by.
Then that lone thief, having thrust his head into an empty jar and being carried along by the current, arrived at that place;
he then boarded the boat and said to the girl:
"Do not make a sound."
"I will not have you executed," he said; she remained silent in terror;
having dallied with her, he departed.
She began to cry out:
"This thief is leaving after having served me!
The guards said:
"When he was attending to you, you remained silent;
now that he has finished attending to you and departed, you weep.
Where shall we look for him now?"
The guards reported what had occurred to the king,
and the king said:
"It was not well done that he was not seized."
Having dallied with a thief, the girl became pregnant;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A son was born;
a certain thief heard of it and reflected:
"I did not feel joy at my son's birth"; having thus disguised himself as a chamberlain, he departed from the royal palace and addressed his attendants: "Sirs, the King commands: 'Plunder the city!'"
They reflected:
"A grandson has been born to the king;
therefore, we have issued this command."
"Let us plunder them! They began to plunder;
a great clamor and loud noise arose.
The king asked, "What is this?
and the ministers explained it in detail; he said:
"Even so, I have been humiliated by him;
I shall either renounce the kingdom or inflict punishment upon him.
Having understood this, he had a wrestling arena constructed.
After diverting himself for some time, he gave this command to his ministers: "Sirs, cause a proclamation by bell to be made throughout the city:
all men who reside here must enter the arena without exception."
"Whoever does not enter shall be punished with death";
thus the ministers caused a proclamation to be made by the ringing of a bell,
and all the men residing in the city entered.
Then the king, having given a garland to that boy, said:
"Give this garland to him who is your father"; and he addressed the guard-men:
"To whichever boy among you this garland gives, he should be taken by you and brought to my presence.
Then, taking that flower garland, he began to wander about, observing the crowds of people;
by him, that thief was seen.
The ripening of the karma of sentient beings is inconceivable;
for that reason, a garland was given to him.
Then, royal officers seized a certain thief and presented him to the king.
The king addressed his ministers: "Sirs, how should we proceed in this matter?
They replied:
"Your Majesty, let him be executed.
The king said,
"Sirs, how can such a heroic man be executed?"
Thinking, "I must show him favor," he gave his daughter, adorned with all her ornaments, to him as a wife,
and shared half of his kingdom with him.
What do you think, monks?
At that time, on that occasion, I myself was that lone thief;
at that time, on that occasion, this Rāhula here was his son.
"Even then he was recognized by me through my garland; even now I am recognized by him through this sweetmeat.
Thus, monks, the ripening of the karma of sentient beings is inconceivable; therefore, you must be devoted to karma."
Yaśodharā sought to bring the Buddha back to her; she reflected:
"If Rāhula’s father enters the inner apartments, he must be attended to in such a way that he does not go out again."
Then, beginning with herself, sixty thousand women, headed by Gopikā and Mṛgajā, adorned themselves with various ornaments and decorated themselves with fragrant garlands, incense, and garments.

Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and—surrounded by a multitude of monks and preceded by the community of monks—entered the inner apartments out of consideration for those to be trained.

Thereupon, sixty thousand women, headed by Yaśodharā, Mṛgajā, and Gopikā, [were filled] with the sounds of their loosened and trembling girdle-sets, which moved and quivered due to the agitation caused by the pride of their beauty, youth, and amorous play.

They displayed their inner state through laughter, sweet singing, the movement of honey-colored eyes and eyebrows, the heaving of breasts, the revealing of their bellies, and the clear manifestation of physical gestures.
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"If I were to eat, there would be a transgression of the proper time for those beings who are to be converted."
These women, overcome by sensual passion, will become unfit vessels for the truths; yet,
there exists a swift supernatural power of an ordinary person that is capable of winning them over.

"Suppose I were to win over the inner apartments by means of a miracle of supernatural power. Having thought this, he rose up into the air in the eastern direction and performed the fourfold deportment:
namely, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
He also enters the fire element;
when the Buddha, the Blessed One, has entered the fire element, various rays of light issue forth from his body—
namely, blue, yellow, red, white, madder-colored, and crystal-colored.
He also displays twin miracles:
his lower body blazes with fire,
while from his upper body cool streams of water flow forth.
The upper part blazes,
while cool streams of water flow from the lower part of his body;
as it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the southern, western, and northern directions— thus in the four directions, in four ways.
Displaying the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), he withdrew his miraculous transformations and sat down upon the seat prepared before the community of monks.

Then, having witnessed the Blessed One’s miracle of supernatural power, those women were deeply moved; like trees whose roots have been severed, they prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood their inclinations, latent tendencies, elements, and natures, delivered a discourse on the Dharma conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, sixty thousand women, headed by Gopikā and Mṛgajā, realized the fruit of stream-entry;
however, Yaśodharā, being excessively overcome by sensual passion, did not attain the vision of the Truths.
The thought occurred to her:
"What if I were to win over the Blessed One through a craving for flavors?
Having understood this, she herself prepared food and drink for the Blessed One and said:
"Today I shall satisfy the Blessed One with my own hand.
Having heard this, the monks informed the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, Yaśodharā wishes to entice the Blessed One with her own hand out of a craving for savory flavors."
The Blessed One said: "Monks, formerly I was possessed of lust, possessed of hatred, and possessed of delusion; I experienced flavors and experienced passion for flavors.
Now, however, I am free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion; I experience flavors, but I do not experience passion for flavors."
"How is it now that Yaśodharā seeks to win him over through a craving for flavors?
Having thus become filled with doubt, the monks questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, Yaśodharā has begun to seek to win over the Blessed One with a 'subduing' sweetmeat."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, I was won over by this woman with a sweetmeat.
Listen to that."
The Story of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain village, there lived a seer in a forest retreat that was well-provided with flowers, fruits, water, and roots.
He was one who practiced severe austerities, subsisting on roots, fruits, and water, and clothed in skins and bark;
by him the five supernormal powers were realized;
even ferocious beasts roam about his hermitage grounds, dwelling there with full confidence.
He set out for a certain spot to urinate;
a doe followed closely behind him;
he discharged urine mixed with semen.
He was drunk by that doe;
her female organ was licked with her tongue;
inconceivable is the ripening of the karma of sentient beings.
She became pregnant; at the time of delivery, she came to that very same place and gave birth;
a boy was born.
Having smelled that odor, she thought, "This is a being of a different kind," and becoming terrified, she voided her urine and excrement,
cast him aside, and departed; meanwhile, when that seer arrived at that place, he saw the boy.
He set about reflecting, "Whose son is this?
and saw that it was his own.
He then took him to his own hermitage, where he suckled him, nourished him, and raised him.
As he was growing, antlers appeared on his head;
because his antlers were like those of a deer, the name "Riṣyaśṛṅga" (Deer-Antler) came to be applied to him. Eventually, that seer became withered and weak.
That seer was attended with appropriate medicines,
yet that illness did not subside; when his terminal agony had arisen, he thought, "I shall not die for long."
Then he said to his son:
"Son, from time to time, sages dwelling in various lands come to this hermitage.
Out of love for me, you should greet them with a welcome and polite conduct, invite them to sit, and provide them with fruits and roots according to your ability. Having said this, he continued:
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; all unions end in separation; for life indeed ends in death.
Thus, being subject to the law of time,
he was consumed by that practice of the ṛṣi-dharma;
overcome by grief for his father, through spiritual urgency, he realized the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā).
At a later time, seeking water, he set out taking a jar with him;
and the god began to rain;
having filled his water-jar, he began to return.
He stumbled and fell;
the ṛṣis are quick to anger,
and so, taking a small amount of water and throwing it, he uttered a curse.
“O Durācāra, you have broken a water jar full of water;
therefore, from this day forward, you shall not cause rain for twelve years.
Thus [spoken], the god began no longer to rain.
A great famine arose in Vārāṇasī; the masses of people fled in all directions; the king summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them:
"Sirs, by whose power does the god not rain?
They replied, "Your Majesty, it is due to the wrath of a seer; if this seer could be moved from his ascetic practice,"
"The god rains thus, and not otherwise";
the king remained absorbed in anxious thought.
The women of the harem, the ministers, and the princes said to him:
"Your Majesty, why are you so preoccupied with anxiety?
He replied:
"Due to the wrath of the seer, the god does not send rain;
and the diviners say thus:
'If that seer is moved from his ascetic practice, then the god will send rain.'"
Otherwise it would not be so;
therefore, it is not understood who is able to cause him to waver from his ascetic heat (*tapaḥ*).
Thus it was said; that king had a daughter named Śāntā, and she said:
"Your Majesty, if this is so, then be free from anxiety."
"I shall act in such a way that this seer wavers from his ascetic practice.
He asked, "By what means?
She replied:
"Teach me the Vedic mantras and other girls as well;
and at the boat-landing, have a hermitage constructed, well-provided with flowers, fruits, and water.
Accordingly, he taught the Vedic mantras to me and to the other girls.
And at the ferry crossing, she had such a hermitage constructed;
then, she filled those fruit-baskets with substances for subjugation and wine,
and had other various and wonderful fruits made as well.
She assumed the guise of a seer;
clothed in robes of bark,
she went to the hermitage while teaching those girls the Vedic mantras.
The disciples informed the preceptor: "O Preceptor, many sages have arrived at your hermitage;
welcome to the sages, let them enter.
They entered.
Having seen them, he spoke this verse:
"Their gait is effortless yet graceful, their faces are devoid of beards, and their chests are unevenly raised; indeed, this dress of these great seers is unprecedented."
Thus, although his mind was agitated by doubt, he invited them with roots and fruits;
after they had eaten those fruits, the seer was addressed by them:
"These fruits of yours are pungent, bitter, and astringent."
"Our hermitage, however, is in the midst of the water where the fruits resemble nectar;
nevertheless, please accept our invitation to stay at our hermitage.
He consented to this.
He was made to board those boats by them, which were like a pleasure garden;
there, coconuts filled with liquor and mixed with intoxicating substances were given to him.
Overcome by the intoxication of liquor due to the application of a subjugating drug, he engaged in misconduct with her and was deprived of his supernatural powers;
the clouds rose up on all sides,
and the seer rebuked the deity, thinking she intended to rain.
Śāntā said:
"Even now you do not know who you are.
Bound by the noose of passion, he was led into the presence of the king by her, [who said], "Your Majesty, this is that seer."
Then the god began to rain;
a time of abundance appeared;
and the king gave her, along with her retinue, to that very seer for the sake of his wife.
Having rejected Śāntā, he began to enjoy himself with those other women;
thereupon, Śāntā, her heart agitated by jealousy, began to treat him with disrespect,
and that became more and more severe.
He was struck on the head by her with a foot wearing a sandal;
he reflected:
"I, who could not even endure the roar of a cloud, have now been so humiliated by a mere woman, bound as I am by the snare of passion."
Having applied himself with vigor, he again realized the five superknowledges.
What do you think, monks? That seer at that time, on that occasion, was none other than myself.
She who was Śāntā is this very Yaśodharā;
even then I was won over by her through a craving for flavors,
and now she has set out to win me over with a sweetmeat.

Yaśodharā attempts suicide: when the Blessed One, having eaten in the inner apartments, was departing, Yaśodharā, having fallen into despair due to her husband’s aversion to affection, climbed onto the roof of the palace and threw herself down.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess the quality of non-forgetfulness;
that [gift] was accepted by the Blessed One through his supernormal power.
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, see how Yaśodharā has cast herself down from the roof for the sake of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, she sacrificed her own life for my sake."

Let that be heard: (SBV II 41) Once upon a time, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī there was a king named Brahmadatta. There was a story of a kinnara and a kinnarī. Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta.
At a later time, he went out for the purpose of hunting deer;
traveling by stages, he entered a mountain cave,
where he saw a kinnara and a kinnarī.
The kinnara was asleep while the kinnarī was awake;
the king, having drawn his bow to his ear, struck the kinnara with an arrow in a vital spot.
Deprived of life;
the Kinnarī was seized by the king for the sake of a wife;
taking her with him, the king set out.
She said:
"Your Majesty, let it be for now; please grant me leave until I have performed the funeral rites for this kinnara's body."
The king reflected:
"Where will he go? Let me first see how he performs the worship of his body."
She was granted permission by him;
then, having propped up that kiṃnara with wood and ignited a funeral pyre, she threw herself into it.
A deity spoke this verse:
"An object intended in one way was transformed into something else;
while thinking 'I shall delight the Kinnarī,' two acts of killing living beings were committed.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that kinnara at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself; she who was that kinnarī was this very Yaśodharā;
even then, she offered herself upon the funeral pyre for my sake.
"Even now, for my sake, she has surrendered her own self from the back of the shelter.
Thus did the Blessed One perceive the conversion of Yaśodharā.
"Now the time for Yaśodharā’s discipline has arrived;

I shall cause her to cross over the wilderness of saṃsāra. Having understood this, he gave her a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths, upon hearing which Yaśodharā shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with twenty peaks.
Having pierced through with the vajra of knowledge, she realized the fruit of stream-entry;
with perfect faith, she went forth from the home to the homeless life,
until she became an arhat.
Because she acted in accordance with the traditions of her own family and because she had attained the Noble Path, she felt extreme shame regarding matters that arose among the bhikṣuṇīs.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus, this is the foremost among my bhikṣuṇī disciples who possess a sense of shame, namely Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula."
Again, monks, filled with doubt, they questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by Yaśodharā, the ripening of which caused her to carry a fetus in her womb for six years?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these deeds were performed and accumulated by Yaśodharā herself in previous births... [as before] ...for indeed, embodied beings must experience the results.
The Story of the Two Ābhīrīs.
Long ago, monks, two Ābhīrī women lived in a certain cow-pen;
they were mother and daughter.
They used to go frequently to the edge of the village carrying jars of churned curds.
Of those two, the daughter was prone to deceitful conduct while the mother was straightforward.
The daughter said: "Mother, take [this]," (A 440b)
"I will make a urine-offering using a jar of churned curds";
having taken it, she set out,
yet through her deceitful conduct, she merely trailed behind.
He did not follow her;
thus, she made that mother carry a jar of churned curds for six krośas.
What do you think, monks?
At that time and on that occasion, this very daughter of the Ābhīra woman was Yaśodharā.

Because she caused her mother to carry a jar of churned curds for six *krośas* through deceitful conduct, as the ripening of that karma, she carried Rāhula in her womb for six years. Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black karmas is entirely black, and so forth, as previously stated.
"Monks, you must train yourselves thus.
Then the monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Rāhula, as a result of which he remained in his mother’s womb for six years?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Rāhula himself; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
Who else shall experience the results of the actions performed and accumulated by Rāhula?"
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element,
nor in the water element, nor in the fire element.
Actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— do not ripen in the element of wind, but rather ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
for actions do not perish even after hundreds of eons.

"Having reached the assemblage of conditions and the [right] time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit. (SBV II 43) Long ago, monks, not far from Vārāṇasī, there was a hermitage rich in flowers and fruits, resounding with the songs of various birds, and frequented by trusting deer and winged creatures.
There lived two seers who were brothers, Śaṅkha and Likhita, subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, and wearing deerskins and bark garments;
Śaṅkha was the teacher and Likhita was his pupil;
they were renowned throughout all the world in Vārāṇasī.
King Brahmadatta also learned:
"In this park there dwell two seers who are brothers, Śaṅkha and Likhita."
In that place, Śaṅkha was the preceptor and Likhita was the pupil.
At another time, Śaṅkha filled his water-pitcher and went to the forest for the sake of roots and fruits;
however, Likhita rose even during the night and departed earlier than him.
Having taken flowers and fruits, he returned quickly;
he inspected his own water-carrier,
and there was very little water.
Afflicted by thirst, he thought, "I shall drink the water belonging to my preceptor," and so he drank it.
Meanwhile, the seer Śaṅkha, having gathered roots and fruits, entered the hermitage with his face overwhelmed by thirst.
He examines the water-pot; he sees that it is empty;
filled with indignation, he says:
"By which thief was the water stolen?
Likhita replied,
"Preceptor, I am the thief."
"I have drunk it;
give me the punishment," he said;
and he replied:
"You are my brother and my disciple; if it has been drunk, it has been well drunk, according to your pleasure.
He replied:
"Preceptor, I am unable to dispel this remorse;
grant me the heavy punishment that is given to a thief.
When he had spoken thus, the seer Śaṅkha—
Enraged, he said:
"I will not inflict punishment;
if you require punishment, go into the presence of the king."
He went into the presence of the king;
at that time, the king had set out for the purpose of hunting deer.
Having greeted him with wishes for victory and long life, he addressed him with a verse:
"I am the thief, O Great King, who would drink this water that was not given;
grant me the heavy punishment that is bestowed upon a thief."
The king said:
"There is no such thing as taking water that has not been given; however, whose water have you stolen?"
Thus it was; he related exactly what had occurred,
and the king said:
"He is both your brother and your preceptor; go, for you are not deserving of punishment.
He replied, "Your Majesty, I am unable to [dispel] my remorse."
"To divert [my grief],
give me the heavy punishment that is given to a thief.
When this was said, the king became enraged and was overcome by intense agitation.
He said:
"If that is so, stay right here and do not depart until I have returned.
Having hunted deer, the king entered through another gate with a specific intention and did not come out again.
On the sixth day, the ministers informed the king:
"Your Majesty, six days have now passed while that seer remains in that very place; you should deign to give him an order."
The king said:
"Let his punishment be removed; let him go—this itself shall be his punishment."
The ministers reported this to the seer:
"O Seer, Your Majesty says, 'This man's punishment has been lifted; let him go, for this itself shall be his punishment.
Having thus freed himself from remorse, he departed."
What do you think, monks?
That King Brahmadatta at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Rāhula;
it was he who, having become corrupted in mind, spoke thus to the ṛṣi.
"Stay in that place;
you must not go," he said;
as the ripening of that karma, he remained in his mother's womb for six years.
"Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black," and so on as before, "in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Then the monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Bhadrika, the ripening of which resulted in his becoming the king of the chief men?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Bhadrika alone; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
Since these actions were accumulated by Bhadrika alone, who else shall experience them?"
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.

Actions performed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, do not ripen in the fire element nor in the wind element, but rather they ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
The Story of the Beggar (Concerning a Previous Birth of King Bhadrika).
Monks, in the past, a certain beggar came from the countryside to Vārāṇasī;
he was [treated] with envy by the beggars residing there.
Having been beaten with kicks, slaps, blows, and the like by his own people, he was driven out;
he stayed outside Vārāṇasī in a royal park.

When the time of spring had arrived and the trees were in full bloom, King Brahmadatta went out to the park grounds together with his harem, as the forest groves resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvañjīvaka birds. Having enjoyed himself there in the park with his harem, he fell asleep.
The womenfolk, greedy for flowers and fruit, began to wander about searching for them.
Meanwhile, King Brahmadatta, having dispelled his drowsiness and lethargy, quickly entered Vārāṇasī;
the attendants of the harem also set out with great haste.
Meanwhile, a certain woman, in her agitation, dropped a pearl necklace and departed;
then that Koṭṭamallaka began to wander about in that park,
and by him that pearl necklace was seen.
He reflected:
"What need have I for this? There is the possibility that, for the sake of what is beneficial, I might bring about what is harmful."
Having tied him to a creeper, he remained in the garden with the thought,
"Whoever possesses this shall take him";
meanwhile, the women of the inner apartments informed the king.
"Your Majesty, a pearl necklace was forgotten in such-and-such a garden";
the king gave an order to his ministers:
"Gentlemen, a pearl necklace has been forgotten in the garden."
"Search thoroughly!
Having gone to the park, they began to search;
eventually, they saw him clinging to a creeper.
They reflected:
"Let us first investigate by whom he has been bound";
they then began to wander through the park.
When they saw Koṭṭamallaka, they said to him:
"O man, by whom was this pearl necklace tied and left hanging on the creeper?"
He related to them exactly what had occurred;
the ministers presented a pearl necklace to the king and reported the events as they had happened.
The king said, "Sirs, summon that Koṭṭamalla;
I wish to see him.
They summoned him.
Questioned by the king, "O man, why did you tie this pearl necklace upon a creeper and leave it there, rather than taking it for yourself?
he replied:
"Your Majesty, I am not entitled to a share of this; it is worthy only of Your Majesty," he said.
The king, being highly pleased, replied:
"O man, you are worthy of a boon."
"Tell me, what boon shall I grant you?
He replied,
"If Your Majesty is well-pleased, then after feeding the Koṭṭamallakas and clothing each one of them with a pair of garments, [grant this to] me."
"Let him be appointed as their leader.
The king gave this command to his ministers: "Sirs, after you have fed the Koṭṭamallakas and clothed each one of them with a pair of garments, appoint this man as their leader."
They caused a proclamation by bell to be made in Vārāṇasī:
"The King commands that all the *koṭṭamallakas* in Vārāṇasī must assemble in this park;
I shall feed the *koṭṭamallakas* and clothe each one with a pair of garments."
They all assembled together and were satisfied with food prepared by the ministers; each was clothed in a pair of garments and addressed thus:
"Your Majesty commands:"
"From this day forward, this Koṭṭamallaka shall be your king;
you must carry out his commands.
Having been satisfied with excellent food and clothed in pairs of garments, they, with joyful minds, said, "As the lord commands."
Thus, that *koṭṭamallaka* became the ruler.
By their very nature, the *koṭṭamallakas* were overcome by hunger and thirst, and they began seizing food and drink from the streets;
since they were honored by the king, they proceeded to seize even more extensively.
The multitude of people who subsist on the city became agitated;
they informed the king,
and the king said:
"You must provide protection with vigilance,
but you must not strike them";
meanwhile, a certain man was walking through the middle of the street carrying some cakes.
The lord of the Koṭṭamallakas snatched the cakes from him;
taking them, he went to a secluded place,
while being pursued by the Koṭṭamallakas.
Being harassed by them, he crossed the Vārakā River and stayed at the foot of a certain tree.

When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas—who have compassion for the lowly and the destitute, who delight in remote lodgings and seats, and who are the sole objects of offerings for the world—appear in the world.
Eventually, a certain Pratyekabuddha arrived at that place by chance.
He saw that he was handsome in body and possessed a peaceful deportment;
he reflected:
"Surely it is because I failed to perform services toward such a truly worthy recipient of offerings that, despite having attained human birth, I have become a scavenger."

"If this Great-souled One would accept cakes from me, I would give them to him"; then that Pratyekabuddha, knowing his thought with his own mind, extended his alms-bowl for the sake of favoring another; he [the householder], having shown great respect, gave the cakes to him.
The teaching of the Dharma by those great-souled ones was physical, not verbal;
having ascended into the sky above, he began to perform the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing light.
Indeed, the supernatural power of an ordinary person is quickly capable of winning over others.
Like a tree cut at its root, he prostrated at the feet of the Pratyekabuddha and began to make this aspiration:
"Since I have performed such services for one who is a truly worthy recipient of offerings..."
"By this root of merit, may I become a king of preeminent men;
and may I please, and never displease, a Teacher even more distinguished than this one.
Then those *koṭṭamallakas* arrived and said:
"Give us a cake as well," they said;
he replied,
"This is a great-souled seer."
"I have bestowed them upon him"; they asked,
"Having bestowed them, what vow did you make?"
He said:
"I would be king of the principal men.
They replied:
"We ourselves shall be those principal men of whom you will be the king," they said;
he replied, "Excellent; let it be so."
"But rather, prostrate at the feet of this seer and make a formal vow (praṇidhāna).
They then prostrated at the feet of that Pratyekabuddha and made a vow, saying, "May we be the chief ministers for whoever shall become this king.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that lord of the Koṭṭamallakas at that time and on that occasion was none other than Bhadrika, the Śākya king;
those who were the Koṭṭamallakas were these very five hundred Śākyas;
and while Bhadrika was a Koṭṭamallaka, he made a formal aspiration before a Pratyekabuddha.
As the ripening of that karma, he became the king of these five hundred Śākyas.
Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black karmas is entirely black, as previously stated, up until: "In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Story of Madhuvāsiṣṭha.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Nādikā in the Guñjikāvasatha.
Now at that time, many alms bowls had been placed out in the open air,
including the bowl of the Blessed One.
Then a certain monkey, having descended from a *śāla* tree, approached the place where the bowls were;
the monks tried to ward him off.
"He will break the bowls.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, do not ward off this monkey."
For what reason?
Because he will not break the bowls.
Then that monkey approached the place where the Blessed One’s bowl was.
Having approached and taken the Blessed One’s bowl, he climbed that *śālāvṛkṣa* tree, filled it with pure, honey-like nectar, and descending slowly and quietly from the *śālāvṛkṣa* tree,
he offered it to the Blessed One; however,
the Blessed One did not accept it, considering it to contain living beings.
Then that monkey, having gone to one side and made [the honey] free of living beings, offered it to the Blessed One;
however, the Blessed One did not accept it, considering it to be unfit.
Then that monkey, having gone to one side and sprinkled it with cool water, offered it to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One accepted it, considering it to be properly prepared.
Then that monkey, perceiving that the Blessed One had accepted his bowl of honey, was thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed.

Filled with intense joy and gladness, with palms joined in reverence, bowing down, dancing, and paying homage to the Blessed One, he gazed at the Blessed One with faith born within him and did not look back;
he fell into a well.
He passed away and was reborn in the very city of Nādika, in a brahmin family devoted to the six duties;
on the very day he took rebirth, a rain of honey fell.
His father summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them;
they replied,
"This is due to the power of this being."
When eight or nine months had passed, that brahmin woman gave birth;
a boy was born,
and on the very day he was born, a rain of honey fell.

His kinsmen, having gathered and assembled together, performed the birth ceremony for the newborn in full detail over three weeks— twenty-one days— and then established his name, asking, "What shall be the name of this child?
The kinsmen said:
On the very day this boy entered his mother’s womb, a rain of honey fell; on the day he was born as well, a rain of honey fell;
and he belongs to the Vāsiṣṭha clan.

Therefore, let the boy's name be established as Madhuvāsiṣṭha. He was reared and grew up until he became a man; when he had become a man, he went forth into homelessness in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Even though he had gone forth as a renunciant, three bowls of honey were produced for him day after day; of these, he would present one to the Blessed One and the second to the Saṅgha.
On the third day, he ate together with those who were affectionate toward him.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Madhuvāsiṣṭha, the ripening of which results in three bowls being provided for him every day?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Madhuvāsiṣṭha alone; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have ripened, and they have arrived like a flood—as before, until: 'Indeed, for embodied beings, actions bear fruit.'"
“Monks, did you see that monkey who offered a bowl of honey to the Tathāgata?
“We saw him, Venerable Sir.
“That very monkey was this Madhuvāsiṣṭha at that time and on that occasion.”
He offered a bowl of honey to the Tathāgata;
as the ripening of that karma, he was reborn into a brahmin family devoted to the six duties, and at both his conception and his birth, a rain of honey fell;
even now, three bowls of honey are produced for him every day.
"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black deeds is entirely black, as previously stated, up until: one should apply oneself only to entirely white deeds.
For what reason?
If the monk Madhuvāsiṣṭha were to first resolve that the great ocean is honey..."
"Even that would be honey;
for thus, monks, is the sacrificial gift to a Tathāgata immeasurable.
Then the monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Upāli, the ripening of which resulted in his becoming a royal barber? The Blessed One said: "Monks, it was by Upāli himself that immeasurable offerings were made to the Tathāgata in former lives. Karmas were performed and accumulated, and having reached their full measure—as previously described—they indeed bear fruit."
The Story of the Royal Barber (Concerning a Previous Birth of Upālin):
Once upon a time, monks, a Pratyekabuddha approached a certain royal barber.
"Noble sir, shave my hair;
it will be a meritorious act.
And he set out for the royal palace.
He said to his nephew:
"Nephew, shave the hair of this renunciant;
I am about to set out for the royal palace."
"And introduce me in such a way that it is as if I were the king";
he reflected:
"It is just as my maternal uncle says."
"Surely there must be merit here";
having thus shown respect, he shaved off his hair and beard.
The Pratyekabuddha reflected:
"Much merit has been produced by this being;

he must be planted with roots of virtue. Having understood this, for the sake of compassion toward him, he rose high into the air and began to perform the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning.
Ordinary people possess a swift supernatural power that inspires conversion;
like a tree cut at its roots, he fell at his feet and began to make a formal aspiration:
"By this root of merit, just as my maternal uncle has become a royal barber, may I too become a royal barber."
What do you think, monks?

This very Upāli, the monk, was that nephew of the royal barber. Because he shaved the hair and beard of a pratyekabuddha and made a formal vow, as the ripening of that karma, he became a royal barber.
Listen further to the vow that he made.
Another story of a barber:
Once upon a time, monks, a householder lived in a certain market town.
He brought a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her,
and while he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him.
Furthermore, as he played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself, a son was born; again, as he played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself, another son was born;
and so on, until in due course seven sons were born.
He had a barber as a friend;
that man was childless,
and he sat there lost in thought with his cheek resting on his hand.
"I have no son and no daughter;
upon my passing, all this wealth will be considered ownerless and will thus fall under the jurisdiction of the king.
He was seen by that householder, who said to him:
"Friend, why are you so preoccupied with anxiety?
He replied: "Friend, how could I not be preoccupied with anxiety, when I possess such a vast accumulation of wealth, yet have neither son nor daughter?
Upon my passing, all of this will fall under the control of the king."
He said:
"If that is so, this is my youngest son; I give him to you."
He accepted him;
later, when the householder passed away,
his sons, whenever they had a quarrel with anyone, were rebuked by him [the monk] as follows:
"You too engage in quarreling because your brother is a barber";
being thus dejected, they reflected:
"Whatever slight we have suffered, all of that is due to the fault of this brother."
"He must be cut off in every way";
thus he was cut off by them, and the barber was [seized]. He then caused all the barbers to make a formal agreement.
"No one shall perform the work of shaving on the sons of the householder so-and-so";
thus they grew with long beards and nails,
and when they were seen by the king, he said to them:
"Sirs, for what reason do you remain with such long hair and nails? They replied,
"All barbers have been forbidden by this barber."
"No one at all should perform the shaving of their beards.
For what reason?
Because they related exactly what had occurred.
The king said:
"A father ought to give his son; why was he seized by you?"
"Give it to him alone";
thus he was released by them against their will.
Having become despondent, they desired to have him killed out of fear of public scandal.
The world consists of friends, enemies, and neutrals;
this was explained to him by others,
and so he said to that barber:
"They wish to have me executed;
give me permission, for I am going forth.
He reflected:
Thinking, "Let him indeed go forth into homelessness; he must not lose his life because of them," he said:
"Son, if it is so, go and become a renunciant;
whatever collection of virtues you may attain, you shall report that to me."
Having received permission, he went forth among the ṛṣis;
without a co-practitioner and without a preceptor, he realized pratyekabodhi.
He reflected:

"I promised his father that I would demonstrate [my power]; I am going now to fulfill this former promise. Having gone into his presence, he performed the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning, until—like a tree cut at its root—he fell at his feet and began to make a formal vow (praṇidhāna):
"By the roots of merit from the services I have rendered to such a truly worthy recipient of offerings, may I become a royal barber," he thought.
Furthermore, having again performed services for five hundred pratyekabuddhas, he made this aspiration:
"By this root of merit, may I become a royal barber."
Furthermore, after performing services for four perfectly enlightened Buddhas, he made a vow, saying: "By this root of merit, may I become a royal barber.
As the ripening of that karma, he became a royal barber on many occasions.
Again, monks, filled with doubt, they questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Upāli, what karma was performed by him such that he was designated as the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya?
The Blessed One said,
"Where was the vow made?"

Upāli is the foremost among those who master and know the Vinaya. Long ago, monks, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years, a Samyaksaṃbuddha named Kāśyapa appeared in the world; as previously described, he [went] to the city of Vārāṇasī.
He dwells having taken recourse in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana;
he has gone forth in this Teacher’s dispensation;
he who has gone forth—(SBV II 52)
Furthermore, that monk was designated by the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa as the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya; yet,
although he practiced the holy life there for as long as he lived,
he did not attain any collection of virtuous qualities.
Therefore, at the time of his death, he began to make this aspiration:
"Although I have practiced the holy life for as long as I lived under the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one, I have not attained any collection of virtues."

"By this root of merit, may I become that very young brahmin named Uttara who was prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One, saying: 'Young man, when the lifespan of humanity is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Truly and Fully Enlightened One named Śākyamuni.'"
"Having gone forth in his teaching, may I realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions;

and just as my preceptor, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, was designated by him as the foremost of those who uphold the Vinaya, may that Blessed One Śākyamuni likewise designate me as the foremost of those who uphold the Vinaya. By virtue of that aspiration, he was designated by the Tathāgata as the foremost of those who uphold the Vinaya.
"Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black, as previously stated, up to: 'effort must be made.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
[The False Announcement of the Buddha’s Death and the Birth of Ānanda]
When the Blessed One, having utterly defeated Māra Pāpīyas along with his retinue of thirty-six million spirits, attained unsurpassed knowledge,
it was announced to the women of the harem, the ministers, and the people of the city and countryside:
"Today the ascetic Gautama has passed away."
King Śuddhodana, together with his harem, princes, ministers, citizens, and countryfolk, began to grieve.
The vision of the deities appeared below him,
and the deities belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm announced:
"The Blessed One has not passed away; rather, the Blessed One has attained unsurpassed knowledge.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana experienced supreme joy;
at that very moment, a son was born to Amṛtodana.
When he was born, an extensive birth ceremony was performed, and his name was established;
they asked, "What shall be the name of this boy? and the kinsmen replied:
This boy was born while Ānanda was present;
therefore, let "Ānanda" be established as the name of the boy. Thus, the boy Ānanda was entrusted to eight nurses.
He was entrusted to two nurses for his portions, two for play, two for milk, and two for cleansing.
While he was in the care of these nurses, the fortune-tellers prophesied regarding him: "This child must perform service to the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Upon hearing that the child had been so prophesied by the fortune-tellers, Amṛtodana reflected:
"If the Blessed One ordains me in this way, he must not even descend before me";
[thinking thus], when the Blessed One arrived at Kapilavastu, then—
He was being led to Vaiśālī;
when the Blessed One went to Vaiśālī, he was then led back to Kapilavastu.
In the meantime, there is nothing whatsoever that is unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

It is indeed the natural law of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are possessed of great compassion, who act for the benefit of the world, who are the sole protectors, who dwell in tranquility and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, who have crossed over the four floods, whose intellects are firmly established on the soles of their feet through the four bases of psychic power, who have long practiced the four means of attraction, and who are free from the five factors and have transcended the five destinies.

For those endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections, who are rich with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, who teach the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling, who possess the ten powers, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vasavartin gods— three times during the night and three times during the day, they survey the world with the Buddha-eye, and their vision of knowledge proceeds.

Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into confinement? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone to the lower realms? Who is leaning toward the lower realms? Whom shall I uplift from the lower realms and establish in heaven and liberation?
Whose unplanted roots of merit shall I plant? Whose planted roots shall I bring to maturity?
Whose matured roots shall I liberate? And it is said:
Even the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might exceed its shore; but the Buddha would never exceed the proper time for those who are to be trained as his children.
The Blessed One reflected: "The boy Ānanda is in his final existence."
"He will go forth in my teaching;

having gone forth, he must attend upon me and uphold my word, and after I have attained final nirvāṇa, he must realize the Deathless. What if I were now to cause the youth Ānanda to enter the teaching?"
Without being noticed, he entered the city of Kapilavastu, went to the residence of Amṛtodana, and sat down on a prepared seat. Prince Ānanda was made to enter a private chamber by Amṛtodana;
however, the Blessed One empowered it such that the door opened of its own accord.

At the very outset, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood behind the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning him; then Amṛtodana, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
When Amṛtodana was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma, after which he rose from his seat and departed.
Even a great power of causes depends upon the power of conditions;
thus, Ānanda, a being in his final existence, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
"Amṛtodana, together with his retinue of the inner apartments, is unable to turn him back.
The Blessed One said: "This is a being in his final existence; you are not able to turn him back."
"Let him not turn back," said Amṛtodana;
"Venerable One, if it is so, we shall perform this for him in due order."
The Blessed One said, "Do so. Then Amṛtodana gave gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, beggars, wandering mendicants, and supplicants;
he performed meritorious deeds.

Having asked his own kinsmen for forgiveness, adorned with all his ornaments, mounted upon the neck of an elephant, and surrounded by many people, he was sent toward the Nyagrodha Grove into the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, as he was traveling through the middle of the street, a handful of blue lotuses was swallowed by the elephant.
The diviners saw him and said:
"This prince must become the foremost among those who retain what they have heard."
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground would allow, he alighted from the vehicle and entered the Nyagrodha Grove on foot.
He approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side.
The Blessed One then entrusted him to Daśabalakāśyapa, saying, "Kāśyapa, ordain this youth."
He was thus ordained and received full admission.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kapilavastu for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Rājagṛha;
traveling by stages on his journey, he arrived at Rājagṛha.
The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
A boil had arisen on the head of the Venerable Ānanda;
the Blessed One gave an instruction to Jīvika, saying, "Provide medical treatment for the monk Ānanda."
"So be it, Venerable Sir," Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared in front of the community of monks and taught the Dharma; the Venerable Ānanda also sat down right there to listen to the Dharma.
Jīvika, the physician to the prince, reflected:
"This is his remedy for the disease;
having attained the momentum of the Dharma, he will not feel [any pain]."
He gave him a digestive medicine for his stomach,
and he was opened right there;
when the medical treatment was completed, Jīvaka said:
“Blessed One, while the Venerable Ānanda was sitting right here, I roasted, split open, and cooked a basket of fish for him.
The Venerable Ānanda said:

‘Even if my body had been cut into pieces as small as sesame seeds, I still would not have fully understood the Dharma as the Blessed One taught it, for my mental continuum was captivated by the serene confidence that follows from the Dharma.’”
Jīvaka was struck with great wonder.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Ānanda, as a result of which a tumor grew upon his back?"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the monk Ānanda himself... [as before] ...for indeed, embodied beings must experience the fruit [of their deeds]. [This concludes] the story of King Kirāta.
(A previous birth of Ānanda:
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain mountain stronghold there lived a ruler of the Kirātas.

When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world—beings who have compassion for the lowly and the wretched, who delight in remote lodgings and seats, and who are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
Then a certain Pratyekabuddha, wandering here and there, arrived at the city of the Kirātas; seeking alms there, he entered the house of the Kirāta king, who,
having become filled with resentment and a corrupted mind, struck him on the back with a pellet.
That Great Being, having destroyed pride and arrogance, departed after realizing his lack of spiritual capacity.
What do you think, monks?
That king of the Kirātas was none other than this monk Ānanda.

Because he, having become resentful and with a corrupted mind, struck a Pratyekabuddha on the back with a pellet, through the ripening of that karma, in whatever place he was born, for five hundred births a boil arose upon his back; even now, in this final existence, a boil has arisen upon his back.

When the Venerable Ānanda follows the Blessed One and displays his mathematical knowledge, then toward the Blessed One there arises in him intense faith and reverence, a sense of shame and dread of blame, and a state of trepidation.
When, through such a transformation, neither such serene confidence, reverence, a sense of shame and dread of blame, nor trepidation arises;
at one time, a certain householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal at his home.
In the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded and preceded by the assembly of monks, entered that householder’s home, ate, and departed.
The monks questioned the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, did you go today with the Blessed One, or rather with a magical creation?
He replied:
I went together with the Blessed One, not as a transformation of a Buddha;
how so? Because when I go together with the Blessed One, there arises within me toward the Blessed One intense faith and reverence, a sense of shame and dread of blame, and a state of trepidation.
When it was [actually] by means of a transformation of a Buddha,
the monks then conversed among themselves,
saying: "The Venerable Ānanda is skilled in signs."
A report spread in all directions and intermediate points that the monk Ānanda was skilled in signs.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagṛha for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Śrāvastī;
traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Śrāvastī.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Then, in the forenoon, the Venerable Ānanda dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.
He was seen by a certain brahmin.
He reflected:
"This is the monk Ānanda, a disciple of the ascetic Gautama,
who is renowned as being skilled in signs."
"I shall first ask him how many leaves there are on this *śiṃśapā* tree";
being thus questioned by him, he said:
"Noble sir, how many leaves are there on this *śiṃśapā* tree?"
He said, "There are this many hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands," and having spoken thus, he departed;
that brahmin then removed a few leaves, counted them, and discarded them.
The Venerable Ānanda, having finished his almsround, returned;
he was addressed again by that brahmin:
"Noble one, now you should know how many leaves there are on this śiṃśapā tree."
He said,
"Previously there were this many hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands;
from that, this many have been subtracted," and having said this, he departed.
That brahmin was struck with great wonder, thinking, "How proficient this noble one is even in calculation!
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
“Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Ānanda, by which he became skilled in signs?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, by Ānanda himself were these deeds performed and accumulated... [as before] ...for indeed, deeds bear fruit for embodied beings.
The Story of the Astronomer (a Previous Birth of Ānanda)
Long ago, monks, in Vārāṇasī there was a certain brahmin who brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
As he was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a son was born to him;
after performing the birth ceremonies for him in detail for three times seven—that is, twenty-one—days, a name appropriate to his family was established;
he was reared, grew up, and reached adulthood.

Having gone to another country, he studied the science of horoscopy (*horāśāstra*) consisting of sixty thousand [verses]; in this manner, as he wandered through cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), he studied the knowledge of horoscopy for five hundred births and taught it to others.
By that cause and by that condition, wherever he was reborn,
there he was born as the foremost among diviners;
even now, in this final existence, he has been born as the foremost among diviners.
The Story of the Rice, the Two Quails, and the Sugarcane (concerning King Prasenajit and a previous birth of his)

Every day at the time of King Prasenajit of Kosala’s meal, two partridges and a stalk of sugarcane would fall into his food-bowl; one of them would fall into the bowl and the second onto the ground. He informed the Venerable Ānanda of this.
Because of this, the monks were filled with doubt and questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir,
what karma was performed by King Prasenajit of Kosala, such that at his mealtime, boiled rice falls into his bowl along with two partridges and a stalk of sugarcane?"
"One of them [fell] into a bowl,
the second onto the ground? The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by King Prasenajit of Kosala himself in previous births, as a result of which, at his mealtime,
boiled rice falls into his bowl along with two partridges and a stalk of sugarcane; of those two, one [partridge] falls into the bowl."
The second [story concerns] the ground.
Once upon a time, monks, there lived in the city of Vārāṇasī a certain householder who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments;
his servants brought fresh śāli rice from the agricultural villages.
There were two partridges and sixty stalks of sugarcane.

When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world—those who have compassion for the lowly and the wretched, who frequent remote lodgings and seats, and who are the sole objects of offerings for the world.
A certain Pratyekabuddha arrived at Vārāṇasī.
Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, he entered the house of that householder while wandering for alms;
he was seen by him, appearing serene in body and serene in mind.
Thinking that fresh food should first be brought to him, he gave him rice with milk, a stalk of sugarcane, and two partridges.
There, one fell into the bowl and the second onto the ground.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks?"
The householder who was at that time and on that occasion was none other than this King Prasenajit of Kośala.
Because he gave fresh śāli rice, a stalk of sugarcane, and two partridges to a pratyekabuddha,
by that karma he experienced divine and human happiness for many years, many hundreds of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years.
Even now, at his mealtime, when there is boiled rice and sugarcane stalks, one partridge falls into his bowl and the second falls upon the ground.
King Prasenajit of Kośala heard:
"The Blessed One has thus prophesied this web of karma for me."
Realizing that this was the ripening of the fruit of his former karma, he became full of faith toward the Blessed One and the community of disciples;
with his mind thus averted from the ripening of karma, he remained there.
Furthermore, a fortune-teller had prophesied that Ārya Ānanda would receive the binding of the turban.
When the night had turned to dawn, a boil appeared on the forehead of the Venerable Ānanda;
King Prasenajit of Kośala heard of it,
and this thought occurred to him:
"Having performed services for those worthy of offerings, there arises a distinguished fruit of merit that is not in vain;
what if I were to personally attend upon him? Thinking thus, he summoned all the physicians.
"Provide medical treatment for the noble Ānanda. They began to treat him;
King Prasenajit of Kośala himself held a hundred-ribbed parasol over the venerable Ānanda.
And when the vein had been released, a cloth bandage was bound upon his forehead.
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

“Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Ānanda, the ripening of which resulted in King Prasenajit of Kośala holding a hundred-ribbed parasol over his head, personally tying a white cloth [around him], and attending upon him? The Blessed One said:
"Monks, by this very monk Ānanda, in former births, actions were performed and accumulated—as before—up until: 'Indeed, for embodied beings, [actions] bear fruit.
The Story of the Physician (a previous birth of Ānanda)."
Long ago, monks, there lived a certain physician in Vārāṇasī. A Pratyekabuddha, being ill, approached him; he was provided with all necessary requisites by that physician.
He himself performed the medical treatment and provided nursing.
What do you think, monks?
That physician at that time and on that occasion was none other than this monk Ānanda.

Because he performed services for a pratyekabuddha and made a vow, through the ripening of that karma, for many years, hundreds of years, and thousands of years, he was attended by kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders; even until now, King Prasenajit of Kośala has held over him a parasol with a hundred ribs.
"And he himself performed service.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Śrāvastī for as long as he pleased;
He set out on a journey toward the hall.

Wandering on his tour in due order, he arrived at Śālā and stayed there in the village of the brahmins. At that time, many very senior elder great disciples were dwelling in dependence upon the vicinity of the Blessed One in forest huts.
Namely: the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya,
the venerable Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Bāṣpa, Mahānāman, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, Subāhu, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the venerable Mahākapphiṇa, the venerable Aniruddha, Nandika, and Kiṃpila.
The Elder Yaśas of Śālāvihārika, the Elder Pūrṇa of Kuṇḍopadhānīya— these and other very senior Elders, great disciples, were dwelling in the vicinity of the Blessed One.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, I am now old, aged, and advanced in years;
I am weary of instructing the four assemblies—the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen.
Monks, you must appoint for me an attendant monk who will serve me agreeably and not disagreeably."
"He will grasp what has been spoken and will not neglect his own welfare.
Then the Venerable Ājñāta-kaundinya rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"I shall attend upon the Blessed One with what is pleasing and not with what is displeasing;
I shall grasp his speech and I shall not neglect my own welfare."
"You, Kauṇḍinya, are old, aged, and advanced in years; you yourself must be attended by your attendant. Sit down, Kauṇḍinya, on your own seat."
The venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya sat down on his own seat;
then the venerable Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Bāṣpa, Mahānāman, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, and Subāhu [did likewise].
The venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila,
the venerable Mahākapphiṇa, the venerable Aniruddha, Nandika, Kiṃpila, Yaśas, the Elder Śālāvihārīyaka, Pūrṇa,
and the Elder Kuṇḍopadhānīyaka rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and approached the Blessed One.
Having bowed with palms joined, they said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, I shall attend upon the Blessed One with what is pleasing and not with what is displeasing,
and I shall grasp whatever he speaks."
I shall not neglect my own duty;
you too are full-grown, aged, old, and advanced in years;
indeed, it is for you first that service by an attendant must be performed.
“Sit down, Pūrṇa, on your own seat. The venerable Pūrṇa sat down on his own seat.
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Which monk, then, does the Blessed One intend to have as his attendant?
Suppose I were to enter such a state of concentration that, with my mind thus composed, I might perceive the mind of the Blessed One."
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he beheld the mind of the Blessed One.

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw that the Blessed One’s mind was fixed upon the Venerable Ānanda: "The monk Ānanda will attend to me with what is pleasing and not with what is displeasing, and he will grasp whatever I say."
He will not fail his own purpose;
and having emerged from that concentration after seeing this, he said to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable one, you should know that the Blessed One’s mind is fixed upon the venerable Ānanda: 'The monk Ānanda will attend to me with what is pleasing, not with what is displeasing.'"
He will grasp what has been spoken and will not fail in his own purpose;

it is just as if, in a gabled house or a hall with a gabled roof, which is long from north to south and long from east to west, rays of the sun entering through the eastern window were to remain resting against the western wall.
In the same way, the Blessed One’s mind was fixed upon the Venerable Ānanda: "The monk Ānanda will attend to me with what is pleasing, not with what is displeasing;
he will grasp what is spoken and will not neglect his own welfare."
"Come, let us go and encourage him.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached the Venerable Ānanda.
Having approached, they exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Venerable Ānanda, and sat down to one side.
The venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were seated to one side; the venerable Śāriputra then said this to the venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, you should take it upon yourself to attend upon the Blessed One."
"Your service to the Sugata will be of great supernatural power;
however, Venerable Śāriputra, I am not able to attend upon the Blessed One. Why is that?"
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are difficult to approach and difficult to withstand;
just as a blazing fire is difficult to approach and difficult to withstand because of its intervening flames,
even so the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are difficult to approach and difficult to withstand.
I do not venture to attend upon the Blessed One;
for just as the lion, the king of beasts,
when he has entered his mountain cave, becomes difficult to approach and difficult to withstand— namely, by virtue of the space between his fangs.

In the same way, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are difficult to approach and difficult to withstand; just as a king’s elephant, a rutting, wild tusker, sixty years of age, with tusks like plow-poles, broad-chested, a veteran of battle who has entered the midst of combat, becomes difficult to approach and difficult to withstand—
that is, even by the space between its tusks.
"In the same way, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are difficult to approach and hard to endure.
Therefore, Venerable Śāriputra, I do not venture to attend upon the Blessed One.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable one, you should know that the Blessed One’s mind is set upon the venerable Ānanda: 'The monk Ānanda will attend to me with what is pleasing and not with what is displeasing;
he will grasp my speech and will not neglect his own welfare.'"

Just as, for example, in a gabled house or a hall with a gabled roof, where it is long from north to south and long from east to west, rays of the sun entering through the eastern window would remain resting against the western wall;
even so, the Blessed One’s mind was fixed upon the Venerable Ānanda: "The monk Ānanda will attend to me agreeably and not disagreeably, and he will grasp what is spoken."
And he will not fail in his own purpose.
Exert yourself, venerable Ānanda, to attend upon the Blessed One; your service to the Sugata will be of great efficacy.
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the Blessed One were to grant me three boons,
