I would not wear a robe that has been worn by the Blessed One, nor would I accept a personal invitation from the Blessed One."
And there would be no improper time for me to approach the Blessed One for the purpose of seeing him and attending upon him;
if, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One were to grant me these three boons, then I would venture to attend upon the Blessed One, and not otherwise.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the Venerable Śāriputra, having encouraged the Venerable Ānanda—the Blessed One’s attendant—to go, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, we have been encouraged by the monk who is the Blessed One’s attendant—namely, the Venerable Ānanda—who spoke thus:

'If, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One were to grant me three boons, then I would be willing to attend upon the Blessed One; I would not wear a robe that has been worn by the Blessed One.'"
I would not accept a personal invitation from the Blessed One;
nor would there be any improper time for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit and for his service.
If the Blessed One would grant me these three boons, [I would accept].
"In this way, I am willing to attend upon the Blessed One.
"Excellent, excellent, Maudgalyāyana! The monk Ānanda is wise; he perceives the future."
From his fellow celibates, he might hear reproachful talk concerning a matter worthy of censure:
"On this account, our fellow celibates would say of me,
'The monk Ānanda attends upon the Teacher for the sake of robes.'"
"Maudgalyāyana, this is a marvelous and wonderful quality of the monk Ānanda; excellent, excellent, Maudgalyāyana! Wise is the monk Ānanda;
he perceives, even before it happens, a dispute or a subsequent argument from his fellow celibates that would be grounds for censure."
"Because of this, my fellow practitioners of the holy life might say:
'The monk Ānanda attends upon the Teacher for the sake of alms-food.
It is well, it is well, Maudgalyāyana! The wise monk Ānanda knows the proper time and understands the proper occasion."
He will know the proper time, thinking: "This is the time for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit; this is not the time.

He will know: "This is the time for the community of monks, the community of nuns, the assembly of laymen, or the assembly of laywomen; this is the time to approach other non-Buddhist wanderers for a visit."
"This is the wrong time;
these wanderers of other sects are capable of engaging in debate with the Blessed One, while those others are not;
this hard and soft food would lead to the Blessed One’s well-being."
"This will not lead to the accumulation of happiness;
Maudgalyāyana, the wise monk Ānanda knows the proper time and understands the right occasion;
he will know the time when it is appropriate for him to approach the Blessed One for a visit."
This is the improper time;

this is the proper time for the community of monks, the community of nuns, the assembly of laymen, and the assembly of laywomen to approach the Blessed One for a visit; this is the proper time, whereas this is the improper time for the wandering ascetics of other sects to approach the Blessed One for a visit.
"These wanderers of other sects are eloquent in debate with the Blessed One; these are not eloquent in debate.
This solid and soft food will lead to the Blessed One’s well-being; this will not lead to his well-being."
This, Maudgalyāyana, is the marvelous and wonderful quality of the monk Ānanda;
excellent, excellent, Maudgalyāyana! Wise is the monk Ānanda; he is skilled in discerning the minds of others.
In this way, he will perceive the Tathāgata having arisen from his afternoon seclusion, either by means of a sign or through a description:
"The Blessed One frequently dwelt in such and such a state of ease; the Sugata frequently dwelt in such and such a state of ease."

And whatever he shall command at whatever time, all that will happen exactly so and not otherwise; this, Maudgalyāyana, is the marvelous and wonderful quality of the monk Ānanda: he will attend upon the Tathāgata with what is pleasing, not with what is displeasing.
He will grasp what has been spoken and will not fail in his own purpose;
for the monk Ānanda, Maudgalyāyana, will attend upon the Tathāgata with what is pleasing, not with what is displeasing.
He will grasp what has been spoken and will not fail in his own purpose;
this, Ānanda, is the marvelous and wonderful quality of the monk Ānanda.
When the venerable Ānanda had been encouraged by the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to serve as the Blessed One’s attendant,
and had been praised by the Blessed One,
the monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Ānanda, as the ripening of which karma he became the Blessed One’s brother, his attendant, and one of great learning?"
"One who retains what has been heard" and "one who accumulates what has been heard";
the Blessed One said:
"Monks, by Ānanda alone were these deeds performed and accumulated... [as before] ...for indeed, deeds bear fruit for embodied beings.
The Story of Bhānumān and Bhānumantah (concerning a previous birth of Ānanda).

Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Bhānu reigned over a kingdom that was prosperous and teeming with many people. He sported, enjoyed himself, and dallied with his queen; while he was thus sporting, enjoying himself, and dallying, a son was born to him.
When he was born, they held a birth festival and established his name,
asking, "What shall be the boy's name?
The ministers said:
"His father is Bhānu;
therefore, let the boy's name be Bhānumān.
Thus, the name Bhānumān was given to him.
He was raised and grew up until he became a man;
he was consecrated by his father as the crown prince.
Furthermore, while he was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a son was born to him.
When he was born, they celebrated his birth-festival and gave him the name Bhānumant;
Prince Bhānumant delighted in renunciation.
He saw his father ruling the kingdom through both righteousness and unrighteousness.
He reflected:
"When my father passes away, I too shall become king; and having ruled the kingdom through both righteousness and unrighteousness, I too shall be destined for hell."
He approached his father, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Your Majesty, grant me permission; I wish to go forth.
He replied:
"Son, for whose sake sacrifices are performed, oblations are offered, and austerities are practiced—that very kingdom is now in the palm of your hand;
for whose sake, then, do you go forth into the religious life? Though he was thus dissuaded, he would not desist.
Knowing his persistent insistence, the king granted him permission;
he went forth among the sages,
and King Bhānumant was consecrated as the crown prince.
Bhānumat, having gone forth in the midst of the ṛṣis, went to a secluded place and, without a teacher or preceptor, realized pratyekabodhi. At a later time, he became ill;
wandering here and there, he arrived at Vārāṇasī.
The king heard that Bhānumat had realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and was staying there; he approached him, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Great Seer, you seek alms-food, while I seek merit;
therefore, dwell right here in my own garden."
"I shall provide you with all necessary provisions to prevent any obstacles";
he consented,
and the king appointed Prince Bhānumant as his attendant.
He set about attending upon him;
the Pratyekabuddha perceived his signs of limited merit and saw that he would pass away after the lapse of seven days.
He was asked by him: "Brother, for what reason do you not go forth?
He replied:
"O Great Seer, I am going forth into homelessness; if it must be so, go, having first taken leave of your father."
He went into the presence of the king and said,
"Your Majesty, grant me permission; I shall go forth into the religious life."
The king said:
"Your brother has gone forth into the religious life; after my passing, you alone shall be king."
"For what purpose do you go forth?
He did not obtain the going-forth;
that Pratyekabuddha then approached the king of his own accord.
Having approached, he spoke in verse:
"Release Bhānumant, O Bhānu; Bhānumant is going forth into the religious life. Forgoing the world, Bhānu, is superior, since it has been praised by the Victors."
The king said:
"Great Seer, you have gone forth into the religious life; after my passing, he shall become the king."
"He will give gifts right here;
he will perform meritorious deeds;
for what purpose does he go forth?"
The Pratyekabuddha spoke this verse: "For things intended in one way turn out quite otherwise;
the life of Bāhu is but short, lasting for no more than seven days."
"Great Seer, how long is his life?
The Pratyekabuddha replied, "Seven days. The king said:
"Great Seer, if it is so, let him be permitted;
let him go forth.
Knowing his own life to be short, he began to attend upon him with intense devotion.
That Pratyekabuddha was afflicted by illness;
as he was eating while holding his bowl in the palm of his hand, his hand trembled due to the wind.
Thereupon, that prince took off his bracelet and [placed it] upon the bowl.
The support was given;
that bowl remained motionless.
Seeing this, he began to make a formal vow:
"Just as this bowl is motionless,
so too may those who enter into the continuum of my Dharma remain motionless through this root of merit of mine."
He first taught the Dharma to him using well-rounded words and phrases;
he said:
"Previously, when you were a householder, you taught the Dharma using very well-rounded words and phrases."
"Now you have realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
for what reason do you not teach it? He replied:
"I do not teach;
who is it that teaches the meaning?
Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones—those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—they teach the Dharma through perfectly rounded words and phrases."
He made this aspiration:
"May I become the brother and attendant of that Blessed Buddha who teaches the Dharma with perfectly rounded words and phrases."
He was ordained by that pratyekabuddha and told:
"Child, you must keep this very thing in mind: I am to die at the end of seven days.
During those seven days, he did not attain anything.
At the time of his death,

he makes this aspiration: "By this root of merit, may I go forth in the teaching of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, and become one who is deeply learned and a retainer of what has been heard."
"Regarding the accumulation of learning:
What do you think, monks? That prince who was the brother of the pratyekabuddha was none other than this monk Ānanda.

Because he performed service for his brother, the pratyekabuddha, and made a formal aspiration, as the ripening of that karma, he has become the brother of the Blessed One, his attendant, and one of great learning."
He was one who retained what he had heard and accumulated what he had heard.
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Ānanda, the ripening of which resulted in his being designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who have heard much, who retain what they have heard, and who have accumulated what they have heard?"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the monk Ānanda himself; their conditions have been met, as previously stated, until: 'indeed, for embodied beings, [actions] bear fruit.
Ānanda is the foremost among the learned monks."

In the past, monks, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was two hundred years, a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Kāśyapa appeared in the world, endowed with knowledge and conduct, [and so forth] up to: a Buddha, a Blessed One;
he [lived] in the city of Vārāṇasī.
He dwells having taken refuge in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana;
he has gone forth in this man’s teaching,
yet therein he has not attained any collection of virtuous qualities.

In whose presence he went forth as a renunciant, and by whom the Blessed One Kāśyapa had declared him the foremost among those who are learned, who retain what they have heard, and who have accumulated great learning;
at the time of his death, he made this aspiration:
"By me, for as long as life lasted, the holy life was practiced under the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one, the unsurpassed object of offerings."

No collection of qualities has been attained by me; yet, by this root of merit, may I become that very young brahmin Uttara who was prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Truly Perfectly Awakened One:
"Young brahmin, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Truly Perfectly Awakened One named Śākyamuni."
Having gone forth in his teaching, may I realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions;

and just as my preceptor was declared by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, to be the foremost among many who possess retentions, who are retainers of what they have heard, and who have accumulated what they have heard.

"In this way, may that Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Sovereign of the Śākyas, also prophesy me as the foremost among those who have heard much, who retain what they have heard, and who have accumulated what they have heard.
"Thus it is, monks: for those actions that are entirely black, and so forth—thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Summary Verse (uddāna):
"Riddhi is the teacher, Tṛkā is the speaker; this Gayā has been visited by a Caṇḍāla, and for him these beings, the dogs, and the jackals are intent upon others. (SBV II 68) [Famine in Rājagṛha]
cf. Matsuda, “A Vinaya Fragment of the MSV from ‘Bendall’s Puka’,” Festschrift Bechert (1997):
The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
At that time, there was a famine—a difficult and desolate scarcity in which alms were hard for a beggar to obtain.

Thereupon, those monks who possessed supernormal powers took from the rose-apple tree (*jambu*) after which Jambudvīpa is named, as many rose-apple fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor as would fill their bowls; they then shared these with themselves and the rest with the other monks.

Or again, from the vicinity of this [mountain], they take a bowlful of *āmalaka* fruits endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor—from a grove of *bilva*, a grove of *kapittha*, or a grove of *āmalakī*—and eat them themselves;
and with the remainder, they share with hundreds of monks.
Having gone to the continent of Uttarakuru, they take a bowlful of uncultivated and unsown rice-grains and eat them themselves.
And with what remains, they distribute it among hundreds of monks;
having gone to the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, they take a bowlful of divine ambrosia and consume it themselves,
and with what remains, they distribute it among hundreds of monks.

Or those districts which are prosperous, even unto being crowded with many people and inhabitants— from there, having taken a bowlful of pure and excellent food, both solid and soft, they consume it themselves and share the remainder with hundreds of monks. (In this way) Devadatta strives to acquire supernatural power.
cf. Matsuda, “A Vinaya Fragment of the MSV from ‘Bendall’s Puka’”, Festschrift Bechert (1997):
Then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
At present there is a famine, a time of hardship and wilderness, and alms-food is difficult for a beggar to obtain.
Those monks who possess supernatural powers take from that jambu tree—after which Jambudvīpa is named—jambu-berries endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, filling their bowls;
they consume them themselves and share the remainder with the other monks.

Or again, from the vicinity of this [mountain], they take a bowlful of *āmalaka* fruits endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor—from a *bilva* grove, a *kapittha* grove, or an *āmalakī* grove—and partake of them themselves;
and with what remains, they share it among hundreds of monks.
Having gone to the continent of Uttarakuru, they take a bowlful of non-plowed, non-sown *śāli* rice with grains of pure *taṇḍula*, and partake of it themselves.
And with what remains, they share it among hundreds of monks;
having gone to the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trayastriṃśa heaven, they take a bowlful of divine nectar and consume it themselves,
and with what remains, they share it among hundreds of monks.
Or those districts which are prosperous, even unto being crowded with many people and inhabitants—from there they take a bowlful of pure, excellent food, both hard and soft, and eat it themselves;
and from the remainder, they distribute portions to hundreds of monks.
"If I too were to possess supernatural power, I too would take a bowlful of rose-apple fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor from that rose-apple tree after which Jambūdvīpa is named."

They would eat it themselves, and with what remained, they would share it with the monks; or alternatively, from the vicinity of that place— whether it be a grove of *bilva* trees, a grove of *kapittha* trees, or a grove of *āmalakī* trees— they would take a bowlful of *āmalaka* fruits endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, and eat them themselves.
And with what remains, they share it with hundreds of monks;
having gone to the continent of Uttarakuru, they take a bowlful of uncultivated and unsown rice-fruit and eat it themselves,
and with what remains, they share it with hundreds of monks.
Having gone to the Cāturmahārājika and Trayastriṃśa gods, they take a bowlful of divine ambrosia and consume it themselves;
and with what remains, they share it among the monks.
Or else, from those districts that are prosperous and filled with many people, they take a bowlful of pure and excellent food—both hard and soft—and consume it themselves.
And with what remained, they distributed it among the monks.
[Devadatta thought: "Now, what gain would there be for me in teaching the path to supernatural power? Then Devadatta approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Devadatta said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One point out to me the path to supernatural power."
Then the Blessed One, knowing that such an evil desire had arisen in Devadatta, said this to Devadatta: "Gautama, apply your mind thoroughly to higher morality,
and you will possess supernatural power."
And furthermore: "O Gautama, apply yourself thoroughly to higher mind and higher wisdom; you will possess supernatural power, and more besides. Then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
Realizing, "The Blessed One does not point out to me the path to supernatural power," he departed;
he went to where the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya was, and having approached him, he said this to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya:
"Venerable sir, please point out to me the path to supernatural power.
Then the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, having observed the mind of the Blessed One and perceiving that Devadatta had such an evil desire, said this to Devadatta:
"Devadatta, attend properly to form."
"And you shall possess supernatural power (ṛddhi) and other [qualities]. Then it occurred to Devadatta:
"Even the Elder Kauṇḍinya does not point out the path to supernatural power to me. Having realized this, the Venerable Aśvajit...
Bhadrika, Bāṣpa, Mahānāman, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, and Subāhu approached the five hundred elders;
having approached, they said this to the five hundred elders:
"May the elders point out to me the path to supernatural power."
Then the five hundred elders, having observed the mind of the Blessed One and that of the senior elder monks, and having understood Devadatta’s such evil inclination,
said this to Devadatta:
"Devadatta, attend to form with proper attention."
And you will possess supernatural power,
and something else as well: Devadatta, attend to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness with proper attention, and you will possess supernatural power.
And furthermore: then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
"Even these five hundred elders do not point out the path to supernatural power; how much less could these venerable ones have previously reached a consensus with the Blessed One?"
For no one was pointing out the path to supernatural power to me.
Then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
"Now, who indeed would be capable of pointing out the path to supernatural power to me?"
Daśabalakāśyapa teaches Devadatta the method for attaining supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
See Matsuda, “A Vinaya Fragment of the MSV from ‘Bendall’s Puka’,” *Festschrift Bechert* (1997).
At that time, the Venerable Daśabalakāśyapa was staying at Rāhagṛha in the Senikā Cave.
Then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
"This Elder Daśabalakāśyapa has for a long time been free from deceit and free from guile."
Thinking, "My maternal uncle Nanda is upright by nature, and the Elder Daśabalakāśyapa is capable of instructing me in the way to supernatural power," he approached the Venerable Daśabalakāśyapa;
having approached him, (SBV II 70)
Having bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Daśabalakāśyapa, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Devadatta said this to the venerable Daśabalakāśyapa:
"May the Elder instruct me in the path to supernatural power."

Then the venerable Daśabalakāśyapa, not having discerned the mind of the Blessed One nor knowing that such an evil desire had arisen in Devadatta among the elder monks, taught him the way to supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Thereupon, Devadatta, dwelling devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, relied upon the first dhyāna and manifested supernatural power.
Being one, he becomes many; having become many, he becomes one;
he experiences manifestation and disappearance through his knowledge and vision.
He passes through walls, through mountains, and through ramparts with an unimpeded body, just as if through space;
he performs the act of diving and surfacing in the earth just as in water;
and he walks upon water without breaking the surface, just as on the earth.

He travels through the sky cross-legged, just like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand these two, the sun and the moon, who possess such great supernatural power and such great majesty.
Then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
"Why should I not take from that Jambu tree—after which the continent is known as Jambūdvīpa—a bowlful of rose-apple fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor, in order to enjoy them myself?"
And [how can you] share the remainder with hundreds of monks?
Or rather, how can you take from the surrounding Bilva forest, Kapittha forest, or Āmalakī forest a bowlful of *āmalaka* fruits endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor,
to enjoy them yourself and share the remainder with hundreds of monks?
Having gone to the continent of Uttarakuru, would you take a bowlful of rice-grain *śāli* that grows without being ploughed or sown to eat yourself,
and with what remains, share it with hundreds of monks;
and having gone to the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trayastriṃśa heaven, would you take a bowlful of divine ambrosia to eat yourself?
And [how can you] share the remainder with hundreds of monks;
or rather, from those districts that are prosperous, even up to being crowded with many people and inhabitants, take a bowlful of pure and excellent food, both hard and soft,
to consume yourself and share the remainder with hundreds of monks?
Devadatta seduced Prince Ajātaśatru; then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
"What if I were to win over a preeminent person in this Magadhan territory?"
When he had turned [the people] toward himself, a great multitude of people would follow him without difficulty;
then this thought occurred to Devadatta:

"This Prince Ajātaśatru, upon the passing of his father, will be established in the sovereignty and lordship of his paternal kingdom; what if I were to win over Ajātaśatru? Once he has been won over, a great multitude of people will follow him with little difficulty."
Then Devadatta, having become a noble, well-bred elephant, would enter Prince Ajātaśatru’s residence by a side gate and exit through the main gate;
or, entering by the main gate, he would exit by a side gate. Likewise, having become a noble, well-bred horse, or even a shaven-headed monk clad in a saṃghāṭī robe, he would do the same.
Even now, though he is but a small boy, having become one wearing a golden girdle, he rolls about, turns over, and wriggles upon the lap of Prince Ajātaśatru;
and Prince Ajātaśatru also embraces, kisses, and hugs this boy.
"He even throws a lump of excrement into his mouth,
and Devadatta consumes it as well, being so overwhelmed and possessed in mind by gain and honor. Thereupon, Prince Ajātaśatru acquired an even greater degree of evil views.
"Ah, the noble Devadatta is indeed possessed of great supernatural power in the presence of the Teacher! Thus he became devoted to him and performed acts of devotion;
accompanied by about five hundred chariots, he went forth both morning and evening to attend upon him.
And for him, about five hundred pots of cooked food were brought at every meal-time;
Devadatta, too, would sit at the head of the meal with about five hundred monks.
The gifts and honors of Ajātaśatru intoxicated Devadatta, and his supernatural powers completely abandoned him.
Then, a great number of monks, having dressed in the forenoon and taken their bowls and robes, entered Rājagṛha for alms.
While wandering for alms in Rājagṛha, those many monks heard that such a kind of gain and honor had arisen for Devadatta.
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, goes out morning and evening with about five hundred chariots to pay his respects;
and at every meal-time, he provides him with about five hundred pots of cooked food;
while Devadatta, together with about five hundred monks, [partakes of] the finest of the food.

"Let us sit down"; having heard this, they again entered Rājagṛha for alms, and having finished their meal and returned from their alms-round, they put away their bowls and robes, washed their feet, approached the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, a great many bhikṣus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, here we, a great many bhikṣus, having dressed in the forenoon and taken our bowls and robes, entered Rājagṛha for alms.
While wandering for alms in Rājagṛha, Venerable sir, we heard [the following]:”
Such was the kind of gain and honor that arose for Devadatta:
Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha and son of Vaidehī, would go out both morning and evening with about five hundred chariots to pay him homage;
and at every meal-time, he would provide him with about five hundred pots of cooked food.
Devadatta also sat down at the head of the meal together with about five hundred monks;
"O monks, do not envy Devadatta’s gain and honor.
For what reason? Because—"
Gain and honor lead to the destruction of Devadatta;
gain and honor lead to the downfall of Devadatta.
Just as, monks, the plantain tree bears fruit for its own destruction, and the plantain tree bears fruit for its own downfall; so it is with Devadatta.
In the same way, gain and honor lead to the destruction of Devadatta;
gain and honor lead to the downfall of Devadatta.
Just as the bamboo and the reed bear fruit for their own destruction,
even so does gain and honor lead to the destruction of Devadatta;
gain and honor lead to the ruin of Devadatta.
Just as a mule conceives a fetus for her own destruction, just as a mule conceives a fetus for her own ruin,
even so, gain and honor lead to the destruction of Devadatta.
"Monks, as long as this kind of gain and honor arises for Devadatta, it will lead to the long-term harm and suffering of that deluded man.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall overcome gain and honor.'"
And gain and honor, even when they have arisen, shall not remain by taking possession of the mind;
thus, monks, you should train yourselves:
"The fruit indeed destroys the plantain tree; the fruit destroys the bamboo; the fruit destroys the reed."
"Honor kills a man, just as its own fetus destroys a mule.
For a fool becomes a source of harm precisely to the extent that he is known.
It destroys the wholesome portion of the fool and even causes his head to fall off.
Then, Devadatta, overcome by gain and honor, his mind completely possessed, this kind of evil desire arose:
"At present, the Blessed One is aged, old, advanced in years, and weary from instructing the fourfold assembly;
oh, that the Blessed One would entrust the community of monks to me!"
"I shall lead the community of monks;
may the Blessed One dwell with little concern, devoted to abiding in happiness in this very life.
As soon as this thought arose, Devadatta fell away from that supernatural power.
Furthermore, having fallen away, he did not even realize, "I have fallen away.

At that time, the monk Kakuda, the son of Kroḍa—a disciple of the Blessed One who had practiced the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One and cultivated the four divine abodes—informed the Buddha that Devadatta was heading toward the assembly. Maudgalyāyana [also] informed the Buddha.
Having abandoned sensual desire for sense-pleasures and dwelling frequently therein, he was reborn in the company of the Brahma-world.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was staying among the Bhārgavas, on Mount Śiśumāragiri, in the Mṛgadāva forest of Bhīṣaṇikā.
Then, the Brahmā Kakuda, perceiving that Devadatta had fallen away from that supernatural power,

just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so did the Brahmā Kakuda vanish from the Brahma-world and reappear before the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana among the Bhārgavas.
Then the Brahmā Kakuda said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Venerable Maudgalyāyana, you should know that Devadatta, overcome by gain and honor and with his mind possessed, has conceived such an evil desire:
'At present the Blessed One is aged, decrepit, advanced in years, and weary from instructing the four assemblies; oh! [SBV II 74]
"Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One entrust the community of monks to me;
I shall lead the community of monks,
while the Blessed One may dwell at ease, devoted to the practice of dwelling in happiness in this very life."
From the very moment that thought arose, he fell away from that supernormal power;
and having fallen away, he did not even realize, "I have fallen away.
"Venerable Maudgalyāyana, it is well! [he said.]

"You should approach the Blessed One where he is; having approached, out of compassion, you should report this very matter in detail to the Blessed One. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to the Brahmā Kakuda by remaining silent.
Then Kakuda Brahmā, perceiving through his silence that the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had consented, bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and vanished right there.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing that Kakuda Brahmā had departed not long before, entered into such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he vanished from the Bhārga country and reappeared in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana related in detail everything that had been the subject of conversation between him and the Brahmā Kakuda.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Maudgalyāyana, was Devadatta not already known to you by pervading him with your mind? Why then did the brahmin Kakuda report it afterwards?"
"So be it, Venerable Sir.
This conversation between the Blessed One and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was thus carried on.
Then Devadatta visited the Buddha and departed in indignation.
Then Devadatta, together with four companions—Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta—approached the place where the Blessed One was.
The Blessed One saw Devadatta from afar, and having seen him, he addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Now, Maudgalyāyana, you must guard [the Sangha]."
"Guard him now, Maudgalyāyana!
Here comes Devadatta;
now this deluded man will himself declare his own fate in my presence."

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, entered such a state of meditative concentration that, while his mind was thus composed, he disappeared from the Bamboo Grove and appeared on Mount Śiśumāra in the Bhīṣaṇikā forest, in the Deer Park of the Bhārgavas.
Then Devadatta approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Devadatta said this to the Blessed One:
At present, the Blessed One is aged, elderly, and advanced in years; he is weary from instructing the fourfold assembly.
Oh, that the Blessed One would entrust the community of monks to me!
I would then lead the community of monks.

"May the Blessed One dwell with little concern, devoted to the practice of dwelling in happiness in this very life; for as long as I have not yet entrusted the community of monks even to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— those two gentle companions in the holy life— how much less, O deluded man, shall I entrust it to you, a corpse, a consumer of spittle?"
Then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
"The Blessed One speaks in praise of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,
yet he addresses me with the reproach of being like a corpse-eating jackal."
Thereupon, Devadatta manifested anger, hatred, pride, hypocrisy, malice, intolerance, and resentment toward the Blessed One; then,
making a sound like "hum" and shaking his head three times, Devadatta departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
The Buddha Assembles the Monks:
The Discourse on the Five Teachers.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda, and assemble in the assembly hall all those who dwell in dependence upon the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having obeyed him, [he departed].
Having gathered all the monks who were dwelling in dependence on the Kalandaka Feeding Ground in the Bamboo Grove, he approached the place where the Blessed One was;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda [addressed] the Blessed One.
He said this:
"Venerable sir, as many bhikṣus as there are who dwell depending on the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, they have all assembled and are seated in the assembly hall."
They had assembled together, [saying],
"It is now time for the Blessed One to do as he sees fit.
Then the Blessed One went to the assembly hall.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared right in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, there are these five teachers who exist and are found in the world."
Which five?
1) Here, a certain teacher, while being of impure conduct, claims: "My conduct is pure and unafflicted. His disciples, through living together with him, recognize this of him:
This Blessed One, the Teacher, while his own moral discipline is actually impure, claims: "My moral discipline is pure and unblemished.
If we were to report this to others, it would cause him displeasure.
Why should we address the Teacher with that which causes him displeasure?
"This Blessed One, the Teacher, acknowledges this himself:
'He remembers us by means of the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines for the sick.
Thus, even his disciples who possess virtuous conduct consider him one who ought to be protected."
A teacher of such a kind expects from his disciples the preservation of moral discipline;
this is the first teacher who exists and is found in the world.
Furthermore, another teacher here, while his own livelihood is actually impure, claims: "My livelihood is pure and unafflicted."
Because of their long association with him, his disciples recognize him thus:
"This Blessed One, the Teacher, while his livelihood is actually impure, claims: 'My livelihood is pure and unblemished';
and if we were to report this to others, it would cause him displeasure."
Why should we behave toward the Teacher in such a way that it would cause him displeasure?
This Blessed One, the Teacher, himself acknowledges [our service];
he takes us into account by means of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
Thus his disciples consider him to be one who must be protected for as long as he lives;
such a teacher expects from his disciples the protection of their virtue.
This is the second teacher who exists in the world.
3) Furthermore, in this case, there is a certain teacher who, while his knowledge and vision are actually impure, claims: "My knowledge and vision are pure and unafflicted.
Because of their long association with him, his disciples recognize him as such:
This Blessed One, the Teacher, while his knowledge and vision are indeed impure, claims: "My knowledge and vision are pure and undefiled.
If we were to report this to others, it would cause him displeasure.
Why should we behave toward the Teacher in such a way that it would be displeasing to him?
This Blessed One, the Teacher, acknowledges this for himself;
he is mindful of us, namely, with regard to the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
Thus, the disciples consider him to be one who must be protected by means of knowledge and vision;
such a teacher expects protection through knowledge and vision from his disciples.
This is the third teacher who exists and is found in the world.
4) Furthermore, in this case, there is a certain teacher who, while his own grammatical exposition is actually incomplete, claims: "My grammatical exposition is complete and unblemished.
Because of their long association with him, his disciples recognize him as follows:
"This Blessed One, the Teacher, while his grammatical exposition is actually incomplete, claims: 'My grammatical exposition is complete and unblemished.'"
If we were to report this to others, it would cause him displeasure. Why should we behave toward the Teacher in such a way that causes him displeasure?
This Blessed One, the Teacher, declares this himself.
"He takes care of us with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick";
thus do the disciples think that he, having received a formal prediction of his attainment, must be protected.
Such is the Teacher who expects from his disciples this protection resulting from their formal prediction of attainment.
This is the fourth teacher who exists and is found in the world.
Furthermore, there is another teacher here who, while his Dharma and Vinaya are poorly proclaimed, claims: "My Dharma and Vinaya are well-proclaimed and undefiled.
His disciples, through association with him, likewise claim this of him.
"This Blessed One, the Teacher, while his Dharma and Vinaya are poorly proclaimed, claims: 'My Dharma and Vinaya are well-proclaimed and uncorrupted.
If we were to report this to others, it would cause him displeasure. Why should we address the Teacher with that which causes him displeasure?"
"This Blessed One, the Teacher, himself acknowledges [this];
he is mindful of us, namely, with regard to the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick";
thus do the disciples consider that he should be protected by them from the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
A teacher of such a kind expects from his disciples the preservation of the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
this is the fifth teacher who exists as a real and existing person in the world. Furthermore, monks, being one whose conduct is perfectly pure, he maintains perfect purity. (SBV II 78)
"I declare that my own morality is unblemished;
my disciples do not consider it necessary to guard my morality, nor do I expect them to guard my morality from me."
"Monks, since my livelihood is indeed completely pure, I declare: 'My livelihood is pure and unblemished.
My disciples do not consider it necessary to guard my livelihood for me, nor do I expect them to guard my livelihood on my behalf."
"Monks, being indeed one whose vision of knowledge is completely pure, I claim: 'My vision of knowledge is completely pure and undefiled';
my disciples do not consider it necessary to guard me regarding my vision of knowledge."
"I do not expect from my disciples any protection regarding my knowledge and vision.
Indeed, monks, being one whose declaration is fulfilled, I claim for myself that my declaration is fulfilled and undefiled;
my disciples do not consider it necessary to protect me on account of my fulfilled declaration."
I do not expect from my disciples the preservation of a formal declaration of perfection;
rather, monks, since my Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded, I claim that my Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded and uncorrupted;
yet my disciples do not consider it necessary to preserve me by means of a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
I do not expect from my disciples that they will preserve the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; rather,
monks, I shall speak to you by repeatedly restraining you and by repeatedly overcoming you.
And I shall not carry you about like a potter with his earthen vessels;
that which is essential shall remain.
"And you should be patient with the words of the Blessed One.
Then Devadatta addressed Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta: "I intend to cause a schism in the Saṅgha."
Thus indeed are Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta;
let us split the entire community of disciples of the ascetic Gautama while he is still present; we shall bring about a schism in the Wheel of Dharma.
Then, when we have passed away, a noble, auspicious report of our fame and renown will rise up in every direction and intermediate direction;

for even while the ascetic Gautama— so powerful and so majestic— is still alive, Devadatta, Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta have caused a schism in the entire community of disciples.
"A schism shall be created, and a division of the Saṅgha brought about.
They replied,
"Devadatta, we shall not be able to split the Blessed One’s entire community of disciples."
For what reason?
Venerable Devadatta, there are disciples of the Blessed One who possess great supernormal power and great majesty, who have the divine eye and know the minds of others;
they see even from afar.
They are not seen even when nearby;
having pervaded their mind with one's own mind, they discern their own minds with their own minds,
thinking, "They will know us as we approach."
He said:
"Kokālika, there is a means.
Let us approach these elder monks with all their requisites and say: 'May the elders have little concern; we shall ensure that the elders lack for nothing in any requisite.'"
"We shall do so;
we will attend to the junior monks and look after them with regard to their alms-bowls, robes, bags, water-strainers, waist-bands, recitation, study, private recitation, yoga, and mental attention.
Venerable Devadatta, this means exists."
There, Devadatta began to strive for the schism of the entire Saṅgha.
Devadatta’s conduct was recognized by the elder monks even as he was moving about within the assembly.
"He is striving for the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha";
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, saying,
"Venerable Sir, Devadatta is striving for the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha."
The Blessed One addressed those monks: "Monks, command Devadatta by means of a formal censure."
Or whoever else is of such a kind must be addressed in this way:
"Devadatta, do not strive for the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha."
"Do not persist in taking up and maintaining a legal dispute that leads to schism; let there be reconciliation for you, Devadatta, with the Saṃgha.

For when the Saṃgha is united, harmonious, in agreement, without dispute, single-minded, having a single objective, and becoming like milk and water mixed together, it illuminates the Teacher’s dispensation and dwells in comfort."
Those monks admonish Devadatta with the *meṣaka* [formal censure];
yet, being thus admonished by the *meṣaka*, he stubbornly clings to that very matter, adheres to it, and persists in asserting:
"Only this is true; everything else is delusion."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, we informed Devadatta by means of a *meṣaka*;
yet, being thus informed by the *meṣaka*, he stubbornly clung to that very same point, adhered to it, and continued to insist: 'This alone is the truth; all else is delusion.'"
The Blessed One said:

"O monks, you must command Devadatta—whosoever else is of such a kind—by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (jñapticaturtha-karman). And it should be commanded in this manner."
Having prepared the seats and beaten the gong, and having exhorted the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṅgha was seated and assembled, one monk should make a motion:
"Listen, venerable Saṅgha!
This Devadatta is striving for the schism of the harmonious Saṅgha."
He persists in taking up and maintaining a legal dispute that leads to schism;

having been admonished by a majority of monks acting as a sheep-shearer (meṣaka), while being so admonished, he stubbornly clings to that very same matter and continues to assert: "This alone is the truth; all else is delusion."

If it seems timely to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha permit it, that the Saṅgha shall command Devadatta by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations: "Devadatta, do not strive for the schism of the harmonious Saṅgha;
do not persist in taking up and maintaining a legal dispute conducive to causing a schism."
Let it be reconciled for you, Devadatta, with the Saṅgha;

for the Saṅgha is harmonious, united, living in mutual joy, without dispute, single-minded, having a single objective, and having become like milk and water mixed together, illuminating the Teacher’s dispensation—may it dwell in comfort.
Therefore, release [your opposition].
"Devadatta, this is the matter that causes a schism in the Saṅgha, being of such a nature";
this is the motion (jñapti); and the formal act (karman) should be performed in this manner.
Let the venerable Saṃgha listen:
this Devadatta is striving for the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha;
he persists in adopting and upholding a legal dispute that leads to a schism.
He, having been admonished by many monks, while being thus admonished, stubbornly clings to that very same matter, adheres to it, and insists: "This alone is the truth; all else is delusion.
Therefore, the Saṃgha formally commands Devadatta by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*):
Do not strive, Devadatta, for the schism of the harmonious Saṅgha;
do not persist in taking up and maintaining a legal dispute that leads to division; let there be reconciliation for you, Devadatta, with the Saṅgha.

"For the Saṃgha is indeed united, harmonious, living in mutual joy, without dispute, single-minded, having a single objective, and having become like milk and water mixed together; may it dwell in comfort, illuminating the teaching of the Teacher.
For those venerable ones for whom it is acceptable, let Devadatta be instructed by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations:
'O Devadatta, do not strive for the schism of the united Saṃgha!'"
Do not persist in taking up and maintaining this legal dispute that leads to schism;

The Story of a Caste-out Man Learned in Magic and a Brahmin Student (Concerning a Previous Birth of Devadatta).
Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned over a kingdom that was prosperous, flourishing, and crowded with many people and inhabitants. (SBV II 87)

There, a caṇḍāla who was a master of spells and mantras, skilled in spells and mantras, having mastered the Gāndhārī spell, used his supernatural power to take flowers and fruits out of season from Mount Gandhamādana and presented them to King Brahmadatta; the king, being well-pleased with him, granted him a private audience. Thereupon, intent on propitiation, he began to perform service for his teacher with due respect;
then, at another time, that outcaste arrived home intoxicated by liquor,

As he was turning over, a corner of his bed broke off;

For this is the nature of drunkards: whichever among them is the strongest, his vomit comes out."
In its first watch, the liquor was digested;
because of the sharp force of the liquor, the youth vomited on his back,
and he reflected:

"If I were to move my body or utter a word, it is possible that the preceptor, hearing the sound, would wake up and no longer remain lying down; therefore, he remained there with deliberate mindfulness.
Eventually, the Caṇḍāla himself woke up and saw him in such a state.
Then he asked, "Who is this? He replied, "Preceptor, I am Somaśarman. "Child," [he said].
"What is he doing in such a state?
He related exactly what had occurred,
and [the king], having gained faith, said:

go, bathe, and return;
I shall bestow the knowledge upon you."
Somaśarman arrived;
he gave the knowledge to him;
for Brahmins are fickle by nature.

By that means, she transformed the spell;

Having gathered flowers out of season, he returned;

therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall be grateful; we will not let even a small favor done to us go to waste, much less a greater one."

the story of the mango tree (concerning a previous birth of Prince Ajātaśatru).
Long ago, monks, in a certain remote village, there was a hermitage of seers in a forest retreat,
well-endowed with various flowers, fruits, and water; there the seers dwelt, subsisting on fruits, roots, and water.
Wearing matted hair and bark garments, subsisting on fallen fruit,
they remained in that hermitage until there stood an mango tree with branches bent down by the weight of its fruit, laden with ripe fruit.
The sages begged for fruits;
the deity who dwelt in that tree, overcome by envy, did not give them.
Thereupon, those sages, seeking roots, left one sage behind at the hermitage and wandered away.
Immediately thereafter, five hundred thieves arrived at the hermitage;
they gave him that tree and said:
"How are these fruits to be enjoyed?
the bandit chief replied,
"Cut the tree down at its root with an axe, and then eat the fruits."
When this was said by the deity, all the fruits were dropped onto the ground;
the thieves ate as much as they desired and departed;
the sages arrived and asked:
"By whom were those mango fruits eaten? "By thieves. That seer then spoke this verse:
"The tree does not give fruit to those who are peaceful and practicing celibacy."
"But it yields fruit for those thieves who have committed evil deeds.
Thus they asked:
"O Sage, what is this?"
He related exactly what had occurred;
they began to reproach him,
for the deity, overcome by stinginess, had not given any fruits to the sages.
"They were given to unworthy recipients and to thieves.

The Story of a Householder and His Son (Concerning a Previous Birth of Jīvaka):
Once upon a time, monks, a householder lived in a certain mountain village.
He was wealthy, possessed of great riches and great enjoyments;
he brought home a wife from a family of equal status,
and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, in the course of time his wife became pregnant;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth,
and a daughter was born.
When twenty-one days had passed since her birth—having celebrated the birth festival for her—the name Valayā was established for her.
Furthermore, while he was playing, sporting, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him;
a name appropriate to his family was also established for that child.
He reflected:
"A debtor and a consumer of my wealth has been born to me; I shall go to another country taking my merchandise."
Again he reflected:
"This wife of mine is beautiful; if I were to go after giving her many kārṣāpaṇas,"
"It is possible that she will become corrupted by other men;
what if I were to give her a few kārṣāpaṇas and then depart?
Having given her a small number of kārṣāpaṇas, he left.

Having placed the remainder in a golden vessel and fastened a pearl necklace around his neck, he buried it at the foot of an aśvakarṇa tree in the cremation ground and, taking his merchandise, departed for another country;
there, a great profit accrued to him.
Having taken a wife right there, he remained settled;
many sons were born to him.
Then, that first wife, Valayā, had both the husband and the son nourished by means of her own physical strength and the power of her kinsmen.
They were nourished and brought up; the two of them said:
"Mother, where has our father gone?
She replied, "Son, there is such-and-such a town in this country; he stays there."
And it was heard that he possessed a great abundance of wealth; "Go, and perhaps some means of livelihood will be found for you there. Seeking his father, he eventually arrived in his presence.
As he was wandering along the street, he was recognized by his father through the reflection in his face; having summoned him, the father said to him:
"From where have you come here?"
"Or where should I go? He related it in detail;
he (the king) reflected:
"This is indeed that son of mine"; he was taken into his own home by him and told:
"Son, you must not tell this to anyone."
"This is my father," he thought, and he began to show him excessive affection.
Then he was addressed by those other sons:
"Father, whose son is this boy?
He replied,
"He is the son of my friend."
They observed: "Since he is so exceedingly affectionate toward her, he must surely be her son";
they then began to converse with one another.
"This is another brother," he thought; he then reflected:
"I shall send him away."
This is the lowest of enmities,
namely rivalry with a co-wife;
it is possible that they will have him killed.
Thinking, "If I give them anything along the way, they will kill me for the sake of the inheritance; what if I were to send him in this manner? he wrote a note and gave it:
"At the village cemetery, one *yojana* from the previous location, at the base of the Hayakarṇa tree."
By digging there with skill and vigilance, you will indeed obtain your own inheritance.
"But that which is on his neck must be given to Valayā.
Taking the letter, he set out; however, on the way, he was seized by his brothers and addressed as follows:
"What did you receive from your father? He replied, "Nothing; this is merely a written note.
They reflected:
"He has been deprived of his inheritance by his father;
let him go";
thus he was released by them.
Having entered his own home in due course, he dispelled the fatigue of the journey;
then his mother asked him: "What have you received from your father?"
He said: "Nothing at all,
but this letter."
She said: "You have been deceived by him, and you have become weary from the journey."
"Nothing has been accomplished," he said;
she replied,
"Mother, he is a great-souled one."
"He will not deceive me," he thought; he then began to read that document: "In the village"—by which is meant the village where one is born.
"Śmaśāna" refers to where one who has died is cremated; "at the root of Hayakarṇa" means that "hayas" are called horses.
*Tatkarṇa* is the name of a tree; thus, it means "at the foot of an *aśvakarṇa* tree";
[the phrase] "from the eastern ground" means:
In the eastern direction;
"at a distance of one yojana" means at a distance of the length of a yoke.
Having thus reflected on the meaning of the verse, he went to the cemetery at the time when the birds had ceased their flight;
there, near it, he saw an aśvakarṇa tree.
Having measured out a space of one yoke’s length to the east of it, he began to dig;
as he dug, he saw a golden jar,
and around its neck was tied a necklace.
Taking it with a joyful heart, he went home;
having removed the pearl necklace, he gave it to Valaya.
What do you think, monks?
The householder at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself;
the son of that householder was this very Jīvaka at that time and on that occasion.
Even then, he understood my intentional speech.
The power of the Buddha. The Buddha heals Devadatta.
Jīvaka reflected:
"The Blessed One possesses a body of diamond-like substance and is of great stature."
"It is not possible to perform the medical treatment with such a small amount of ghee.
Therefore, taking a vessel and weighing out thirty-two *pala* measures of ghee using a scale, he offered it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One then distributed what remained in the vessel among the monks.
The monks,
regarding it as the remnants from the Blessed One’s bowl, paid homage to it.
Devadatta reflected:
"I too shall drink ghee. He then asked Jīvaka:
"Jīvaka, what quantity of ghee was drunk by the ascetic Gautama?"
Thus it was said; he replied: "Thirty-two palas"; he said:
"I too shall drink thirty-two palas," [said the king].
Jīvaka replied: "The Blessed One has a body like diamond and is large of stature."
"He is able to digest such a quantity, whereas you will not be able to digest it";
he said:
"I too possess a vajra-body;
why then do I not digest it? Thinking thus, he forcibly drank thirty-two palas of the dose.
For the Blessed One it was properly digested,
but for Devadatta it was not digested;
on the very next day, Jīvaka gave a gruel to the Blessed One.
Out of pride, Devadatta, thinking "the Blessed One drinks [this]," drank the scum of ghee while the ghee was still undigested;
a sharp pain arose,
and a sensation constricting the vital organs appeared.
On account of that, he experiences painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and unpleasant sensations;
neither by night nor by day does he obtain sleep.
The Venerable Ānanda, being affectionate toward his kinsmen,
reported that matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One extended his arm, which resembled the trunk of an elephant, and having split the Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain with a wheel marked by a thunderbolt, a svastika, and a nandyāvarta, [he emerged].
Placing his hand—which was born from hundreds of manifold merits and provides consolation to the terrified—upon Devadatta, he made a vow of truth:
"By that truth, by which my mind toward Devadatta is exactly the same as toward my beloved only son Rāhulabhadra, neither less nor more, by that truth may his pain be stilled.
Immediately following the moment of this vow of truth, Devadatta’s pain subsided.
Having regained his lost life-breath, he gazed at the Blessed One’s hand;
he recognized it perfectly and reflected:
"This is the hand of the ascetic Gautama"; yet,
although his followers were overcome by the intoxication of pride arising from their practice of extensive and long-standing deceit,
they spoke thus, their afflictions stilled by the majesty of the Buddha:
"Siddhārtha, you have mastered an excellent medical science;
you will be able to provide for your livelihood with this.
Thus the news spread throughout the surrounding area.
Devadatta, having been restored to health by the Blessed One through a prayer of truth after being overcome by intense agony and on the verge of losing his life—
having heard this, even those on Devadatta’s side who were extremely obstinate acknowledged their wonder toward the Blessed One, saying: "Oh, how perfectly perfected is his loving-kindness!"
"Oh, how well-cultivated is compassion toward sentient beings! Thus was Devadatta addressed by the monks:
"Devadatta, you have been restored to health by the Blessed One."
"Otherwise, you would be deprived of your life-breaths";
he replied,
"That man knows the illusion of compliance."
"By which he causes the world to follow along"—thus it was said; the monks replied:
"Devadatta, enough of this boasting!"
"Regain your own mind; you have been restored to health by the Blessed One. He replied:
"What has he done for me? My pain was relieved when the ghee was digested.
Thinking, "This man is ungrateful and does not recognize what has been done for him," they departed.
They approached the Blessed One;
having approached, being filled with doubt, they questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, Devadatta is ungrateful and unthankful."
The Blessed One said: "Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, this man was ungrateful and unthankful."
Listen to that.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) is:
Kauśika, Mahendrasena, the mangoes, and Dārukoṭaka.
The two bears, Śibi-rāja and Vidāra, and Jujjuka.
The Story of a Sage and an Ungrateful Elephant (concerning a previous birth of Devadatta):
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain remote forest retreat, there was a park endowed with various kinds of flowers, fruits, and water.
In that place lived a seer of the Kauśika clan,
who subsisted on discarded fruit and fed upon roots, fruits, and water, and was clothed in deerskins and bark garments;
in the vicinity of his hermitage, deer and birds dwelt with full confidence, roaming about as they pleased.
Not far from him, a female elephant had given birth; immediately upon that birth, a lion let out a roar, whereupon she,
terrified and trembling, abandoned her calf and fled, voiding urine and dung.
When that seer had emerged from his hermitage grounds and began to wander about, looking toward the various directions in the vicinity of the hermitage,
he saw that newborn young elephant calf.
Then, his heart shaken by compassion and his mind intent on searching for its mother, the seer began to look all around.
When he did not see him in any state whatsoever, he took him and entered the hermitage;
there he was suckled, nourished, and raised by him like a son, until he grew up to be a great man.
Then he commits an offense in that seer’s hermitage;
he uproots flowering branches and breaks off the limbs of fruit-bearing trees.
He commits these and thousands of other offenses;
the seer rebukes him, and being rebuked by the seer, he falls into a state of contraction.
When he became filled with passion, even though he was being rebuked, he showed contempt;
eventually, at another time, having been severely threatened by the seer,
he rushed toward that very seer in order to kill him.
Having torn a portion of the seer’s body, he fled;
then a deity spoke this verse:
"O Bhadrika, there is no association with a base man, a most cruel being who is ungrateful."
"Even after following him for a long time, he commits an evil deed, just as the Naga did to Āśramakauśika.
"Why then do you serve a wicked person with such devotion—with food, with drink, and with both?
In the end, he will surely destroy his friend, just as the Naga destroyed Āśramakauśika. Thus [he spoke].
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? That seer at that time, on that occasion, was none other than myself."
He who was that elephant-king was none other than this Devadatta at that time and on that occasion;
even then he was ungrateful and unthankful,
and now too he is ungrateful and unthankful.
Furthermore, hear how this man was ungrateful and failed to acknowledge what had been done for him.
The Story of Mahendrasena.
(Concerning a former birth of Devadatta:

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Mahendrasena reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
He had a queen named Candraprabhā, whose dreams were true.
Whatever one sees in a dream, all that comes to pass exactly so;
and in the realm of that king, there was a Bodhisattva named Suvarṇapārśva who had been reborn among the deer as their sovereign.
By virtue of his inconceivable form and power, he brought delight to the minds and eyes of the entire world.
And he was to be longed for;
whoever saw him remained gazing right there,
and as he looked at him intensely, he became filled with apprehension.
He wanders about, terrified by the fear of hunters and the fear of other people;
for it is the nature of things that when the world has recently come into being, even animals become capable of uttering speech.
Now, a certain crow—
He approached him,
and being filled with affection, love, and happiness in his company, he said: "O uncle, why do you wander about so terrified?"
Thus he spoke; he said:
"Nephew, this form of mine is auspicious to all the world and worthy of being prayed for;
yet I am utterly terrified by fear of the world and fear of hunters."
"I am traveling," he said; the other replied, "I too have a very great fear of owls; therefore, let us protect one another."
"I shall protect you by day;
you protect me by night. Having thus established their agreement, they remained so settled.

Meanwhile, a certain man, his arms bound tightly behind his back by his enemies, was cast into a river of swift current filled with fresh water, which was lined with golden chains and golden ornaments;
being carried away there, he lamented and wailed with a cry of distress.
"To whom shall I be a servant, or to whom a follower, who might today grant me life, which is so very difficult to obtain in the worlds? Thus he thought;
then, by chance, that lord of deer approached the vicinity of the river from his watery abode, surrounded by a herd of deer.
Then, hearing that human cry, those deer fled in all directions;
for such is the nature of Bodhisattvas that even if they fall away from their bodies, they do not fall away from their minds.

Then that lord of beasts, his heart moved repeatedly by compassion, suddenly began to descend into the river; and the crow, his mind fixed upon the former agreement, followed closely behind him for protection.
Perceiving that the man had resolved to rescue himself, he spoke thus:
"Enough, enough, O Lord of Beasts! Do not act rashly;
for these humans are ungrateful and do not acknowledge a favor."

Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, are those who do not turn back; having treated that man’s words as no words at all, he plunged into the river, mounted the man upon his back as if he were a beloved only son,
and reached the far bank of the river.
Having loosened his bonds and rested for a moment,
he said: "My son, go by this path as you please."
Then that man, with palms joined in reverence, fell at the feet of the lord of beasts and said this to him:
"O Father, I am indeed your slave; I am your very servant.
By you my life has been granted, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain in all the worlds. Thus he spoke.
He said: "May you not be my slave today, nor even my servant;
do not speak of me to others, lest they kill me for the sake of my skin."
"Moreover, my child, this must be done by you:
once the service has been rendered, you must not reveal me to anyone,
for this body of mine is exceedingly alluring and would be sought after by the whole world."
Then that man, having agreed saying "So be it," circumambulated the lord of beasts three times, prostrated at his feet, and departed. Subsequently,
at another time, Queen Candraprabhā, exhausted by the fatigue of pleasure, was lying upon her great couch.

Having fallen asleep during the final watch of the night, she saw a dream: the lord of beasts, a lion of exceedingly beautiful form, seated upon a lion-throne in a great royal assembly, teaching the Dharma.
Having seen this, as if it were before her very eyes, and filled with joy born from the vision of the dream, she rose very quickly from her great couch and informed the king.
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with great wonder, thinking:
"How indeed can one who has been reborn in an undesirable state sit upon the lion throne and teach the Dharma in the great assembly of the court?
Then Queen Candraprabhā, having comforted the king for a moment through her endearing, sweet, and clever speech and conduct, said:
"Your Majesty, let an effort be made to bring that deer back.
Thereupon, the king gave an order to his ministers: "Sirs, all the deer-hunters who dwell within my realm must be brought into my presence."
The ministers issued orders to the royal officers in each respective district:
"His Majesty commands that all hunters residing in my territory must come here;
therefore, you must dispatch all the hunters to this place."
By them, all the deer-hunters dwelling in the region were sent into the presence of the king;
they were brought before the king by the ministers,
and the king said:
"Gentlemen, I have heard that in my realm there is a deer with an exceedingly beautiful form.
You must capture him with soft and loose bonds, bring him to me without distressing him.
They replied:
"Your Majesty, we are indeed those who live by this very thing;

yet, while wandering through Your Majesty’s realm for so long a time, never before have we heard of such a preeminent deer, much less seen one. Therefore, it behooves Your Majesty to search for him through a succession of reports, until it is known that he stands in such-and-such a place."
"To learn from us;
in this way we shall certainly carry out the command of Your Majesty.
Thereupon, the king gave his command to the ministers:
"Gentlemen, have a proclamation made by the sounding of bells in Vārāṇasī:
'The King commands that there is a lord of deer with an exceedingly beautiful form;
whoever reports news of him to me, I shall honor him with great hospitality.'"
"And I shall grant him five excellent villages.
Having promised this to the king, the ministers caused a proclamation by bell to be made in Vārāṇasī:
"Listen, O citizens dwelling in Vārāṇasī and all people arrived from various lands!"
"Your Majesty commands thus: 'In my realm there is a lord of deer with an exceedingly and most beautiful form;
whoever reports news of him to me, I shall honor him with great hospitality and grant him five excellent villages.'"
Then, as that man beheld this, the thought occurred to him:
"Should I continue to maintain my family, or rather, should I practice gratitude?"

Thus it is said: "For one who indulges in sensual desires, there is indeed no evil deed that should not be committed. Consequently, his heart tormented by the fierce fire of hatred arising from the cause of those desires, he reflected:
"Let gratitude be set aside!"
"The time has arrived to exact vengeance upon my enemy;
why should I again allow myself to fall into such a state?
For now, I shall exact my revenge upon him."

When the night had turned to dawn, while the king was seated in his assembly hall presiding over royal affairs, [the man], having brought various kinds of wonderful and fragrant flowers, passed through the unguarded palace gates, announced himself through a succession of doorkeepers and ministers, entered the assembly, and after performing the customary rites of honor, made his report to the king:
"In that region, adorned with groves of various trees and filled with trusting deer and birds, there dwells a lord of deer named Suvarṇapārśva, surrounded by a multitude of deer;
I shall show Your Majesty that supreme deer of most delightful form.

Then the king, his heart filled with joy upon hearing this, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of ministers and by the citizens and country folk residing in Vārāṇasī who had gathered from various lands out of curiosity, [set out].
Following the path shown by that man,
he reached that region in due course;
meanwhile, that crow, who had been appointed by the Bodhisattva as his lookout for the directions, was perched upon the top of a tree in that forest thicket.
He saw a great multitude of people heading toward the forest grove;
hurrying as fast as possible, he approached the lord of the deer and said:
O King of Beasts, I told you before that humans are ungrateful, unthankful, and do not acknowledge a favor received.
"This man has arrived with a great gift";
hearing that sound, the deer fled in all directions out of fear.
The Bodhisattva, the lord of the deer, reflected:
Thinking, "If I do not protect these beings,
they will meet their end this very day;
it would be better for me to lose my own life than to neglect these sentient beings," he went out to meet the king.
Then that man, whose heart was devoid of compassion, who had abandoned the world beyond, and whose mind was captivated by Mṛgadarśanā, pointing out that best of deer with both hands, said:
"Your Majesty, this is that lord of deer.
For actions that are exceedingly powerful and fully ripened do not wait for the time of their fruition.
Immediately after the man had uttered those words, both his hands fell to the ground;
thereupon the king, overcome with agitation, asked that man:
"O man, what is this?"
Thus he spoke; struck by painful sensations, he uttered this verse with a faltering voice:
"He is not a thief, O Great King, who robs another of wealth after having slain him.
But he is a thief, O Great King, who possesses no gratitude. (SBV II 100)
The king asked, "What is the meaning of this statement? and he explained everything to him in full detail.
Then the king addressed the ungrateful man with a verse:
"How is it that you, the lowest of men, do not sink into the earth?
How is it that your tongue does not split into a hundred pieces?"
"How is it that the Guhyakas do not strike your body here with thunderbolts, spears, javelins, or lances?
Then the king, having recognized the greatness of the Bodhisattva's power, addressed his ministers:
"This high-souled lord of deer is here for the sake of honor; go,
and have the city beautified and the road decorated."
By those means, that city was prepared, cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;
it was sprinkled with sandalwood water, set with fragrant incense burners, with banners and flags raised high, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and cords, strewn with various flowers,
and delightful like the Nandana grove of the gods.
Thus the beauty of the road was prepared;
the multitude of people residing in Vārāṇasī came out to meet him, carrying offerings of flowers and perfumes.
Then the king, having led that lord of deer—whose form was exceedingly beautiful—with great magnificence into the city of Vārāṇasī, seated him upon a lion-throne.
Then, with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, the king sat down, surrounded by his harem, princes, ministers, and the people of the city and countryside.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, the Lord of Deer, surveyed that assembly on all sides and taught such a Dharma to the king and that assembly that,
having heard it, the king together with his retinue took up the five precepts.
And many beings acquired roots of merit;
then the king granted safety from fear to the Bodhisattva deer,
and granted safety from fear to all living beings.
What do you think, monks?
At that time, on that occasion, he who was the lord of deer with golden flanks was none other than I myself;
and he who was that man was none other than Devadatta at that time, on that occasion.
Even then he was ungrateful and failed to recognize what had been done for him; even now he is ungrateful and fails to recognize what has been done for him.
Listen again to how Devadatta was likewise ungrateful and failed to recognize what had been done for him.
The Story of a Lord of Monkeys and a Garland-Maker (concerning a previous birth of Devadatta):
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain mountain village there lived a garland-maker.
There, on the far bank of the river, was a flower garden;
he gathered river flowers every single day.
Then, at another time, as he was crossing the river, he saw a mango fruit being carried away by the current, out of season.
Having taken it, he gave it to the doorkeeper; the doorkeeper gave it to the usher; the usher gave it to the king.
The king gave it to the queen;
the queen tasted it,
and having tasted it, being greedy for its flavor, she informed the king:
"Your Majesty, you ought to give me such mangoes as these.
The king asked the doorkeeper: "Where did you get these mangoes?"
Thus he spoke;
he replied, "It was given by the doorkeeper"; the doorkeeper was then questioned.
He said:
"It was given by the garland-maker";
the king said:
"Sirs, let the florist be summoned.
He was summoned by the king's men,
and the king said:
"O gardener, from where did you obtain this mango fruit?
He related exactly what had happened;
the king gave him this very command: "Go!"
"Bring such mangoes as those.
The command of kings is not to be disobeyed;
with his heart overcome by apprehension, he began to search for the mangoes.
Taking provisions according to his previous experience with mango fruits, he went on his way and saw that mango tree on a certain part of the mountain;
it was accessible to monkeys,
but not to humans.
Then that gardener looked here and there at the tree, intending to climb it;
however, because its precipice had grown so high, it was inaccessible to humans,
and many days passed for him there in his longing for the mango fruit.
His provisions were completely exhausted,
and he reflected:
"In this way, due to the lack of provisions, I shall be parted from my life."
"Whether it be this way or that, I shall climb up"; grasping hold of stone after stone, he began to ascend,
but before even reaching the mango fruits, he fell into a pit.
And on that mountain, the Bodhisattva, having become a monkey, was the leader of a troop of monkeys;
by chance, he arrived at that place after leaving his troop on the mountain;
there he saw the gardener who had fallen into a state of extreme distress, peril, and confinement.
Bodhisattvas are skilled in various arts and crafts;
because he was intent on bringing about his welfare, [the Bodhisattva] realized that he could not be lifted out without a step-by-step process, so he began to practice with stones.
When the man recognized, "I am able to lift him out," then he was gradually raised from the precipice by him.
He was utterly exhausted from the exertion of moving stones and from lifting that gardener;
and at that time, animals spoke in human voices,
so he questioned them.
"For what reason have you fallen into such a peril? He related exactly what had occurred;
the Bodhisattva reflected: "He has gone... (SBV II 102)
"Even this man will meet with misfortune if he is deprived of mango fruits;
I shall give him some.
With his resolve unflagging and intent on securing the welfare of others, that Great Being, though exhausted, climbed that tree and began to shake down the mango fruits.
