That man ate as many mango fruits as he could obtain and filled his lap;
then that lord of monkeys descended.
The Bodhisattvas have confidence in all sentient beings;
he said to that man:
"O man, first of all, look around in the directions."
"I am exhausted;
I shall sleep for a moment," he said;
and he replied:
"Do so"; he fell asleep;
the man reflected:
"I have exhausted my provisions for the journey; if I go along eating mangoes, what shall I give to the king?
Therefore, I shall kill this very monkey, prepare dried meat like *śuṇḍī*, and proceed on my way.
With a heart devoid of compassion and having abandoned the world beyond, he deprived that monkey of life with a large rock.
A deity recited this verse:
"They say that a friend is characterized by helpfulness and likewise recognizes the help rendered;
yet some people do not acknowledge the assistance they have received."
What do you think, monks?
He who was that lord of monkeys at that time, on that occasion, was none other than I.
He who was that gardener at that time, on that occasion, was this very Devadatta.
Even then he was ungrateful and unappreciative; even now he is ungrateful and unappreciative; hear again how he is ungrateful and unappreciative.

The Story of a Lord of the Dārukoṭaka Birds and a Lion (Concerning a Previous Birth of Devadatta): Monks, in the past, when the Bodhisattva was situated in the indeterminate group, he was reborn among the birds in a certain remote forest region, a mountain cave on a slope rich in flowers and fruits.
There was a woodpecker;
and on that very same part of the mountain, a lion, the king of beasts, having repeatedly slaughtered deer for his own pleasure and sport, would devour them.
At another time, as he was eating meat, a bone became stuck between his teeth.
His body being oppressed by the pain of colic,
he became despondent even though his fear and terror had vanished;
he was unable to take food.
By chance, that woodpecker, through his habit of moving from tree to tree, arrived at the very spot where the lord of beasts was;
there he saw the lion struck by agonizing pain and said to him, "Uncle, why are you so distressed?"
He said: "Nephew, I am struck by painful sensations; what kind of suffering do you have?"
He explained it in detail,
and he said:
"Uncle, I shall treat you."
For you are the lord of all four-footed creatures; you are capable of providing every assistance;
therefore, you must provide for my sustenance from time to time.
He said: "So be it; I shall do so."
That Dārukoṭaka reflected:
"I shall treat him in such a way that he does not even know when treatment has been performed,
yet he becomes aware of it once he has recovered."
Intent on bringing about his welfare, he remained there, observing the king’s conduct and movements;
meanwhile, that lord of deer, his mouth stilled by the touch of a pleasant breeze, lay down upon his left side with his head upon a large rock on the ground and fell asleep.
Then Dārukoṭaka approached the presence of that lord of deer.
He sees him living in such a state of deception; he reflects:
"This is the time for his treatment."

Having understood this and having carefully examined it, he suddenly extracted the bone stuck between the teeth by the stroke of his wing, drew it out from the cavity of the mouth, and remained perched upon the tree watching him closely. Then that lord of deer, his mind filled with joy at the removal of the bone-thorn, dispelled his fatigue from sleep and, having risen, departed.
Then Dārukoṭaka, perceiving that the lord of deer was free from suffering and dejection, approached him with a joyful mind and said:
"Uncle, here is that bone which was the cause of your distress.
Thereupon, the lord of deer was struck with great wonder and said:
"Nephew, I must certainly repay this kindness of yours at the appropriate time; you should come to visit me from time to time.
"Very well, let it be so," having said this, Dārukoṭaka departed.
Then, at another time...
The lord of beasts was eating meat,

and that woodpecker, having slipped from the talons of a hawk and considering himself as good as dead, approached the lord of beasts with his heart overcome by hunger; having announced his distress, he said:
"Uncle, I am overcome by hunger;
give me a little meat."
He spoke this verse:
"Today, you who have been caught between the fangs of me— a fierce doer of evil who takes life— do not hold yourself in high regard while still living."
He too spoke this verse:
"Lost is what has fallen into the ocean; lost is what is imagined in a dream;
lost is service rendered to a base man, and whatever is done for one who is ungrateful."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks?
That Dārukoṭaka at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself."
He who was that lion, the king of beasts, was none other than this Devadatta at that time and on that occasion;
even then he was ungrateful and unappreciative,
and even now he is ungrateful and unappreciative.
Furthermore, hear how he was ungrateful and failed to acknowledge what had been done for him. [This is] the story of a lord of bears and a poor man (concerning a previous birth of Devadatta).
Long ago, monks, there lived in the city of Vārāṇasī a certain poor man who made his living by selling wood.
On another occasion, rising very early in the morning, he took up an axe and a basket and went to the forest in search of wood.
A great and untimely cloud, preceded by wind and rain, arrived; then that man, thinking "this is appropriate" or "this is right," went from tree to tree in search of another place,
yet he was still drenched by the heavy rain.
Moving through the midst of the trees, he gradually entered a mountain cave;
and in that cave there was a bear.
Upon seeing it, he became terrified and began to flee.
The bear said:
"My son, why are you terrified?
You have no cause for fear from me."
"Stay! he said.
Although filled with apprehension, the man was unable to move due to his trepidation;
then, that bear took hold of him with its two forepaws and supported him.
He was satisfied with roots and fruits,
and for seven days a storm of foul weather occurred;
the god continued to rain.
He did not remain;

after seven days had passed, on the eighth day, when the sky was cloudless and the rain had ceased, the bear looked out in the four directions, gave him abundant roots and fruits, and said to that man:
"My son, this foul weather has passed."
"The day has passed;
the sky is free of clouds;
go as you please."
That man fell at his feet and said:
"Father, I am going;
nevertheless, I must perform a service for you in return."
He said,
"My dear child, you have done exactly this for me: that you do not report this to anyone."
He said,
"Father, let it be so.
Having circumambulated him and prostrated at his feet, he departed.
He was entering Vārāṇasī when a certain deer-hunter was going out to hunt deer;
he saw him and said:
"O friend, you have come here after such a long time;
your wife and children have become distressed and are crying out piteously."
"It is said that you were killed by an untimely storm lasting seven days or by a wild beast;
many deer and birds have been killed by such an untimely storm lasting seven days, so how is it that you alone have escaped?"
Thus he spoke; he reported everything exactly as it had occurred, and he said:
"Friend, I shall maintain my livelihood by whatever means or in whatever way."
"I shall not enter the forest again.
Thus enticed by him with two portions of meat, he set out, showing the way as he proceeded; and so, in due course...
Having reached the cave where that great-souled bear was staying,
he then resorted to cruelty and ingratitude and said:
"This is the cave where he stays."
Then that hunter, who deprives others of their lives, set fire to the cave;
thereupon that Great-souled bear, his mind distressed by the smoke and his eyes clouded with tears, spoke this verse:
"Whose [suffering] has been removed by my dwelling in this mountain cave?"
Subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, he maintained a mind intent on the welfare of all living beings.
Now that the time of death has arrived, what shall I do?
For embodied beings, whether desirable or undesirable, their own karma must inevitably follow them.
Having said this, he passed away;
then, after they had divided the flesh into portions for dismemberment, they said to that ungrateful man:
"Take two shares of the meat."
He stretched out his hands, thinking, "I shall seize him," but they fell to the ground.
Then, seeing him treated so cruelly, that deer-hunter cried out, "Alas, what a tragedy! Alas, what a tragedy! and having abandoned even his own share, he departed.
Having heard this most wonderful account, a great multitude of people gathered in that place;
King Brahmadatta, filled with curiosity, went there as well;
and on one side of that mountain was a monastery.
Then King Brahmadatta, having taken his hide with eyes wide open in amazement,
went to that monastery thinking, "I shall announce this matter to the community of monks.
Having placed the hide in the lotus pond, he sat at the end of the row of elders and related this matter in detail to the Saṅgha.
And there the elder of the Saṅgha was an Arhat;
he addressed the king in verse:
"This is no bear, O Great King, but the Bodhisattva Dyutindhara."
"O best of men, he is to be honored by the three worlds and by you as well.
Thus the king reflected: "I must perform his worship."
The monks said:
"Your Majesty, this is a Bodhisattva belonging to the Fortunate Aeon;
honor should be prepared for him."
Then King Brahmadatta, together with his harem, princes, ministers, citizens, and countryfolk, took all kinds of fragrant wood and went to that place.
Having had all that flesh, bone, and corpse gathered into one heap, he said:
"Sirs, having piled a funeral pyre with all kinds of fragrant wood, cremate him with great honor."
And in that place, a great stūpa was erected; umbrellas, banners, and flags were raised; and a festival was instituted.
And those who performed acts of service there all became intent upon liberation.
What do you think, monks?
That bear at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself.
That man who was ungrateful at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this Devadatta;
even then he was ungrateful and unthankful,
and even now he is ungrateful and unthankful.
Furthermore, listen to how he was ungrateful and unthankful;
this is another story concerning a bear and a poor man [relating to a previous birth of Devadatta].
Long ago, monks, there lived in the city of Vārāṇasī a certain poor man who made his living by selling firewood.
On another occasion, rising early at dawn, he took up an axe and a basket and went to the forest in search of wood.
In that mountain region, adorned with various groves of trees and abundant with many kinds of flowers and fruits, the Bodhisattva had been reborn among the bears, dwelling in no fixed place.
Now, while this wood-gatherer was searching for firewood, he was attacked by a tiger in a certain spot;
terrified by the fear of death, by chance he [encountered] him...
He climbed the tree upon which the Bodhisattva-Ṛkṣa was staying; seeing him, he became even more terrified,
but that Great Being comforted him and held him upon his lap.
And that tiger, greedy for food, did not leave the foot of that tree at all;
and he said:
"O Great-souled One, these humans have black heads and are ungrateful."
"Strike him down! Having devoured him, I shall depart.
For even other human beings are generally compassionate toward those who have come for refuge.
How much more so, then, the bodhisattvas!
He said: "This one has come to me for refuge."
"I am not causing him to fall," he thought;
nevertheless, that tiger, longing for flesh and blood, remained right there and did not move away from him.
Then that bear said to the man:
"I am weary; you stay here for a moment while I rest."
Seated upon his lap, exhausted and weary from fatigue, he fell asleep;
the watchman then said: "O man, how long must you remain here?"
"Throw him down! Having devoured him, I shall depart.
Thus he reflected, a man of pitiless heart, an evildoer who had abandoned the world beyond.
"He speaks well;
for how long must I remain here?
I shall cause him to fall."
He was struck down by him;
as he was falling, that great-souled one cried out, "Alas! Not so! Alas! May no harm come to you," and having said this, he fell;
thus was he brought to ruin by the wicked tiger.
Having heard his intentional speech, he reflected: "He wishes to share something with me, which is why he speaks thus."
The lamentation of that man, blinded by craving, became fixed; with his mind deranged, wandering here and there, he spoke thus:
"Alas! No, indeed! Alas! What shall I do?"
He was led home by his kinsmen;
yet he continued to rave and could not remain still.
They consulted those who held spells and mantras, physicians for spirit afflictions, and other ascetics and brahmins, as well as friends, relatives, and kinsmen.
They spoke of it in many ways, yet no one provided medical treatment.

Now at that time, not far from Vārāṇasī, in a hermitage adorned with various groves of trees, abundant in flowers, fruits, and water, and resounding with the songs of many kinds of birds, there lived a seer endowed with the five superknowledges.
The kinsmen of that man took him with them, went into the presence of that seer, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Great Seer, this is our kinsman; he speaks thus repeatedly."
"What should be done with him? This being is an evildoer;
by this wicked-souled one, the Bodhisattva, who had rendered him assistance, was cast down before a tiger."
That Great Being thought, "I shall teach him the Dharma," but he was felled by this [being].
As he fell, reeling, one syllable from each of ten verses occurred to his mind: *hā naivā te hā kiṃ cid duḥse mi*.
The disciple of that seer said, "Preceptor, tell me first, what are those verses like?
That seer then began to recite those verses in their proper sequence.
Alas, what a tragedy! Indeed, there is a terrible unrighteousness in this world; for while these men are alive, violence is being committed against their own friends. (1)
Neither on a seat, nor on a bed, nor even while walking, nor in any state whatsoever, does one who betrays a friend find happiness. // 2 //
O evil-minded one, that speech which was uttered by me out of compassion now consumes you, just as the blazing Khāṇḍava forest burns.
Therefore, you shall experience that feeling in the next world.
Having performed extremely terrible deeds that result in unpleasant contact with suffering. // 4 //
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", you shall experience great suffering in the most dreadful Raurava hell, O base one, lowest of the low. (5)
What [action] is not natural to you, who are fierce and of evil deeds?
For among these untruthful men, violence toward friends is found.
They determine that the mind is evil, for the destruction of the Dharma is terrible;
remember the bear and the tiger, and the evil that was committed by you. (7)
O evil-minded one, you do not know how to behave toward friends;
the killer finds himself killed, and the enemy encounters his own enmities.
"You were served by me for a long time when the great danger of the tiger arose;
you were protected by me even while lying down—why was he not protected by you? (9)
"Those who speak of the Dharma say that the breaking of friendship is the most censurable act;
O evil-minded one, after the dissolution of the body, you will be reborn in the hells.
"What do you think, monks? [the Buddha asked].
He who was that bear was none other than myself at that time, in that period;
he who was that ungrateful being was this very Devadatta at that time, in that period;
even then, he was ungrateful and failed to recognize what had been done for him.
Even now, he remains ungrateful and unappreciative;
listen again to how he was ungrateful and unappreciative.
[The Story of King Śibi]
(Briefly concerning a previous birth of Devadatta:

Once upon a time, monks, in the royal capital of Śibighoṣā, a king named Śibi reigned; his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.

And that king was faithful, auspicious, of noble intent, dedicated to his own welfare, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of all, one who renounces without attachment, and he abides in great generosity. There was nothing whatsoever that he had not given away or relinquished— namely, to ascetics, brahmins, the wretched, beggars, travelers, and supplicants.
For the most part,
it was the custom of that king to rise very early in the morning, pay homage to his mother and father, visit the sick, and then sit in the court of justice;
at that time, a certain man fell ill.
Rejected by all physicians, indifferent to life and facing death, he wandered here and there until he reached the royal capital of Śibighoṣā.

At that time, when the spring season had arrived, the king— surrounded by his harem— set out for the pleasure grove, where the trees were in full bloom and fruit, and the forest thickets resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, cuckoos, and jīvañjīva birds.

And that sick man, his mind distressed by the torment of intense pain, his body repeatedly obstructed by labored breathing, his eyes clouded with tears, and holding a staff in his hand, slowly approached the king, bowed his head in salutation, and said: "Your Majesty, protect me from this disease!"
"Grant him his life!
Then King Śibi, hearing those words of the sick man spoken in piteous, distressed, and faltering syllables, his heart trembling with compassion, turned back right there and addressed his ministers:
"Let the physicians residing in my realm be summoned."
All those physicians were summoned and brought before the king;
then the king, having called that man to him, said:
"Sirs, provide medical treatment for him. The physicians, having deliberated, spoke with one accord:
"Your Majesty, if a man who has never before been angry with anyone is used to prepare a gruel with his blood, and if it is eaten, [he will recover]."
"In this way he will recover,
and not otherwise";
having heard this, the king reflected:
"What is the use of this kind of life for me, or this sovereignty and dominion over a kingdom,
since I am unable to bring peace to others who are afflicted by suffering?"
Having reflected thus, the king began to examine his own lineage;
he asked his nurse, "Mother, have I ever been angry with anyone before?"
She said: "Your Majesty,
when you were situated within my flesh, even then I had never before been angry with anyone,
let alone now."
Then, having approached his mother, he said: "Son, when you were in my womb, I never before became angry with anyone, much less now that you have been born."
The king said,
"Now the medicine has been prepared"; he then spoke to the physicians:
"Release the veins from my five limbs," he said;
they replied:
"Your Majesty, we shall not let a weapon fall upon the body of Your Majesty for the sake of an ordinary man.
Bodhisattvas are skilled in various arts and crafts;
therefore, he himself released the veins in his five limbs.
A skull-bowl was filled with blood; then, having prepared a gruel from it, he gave it to him.
That king was beloved by the people of both the city and the countryside.

The women of the inner apartments, the princes, the ministers, the townspeople, and the countryfolk began to cry out; and the multitude of people gathered from various lands began to speak in protest:
"How is it that for the sake of a single ordinary being, so many beings are being sacrificed?"
Thus it was; then the king comforted that multitude of people;
by this means, for six months, he had his veins opened in five parts of his body and was fed only with barley gruel.
King Śibi’s body became like a winnowing basket;
his vital energy began to decline.
The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm perceived this:
If a Bodhisattva belonging to the Fortunate Aeon (bhadrakalpika) should thus fall away,
it is not good;
they bring him vital energy (ojaḥ) every day.
By means of this he sustained himself;
when that man's illness had subsided,
he was then provided with five excellent villages by King Śibi.
He was born as one highly esteemed in Vārāṇasī; at that time, a report spread throughout the surrounding region that King Śibi had opened his veins in five parts of his body.
"For such a long time you have attended to the sick man with your own blood,
and he has been restored to health";
then, filled with curiosity, beings approached and questioned that man:
"O man, is it true that King Śibi has indeed served you for all this time?
He replied,
"What has he done for me?"
"If corrupt blood were to be spilled upon the earth or given to another,
what would be the wonder in that?"—
no sooner had these words ended than fire fell upon his house.
By whom his entire house and all his wealth were burned.
What do you think, monks?
That King Śibi at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself.
That ungrateful man was none other than this Devadatta at that time and on that occasion; even then he was ungrateful and failed to recognize what had been done for him,
and even now he remains ungrateful and fails to recognize what has been done for him.
Furthermore, listen to how he was ungrateful and failed to acknowledge what had been done for him. [This is] the story of Kalyāṇakārin (concerning a previous birth of Devadatta).
Long ago, monks, in a certain royal capital, a certain king reigned over a kingdom that was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
At a later time, he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with his queen;
as he was thus sporting, dallying, and enjoying himself, (SBV II 111)
In the course of time, the queen became pregnant;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, golden-colored, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, joined eyebrows, and a prominent nose.
He was endowed with all major and minor limbs;
at his birth, many thousands of auspicious signs appeared;
and having performed the birth festival upon his birth, his name was established.
"What shall be the name of the boy? The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, at his birth, many thousands of auspicious signs appeared."
"Therefore, let the boy's name be Kalyāṇakārī.
Thus the name Kalyāṇakārī was established for him;
the boy Kalyāṇakārī was entrusted to eight nurses.

He was raised by eight nurses— two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to cleanse him, and two to play with him— and he grew quickly, nourished by milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the cream of clarified butter, and other various highly refined delicacies,
like a lotus in a pond.
Again, that king played, took pleasure, and amused himself with the queen;
while he was playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, the queen became pregnant;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A boy was born;
at his birth as well, thousands of inauspicious things appeared,
and thus he was given the name Akalyāṇakārī (the Doer of Evil).
He too was raised and grew up to be a great man; Prince Kalyāṇakārin was friendly by nature, compassionate, full of pity for all beings, fond of giving, and delighted in generosity;
he bestowed gifts upon ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the indigent, and beggars.
He was told by his father:
"Son, do not give gifts constantly;
from where will we have such a quantity of wealth that I might give in this manner every single day?"
For this is the natural law (dharmatā) of a donor, a master of giving: he becomes dear and pleasing to many people;
and his noble, auspicious fame, renown, and verses of praise rise up in all directions and intermediate points.
Having heard of the greatness of his virtues from another king in a different land, that king gave him his daughter.
He was installed by the king with great royal splendor;
Kalyāṇakārī said:
"I will not yet take a wife."
"Father, please permit me until I have acquired wealth;
I shall set out upon the great ocean."
He said, "Do so";
taking his merchandise, he set out for the great ocean.
His brother, who was a doer of evil, reflected:
"This man is dear and pleasing to the great multitude;
if he returns from the great ocean with a successful ship, he will become even more beloved by the people."
And he is pleasing; it is possible that while his father is still alive, he may exercise the sovereignty, lordship, and dominion of the kingdom.
In every respect, what is the appropriate course of action here?
I too shall descend along with him.
"I shall deprive him of life right here;
thus, even against my will, the consecration for the position of crown prince will be mine.
Having realized this, he approached his father and said:
"Your Majesty, Kalyāṇakārī has set out for the great ocean;
I too shall go with him. He replied, "Do so."
Then Kalyāṇakārin had a proclamation made by the ringing of a bell within his own domain:
"Listen, you merchants dwelling in the city!
Prince Kalyāṇakārin is setting out for the great ocean."
"Whoever among you is able to set out upon the great ocean with the caravan leader Kalyāṇakārin— free from customs duties, free from tolls, and without payment for crossing—
let him gather the merchandise suitable for a voyage to the great ocean.
Thereupon, many hundreds of merchants gathered the merchandise suitable for a voyage to the great ocean.
Then the merchant Kalyāṇakārī, having performed the festive rites, auspicious ceremonies, and benedictions together with his brother Akalyāṇakārī,

set out accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of merchants, taking with him a vast amount of merchandise suitable for the great ocean, carried on carts, loads, bundles, baskets, camels, oxen, and donkeys.
Traveling by stages through villages, market towns, royal capitals, and kingdoms, he surveyed the ports and reached the seashore.

Having hired a ship for five hundred *paurāṇas* and taken five crew members— a food-provider, a waste-disposal man, a sailor, a fisherman, and a helmsman— and having made a proclamation three times by the ringing of a bell,
he set out upon the great ocean.
When the ship had set sail, he said to his brother, who was intent on doing him harm:
"If that ship should meet with disaster while we are in the midst of the great ocean, you must cling to my neck."
"Do not become despondent," he said;
he replied, "Excellent; let it be so."
When that ship, driven by a favorable wind, reached the Island of Jewels,
the helmsman said:
"Listen, O merchants of Jambudvīpa!"
"That which is heard of as the island of jewels (Ratnadvīpa), the source of gems such as diamonds, lapis lazuli, sapphire, and emerald—that we have reached;
gather as many jewels as you desire!
Then, with joyful minds, they examined them.
That vessel was filled with jewels,
just like sesame, rice, jujubes, and mung beans;
for Bodhisattvas are both skillful and expert.
The prince Kalyāṇakārin had fastened highly precious jewels around his waist;
then that vessel turned over,
and not far from the shore, it was brought to ruin by a crocodile of the fish species through its wickedness.
Then the doer of evil clung to the neck of the doer of good;
he was pulled off by him with great effort,
and having become exhausted, he fell into a deep sleep.
As he was turning around, he saw the jewels fastened to the waist of that evildoer;
he reflected:
"This man will surely take these jewels and depart."
Thinking, "I shall depart with empty hands," he realized this and, while [the king] was held fast by a deep sleep, he stole those jewels and plucked out his eyes with thorns.
Having abandoned that blind man on the shore of the ocean, he departed;
by chance, some cowherds tending cattle arrived at that place,
and they saw him and questioned him:
"O man, who are you, and why are you like this?
He related everything exactly as it had happened;
having heard it, compassion arose within them.
They led him to the house of Pālabandhu; there he began to play the lute for him. Hearing the sound of the lute, Pālabandhu’s wife, impelled by the intoxication of youth, set out to solicit him.

Recalling his ungrateful conduct, he covered his ears and remained there, refusing to consent. [The woman thought: "For those possessed by lust, there is nothing that cannot be done. Thus she incited her husband, saying, "This blind man is making advances toward me."
"You are gathering such people together";
this enmity, namely enmity toward women, is the most base of all enmities;
he reflected thus:
"This man has been punished;
there is nothing further to be done for him except banishment.
Thus, he was banished from his home by him, and he makes a living with his lute in the streets, lanes, squares, and crossroads.
His father had passed away,
and his brother— who acted unrighteously— was established in the sovereignty and lordship of the kingdom.
He, too, in due course, arrived at the city of a neighboring king to whom he had previously given his daughter in marriage.
She grew up to be a woman,
and princes and sons of priests dwelling in various lands came as suitors for her hand; she was then addressed by her father:
"Daughter, the prince Kalyāṇakārin, to whom you were given in marriage, has gone to the great ocean; there he met with disaster due to his own misconduct.
Now, suitors are coming for you."
"But he to whom I shall not give you will become dejected; how, then, should one proceed in this matter?
She said:
"Father, if it is so, then have the splendor of the city prepared;
I shall descend for the svayaṃvara," he said.
The king replied:
"Daughter, do exactly so.
Thereupon, the announcement of the svayaṃvara was proclaimed throughout various regions and various cities;
and that city was prepared, cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel, and sprinkled with sandalwood water.
It was furnished with censers of fragrant incense, with banners and flags raised aloft, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, strewn with various flowers,
and as delightful as the Nandana grove of the gods;
and a proclamation by the ringing of bells was caused to be made:
"Listen, O citizens dwelling in the city and the multitude of people arrived from various lands:
tomorrow the princess will descend for her *svayaṃvara*."
"Therefore, you must assemble according to your respective means.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, that princess— adorned with various ornaments, surrounded by many young maidens,
and shining most brilliantly like a forest goddess in the midst of a flowering grove— appeared in the center of the city with a great display of splendor.
When many hundreds of thousands of living beings had assembled for the self-choice marriage ceremony (svayaṃvara),
Kalyāṇakārī was standing in a certain place playing his lute;
indeed, it is the very actions (karma) of sentient beings that join them together with one another.
"Even a powerful force of causes depends upon a counter-force";
therefore, that princess, her heart captivated by the sound of the lute, became infatuated with the lute-player Kalyāṇakārī;
she threw a garland of flowers at him.
"This man is my master!
Thus the multitude of people became dejected;
some, unable to restrain their agitation, began to revile him.

"How indeed could the Prince have rejected the sons of kings, ministers, and priests who had arrived from various lands, as well as other leading citizens residing in the city, and chosen a blind man as his lord, when the Princess herself was endowed with such beauty, youth, and mastery of the arts? Thus did the attendants, dejected and averse, inform the King.
"Your Majesty, a princess who had descended for a svayaṃvara has chosen you as her husband.
The king asked, "Of what sort? [The messenger replied,] "Your Majesty, he is blind."
Having heard this, he too became dejected;
then he summoned her and said,
"Daughter, there exist kings, wealthy merchants, caravan leaders, sons of ministers, and sons of priests."
"And they are endowed with beauty, youth, and wealth;
why have you chosen such a master?
She replied:
"Father, he alone pleases me," [the prince] said.
The king asked,
"If that is so, why do you remain here?"
She approached him and said,
"I have chosen you as my husband"; "You have not done well," he replied.
"What are you thinking?
This man is blind;
I shall enjoy myself with other men."
She said,
"I am not the doer of such a deed"; he replied:
How is this known?
She began to make a vow of truth:
"By that truth, by that word of truth, through which passion arose in me toward that prince who performs good deeds and toward you..."
"Of no one else;
by this truth, by this word of truth, may your one eye become as it was before.
Immediately upon this empowerment by truth, his one eye became restored as it was before.
He said:
"I am that very same doer of good; I have been brought to this state by my brother, who does what is not good."
She said,
"How is it known that you yourself are that doer of good?
He too began to make a vow of truth:
"By this truth, by this word of truth— that even as he was plucking out my eyes, not even the slightest malicious thought arose in me toward him—
by this truth, by this word of truth, may my second eye become as it was before! With that utterance of truth, his second eye became restored just as it had been before.
Then that princess, taking Kalyāṇakārin— who possessed unimpaired faculties— went into the presence of the king and said,
"Father, this is indeed that Kalyāṇakārin.
The king did not believe her.
He reported the matter exactly as it had occurred;
the king was struck with great wonder,
and thereupon he gave his daughter in marriage to him with a magnificent display of splendor.
And that doer of good, having gone to that city with a great host of forces, deposed the doer of evil and established him in his father’s kingdom.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that doer of good at that time, on that occasion, was none other than I; he who was that doer of evil at that time, on that occasion, was this very Devadatta;
even then, he was ungrateful and failed to recognize what had been done for him.
Even now, he remains ungrateful and unappreciative;
listen again to how he was likewise ungrateful and unappreciative.
[The Story of Viśākha]
(Concerning a previous birth of Devadatta:
Once upon a time, in a certain royal capital, a certain king was ruling a kingdom that was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants;
he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself together with his queen.
As he was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, four sons were born to him in due course:
Śākha, Praśākha, Anuśākha, and Viśākha;
they were raised, nurtured, and grew up to be adults.
They were married to the daughters of kings from other lands;
they began to plot against the king,
and consequently, they were banished by the king to their respective homes.
Taking their wives, they set out;
as they proceeded along the wilderness path,
their provisions for the journey were exhausted.
They made a mutual agreement among themselves:
"Having deprived each woman of life, let us cross the wilderness paths with her flesh. Viśākha reflected:
"It would be better for my own life to perish than for another's life to be obstructed; what is appropriate here? I shall take my wife and flee."
Taking his wife with him, he fled; but his wife, distressed by the lack of food and drink and by the exhaustion of the journey, became despondent and said,
"Noble son, I shall part from my life."
Viśākha reflected:
"I have rescued her from the midst of the rākṣasas;
if she should die now,"
"It is not right," he said;
thereupon, having cut the flesh from his own thigh, he gave it to her to eat,
and having severed his head from his arms, he made her drink his blood.
Having taken her, he gradually approached a certain mountain;
there he sustained himself on roots and fruits,
and near that mountain flowed a river.
In that river, a man who had been deprived of his hands and feet by an enemy was cast in; being carried away by the current, he cried out with a piteous voice,
while Viśākha was uprooting roots in another part of the region.
He heard that cry of the man;
with his stream of consciousness overflowing with compassion, he climbed the mountain and began to look all around,
until he saw that man being carried away.

He descended from the mountain very quickly, plunged into the river, and having mounted that man upon his back, carried him across the river and set him down on the bank. With a heart tormented by grief, he asked, "My son, what is this? and the man related everything exactly as it had happened.
Then he was comforted by him;
having been satisfied with roots and fruits, he was entrusted to his wife,
who then attended to him.
While attending upon him, she approached him again and again with affectionate cheerfulness and waited on him with various kinds of conversation;
for it is the nature of Bodhisattvas that they are by their very essence of little passion;
thus Viśākha sometimes dallied with her and sometimes did not.

And by the power of the Bodhisattva, those roots, tubers, and fruits became exceedingly potent; while consuming them, she— due to the intensity of her afflictions— began to solicit him who was deprived of hands and feet, but he did not consent.
And she said: "I have now somehow returned to life with my breath restored;
yet if I were to do such a thing again, it is possible that this husband of yours would deprive me of my life entirely."
He was entreated by her again and again;
the afflictions are difficult to conquer; he misconducted himself with her.
Because of her extreme passion for him due to that very joy and gladness, she did not go to his presence even when she was being sent;
he reflected:
"Just as this... (SBV II 117)
She was determined, thinking: "This is the lowest of all enmities, namely enmity with women;
now I am ruined."
He conversed with her, saying:
"This is your husband; if he learns of our union, he will certainly bring about your ruin and deprive me of my life."
She reflected:
"What he says is excellent;
I must devise a stratagem."
The woman Asitapaṇḍitā wrapped her head in a cloth, sat down upon a mountain rock, and remained there; meanwhile,
Viśākha returned, having gathered roots and fruits.
He saw her treated in such a manner,
and then he asked:
"O blessed lady, what is this?"
She said:
"Noble son, a headache afflicts me excessively.
Viśākha said:
"What should be done in this matter? She saw a *pāṣāṇabheda* plant on a mountain slope and said,
"Noble son, previously too I had this headache, and the physician prescribed *pāṣāṇabheda*."
"He has been restored to health by him";
Viśākha said,
"I shall search for a stone-splitter."
She said:
"Noble son, he is seen there on the mountain slope; I shall support you with a rope."
"Uproot it!
That noble being was upright and did not perceive her deceit; he consented.
"So be it; hold on, I shall pull you up.
He was drawn up by her with the rope;
then he released the rope with one hand.
And it was released by her;
he fell into the river;
that being was long-lived.
And the pleasures of sovereignty must be experienced;
he is not dead,
but being carried away by the current, has reached a certain royal capital.
And there, the king, being childless, passed away;
the ministers, together with the citizens and the people of the countryside, all assembled and deliberated: "Sirs, the king has passed away."
"Upon whom shall we now establish the kingdom? They dispatched men skilled in the science of marks, saying: "Sirs, search thoroughly."
"Whosoever is a being renowned for great merit, him we shall establish in the kingdom.
Thus they began to search from place to place.
"Actions do not perish, even after hundreds of eons."
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Because the ripening of the karma conducive to sovereignty had arrived, Viśākha, having crossed the river, sat down in one spot;
through the power of the Bodhisattva, that spot remained as if adorned,
until the men who were examiners of the marks [arrived].
Having come to that region, they saw that great-souled one, endowed with the marks of royalty;
with joyful minds, they went to the ministers and said,
"We have found the being of great merit and power who is worthy of the kingdom."

Then, those ministers, having prepared the adornment of the roads and the adornment of the city, led him into the city with a great display of splendor and consecrated him in the kingship according to the sequence of the day, lunar date, auspicious moment, and constellation. Since he had no queen, the ministers, priests, neighboring kings, and other wealthy merchants, guild-leaders, and caravan-chiefs came to that city, bringing their respective daughters adorned with every ornament, thinking, "The king will marry them."
That king, deceived by his wife, did not accept [the truth];
the ministers said:
"Your Majesty, there are those who are princes of the harem, ministers, townspeople, countryfolk, wealthy men, and kings."
"Let the inner apartments be brought forward;
let the leading men dwelling in various countries, the kings from foreign lands, and the principal men from here and there, having prepared their daughters, stand ready;
let her face them."
Nevertheless, he does not understand it;
moreover, he feels revulsion toward women;
yet, through the power of merit, the enjoyments of sentient beings become vigorous and come to fruition.
When the Bodhisattva was released from that ungrateful woman on the mountain, the roots and fruits on that mountain became sparse and devoid of vitality.
Then, terrified by the fear of famine and untimely death, the woman placed that man, whose hands and feet were mutilated, upon her shoulder and set out toward the edge of a village.
She wanders for alms through the streets, lanes, crossroads, and squares;
and when questioned, she says, "I am a devoted wife.
For this is the law of the world: whatever woman is devoted to her husband is honored in the world.
Wherever she entered, there she received alms;
in due course, she arrived at that royal capital,
and the people heard of it.
He was filled with supreme wonder;
some, overcome by curiosity, went outside to see her; and the multitude of city-dwellers found an opportunity to descend [upon the scene].
They reproached him, reviled him, and spoke ill of him, saying: "Sirs, this king loathes all women;
yet he does not see this virtuous, faithful wife wandering about with a man deprived of hands and feet carried upon her shoulder."
That account was reported to the king by the domestic priest; and the king, having perceived it, said:
"Let that woman be summoned; I wish to see her. She was summoned and seen by the king, and he spoke this verse:
Having eaten the flesh of my thighs and drunk my blood,
you now carry my headless trunk upon your shoulder, O devoted wife!
"Having cast me down a precipice for the sake of splitting a rock, you now carry my mangled corpse upon your shoulders, O devoted wife! Monks, what do you think?
The prince who was at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself;
the wife who was then was this very Devadatta.
Even then, he was ungrateful and failed to recognize what had been done for him.
Even now, he remains ungrateful and unthankful; hear again how he was ungrateful and unthankful.
[The Story of Viśvantara]
(Beginning with a previous birth of Devadatta:
Once upon a time, monks, in the royal capital of Viśvapuri, a king named Viśvāmitra reigned;

his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, tumults, and disturbances, and devoid of thieves, disease, and calamities.
It was abundant with rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo;
the righteous King Dharmarāja governed the kingdom according to the Dharma.

That king was faithful, auspicious, and of noble intention; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, and affectionate toward his subjects as if they were his own children.
At a later time, he played, enjoyed himself, and dallied with the queen;
while he was thus playing, enjoying himself, and dallying, after some time his wife became pregnant;
and after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.

A boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, joined eyebrows, a prominent nose, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
Upon his birth, a birth-festival was held, and his name was determined:
"What shall be the name of this boy?"
Thus it was said; the kinsmen replied, "This boy is the son of King Viśvāmitra;
therefore, let the name of this boy be Viśvantara."
The boy Viśvantara was entrusted to eight nurses:
two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
Raised by these eight nurses, he grew quickly on milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and various other most excellent nourishing foods.
He was like a lotus situated in a pond. When he had grown up, he was introduced to writing, arithmetic, calculation, and seal-engraving—
those skills which belong to anointed Kṣatriya kings.
For those who have attained the power and vigor of sovereignty over their territories and dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth,
there arise various crafts and occupations, such as: [skill] on the neck of an elephant, on the back of a horse, in chariots, in swordsmanship,
in archery, in retreat, in advance, in the handling of the goad, in the handling of the noose, in the handling of the lance, and in cutting, splitting, and piercing.

In the binding of the fist, the binding of the foot, the binding of the topknot, in shooting from a distance, shooting by sound, shooting at vital points, and shooting without missing the mark— he became accomplished in these five areas of firm striking.
Prince Viśvantara was faithful, auspicious, of virtuous intent, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, and compassionate.

That great-souled one, who loves righteousness, is affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of all, and a renouncer free from attachment, abides in the practice of great renunciation;
having heard of the extent of his generosity, seekers come to him even from a distance of a hundred yojanas.
He sent them all away with their desires completely fulfilled.
Then, on one occasion, the Bodhisattva [mounted] steeds that were illuminated by jewels, gold, silver, diamonds, beryl, musāragalva, and sapphire;
they were adorned with the finest heartwood of sandalwood, draped in the skins of lions, tigers, and leopards, and possessed a speed equal to the force of the wind.
Mounting an excellent chariot yoked with four horses that resounded with the tinkling of bells made of gold, silver, and jewels, he set out from the city toward the park;
then, certain brahmins learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas approached Viśvantara and said:
"Victory to you, O prince of the Kṣatriyas! he said, "In all the worlds you are indeed renowned as the giver of all things;
it behoves you to bestow this chariot as a gift upon the twice-born."

Having been addressed thus, the Bodhisattva Viśvantara quickly alighted from that chariot; with a heart joyful, contented, and gladdened, he pointed out that excellent chariot to those twice-born ones, saying:
"Just as this chariot has been given by me to the brahmins with supreme joy, so may I, having abandoned the three realms of existence, touch the highest enlightenment."

Thus it was said; and at a later time, having mounted his excellent elephant named Rājavardhana—who was white as a kunda flower, a water-lily, snow, or silver clouds; whose seven well-formed feet were firmly planted upon the ground; who moved with the graceful gait of Airāvaṇa;

and who was a visible manifestation of merit adorned with the marks of supreme natural beauty—he set forth, surrounded by contented servants, friends, attendants, and followers, like the moon encircled by the hosts of stars. When the time arrived...
At the time of spring, when the trees were in full bloom and the forest groves resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, jīvañjīvas, and vakas,
he went out to the pleasure gardens. Then, certain brahmins dispatched by his adversaries approached Prince Viśvantara in great haste and said:
"Victory to you, O prince of the kṣatriyas! he said, "And you,
who are renowned throughout the worlds of the Daityas and the gods as the Giver of All,
it behooves you to grant this excellent elephant to us here."
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva quickly alighted even from that excellent elephant, and with a mind joyful, contented, and delighted, he pointed out that excellent elephant to them and said:
"Just as I have given this elephant to the brahmins with supreme joy,
so shall I, having abandoned the three worlds, touch the highest awakening."

And King Viśvāmitra heard that his son, Viśvantara, had given the excellent elephant named Rājyavardhana to those who were employed by his enemies. Upon hearing this, King Viśvāmitra, provoked to anger, summoned Prince Viśvantara and said to him:
"Go, prince; you must not dwell within my domain.
Then Prince Viśvantara, having been abandoned by his father, reflected:
"By me, who have made a firm resolve for awakening and have donned the armor for the sake of benefiting all the world, this elephant has been given away."
Therefore, one living in the household should give gifts according to one's ability;
or, having resorted to a penance grove, one should observe the highest discipline.
"Therefore, having abandoned this home, I shall depart for the forest of asceticism.
However, when entreated, I cannot bring myself to speak the words, 'I will not give.
Having thus resolved, the Bodhisattva approached his wife Mādrī and informed her of this in detail.
Then, as soon as she heard this, Mādrī— her heart apprehensive at the prospect of being separated from her beloved— joined her palms and said to the Bodhisattva:
"Noble Son, if it is so, I too shall go to the forest of asceticism."

"Separated from my noble son, I am unable to sustain my life for even a moment. For how could it be? A woman separated from her husband would be like the sky without the moon, like the earth deprived of its crops, or like a lotus pond without water."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Inevitably, at the end, we must be separated; this is the very nature of the world."
And you, accustomed to excellent food, drink, beds, seats, and clothing, with a body most delicate,
must sleep upon the ground covered with grass and leaves in the forest of asceticism,
and roots and fruits shall be your sustenance.
One must walk upon ground strewn with *darbha* grass, stones, and thorns;
one must frequently observe the fast;
and one must present oneself before all people.
Guests must be honored with every effort;
moreover, I must certainly give gifts there according to my ability,
and you should not feel any regret regarding this.
"Let this matter be considered once more," he said;
Mādrī replied,
"Noble son, I shall follow the noble son to the best of my ability."
The Bodhisattva said:
"If this is so, you must remember this promise.
Then the Bodhisattva approached his father, prostrated with his head at his feet, and spoke.
"Forgive me, O Father, for whatever offense I have committed regarding the gift of the elephant, O Lord of Kings.
I shall depart from this city to the forest; let there be no depletion of your treasury, O King.
Thereupon, the king, distressed by the separation from his son, spoke with a throat choked and faltering with tears:
"Son, stay! Let your mind be turned away from this gift.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Even if the earth, together with its mountains, were to turn back..."
O lord of the earth, I would not turn my mind away from making this gift.
Having said this, he departed.
Then, accompanied by his sons, daughters, and wife, and filled with grief and longing, he went out from that city followed by thousands of citizens and countryfolk.
A certain man, hearing that sound of weeping and lamentation and seeing the great multitude of people departing through the city gate, spoke to another man:
"O man, what is this sound of weeping from the great multitude? He replied, "Do you not know?
From this city, the king has banished his own son, Sudaṃṣṭra."
"He who is firm in resolve and devoted to giving shall attain Nirvana"—
hearing this, the citizens gathered together and, approaching him as he set out for the forest with his wife and son, wept most piteously. Thus it is said.
Then the Bodhisattva approached the citizens who had come out from that city in the proper manner and said to them: "Return, sirs;
for even after a very long period of union with those dear to us, it must inevitably end."
It ends in separation;
for the company of kinsmen is like a tree by the roadside providing shelter for travelers;
the separation from loved ones is inevitable—how could it be otherwise?

"Thinking that for every living being in all worlds who is powerless, separation from loved ones inevitably occurs, you must, with every effort on this earth, establish a firm and unshakable resolve for the sake of peace. Thus he spoke. Then, seeing the Bodhisattva at a distance of thirty yojanas, a certain brahmin approached and said:
"O Kṣatriya prince, the city is about thirty *mātra*s from here;
it was because I had heard of your virtues that I came.
Therefore, you ought to make my labor fruitful by accepting this excellent chariot."
Then Mādrī, filled with indignation, spoke to that brahmin in harsh words:
"Aha! How cruel is this twice-born man's mind, that even in the forest he makes such a request of the prince!
Surely no compassion arises in him for the son of a king who has been deprived of royal splendor."
The Bodhisattva said:
"By no means, by no means should you revile the brahmin. Why?
Because, O Mādrī, if these seekers of wealth were not there to receive [the gift],"
"What man on earth could attain awakening without the gift of all things?
It is through the six perfections—beginning with generosity—that the Bodhisattvas of supreme virtue always and invariably attain unsurpassed omniscience. Thus it is said.
Then the Bodhisattva, with even greater joy, gave that horse-chariot to the brahmin and said:
"O twice-born one, by this gift of a chariot which washes away the stain of stinginess,
may I here [obtain] the great, stainless chariot made of Dharma, which has been set in motion by the true Great Sages."

Then Viśvantara, with a heart full of joy, having given even that excellent chariot to the brahmin, placed the young girl Kṛṣṇājinā upon his shoulder and Mādrī with the boy Jālini, and set out toward the forest of asceticism; in due course they reached the penance grove, whereupon Viśvantara, having undertaken a vow that brought delight to his own heart, dwelt there in that forest of asceticism.
Meanwhile, while Mādrī had gone out for roots and fruits, a certain brahmin approached Viśvantara from the ascetic grove and said:
"May you be victorious, O prince!
Deprived of my attendants, I wander about with only my daughters-in-law.
For that reason, you ought to give me these two children. Thus he spoke.
Thus addressed, the Bodhisattva Viśvantara became lost in thought for a moment regarding the renunciation of his beloved children;
then that brahmin said to the Bodhisattva Viśvantara:
"Since I am making this request of you..."
"So why is this being deliberated?
You are renowned everywhere upon the surface of the earth as one whose nature is compassion;
just as Śibi is constantly heard of, so you ought to act. Thus [he spoke].
Thus addressed, the Bodhisattva said to that brahmin:
"O Great Brahmin,
I have no hesitation whatsoever regarding the sacrifice of my own life."
How much less, then, could my mind be otherwise regarding the abandonment of my own son?
Moreover, O Great Brahmin,
these two children, raised in the forest and accustomed to comfort, have been abandoned by me;
how will they survive, being so compassionate and deprived of their mother?
"May no one say of me: 'The prince is utterly merciless; he abandons his two young children and not even himself. O virtuous Brahmin, lead me away.
Then that Brahmin—
He said to Viśvantara: "O prince, this is not worthy of you— one born of a great royal lineage,
whose fame is renowned throughout the entire earth, who is devoted to compassion and pity for all living beings, and who is a scent-elephant of generosity, honor, and hospitality."

For one who honors ascetics, brahmins, guests, and elders; who provides for the wretched, beggars, the helpless, and the poor; who fulfills all desires and whose very sight is never in vain—should my arrival ever be fruitless, or my journey through the road in vain, or my sight of him useless?
That hope is fruitless, or rather, the one who hoped has long been waiting in his heart;
therefore, let there be an end to this mental chariot of my resolve, which has been turned back by the denial of your words.
For what reason, then, should you not dismiss me with my desire fulfilled?
She whose garment is the ocean, whose eyes reach to the ends of the planets, and whose head is adorned by the full breasts of the best of mountains;
"Having searched the earth with its cities and towns,
there is no one equal to you in the power of giving, O Sudanṣṭra. Having heard these words of the brahmin, the Bodhisattva Viśvantara, overwhelmed by affection for his son, fell into this reflection:
If I were to give my two sons to the brahmin,
both Mādrī and I would suffer the pain born of separation from our children.
If I do not give this to him, I shall be one who has broken his vow;
and this Brahmin, having lost all hope, will depart just as he came.
"Granted, I shall suffer grief on this earth due to the separation from my son;
however, I shall never be one whose promise is broken or whose vow is shattered.
Then, having made his resolve regarding the renunciation of his beloved son, the Bodhisattva Viśvantara said: "O sir, this..."
"The world is sinking in a terrifying ocean of suffering; to rescue those who are deeply distressed, I shall construct a raft of the Path through hundreds of most difficult tasks.
Having said this, his face filled with pure water, he spoke with a countenance free from anger.
With eyes filled with the water of tears, he gave the two children to that brahmin and said:
"May I obtain the vast fruit of this gift of my children."
"By this merit, may I ferry the world across the ocean of saṃsāra.
As soon as those two young children had been given away, this earth shook in six ways;
then, because of that earthquake, the ascetics dwelling in that forest were terrified and said to one another:
"What is the cause of this most terrible trembling of the earth?
It must be clearly understood here whose power it is that is such. Thus spoke a certain aged ascetic there, of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, who was skilled in the knowledge of omens.
He informed those sages of this matter:
"Surely my two young sons, who delight in the penance grove, subsist on fruits and water, and are beautiful and pleasing to the eye."
"For the sake of liberating the world afflicted by suffering,

Viśvantara renounces that which makes the earth tremble. Then, perceiving their father’s intention toward such total renunciation, those two young children, weeping most piteously, fell at the feet of Viśvantara and, joining their palms in reverence, said:
"Be gracious, father; do not abandon us both. Deprived of our teacher, where shall we go now?
"Ambā has departed, father, and you ought to give us [to the teacher]."
"As soon as we see her, you will give her to us.
Then the Bodhisattva, overwhelmed with affection and with eyes clouded by tears, abandoned those two young children and said: "My little sons..."
"My heart is not unaffectionate, nor is it devoid of compassion or cruelty;
rather, for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, I renounce [my own happiness] because I perceive its virtues.
Thus, having myself attained supreme, auspicious awakening, I shall [act].
"May I, without any support, ferry across the world that has fallen into the ocean of suffering.
Then, those two young children, perceiving their father’s resolve to renounce them, fell at his feet with words faltering from compassion and distress; joining their palms in reverence, they said:
"If such is your determination, then by our word you [must not go]."
"O father, our mother must be told; O mother, you ought to forgive us.
And furthermore, father, whatever offense we have committed against our guru because of our childish nature toward you—
If an unpleasant word has been uttered or something else spoken,
and the service rendered has not been fully completed,
that should indeed be forgiven as a fault of a fool.

Having spoken thus, they saluted their father, circumambulated him three times, and—eager for the words of their teacher, turning back again and again with eyes overflowing with tears—they departed from that hermitage. Then the Bodhisattva, his heart overwhelmed by those most piteous words of the young children, set his mind upon awakening and entered a leaf-hut in the penance grove. As soon as the two young children had departed, this great trichiliocosm world-system shook in six ways.
And with many thousands of deities, the atmosphere was filled with cries of "Alas! Alas! [exclaiming]:
"Oh, the greatness of this gift! Oh, indeed, what firm resolve he possesses, that having abandoned these two infant sons, his mind does not waver! Thus they spoke.
At that time, Mādrī, having gathered roots and fruits, set out toward the hermitage;
due to that great earthquake, she hurried toward the site of the hermitage;
then a certain deity, assuming the form of a lion, stood blocking the path.
"Lest Mādrī should create an obstacle for the Bodhisattva, who has exerted himself to liberate all sentient beings, in his practice of the perfection of generosity"—
thereupon, Mādrī said to that queen of deer,
"O playful queen of deer!"
"Why do you stand here obstructing me?
Since I am certainly a devoted wife,
move quickly out of my path!"
Moreover,
you too are the wife of a king of beasts, and I am the wife of a lion among kings.
"By right you are my sister, O queen of deer; give me passage.
When she had been addressed thus, that deity who had assumed the form of a lion moved away from the path.

Then Mādrī, perceiving that these were inauspicious omens, reflected for a moment: "From the way this sound of weeping is heard in the sky, and from the way the cries of distress of the forest-dwelling beings are heard, it is clear that some misfortune will befall the hermitage. And she said:
From the way my eye throbs and the way the bird cries,
it is certain that those two children have been abandoned, for such is the anxious thought in my mind.
"Just as this earth trembles and my heart shakes,
so too do my limbs fail me now that those two children have been clearly abandoned.
Thinking thus of hundreds of thousands of misfortunes, she went to the hermitage.
Having entered the hermitage, she looked about in agitation;
she did not see her two sons.
Then, with a distressed heart and trembling, she reflected, following the tracks of their footsteps:
In this place, Prince Jālinī frequently played with his sister and young deer;
these were the sand-castles built by the two of them.
"These are their toys,
yet I do not see them;
or perhaps, thinking 'Mother is not seen,' they have entered the leaf-hut and are lying down"— thus her heart was overwhelmed with apprehension.
Eager to see her son, she set aside the roots and fruits in a secluded spot, and with eyes overflowing with tears, she fell at her husband’s feet and asked:
"Noble Lord, where have the young children gone?
Viśvantara replied:
"A brahmin has approached me with great devotion; I have given those two boys to him. You ought to grant your permission.
When she had spoken thus, Mādrī fell to the ground like a doe pierced by a poisoned arrow.
Like a fish pulled from its watery abode, she wallowed and rolled upon the ground; like a female osprey whose young has been snatched away, she wailed most piteously;
like a cow that has lost her calf, she lamented with various lowing cries. And she said:
Their faces were like young lotuses,
their hands as delicate as lotus petals;
though they had never experienced suffering, they were pained by the suffering [of others].
To what destination have my two sons gone?
How is it that today my two little sons, who delighted in the hermitage with the fawns and were as gentle as fawns themselves with eyes like those of deer, are not here?
As he departed, they did not come under his control;
with eyes overflowing with tears, crying out piteously and deeply distressed, they were full of sorrow.
And today my two fine horses have been slain;
the wretched people live in misery.
Those two, who grew up in my lap, feeding on roots, flowers, and fruits,
were always patient, gentle, and devoted to their teacher.
For my two sons are indeed suffering greatly.
Deprived of their kinsmen and mother, and suddenly cast out by their relatives,
they approached wicked and evil people.
For my two sons are indeed suffering greatly.
Whose control will those two ever come under, their very selves perpetually overcome by hunger and thirst,
and tormented by affliction and suffering?
Of one who will certainly fall into the state of a servant.
Surely some very cruel and evil karma was committed by me here in another birth,
whereby living beings were separated from hundreds of their loved ones.
Because of which I low like a cow that has lost her calf.
By that word of truth through which my mind has always attained equanimity toward all sentient beings,
by that word of truth, [may it be so] for my two sons.
"May he be released from his state of servitude!

Then Mādrī, seeing those trees which had been planted and nurtured by her two young children now covered with new sprouts, embraced them in agitation and said: "O trees watered by the pitchers of my young sons!"
With drops of tears falling from their sprouts,
the young trees seem to weep like sentient beings,
like infants deprived of their breasts.
Furthermore, seeing those two young children playing with the fawns of the hermitage dwellers, he spoke these words in a voice faltering with compassion and distress:
"This is indeed another great sorrow,
that these fawns wander about."
Eager to see her companions and longing to search for them at their usual places,
she followed the path by which those two young children had gone; and seeing their crooked footprints here and there, she was struck by intense grief.
He spoke again:
"O cruel one, O best of the twice-born! You have surely led us to our downfall, moving as if lingering at every step, yet at times proceeding with a swift gait."
With throats choked by sobbing and tears, with beautiful lower lips trembling,
those two of mine have eyes as restless as those of a deer.
"How did you go with such tender feet?
Then, seeing her thus lamenting, the Bodhisattva, instructing her in many ways through various teachings connected with impermanence, said:
"It was not out of pride nor out of hatred that I abandoned my two children."
However, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, those two sons, though so difficult to abandon, were renounced.
"Having abandoned even their own sons and wives, which are most difficult to renounce, great beings attain supreme enlightenment like Śibi. Thus,
from the basis of renunciation, O Mādrī, those two sons [were born].
"These two, which are difficult to abandon, have been renounced for the sake of liberating the world.
I would give away my own wife, my vehicle, and all my wealth to everyone; this is my resolve. Thus he spoke.
Then Mādrī, summoning her courage, said to the Bodhisattva with her mind:
"I shall not create an obstacle for you; let not your thought turn otherwise.
If you wish to give me as well, bestow me upon him without hesitation."
"Moreover, O steadfast one, quickly attain that goal for which you abandon your own kin, overwhelmed by affection; for by crossing over existence, you shall deliver the world. Thus [he spoke].

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having learned of that most wonderful and exceedingly difficult resolve of Mādrī and the Bodhisattva, surrounded by the hosts of the Thirty-three, approached that hermitage through the air above. Illuminating that forest with a magnificent radiance, he addressed the Bodhisattva while remaining in the expanse of the sky: "In this world of fools, whose minds are agitated by the grasp of evil thoughts..."
"Since your mind is unattached to worldly enjoyments and you have been bound by the snares of sons, you alone, being free from attachment, renounce those children who cause affection;
you will surely attain the secure, peaceful, stainless, and dustless state. Thus [he spoke].
Having thus encouraged the Bodhisattva, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, reflected:
"He is alone and, being without an attendant, will fall into exhaustion;
what if I were now to request this [maiden] from him?"

Then, departing from the presence of the Bodhisattva and assuming the guise of a brahmin, he spoke again to the Bodhisattva: "Give me this woman, whose limbs are entirely faultless, who is devoted to her husband and faithful to him, who brings honor to her family, and who shall share in the status of my servant. Thus he said.
Then Mādrī, filled with indignation, said to the brahmin:
"You are shameless and greedy; you are the lowest of brahmins, since you desire me, a devoted wife who is intent upon the true dharma. Thus she spoke.
Then the Bodhisattva Viśvantara, his heart overwhelmed with compassion, began to look at Mādrī;
thereupon Mādrī said to the Bodhisattva Viśvantara,
"I do not grieve for myself, nor do I have any concern for my own self."
"Just as I grieve for you, how will you be alone?
Then the Bodhisattva said to Mādrī:
"O Mādrī, I am not to be grieved for here on this earth."
"Examine this imperishable state free from sorrow;
follow this twice-born man, O Viśoka,
while I shall go to the hermitage in the deer-sanctuary."
Having understood this, with a mind thrilled, satisfied, and joyful, he reflected:
"In this forest, this will be my final act of giving;
and by relinquishing Mādrī, I shall become free from worldly attachments."
Having understood this, he took Mādrī by the hand and said to that brahmin:
"O best of the twice-born, accept this wife of mine, who is devoted to her husband, intent on service, of virtuous conduct, and sweet-spoken."
Then, as he was abandoning the wife of Sudaṃṣṭra out of a desire for enlightenment,
the entire earth shook in six ways, like a boat upon the water.
Then Mādrī, her voice faltering as it was choked with tears, having fallen under the power of the brahmin and being deprived of husband, sons, and daughter, spoke these words:
"What ignoble deed did I commit in previous births,
because of which I cry out in this lonely forest like a cow that has lost its calf?"
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having made his brahmin disguise disappear and standing in his own form, said to Mādrī:
"I am not a brahmin, O blessed lady, nor am I a mere mortal;
for I am Śakra, the lord of the gods, the destroyer of the asuras."
"I am pleased with this supreme discipline of yours;
therefore, tell me what boon you desire from me here.
Then Mādrī, her mind filled with joy by those words, bowed to Śakra and said:
"O Thousand-eyed One, release my two sons from their state of servitude,
and let them reach the presence of the Grandfather, O Lord of the Thirty-three!
Having said, "So be it," Mahendra entered the hermitage once more and approached the Bodhisattva.
Taking Mādrī by his left hand, he said to the Bodhisattva:
"I give this Mādrī to you as a female attendant;
she must not be given to anyone else, for the betrayal of a trust is contemptible."

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, so utterly deluded the man who had taken charge of the young boy that, suspecting it was another city, he returned to that very same city. When the ministers saw those two young boys for sale, they informed the king:
"O King, these two sons of yours are here in this best of cities with a brahmin."
"And that most cruel man sells Jālin and Kṛṣṇā as well!
Having heard this, the king, his mind bewildered, said quickly: "Show me the two princes at once!"
The women staying in the inner apartments raised a cry, and the citizens quickly came into the presence of the king.
When another minister brought the two grandsons before the king, the monarch gazed upon them as they were presented to him;
their voices were faint, their bodies emaciated, and their limbs smeared with filth.
He suddenly fell from the lion-throne to the surface of the earth; the citizens, the hosts of ministers, and the women all cried out in lamentation.
Then the king addressed his ministers:
"Bring that Sulocana here quickly, together with his wife— his mind remains devoted to acts of giving even while dwelling in the forest."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, bowed to the Bodhisattva and returned to his own abode.

Later, after King Viśvāmitra had passed away, he went together with the brahmins, ministers, and the people of the city and countryside to that hermitage. Having requested the Bodhisattva, he brought him back to his own city and established him on the throne.
Thereupon, King Viśvantara became a giver of all things.

Having bestowed various kinds of gifts upon ascetics, brahmins, beggars, friends, relatives, kinsmen, dependents, and the destitute, and having performed meritorious deeds, he spoke this verse while aspiring for enlightenment: "A confident person, desiring awakening, should give gifts to a kṣatriya, a brahmin, a vaiśya, a śūdra, and even to a caṇḍāla or a pukkaśa."
Gold, fine gold, cattle, horses, jewels, and earrings.
Likewise, he should give a slave or a laborer to those who are endowed with virtuous conduct.
"By renouncing their children and wives with a liberated mind, men attain purity in this world and in the next.
When King Viśvāmitra, for the sake of Viśvaṃtara, gave abundant wealth to the brahmin Jujjuka, he became one of vast fortune; of him—
Friends, relatives, kinsmen, and companions approached and said,
"Whatever splendor you possess has come to Prince Viśvantara";
he replied:
"What has been done for me by Viśvantara? I am born of the highest caste;
I am worthy of offerings from the world; it is because of this that enjoyments come to me."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks?
That prince named Viśvantara was none other than myself at that time and on that occasion."
He who was that Jujjuka was none other than this Devadatta at that time and on that occasion;
even then he was ungrateful and unappreciative,
and even now he is ungrateful and unappreciative.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall be grateful and appreciative; we will not let even a small favor done for us go to waste, much less a great one.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Story of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove at Kalandakanivāpa.
Now at that time, there lived in Campā a householder named Potalaka.
He was wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, with vast and extensive possessions, endowed with wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa;
he took a wife from a family of equal status,
and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.

While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, in the course of time his wife became pregnant. She was attended to with cold appliances in the cold season and warm appliances in the warm season, and provided with food prescribed by physicians that was neither too bitter, nor too sour, nor too salty, nor too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent— being entirely free from the qualities of bitterness, acidity, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency.
Her body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, she moved like an apsaras wandering in the Nandana grove, descending from couch to couch and from seat to seat until reaching the ground below;
and for as long as it took for the fetus to reach maturity, she did not hear anything unpleasant.
At that time, the householder Potalaka had gone to Rājagṛha on some business.
After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth under the constellation Śravaṇā;
a boy was born, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold;
on the undersides of his two soles, hairs four finger-breadths long grew, the color of gold.
When the personal servant of the householder Potalaka had gone very quickly to Rājagṛha, he said to the householder Potalaka:
"Householder, congratulations! A son has been born to you."
Filled with joy and gladness, he asked again, "What do you say, householder? A son has been born to you?
He asked again, "What do you say?
Then this thought occurred to that man: "Why does this householder ask again and again?"
Realizing, "He wishes to make me talk," he remained silent;
the householder said:
"O man, you have failed."
"If even a hundred words had been uttered by you, my mouth would have been filled with gold for you";
then the householder Potalaka filled that man's mouth with gold three times.

It was filled, and the treasurer was instructed: "Give twenty crores of gold for the price of the boy's sweetmeat. The householder Potalaka, with a joyful mind, approached the king and said, "Your Majesty, a son has been born to me.
The king replied:
"Excellent! I shall give him as a gift in Campā a common herd of seven elephants.
Having addressed King Bimbisāra in this way, the householder Potalaka returned to Campā.
Then the householder’s kinsmen, having celebrated the birth festival for twenty-one days— three weeks— established the boy's name, asking, "What shall the child's name be? Others said,
"This boy was born under the asterism Śravaṇā."
At his birth, his father gave twenty crores of gold as the price for the sweetmeat;
therefore, let the boy's name be Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa.
Thus, the name Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa was established for him.
The boy Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa was entrusted to eight nurses:
two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
Raised by these eight nurses, he grew rapidly on milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various excellent nourishments.
Like a lotus situated in a pond, when he had grown up, he was introduced to writing, arithmetic, calculation, and finger-reckoning;

to the extraction [of roots], deposits, and consignments; and to the examination of goods, the examination of garments, the examination of gems, the examination of timber, the examination of elephants, the examination of horses, the examination of young men, and the examination of young women.
