Thus, he became proficient in the eight examinations, an expounder, a scholar, and one of swift conduct.
Having heard of his great merit and majesty, many girls of equal lineage were given to him.
His father had three dwelling-houses constructed for him: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season.
Three pleasure gardens were laid out: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rains;

three harems were established: the senior, the middle, and the junior; and he, having gone to the upper terrace of the palace, played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself with musical instruments performed by women alone.
Every day, five hundred pots of cooked food were prepared for him to eat;
yet, incited by Devadatta, Ajātaśatru sought to take the life of his father, King Bimbisāra, but failed in his attempt.
Devadatta instigated Prince Ajātaśatru, saying:
"Prince, when gray hair has appeared on the heads of all kings, then [the throne] belongs to the eldest prince."
"Having established [his sons] in sovereignty, lordship, and dominion, he goes forth into homelessness;
yet your father’s hair has turned to a third color,
and nevertheless, being still intent upon sensual pleasures, he does not attain tranquility."
Ajātaśatru said,
"What shall I do for him?
Devadatta replied, "Exert your prowess!"
For those driven by desire, there is nothing that cannot be done.
King Bimbisāra, having set aside a portion of the cream of ghee for the Blessed One who wished to drink it after his meal of ghee, set out for the Bamboo Grove;
he was seen by Ajātaśatru.
He threw a golden coin;
the king was skilled at sound,
and by it he broke the vessel containing the gruel.
The king turned back from that very spot.
Desiring to convert Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, the Buddha sent Maudgalyāyana to him.
He appears to him within the orb of the sun and speaks to him of the Buddha;
meanwhile, there is nothing whatsoever that is unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Blessed Buddhas. In that regard:
The Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Maudgalyāyana, Ajātaśatru, being ensnared by an evil friend, has caused the Tathāgata’s alms-food to be ruined.
Go to Campā and bring back alms-food from the son of Potalaka."

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the Blessed One. Having entered into such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he vanished from Rājagṛha and appeared in Campā before Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, who was devoted to the sun.
Day after day, Śroṇa would rise early in the morning and pay homage to the sun.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana descended by means of his supernatural power, having split the solar disk;
then Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, seeing this, was struck with great wonder, thinking:
"I am actually beholding the sun in its own form!"
And having seen it, he spoke this verse:
"Who is this that, having pierced the sun, now approaches his own abode from the surface of the earth with such equal swiftness?"
"Could this be the sun, or the Giver of Wealth, or the moon, or perhaps Śakra, the lord of the gods, who has descended here all at once?
Thus the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having discerned his mind with his own mind, spoke this verse: (SBV II 137)
I am not the sun with its thousand blazing rays, nor am I the lord of the stars;
I am neither Vaiśravaṇa, nor am I the Blessed Lord Īśvara of firm vows.
Know me to be the son of the Buddha, whose mind is peaceful and whose splendor is radiant.
"I have approached you for the sake of alms; furthermore, I have need of a morsel of food.
Śroṇa replied, "Are you a sage?"
He speaks this verse:
"Just as a mustard seed might reach Mount Meru, the golden mountain,
or as a firefly on the earth might become equal to the sun when it has reached the sun."

"Just as the ocean, though rich with jewels, might here become a mere cow's footprint when it meets [the sea], so too, having encountered the Buddha, the Teacher’s own son, me— the Guru, the Supreme among Men— know this. Thus spoke Śroṇa.
By this very inference, we indeed clearly understand your leader to be one who possesses great ascetic power.
"Command me, what is the purpose of your visit?
He replied,
"Please offer almsfood to the Blessed One."
"Who is this Blessed One?

Householder’s son, there is a śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who went forth from the Śākya clan, shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and out of perfect faith left the household life for homelessness; he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
This very son of a householder was named Buddha;
upon hearing that sound "Buddha"—a name he had never heard before—his hair stood on end with thrill.
With a mind full of faith, he offered that very five-hundred-portioned meal to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa filled his alms-bowl with food of extraordinary fragrance, which Mahāmaudgalyāyana took back to the Buddha.

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having taken the alms-food from him, entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he vanished from Campā and reappeared in Rājagṛha.
In the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place; he offered almsfood to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One began to eat.
King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha, taking a second vessel of cooked rice, approached the presence of the Blessed One;
there he saw the entire Bamboo Grove filled with various kinds of [offerings].
It was filled with the fragrant scent of food;
he reflected, "Surely Śakra, the lord of the gods, and other deities have brought alms-food for the Blessed One,
since this Bamboo Grove is suffused with such various kinds of fragrant food-scent."
Having understood this, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, was alms-food offered to the Blessed One by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, or by other deities,
such that the Bamboo Grove is filled with various kinds of fragrant scents from food?"
The Blessed One said:
"Great King, he was not brought here by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, nor by any other deities;
rather, in your own realm at Campā, a meal of five hundred portions is prepared day after day for the son of Potalaka."
Hearing that he had been brought there by the monk Maudgalyāyana and that the Blessed One had begun to speak his praises, a desire to see him arose within him.
The Blessed One, knowing his thoughts with his own mind, said:
"O Great King, that being is one of great merit and power;
do not give him an order,
lest your own store of merit be exhausted."
"Nevertheless, Great King, please partake of the remnants in the bowl.
He replied,
"Venerable sir, I am a king."
"Venerable sir, I am an anointed kṣatriya;
never before have I consumed the remnants from anyone's bowl.
However, by the very nature of things, the Blessed One is my father."
"If the Blessed One commands it, then I shall eat," he said, and began to eat.
The Blessed One said:
"Great King, have you ever before eaten food and drink of such a kind?
The king replied:
"Venerable Sir, this man is an elder in the royal family and has now become king; he has never before tasted such food and drink.
That being who partakes of such food and drink is a great king of vast merit and majesty."
King Bimbisāra desired to see Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed from the presence of the Blessed One;
he gave an order to his ministers:
"Prepare the fourfold army, sirs;
I shall go to Campā. For what purpose? To see the son of Potalaka."
"He is a resident of the King's domain;
let him be summoned right here; he is a being of great merit and renown."
"His command must not be given;
Your Majesty, we shall act in such a way that we do not give him our command."
"He will come;
act in this manner. They then sent a letter to Campā.
"Gentlemen, beautify the city; provide fodder, equipment, and seats;
the king will arrive."
Having heard this, they were highly pleased; a further letter was sent: "Sirs, the king will not come."
"But the prince is coming," they said;
and they were terrified, thinking, "The prince is fierce; perhaps when he arrives, he will cause us harm."
It was written again:
"Neither the king comes, nor does the prince."
"Moreover, you must dam the Ganges in such a way that it flows upstream.
Hearing this, the citizens residing in Campā assembled and said, "Sirs, surely the king wishes to punish us."
Thinking, "By whom was this written? they sent a letter to the ministers for this purpose; and having read it, they replied to them truthfully:
"Sirs, this is the ultimate truth."
The king does not come; nor does the prince;
nor is there any purpose in binding the Ganges.
"Rather, Your Majesty desires to see the son of Potalaka";
they then dispatched a messenger.
He also explained it in exactly this way;
then they went together into the presence of the householder Potalaka and said,
"Householder, the King wishes to see Śroṇa Koṭiviṃśa."
"Send [a message] to our ministers exactly as it was instructed;
even by the secret agent, that very same matter has been reported.
He said:
"Gentlemen, I will not send him;
even if one were to bind my share with lumps of gold, I would still not send him," he said;
they replied:
“Householder, even if it be so, nevertheless the later generation must be shown compassion.
He replied, “Sirs, if it be so, I grant permission on this condition.”
"If even your sons go along with Śroṇa," they said; he replied,
"Householder, let it be so."
"Go, sirs!
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went to Rājagṛha to visit Bimbisāra. Then the householder Potalaka approached Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
Having approached Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, he said this to him:
"Son, these townspeople are saying such-and-such. He replied:
"Father, if it is so, I shall go.
"Son, surely that king wishes to see the golden-colored hairs on your feet;
you must not lift up your feet to show them to him."
Kings are prone to anger at inappropriate occasions;
they may bring you misfortune.
Here is a pearl necklace.
"Having placed this at the king's feet, having prostrated, and having sat down cross-legged before him,
he will then see the body hairs.
Then the householder Potalaka reflected:
By which vehicle shall I send Śroṇa?
By an elephant-vehicle or by a horse-vehicle?
"By chariot or by boat?
Then this thought occurred to him:
"A boat-vehicle is best for them;
I shall send them by boat," he thought;
accordingly, he had a boat-bridge constructed across the river Gaṅgā.
There, a magnificent garden was constructed, endowed with various flowers and fruits, resounding with the warbling of birds such as swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos;
various musical instruments were set up,
and women adorned with diverse ornaments were stationed there.
Thus, sent forth by way of the water with such magnificence,
he arrived in due course near Rājagṛha;
King Bimbisāra heard that the son of Potalaka was coming.
Therefore, having dug a trench from Rājagṛha as far as the river Gaṅgā and filled it, he drew the boat through its middle;
and that city of Rājagṛha was prepared, cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel, and sprinkled with sandalwood water.
It was adorned with fragrant incense burners, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, with banners and flags raised aloft, and strewn with various flowers—
delightful like the Nandana grove of the gods;
he was led into the city of Rājagṛha with such splendor.
Then, having placed a pearl necklace at the feet of the king as he sat upon his lion throne,
and having bowed his head in prostration,
he sat down before him with his legs crossed in the lotus posture.
Seeing the golden-colored hairs on the soles of his feet, the king was struck with great wonder, exclaiming:
"Oh, how truly one of great merit and power is Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa!
Then Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa and King Bimbisāra went together to the Bamboo Grove in order to see the Buddha.
Having seen him, he said:
"Śroṇa, have you seen the Blessed One?
"No, Your Majesty. "Come, let us go."
He asked, "Your Majesty, does the Blessed One travel by vehicle, or rather on foot? The king replied:
"He has gone forth as a monk;
what need has he for a vehicle?
he said. To this, the other replied:
"Your Majesty, if that is so, I too shall go on foot alone," he said,
and set out on foot.
His attendants spread garments upon the ground for him.
He asked:
"Does the Blessed One walk upon what has been spread out, or rather upon what has not been spread out?"
Thus they said: "By one who has not spread [a seat]";
he replied:
"Bring garments."
"I too shall go upon what is not spread out";
the attendants removed the cloths,
but non-human beings spread them out.
He said: "Sirs, have you been forbidden by me?
They replied:
"O King, they were forbidden; by whom, then, were they spread out again?
"O King, you are one of great power through merit."
"They have been spread out by non-human beings. With this intention, he uttered these words: "May the non-humans remove the garments!
They removed them.
He placed his foot upon the earth;
the earth shook in six ways,
and this great earth trembled.
It trembles,
it trembles greatly;
it wavers, it wavers greatly, it wavers intensely.
The eastern quarter rises,
while the western sinks;
the western rises.
The east sinks down; the south rises up; the north sinks down.
The north rises, the south sinks; the edge rises, the center sinks.
The middle sank down; the middle rose up, and the ends sank down.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
Monks, from ninety-one eons ago until now, the son of Potalaka has never placed his foot upon the ground that was not covered with a rug;
today he has placed it down out of reverence for the Dharma,
and not because his merit is exhausted.
"Therefore, this earthquake of sixfold movement has occurred.
Then Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, gave such a teaching on the Dharma that penetrates the Four Noble Truths;
upon hearing it, Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose with twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the Truth, he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and may I lead the holy life under the Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"Indeed, householder’s son, neither Tathāgatas nor the disciples of the Tathāgata ordain or grant full admission to a noble son who has not been permitted by his mother and father.
Go and look after your parents."
The king said: "Venerable sir, I am the master of all legal matters; by my own will and in accordance with the law, this son belongs to me alone;
I grant him permission."
"May the Blessed One ordain me as he pleases.
Then the Blessed One addressed him with the "Come, monk" formula: "Come, monk, lead the holy life.
Immediately upon the conclusion of those words, his head became shaven.

Clad in the saṅghāṭī robe, with bowl and water-pot held in his hands, his hair and beard shorn seven days prior, he stood with the deportment of a monk who had been ordained for a hundred years. And regarding this, it is said: "Come," was the word spoken by the Tathāgata to him.
With his head shaven and his body wrapped in the saṅghāṭī robe,
his senses immediately became tranquil; thus he stood,
clothed in the very desire for the Buddha.
The group of six began to mock that, saying,
"This one has already finished his alms-food."
"What special distinction will he attain in this teaching, which is so exclusively devoted to practice?
Thus insulted by them, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, which concentration conducive to yoga was taught by the Blessed One for a monk who is intent on solitude?
"Venerable Śroṇa, the Blessed One said that if one walks in the walking posture, the concentration will remain undispelled and endure for a long time.
Therefore, having gone to the Śītavana cemetery, he established himself in the walking posture."

There, the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa dwelt at Rājagṛha in the Śītavana cemetery, applying himself with diligence, constancy, and discernment to the practice of yoga in the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening.
Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa gave himself over to rigorous ascetic practices. [The Example of the Lute]
Then, while the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was alone, in seclusion, and in retreat, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Of all the disciples of the Blessed One who dwell with aroused energy,
I am indeed one among them."
And yet, my mind is not liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
moreover, I possess abundant wealth among my kinsmen;
what if I were to sit down and enjoy sensual pleasures?
"I shall give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the thought in the mind of the venerable Śroṇa, addressed a certain monk:
"Come, monk; go to where Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa is.
Having approached him, speak thus to Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa: 'The Teacher, Śroṇa, calls for you.'"
"So be it, Venerable Sir," that monk replied to the Blessed One and approached the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa.
Having approached him, he said this to the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa: "The Teacher, venerable Śroṇa, calls for you."
"So be it, venerable sir," the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa replied to that monk. Having done so, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
The Blessed One then said this to the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa:
"Śroṇa, did not such a reflection arise in your mind while you were alone, in seclusion, and in retreat:
'Of all the disciples of the Blessed One who dwell with energy aroused,
I am one of them'?"
And yet, my mind is not liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
moreover, there exist abundant riches among my kinsmen.
"What if I were to sit down, enjoy sensual pleasures, give gifts, and perform meritorious deeds?"
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa:
"The Blessed One knows my mind with his own mind.
Realizing this, he became afraid, terrified, and agitated, and with the hair on his body standing on end, he said this to the Blessed One:
"So be it, Venerable One.
In that case, Śroṇa, I shall ask you a question;
answer it as you see fit."
"What do you think, Śroṇa? Were you formerly, while still a householder, skilled in the sound of the strings of the lute?
"It is true, Venerable Sir, that formerly, while still a householder, I was skilled in the sound of the strings of the lute."
What do you think, Śroṇa?
At the time when the strings of a lute are too tightly stretched, would it [sound] at that time?
“Is the lute of beautiful sound?
Or of pleasing sound, or possessed of tone, or functional?
“No, Venerable Sir.”
At what time, when the strings of a lute are too loose, would that lute at that time produce a pleasant sound,
or a charming sound, or a melodic sound, or be fit for performance?
"No, Venerable Sir."

Furthermore, at what time, when the strings of the lute are neither too tight nor too loose, but are properly tuned along with their qualities— at that time, would the lute not indeed produce a beautiful sound,
a pleasing sound, a resonant sound, or one that is serviceable for performance?
"So it is, Venerable Sir;
even so, Śroṇa, energy that is over-exerted leads to restlessness,
and a mind that is overly slackened leads to indolence."
Therefore, Śroṇa, you should practice equanimity;
yet do not be conceited because of it, and do not be negligent regarding it.
And grasp that sign;

by dwelling in this dwelling, Śroṇa, before long, through the destruction of the outflows, you will realize for yourself through direct knowledge in this very life the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, you will declare: "Birth is exhausted for me."
"The holy life has been lived;
what was to be done has been accomplished;
I know no further state of existence beyond this."

Then the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, having rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had spoken, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the presence of the Blessed One. Following the advice of the Buddha, in a short time he became an arhat.
Then the Venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, having been instructed by the Blessed One with this lute-like instruction, dwelt alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute,
he attained that goal for the sake of which sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having properly donned [the robes] with faith, they go forth from the home to the homeless state;
having realized for themselves through direct knowledge and attained that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life in this very life, they declare:
"Birth is exhausted for me."
"The holy life has been lived;
what was to be done has been accomplished;
I know no further state of existence beyond this."
The Venerable One realized [the truth] and became an Arhat, his mind perfectly liberated.
Then, as the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had attained Arhatship and was experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation, this thought occurred to him:
"Now is the time for me to go to see the Blessed One."
"For the sake of attending upon [the Blessed One]";

then, in the evening, the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa rose from his seclusion and approached where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa sat to one side, he said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir,
regarding that monk who is an Arhat, whose taints are exhausted, who has accomplished his task, completed what was to be done, and laid down the burden— "
Having attained his own goal, with the fetters of existence completely exhausted, and with his mind rightly liberated through perfect knowledge, at that time he becomes intent upon six points;
he becomes intent upon renunciation.
He becomes resolved in his mind upon the exhaustion of craving, the exhaustion of clinging, and non-delusion.
Indeed, Venerable Sir, it may happen that some person here possesses merely a measure of faith, thinking: "Ah, this venerable one, by relying on this, is resolved upon renunciation."

Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way: "Venerable sir, because of the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion, he has become one who is intent upon renunciation.
For it might be that some person here thinks, "Ah, this venerable one, relying merely on moral discipline, is intent upon non-affliction"; yet indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
"Venerable sir, through the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion, one becomes intent upon the state that is free from affliction.
It may well be, venerable sir, that some person here thinks: 'Alas, this venerable one is merely seeking gain, honor, and fame, yet he is intent upon seclusion.'"
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way;

for, Venerable Sir, through the destruction of passion, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion, one becomes resolved in the mind upon the destruction of craving, the destruction of grasping, and the non-forgetfulness [of the Dharma]; such, Venerable Sir, is the monk who is an Arhat.

At that time, one whose outflows are exhausted, who has accomplished what was to be done, who has laid down the burden, who has attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed, and whose mind is well-liberated through right knowledge, becomes intent upon these six points: "Venerable sir, that monk who is a trainee (śaikṣa) and has not yet reached the goal dwells frequently in a state of aspiring for the supreme security of Nirvana."
At that time, he becomes endowed with the virtues of one in training and with the faculties of one in training;

at a later time, through the destruction of the outflows, he realizes for himself in this very life, by his own direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, attains it, and declares:
"Birth is exhausted for me."
"The holy life has been lived;
what was to be done has been accomplished;
I know no further state of existence beyond this."
At that time, he becomes endowed with the precepts of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and with the faculties of one beyond training;
just as, for example, a small, young, ignorant infant lying on its back at that time is endowed with the precepts of an infant and with the faculties of an infant,
so too, at another time, through the process of growth, he [becomes endowed with those of an adult].
Through the maturation of his faculties, at that time he becomes endowed with mature virtues and mature faculties;
in the very same way, that monk who is still a trainee (śaikṣa) and has not yet attained his goal dwells frequently in a state of longing for the higher security of nirvāṇa;
at that time, he is endowed with the qualities of a trainee and with the faculties of a trainee.

Then, at a later time, through the destruction of the outflows, he personally realized, in this very life, by his own higher knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; having attained them, he declared:
"Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived."
"What was to be done has been done;
I know no further state of existence beyond this"—
at that time, he becomes endowed with the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and with the faculties of one beyond training.
Even if very intense forms cognizable by the eye should come into range of his vision, they do not overwhelm his liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom;
his mind remains steadfast,
inwardly undistorted, well-liberated, and well-cultivated.
And he perceives its passing away;
even if very intense sounds cognizable by the ear, odors cognizable by the nose, tastes cognizable by the tongue,
tangibles cognizable by the body, or mental objects cognizable by the mind should come into range of his mind, they do not [overwhelm] him.
He attains liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom;
his mind remains steadfast,
inwardly non-erroneous, well-liberated, and well-cultivated.
And he perceives its destruction:
for example, not far from a city or a town, there might be a great mountain,
unbroken, without fissures, without holes, well-rounded, and solid as a single mass.
If a violent gust of wind were to come from the eastern direction, it would not move it, it would not shake it,
nor would it carry it away toward the western direction.
If a force of wind were to come from the southern, western, or northern direction, it would not move it, it would not shake it, nor could it carry it away toward the southern direction.
Even if a violent gust of wind should come from this direction or that, it would not move it, it would not shake it, nor could it draw it hither and thither.
In the same way, even very intense forms cognizable by the eye may come within the range of his vision;
yet they do not overwhelm his liberation of mind or liberation by wisdom.
His mind remains established inwardly, unerring, well-liberated, and well-cultivated.
"And he perceives its passing away.
This is what the Venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa said;
having spoken this, the Elder Arhat then said the following:
For one intent on renunciation, for a mind free from affliction,
for one intent on seclusion, and for one who delights in the destruction of craving.
For one who is resolved upon the exhaustion of grasping and possesses a mind free from delusion,
having understood the arising of the sense-bases, the mind is thereby liberated.

Then, for one whose mind is liberated, whose mind is peaceful, and who is a protector, once what was to be done has been accomplished, there remains nothing further to be done. Just as a mountain or a rocky peak is not shaken by the wind, so too is he unmoved.
In this way, there are forms, sounds, touches, smells, and likewise tastes.
"Desirable and undesirable phenomena cause trembling in others,
but for the Protector whose mind is established and unswayed, he perceives their passing away.
Thus, monks, having conceived a doubt, they questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Śroṇa, as a result of which he was born into a family that is wealthy, affluent, and of great possessions;
on the soles of his feet hairs have grown that are golden in color;
and every day, five hundred pots of cooked rice are served to him?"
From ninety-one eons ago until now, he has never once placed his foot upon a patch of ground that was not covered with a rug;
as soon as he was born, he received twenty crores of gold for the price of a sweetmeat;
and having entered the teaching of the Blessed One, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa alone; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have ripened, they have arrived like a flooding torrent, and they are inevitable.
Who else shall experience the results of the actions performed and accumulated by Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, once their conditions have been gathered?"
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind; rather, only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do the deeds performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen.
Deeds do not perish even in hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
The Story of Vipaśyin (concerning a previous birth of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa): Long ago, monks, in the ninety-first aeon, a Perfectly Awakened One named Vipaśyin appeared in the world.
He was endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Accompanied by a retinue of sixty-two thousand monks, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, he arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
At that time, many guildsmen were residing in the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
They heard that the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, accompanied by a retinue of sixty-two thousand monks, had arrived there while wandering through the countryside.
Having heard this, they all gathered together and approached the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin.
Upon arrival, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin and sat down to one side.
As the many members of the assembly sat to one side, the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.

Then a great number of lay devotees rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and extending their joined palms toward Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One, they said this to Vipaśyin,

the Perfectly Awakened One: "May the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha, accept our invitation for the three-month period to provide robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
The Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin, consented to the many members of the assembly by remaining silent.

Then, the many members of the assembly, understanding his consent through the Blessed One’s silence, rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Blessed One. Having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they rose from their seats and departed.
Having assembled in the assembly hall, they began to deliberate:
"Sirs, how should we feed the Blessed One? Should we do so collectively, or individually? Thereupon, some said:
"If he is to be fed together with us day after day, our agricultural work will be interrupted;
therefore, if it pleases you, let us feed him by turns.
They then began to feed him by turns, subjecting him to the authority of the group.
And according to their means, they each gave her something from their own possessions.
Among them was a poor young brahmin;
he approached his mother and said:
"Mother, a formal agreement has been made by the cowherd community that the Blessed One should be fed in turn, one day at a time;
however, I am of meager means."
"How am I to feed him? she asked.
He replied, "Son, if that is so, take today as the very last day."
"By this much time, you will have gathered something;
furthermore, there will be something from the community that is subject to distribution.
Thus, he took the final day.
In that regard, from what belonged to the community, there was an abundance of material suitable for a formal purification ceremony; he himself also gathered some of it,
and then by him—
A dwelling was constructed;
it was covered with cloths;
and five hundred kārṣāpaṇas were placed in the corners.
A bear-skin was also provided for him;
that too was spread at the entrance of the cave.
Then, having prepared a meal for five hundred people, the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin was fed with great honor.
Prostrating at his feet, he made this aspiration: "By this root of merit, may I be born wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments;

may I never place my feet upon a patch of ground that is not covered with a rug; and may the golden-colored hairs on the soles of my feet be exactly like those of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, which were four finger-breadths in length."
"May it be so for me as well;
may I become a possessor of such qualities;
and may I please a Teacher of just such a kind."
"Lest I should become disenchanted"—
what do you think, monks?
That young brahmin Goṣṭhika was none other than this Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa at that time and on that occasion.
Because he made offerings to the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin and formed a prayer,
as the ripening of that karma, he was born into a family that is wealthy, affluent, and of great means;
moreover, golden-colored hairs, four finger-breadths in length, grew upon his feet.
From ninety-one eons ago, he has never placed his feet upon a patch of ground that was not strewn with gold;
as soon as he was born, twenty crores of gold were obtained for him;
and having gone forth in my teaching, through the abandonment of all afflictions, he realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white;
and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.

"Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are entirely black and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to actions that are entirely white. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves. Now, when Ajātaśatru—being ensnared by the evil friend Devadatta—threw molten gold at King Bimbisāra, the citizens residing in Rājagṛha began to murmur in reproach against both Ajātaśatru and Devadatta.
There, some spoke into the ear of the king, saying, "This one has been prophesied to be an enemy of his father;
why was he not killed as soon as he was born?
Others said:
Sirs, it is not the king's fault;
for does a prediction ever come true for everyone?
This prince is indeed well-disciplined.
"Rather, he has been deceived by Devadatta, that evil friend,
by whom he is thus incited to such actions," others say.
Sirs, it is not the fault of the King, nor is it the fault of Devadatta; rather, the fault lies solely with the Blessed One,
by whom Devadatta was ordained.
"But he was not taken away and established in another world-system";
others say:
"This is not the fault of the Blessed One."
"Rather, it is because the formal act of suspension (*utkṣepanīya-karman*) has not been performed against him by the Saṅgha.
In that regard, he who speaks behind the king's back does not cause the king distress, thinking: "These actions were committed and accumulated by me in other previous births."
But he who speaks ill of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha causes the king to suffer exceedingly,
thinking: "Because of my own misconduct, the world speaks ill of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha."
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, that while others have committed the offense,
others are stained by the fault."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, others committed offenses and others were stained by their faults."
Let that be heard:
the story of Kūla and Upakūla (concerning a previous birth of Devadatta and Ajātaśatru).
Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned.
His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people;
he had two dogs, Kūla and Upakūla.
The two of them ate the king’s equipment for his horse-armor;
then, at another time, when King Brahmadatta’s battle was imminent,
he gave an order to his ministers.
"Examine, sirs, the equipment for the horse's armor," he said;
they began to examine it and saw that it was all cut to pieces and shattered.
They informed the king:
"Your Majesty, the horse's harness and equipment have been eaten by a dog";
the king said:
"Gentlemen, since the dogs have thus been abandoned by me," some were killed there,
while others fled.
Meanwhile, a certain village dog was traveling from the countryside to Vārāṇasī;
he saw them fleeing and asked: "Sirs, for what reason are you so terrified?"
They related exactly what had happened, and he said:
"Why did you not inform the king?"
They said:
"Who is able to petition the king? Others have been executed; we have somehow managed to escape."
He said:
"Wait;
I shall petition the king on your behalf."
Comforted by him, they turned back;
then, at the time of their arrival, he stood in the vicinity of Śravaṇa and addressed the king with a verse concerning the two dogs who resided in the royal palace.
"Those two, endowed with strength and beauty, are on the bank and near the bank;
they are the ones to be slain here, while we are not to be slain.
For it is not fitting for Your Majesty to kill those who should not be killed. Thus [he spoke].
The king heard this;
when the night had turned to dawn, he gave an order to his ministers:
"Sirs, search for him by whom I was addressed with a verse during the night."
They gave an order to the guards:
"Search, sirs, to find out by whom the Lord was addressed with a verse during the night.
They reported: "By a village dog."
The king said:
"Sirs, investigate whether it was eaten by those on the near and far banks, or rather by other dogs.
The ministers, having assembled, began to deliberate among themselves:
"Gentlemen, the King himself has given the command: 'Examine the dogs.
Therefore, how is this examination to be conducted?
Others said:
"What is to be examined here? Let them be made to vomit by giving them a hair-net.
Then, pieces of leather were cast up from both the near and far banks;
this was reported to the king.
They were abandoned by the king,
and safety was granted to the remainder.
What do you think, monks?
Those two, Kūla and Upakūla, were at that time and on that occasion Devadatta and Ajātaśatru;
even then, it was these two who committed the offense while others were smeared with the fault, and even now, it is these two who have committed the offense while others are smeared with the fault.
Furthermore, listen to how Devadatta was ungrateful and failed to recognize what had been done for him. [The story of a hunter and an ungrateful man,
concerning a previous birth of Devadatta.]
Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned.
At that time, a certain man, taking an axe and seeking wood, went into the forest.
While he was searching for wood there, he was attacked by a lion; as he fled, he fell into a well, and the lion, intent on devouring him, fell right after him.
A mouse, pursued by a venomous snake, fled;
a hawk, lusting after the mouse, gave chase;
eventually, they all fell into a well.
Consequently, they all became malevolent; they desired to kill one another.
Then the lion said:
"Sirs, you are all accessible to me; however, we have fallen into a state of hardship, distress, and confinement; remain steadfast."
"This is not the time for hostility.
Just then, by chance, a deer-hunter arrived at that place while searching for deer;
he began to look down into the well. (SBV II 152)
Thereupon, the deluded ones uttered these words:
"O man, save us!
Then, having understood this, the hunter first rescued the lion.
Falling at his feet, he said:
"I shall be grateful to you;
however, a black-headed one remains here."
"You must not pull that one out;
for they are ungrateful," he said, and departed.
Meanwhile, the hunter gradually pulled all of them out one after another.
Then, at another time, a deer was deprived of life by a lion;
the deer-hunter arrived at that place,
and the lion, recognizing him, made the deer prostrate at his feet and gave it to him.
At another time, King Brahmadatta went out to the park grounds together with his harem;
having enjoyed himself there in the park, he fell asleep.
The members of the harem, dwelling in confidence, walked about, stood, sat, and fell asleep in the park.
She cleansed the garments;
having removed her ornaments, she set them aside.
Then, a certain woman of the inner apartments, having unfastened her ornaments and set them aside, fell into a deep sleep.
The hawk, having carried it off, gave it out of gratitude to that hunter; King Brahmadatta, having dispelled his fatigue from sleep, entered Vārāṇasī very quickly,
and the women of the harem, the princes, the ministers, and the people of the city and countryside also went with great haste.
When that woman of the harem was searching for her ornaments and did not see them,
she informed the king:
"Your Majesty, my ornaments have been stolen from the park.
The king gave an order to his ministers: "Sirs, ornaments have been stolen from the park."
"Search for who has seized him";
they began to search,
and that black-headed one would approach that deer-hunter from time to time.
As he was approaching his house, he learned in secret that the man possessed ornaments;
out of ingratitude, he went to the king and reported this.
Then, the king, provoked by extreme anger, had the hunter summoned by royal officers and said to him:
"O man, you have stolen an ornament from the park.
Thereupon, the terrified man related the facts exactly as they occurred and returned the ornament to the king;
nevertheless, that man was bound and placed in prison.
The mouse went and informed the venomous snake: "That black-headed evildoer has had our spiritual friend imprisoned by the king in a dungeon.
The venomous snake said:
"O hunter, I shall bite the king; you must treat him with these mantra-words and these medicinal herbs.
In this way, the king, being well-disposed toward you, will certainly release you."
"And he shares his enjoyments with him.
He replied, "Excellent; do exactly so."
The king was bitten by a venomous snake;
a hunter went there and treated him with mantras and medicines,
whereupon the gratified king released him from his bonds.
And having shared his enjoyments with him,
the Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks?"
He who was that hunter was none other than myself at that time and on that occasion;
he who was that ungrateful man was this very Devadatta at that time and on that occasion;
even then, he was ungrateful and failed to recognize kindness.
Even now he is ungrateful and does not acknowledge what has been done for him; hear again how he is ungrateful and does not acknowledge what has been done.
[The Story of Nanda]
The Mongoose (concerning a previous birth of Devadatta):
Once upon a time, monks, an unseasonable cloud appeared for seven days.
While it was raining, a mongoose entered the hermitage;
a mouse also entered there,
and a venomous snake, wandering about out of fear of the rain, likewise entered that very place.
Just as that mongoose began to rush toward the mouse,
the venomous snake said: "Sirs, we have fallen into a state of hardship, peril, and distress."
"Practice non-harming toward one another;
remain motionless.
Therein, he gave the venomous snake the name Priyasena.
The name of Nakula was Nanda,
and that of the mouse was Gaṅgadatta;
thus was Gaṅgadatta addressed by Priyasena and Nanda.
"Go without being observed and seek food for us," he said;
and he was upright and of noble intent.
With the intention of seeking food for the sake of those two, he began to search; he did not obtain any.
Nanda spoke to Priyasena.
"If Gaṅgadatta comes without food,
he alone must be eaten by me";
thus Priyasena reflected, "Even though he has fallen into a state of hardship, distress, and confinement, he still exerts himself for his own destruction."
"How much more so if he comes without food;
in every way, he must be informed.
He then sent word to him.
Nanda spoke thus: "If Gaṅgadatta returns without food, he alone shall be eaten by me.
While Gaṅgadatta was searching for food, he obtained nothing at all.
He reflected, "Surely he intends to devour me";
he then sent a message to Priyaseṇa:
"Men who have reached the end of their lives become devoid of compassion."
"Afflicted by the exhaustion of hunger and thirst,
you must say this to that ungrateful being: 'Gaṅgadatta will not come again.'"
What do you think, monks?
He who was Gaṅgadatta at that time and on that occasion was none other than I;
he who was the mongoose named Nanda at that time and on that occasion was none other than Devadatta.
Even then he was ungrateful and unthankful; even now he is ungrateful and unthankful. Summary verse:
"Eat! The scribe, the actor, the crow, the ruddy goose, the crocodile, the sandalwood;
the body, the poet, the jewel, the beggar, the maiden, and the guardian of wealth."
King Bimbisāra made exceedingly great gifts to Ajātaśatru.
When Ajātaśatru threw gold at King Bimbisāra, he was rebuked by the king:
"Prince, for what reason have you thrown gold at me? He replied:
"O King, it is because of your anger: the enjoyments of the king are available to you, but they are not available to me.
The king said:
"My son, if it is so, go; let Campā be common to you both.
Delighted, satisfied, and overjoyed, he went to Devadatta and said, "Noble sir, I have obtained Campā as our joint possession."
He said:
"Prince, have you seen the fruit of your prowess? "Noble sir, I have seen it. "Exert your prowess further!"
"Your prosperity will become excessive";
he then began to oppress the people of Campā by means of forced labor; being thus oppressed, the great multitude of people began to flee.
Some went to Rājagṛha;
some went to other countries; and the ministers dispatched a messenger to the king.
"Your Majesty, Prince Campā is harassing the people; the populace, being thus oppressed, is fleeing.
Therefore, it behooves Your Majesty to put a stop to the prince."
The king said:
"Prince, why do you oppress the countryside? He replied:
"Your Majesty, the ritual does not succeed.
The king said,
"If that is so, then leaving Rājagṛha alone, take the Magadha territory."
Having seized the territory of Magadha, he went to Devadatta and said, "Noble sir,
with the exception of Rājagṛha, I have acquired the entire territory of Magadha.
He replied:
"Such is the fruit of valor; exert yourself further!
he said, and he began to destroy the territory of Magadha.
The multitude of people residing in the Magadha territory petitioned King Bimbisāra:
"Your Majesty, the prince is destroying the Magadha territory; let him be turned back."
He was summoned by the king and asked, "Prince, for what reason are you destroying the Magadha realm? He replied, "Your Majesty, the vast population is not thriving.
The king said:
"Prince, if that is so, let everything except one treasury be yours alone.
Having taken even Rājagṛha, he went into the presence of Devadatta and said: "Noble sir, having set aside one treasury by me..."
"All enjoyments have been obtained," he said; "this is the fruit of valor;
moreover, kings are indeed powerful through their treasury."
"He who has a treasury is a king; exert yourself for the sake of the treasury! Thus he began to destroy even Rājagṛha.

The multitude of people residing in Rājagṛha, as well as all others dwelling in Magadha and Campā, became utterly terrified. So that Ajātaśatru would not see them, they began to petition the king by dispatching messengers, saying:
"We have been protected by Your Majesty like your own sons."
"The prince has utterly dispossessed us;
the districts of Your Majesty have for the most part fled;
we too shall flee."
That king was devoted to righteousness and possessed a compassionate nature;
therefore, with rising indignation, he summoned Ajātaśatru, and after stroking his head with words that were affectionate, sweet, and agreeable, he said:
"My son, all the provinces have been given to you by me;
for what reason do you cause such agitation? Wait!"
He said:
"Your Majesty, kings possess the strength of a treasury; I have no strength of a treasury."
"What shall I do? he asked.
She replied, "If it is so, let everything belong to you alone, with the exception of the inner apartments."
Nevertheless, being of a wicked nature and having evil companions, he continued to cause destruction and would not remain still;
thus the king addressed him with reproach:
"The treasury, the storehouses, and the countryside have been given to you alone;
for what reason do you now destroy them? Thus [the ministers spoke] as they cast Ajātaśatru's father into prison.
There he was to die of hunger;
being thus addressed, he became enraged and said to his ministers: "Sirs, whoever reviles a consecrated Kṣatriya king—"
"What shall be his punishment?
the ministers replied,
"O King, the punishment is death."
He said: "He is my father; how can I kill him?
Go! Place him in prison."
He was cast into prison;
that king was beloved by the people of both the city and the countryside, and the multitude of inhabitants dwelling in his realm, having heard [of this], [acted accordingly].
He became dejected;
and because Ajātaśatru was fierce, impetuous, and harsh, no one spoke ill of him;
meanwhile, King Bimbisāra remained in prison, devoted to his labors.
And Vaidehī causes a pot of cooked food to be brought to him;
Ajātaśatru asks the prison guards: "Sirs, how is the aged king faring?"
Thus they said:
"Your Majesty, your mother is bringing in a vessel of cooked food";
Ajātaśatru then gave the command.
"Provide food and drink [only] such that he does not enter again";
and an order was issued within the inner apartments: "No one at all shall bring food or drink into the prison;
whoever brings it in shall be punished with death."

Knowing his fierce nature, no one prepared food for him, much less would they allow him entry. Then Vaidehī, her heart constrained by love for her husband, smeared her limbs with a paste of barley meal, filled her anklets with water, and began to enter.
He sustained himself by that means;
the warders also discovered this stratagem,
yet out of affection for King Ajātaśatru, they did not report it.
Again, Ajātaśatru asked the wardens: "Sirs, how is the aged king faring? They explained it to him in detail.
He said: "Sirs, keep Vaidehī confined so that she does not enter again."
Then the Blessed One, for the sake of planting roots of merit in him, began to walk back and forth on Vulture Peak Mountain facing toward the window;
King Bimbisāra, seeing the Blessed One through the window, felt such joy that he was not deprived of his life;
and Ajātaśatru again asked his prison guards, "Sirs, has food and drink been withheld?"
"Now, how does the aged king pass his time?
They replied,
"For the sake of showing him favor, the Blessed One is walking back and forth on Vulture Peak Mountain."
Standing there, he examines him every day;
he says, "Close the windows,
and scrape his feet with a razor."
They closed the windows and scraped his feet with a razor.
Afflicted by the sensation of pain, his throat choked with sobs and his eyes clouded with tears, he reflected:
"The Blessed One does not take heed of me, who have fallen into such hardship, peril, and distress.
At that moment, there is nothing whatsoever unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. [The Buddha] then sent Maudgalyāyana to visit and console the aged king.

It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— those who possess great compassion, who are engaged in favoring the world, who are the sole protectors, who dwell in tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery (*tridaṃathavastu*), who have crossed over the four floods (*oghā*), whose minds are firmly established on the soles of their feet through the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), who have long practiced the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), who are free from the five factors (*pañcāṅga*), and who have transcended the five destinies (*pañcagati*).

For those endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections, who are enriched by the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, who show the way of the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments, who possess the ten powers, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods— three times during the night and three times during the day, having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, their vision of knowledge proceeds:
Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into danger?
Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and danger? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone to the lower realms? Who is leaning toward the lower realms?
Whom shall I lift out from the lower realms and establish in heaven and liberation?
Whose unplanted roots of merit shall I plant? Whose planted roots shall I bring to maturity? Whose matured roots shall I liberate?
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Go, Maudgalyāyana, and convey my words to King Bimbisāra, wishing him health."
He should speak thus:
"The Blessed One says:
'Whatever ought to be done by a spiritual friend has been done for you by me.'"
One foot of yours has been lifted from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
you have been established among gods and humans;
and saṃsāra has been brought to its end.
The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up;
the mountains of bones have been crossed;
the gates to the lower realms have been closed.
The gates to heaven and liberation are wide open;

however, these very actions were performed and accumulated by you alone. Their conditions have been met, their causal factors have ripened, they have arrived like a surging flood, and they are inevitable.
Since these actions were performed by you alone, who else shall experience their results?
Great King, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, deeds performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Deeds do not perish, even after hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

"Therefore, Great King, you should be devoted to karma. "So be it, Venerable Sir," the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the Blessed One, and having so responded, he entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he [appeared] at Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Having vanished from the prison,
he stood before King Bimbisāra and spoke thus:
"Great King, the Blessed One greets you with his blessing."
"I pay homage to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and to the Blessed One.
Your Majesty, the Blessed One has said this:
'Whatever ought to be done by a spiritual friend has been done for you by me.'"
You have been uplifted from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
you have been established among gods and humans;
and saṃsāra has been brought to its end.
The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up;
the mountains of bones have been crossed;
the gates to the lower realms have been closed.
The gates to heaven and liberation are wide open;
however, these very actions were performed and accumulated by you alone, their conditions have been met, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
Having performed and accumulated these actions, who else shall experience their results but you?
Great King, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, deeds performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Deeds do not perish, even after hundreds of eons.
Having reached the collection of conditions and the right time, [karmas] indeed bear fruit for embodied beings.
"Therefore, Great King, you must be devoted to your actions.
And he, imprisoned in a dungeon and afflicted by the sufferings of being scratched with razors on his feet and deprived of food and drink, asked:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, where is exquisite food eaten?"
He replied:

"Great King, among the gods of the Four Great Kings' realm. Having said this, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered such a state of meditative concentration that, while his mind was thus composed, he vanished from the prison and reappeared on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Regarding the belated repentance of Ajātaśatru and the death of Bimbisāra: a boil arose on the finger of Udayabhadra, the son of Ajātaśatru; weeping, he approached Ajātaśatru.
Having placed him on his lap, he embraced him, kissed him, and held him close;
yet even so, the boy continued to weep and would not remain still.
Ajātaśatru placed that finger from his mouth into his own mouth;
a boil burst open in his mouth,
and Ajātaśatru spat the pus and blood onto the ground.
When Prince Udāyibhadra saw the pus and blood, he began to weep even more;
and when Ajātaśatru saw the withered flowers of Vaidehī, he said:
"Mother, what is this?"
She said:
"Son, this is a hereditary disease of yours that your father also suffered from;
it was when your father placed his finger in his mouth that the pustule burst."
"Do not weep," he said, "for pus and blood have been consumed by me;
it was not cast upon the earth. He then spoke:
"Mother, I was so dear to my father. She replied, "You were indeed so dear. Thereupon, Ajātaśatru’s state of being obsessed with hatred toward his father vanished.
Affection arose within him,
and he said to his ministers: "Sirs, whoever tells me that the old king is still alive,"
"I shall give him half of my kingdom.
That king was beloved by his city-dwellers and country-folk;
and a great multitude of people began to run toward the prison.
Hearing the sound, the king reflected: "Now he will inflict some lowly punishment upon me";
thus terrified, he sighed deeply and passed away.
Having accepted the status of being the son of the great king Vaiśravaṇa,
he sat upon his lap and partook of divine ambrosia;
then Vaiśravaṇa said:
"Who are you? he asked.
He replied, "I am Jinarṣabha, O Great King."
Monks, the designation "Jinarṣabha" (Bull among Conquerors) arose for him. Having become filled with doubt, they questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by King Bimbisāra, the ripening of which resulted in his birth into a royal family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments?"
"In the presence of the Blessed One, he attained the vision of the Truths;
his feet were scraped by a razor;
and while bound in prison, overcome by hunger and thirst, he passed away."
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by King Bimbisāra himself. Having reached their full measure and with conditions having ripened, they have arrived like a flood and are inevitable.
Who else shall experience the results of the actions performed and accumulated by Bimbisāra?"
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, deeds performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Deeds do not perish, even after hundreds of eons.
Having reached the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
The Story of the Potter (concerning a previous birth of King Bimbisāra):

Once upon a time, monks, when Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world— those who have compassion for the lowly and the wretched, who frequent remote lodgings, and who are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
Then a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at Vārāṇasī;
he took up residence for the night in the workshop of a certain potter in Vārāṇasī.
And the caravan stayed in that very hall; there,
one man voided excrement.
The caravan set out early in the night;
however, because the knowledge and vision of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas does not function without focused attention,
the Pratyekabuddha remained right there.
"I shall go for alms right here.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the potter entered his workshop and saw that it had been ruined by filth.
Ordinary people are lacking in discernment;
therefore, he conceived a malicious thought toward the Pratyekabuddha, and with that corrupted mind, he said:
"O renunciant, why have your feet been scraped with a razor?
For this reason, you voided excrement in the workshop and did not go outside."
Therefore, having bolted the door, he was placed there with the words, "Die right here from hunger!
That Great Being reflected:
"This poor man has been harmed."
"If I go away after opening the door, he will be even more deeply wounded," [he thought];
thus he remained silent until the time for the potter's meal drew near.
His obsession with hatred vanished;
he said, "O renunciant, come! Let us eat."
The Pratyekabuddha said:
"O gentle-faced one, we eat only at the proper time;
the time has passed."
He said,
"If that is so, you shall eat right here tomorrow and then depart";
out of compassion for him, he consented.
On the following day, he was satisfied by them with excellent food and drink;
the teaching of the Dharma by those great-souled ones was physical rather than verbal,
as he rose up into the air above and began to perform the miraculous displays of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning.
The supernatural power of an ordinary person is quickly captivating;
like a tree cut at its roots, he fell at his feet and said,
"Descend, O one most worthy of offerings!"
"Grant me, who am sunk in the mire of sensual desire, a hand to pull me out.
He descended,
and falling at his feet, he made a formal aspiration.
"May I not be a partaker of this karma for having committed an injury toward such a truly worthy recipient of offerings;
rather, by this root of merit through my service, may I be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments."
"May I be a recipient of such qualities as these;
and may I please, and not displease, a Teacher even more distinguished than this one"—
what do you think, monks?
The potter at that time and on that occasion was none other than King Bimbisāra.
Because he harbored malice toward the Pratyekabuddha and uttered harsh words, as the ripening of that karma, his feet were scraped away;
and while imprisoned in a dungeon, he died of hunger.
As for the vow he made, through the ripening of that karma, he was born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments;
and in my presence, he shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks.
Having pierced through with the vajra of knowledge, the fruit of stream-entry was realized.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
"For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.

Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to actions that are exclusively white. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. [The grief of Ajātaśatru at the death of King Bimbisāra]
The ministers informed Ajātaśatru: "Your Majesty, the elder king has passed away," at which point a dancer arrived from the south, and there were extraordinary effects from the Buddha’s smile.
Upon hearing this, he fainted and fell to the ground;
when his life-breath was restored by the sprinkling of water, he entered a chamber of mourning and remained there,
such that no one was able to console his mind.
The ministers began to search for a means to divert his mind;
meanwhile, an actor arrived from the southern region.
He was made to dance before him by the ministers;
Ajātaśatru remained ill-tempered and was not told "well done" by anyone;
having finished dancing, he departed.
The Blessed One arrived at that place;
he saw the Blessed One and reflected:
"If there were such a virtuous person there, he would have given me his approval";
having thus conceived a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed One, he struck his drum.
Then the Blessed One smiled.

It is the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some go downward and some go upward.
Those that go downward reach the Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṅghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, and Tapana hells.
Having gone to the Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma hells, they fall as a cooling balm upon those who are in the hot hells,
and they fall as a warming balm upon those who are in the cold hells.
By that means, the specific causes of suffering for those beings are stilled;
they think to themselves:
"Friends, have we passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?"
In order to generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation;
upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Sirs, we have certainly not passed away from here."
"Nor have they been reborn elsewhere; rather, this is a being never seen before,
by whose power our particular sufferings have been stilled."
Having developed serene faith in that emanation,
they exhaust that karma which was to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans, where they become vessels for the truths;
those who proceed further upward go to the realms of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, and the Nirmāṇarati.

Having gone to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahman, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
And they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket!"
"For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Then those rays of light, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One intends to proclaim past karma, they vanish behind the Blessed One; if he intends to proclaim future karma, they vanish in front of him.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear into the soles of his feet;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts, they disappear into his big toe; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans, they disappear into his knees;
if he wishes to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful wheel-turning monarch, they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

If he wishes to prophesy the attainment of the kingdom of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), they disappear into the palm of his right hand; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the gods, they disappear into his navel;
if he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a disciple (*śrāvakabodhi*), they disappear into his mouth.

If he wishes to prophesy solitary awakening (*pratyekabodhi*), they vanish into the circle of hair between his eyebrows (*ūrṇā*); if he wishes to prophesy unsurpassed perfect awakening (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*), they vanish into the crown of his head (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Then those rays [of light] [circled] the Blessed One...
Having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, they vanished into the ūrṇā between his eyebrows;
then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with thousands of diverse colors..."
A bundle [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And the Buddhas, who have transcended rebirth, who have abandoned wretchedness and pride, and who are the supreme causes for the world, speak these verses:
The Victors, who have conquered all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.
At that time, O steadfast one, having realized it yourself through your own wisdom,
O Śramaṇa, Lord of Jinas, for the sake of the listeners who long for it,
[speak] with your firm and supreme words, O Bull among Munis.
Dispel this arisen doubt with your auspicious words;
for the Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without a cause.
"The multitudes of people long to hear that for which the wise display a smile.
"Venerable sir, has that actor been seen by you, who, having inspired a mind of faith toward me, struck the drum? "He has been seen, Bhadanta."
Ānanda, this very actor, through this root of merit and this production of the thought of awakening, will become a Pratyekabuddha named Dundubhīśvara;
his gift is this clarity of mind toward me.
(Devadatta has gilded himself with gold.)
Devadatta said to Ajātaśatru:
"I established you in the kingship;
now establish me also in Buddhahood."
He said: "The body of the Blessed One is golden-colored;
first of all, you do not even possess that very golden color."
He said: "I shall produce a golden complexion";
he then summoned a goldsmith and spoke to him.
"Spread gold over my body," he said;
the other replied, "Noble sir, if you are able to endure the pain."
He said, "Apply it; I shall be able.
Having smeared his body with that oil of *cuñcu* seeds, he applied a gold leaf to his skin.
He experiences a painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensation;
the monks asked Kokālika, "Where is Devadatta?"
He said,
"In that place, one brings about a golden complexion";
the monks went to that place.
They heard him crying out, afflicted by painful sensations;
they approached the Blessed One,
and the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, venerable sir, how Devadatta, on account of his golden complexion, experiences a painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensation," [said Ānanda].
The Blessed One said: "Monks, it was not only now."
Just as in the past he also met with disaster through misconduct for the sake of a golden cap (*suvarṇakholā*);
let that be heard:
The Story of the Crow and the Golden Cap.
(Begins concerning a previous birth of Devadatta:
Once upon a time, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain woman whose husband had gone away on a journey;
before her, a crow cawed very sweetly.
She said:
"Fly away, fly away, crow!
If my husband returns in safety and well-being,"
"I shall give you a golden helmet," he said.
Just then, her husband returned safely;
the crow began to warble most melodiously before her for the sake of the golden helmet.
Then she gave him a golden helmet;
with it fastened on, he wandered here and there,
until his head was cut off by the crow Alikā because of that golden helmet.
A deity spoke this verse:
"Even that which appears to be meaningful may lead to misfortune if it is connected with harmful consequences,
as was sought by the *kelikāka* bird, whose head was made of gold."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? That crow who was there at that time and on that occasion was none other than Devadatta."
Even then, for the sake of a golden bowl, he met with ruin through his own misconduct;

even now, for the sake of a golden complexion, he experiences painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations— Devadatta has the mark of a wheel on his feet, which was impressed by glowing-hot iron.
Again, Devadatta said to Ajātaśatru:
"I have established you in the kingdom;
you too must establish me in Buddhahood."
He said,
"The Blessed One possesses the mark of the wheel-sign on the soles of his feet;
you, however, do not possess the mark of the wheel-sign on the soles of your feet."
"I shall cause the mark of a wheel on the soles of my feet to be produced," he thought;
therefore, he summoned the smiths and said to them,
"Will you be able to fashion the mark of a wheel on the soles of my feet?"
They said, "Noble one, if you are able to endure the pain.
He replied, "Do it; I shall be able."
They reflected:
"This man is powerful; if we mark him in this very way,"
"It is possible that he will deprive us of life with a blow from his heel";
having said this, they tore a hole in their patched cloak and said to him,
"Noble sir, insert your feet through this hole in the cloak."
He thrust his two feet through that opening in the neck;
the smiths, having heated a wheel to the color of fire, branded his feet;
he experienced feelings that were painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable.
The monks asked Kokālika, "Devadatta, where is he? He replied,
"In that region, he is manifesting the mark of a wheel on his feet."
The monks went to that place;
they heard him crying out, afflicted by painful sensations,
and they approached the presence of the Blessed One.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, behold how Devadatta experiences painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations for the sake of the mark of the wheel-sign on the soles of his feet.
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is not only now;
even in the past, he met with disaster through improper conduct regarding the footprint.
Listen to that.
Monks, once in the past, an elephant from the Himalayas descended to drink water; [at that time, Devadatta] was a jackal who measured the elephant's stride with his own.
A jackal followed behind him;
seeing the elephant's footprint, he began to measure it with his own footprint,
and he reflected:
"These are my footprints," he said;
leaping up again and again as he placed his footsteps down, he was impaled upon the stake with a stroke as smooth as a split bamboo shaft;
then a deity spoke this verse:
O fool, your footprint is by no means equal to the footprint of an elephant;
abandon this useless notion.
"You will come to grief in vain.
(SBV II 166) What do you think, monks? That jackal at that time and on that occasion was none other than Devadatta.
Even then, he met with disaster through an improper course of action for the sake of a foot.
Even now, for the sake of the mark of the wheel on the soles of his feet, he experiences painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations.
Thus, Devadatta summoned a skilled master mechanic and had him construct a catapult in front of the Blessed Buddha’s dwelling.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, in the abode of the yakṣa Kumbhīra.
Devadatta spoke again to Ajātaśatru:
"I established you in the kingdom;
are you not able to establish me in Buddhahood?"
"Now I shall deprive the ascetic Gautama of his life; you must not investigate by whom he was killed or where he was killed. He said:
"So be it.
Meanwhile, a master of mechanical arts arrived from the southern region;
he was [summoned] by Devadatta.
He was summoned and told: "O Teacher, will you be able to construct such a machine that it can be turned by five hundred men?
He replied:
"Noble sir, I shall be able."
He gave him a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold],
and he also gave him a thousand men, and said:
"Prepare a mechanical device on top of Vulture Peak facing the place where the Blessed One stands";
there, five hundred men were stationed.
Those who repeat that mantra;
two hundred and fifty [arrows] were placed in another location and it was said:
"If the ascetic Gautama is not struck down by the machine..."
"He is to be executed by you";
likewise, for that same purpose, two hundred and fifty men were stationed in another place,
and all were commanded:
"Those among you for whom the ascetic Gautama has become a share must kill him," he said,
while he himself stood in another place.
"If he escapes from these, he must be executed by me.
Then those five hundred men began to wind the machine and spoke among themselves:
"For whose sake is the machine being repeated? Thus the workmen refused to kill the Buddha and departed.
They sat down at his feet and were converted by him, until they saw the Blessed Buddha below them.
They said:
"Sirs, it would be better to sacrifice our own lives."
"But there shall be no taking of life against the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is honored by gods and humans; abandon the mechanical device!
Having abandoned the device, they wandered here and there upon Vulture Peak.
"By which way shall we lower the machine, so that Devadatta may not see it?
Having known their thoughts with his own mind, the Blessed One manifested a staircase.
Seeing those stairs, this thought occurred to them: "Sirs, from where do these stairs come?
This is the power of the Blessed One."
Having inspired their minds with even greater clarity, they descended by means of the staircase and approached the place where the Blessed One was;
the Blessed One, out of consideration for their conversion, remained walking back and forth on Vulture Peak Mountain.
