Then, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One, knowing their inclinations, latent tendencies, elements, and dispositions, gave such a teaching on the Dharma that penetrates the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard it, they shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, they uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
"Venerable Sir, this was not done for us by our mother, nor by our father; nor by the king, nor by our beloved kinsmen and relatives, nor by our deceased ancestors."
"Nothing has been done for us by any ascetics or brahmins such as that which has been done for us by the Blessed One;
he has pulled our foot out from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts."
He has established himself among gods and humans; he has brought an end to saṃsāra;
he has dried up the oceans of blood and tears.
The mountains of bones have been leaped over; the gates to the lower realms have been closed;
the gates to the heavens have been opened.
Having shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time, I have realized the fruit of stream-entry;
we have gone beyond, O Venerable One; we have truly gone beyond.
"We go for refuge to the Blessed One,
and to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikṣus;
may the Blessed One accept us as lay followers from this day forward for as long as life lasts, with our very lives."
Having said, "We have come for refuge" and "We have full confidence," they began to receive the five precepts from the presence of the Blessed One.
Devadatta perceived that both the laborers and the mechanical engineer had fled,
and he himself managed to hurl a stone from a catapult at the Buddha.
(yantrakalācāryo ’pi)
Realizing that this man was about to kill the Buddha, the Blessed One, he immediately descended from the stairs after them,
took a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and fled.
Devadatta, intent on hurling down the rock, watched again and again, thinking, "It does not fall. Having done so, he himself took those other five hundred men and began to ascend Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
He saw that they were listening to the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One;
having seen this, his indignation increased all the more, and turning away, he climbed Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa,
where he saw that even the master of mechanical arts had fled.
Accompanied by his own retinue of five hundred, he himself began to operate the machine.
The Blessed One reflected:

"These very actions were performed and accumulated by me alone; their conditions have been gathered, their causal factors have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable."
Having understood, "I alone have performed and accumulated these actions; who else shall experience their results?", he said this to those five hundred men:
"Sirs, Devadatta, possessed by intense obsession, has ascended Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa."
"Go!
These deeds were committed by me.
Thereupon, those five hundred men fled.
The vision of knowledge of the deities extends downward.
While the yakṣa Kumbhīra sacrifices his life in attempting to seize the rock,
a fragment strikes the Buddha on the foot.
Then it occurred to the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi: "Devadatta is striving for the sake of the Blessed One's death. Having understood this, he approached the yakṣa Kumbhīra;
having approached, he said this to the yakṣa Kumbhīra:
Devadatta has begun to hurl a rock at the Blessed One from Gṛdhrakūṭa by means of a machine;
and since the Blessed One is staying in your residence,
I shall exert myself to crush this rock into powder with my thunderbolt while it is still in the air.
"You too must provide assistance;
perhaps a fragment of her, once crushed, might fall upon the Blessed One.
He replied:
"So be it";
having said this, the Blessed One stood in the open air and entered a mountain cleft.
Devadatta, with a retinue of five hundred, activated a mechanical device and hurled a rock at the Blessed One.
He was crushed by the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi;
half of him, wishing to fall upon the Blessed One's spot, was not properly caught by the yakṣa Kumbhīra,
and he was killed by him.
The Blessed One’s foot was wounded by a pebble thrown by one who had leaped up;
at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean..."
"Nor by entering a cleft in the mountains;
there is no spot on earth where, once situated, one would not be overcome by karma. Thus it is said.
The yakṣa Kumbhīra also passed away with a virtuous mind;
having died, he was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Now, it is the natural law that when a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods has been reborn not long ago, three thoughts arise:
"From where did he pass away, where was he reborn, and by what karma? He saw:
"He passed away from among the yakṣas and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven, [due to his service] to the Blessed One."
"having inspired serene confidence in his mind";
then this thought occurred to the son of the gods who had formerly been a yakṣa: "It would not be fitting for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit while my probation is still unfulfilled;
what if I were to approach the Blessed One for a visit even before my probation is fulfilled?"
Then that son of the gods, who had previously been a yakṣa, wearing shimmering, stainless earrings and his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces,
filled the fold of his garment with divine flowers— blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-lotuses, white lotuses, and māndāraka flowers— that very night;
having illuminated the entire Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain with a magnificent radiance, he [honored] the Blessed One with those flowers.
Having scattered [flowers], he sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, gave such a teaching on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths, upon hearing which the son of the gods who was formerly a yakṣa shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose with its twenty peaks.
Having pierced through with the vajra of knowledge, he realized the fruit of stream-entry;
having seen the truth, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
"Venerable Sir, this was not done for us by our mother, nor was it done by our father."
Neither by our own circle of kinsmen and relatives,
nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our deceased ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas has that which has been done for us by the Blessed One ever been done:
the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up.
The mountains of bones have been leaped over, the gates to the states of woe have been closed, and the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened;
we have been established among gods and humans. And he said:
"By your power, the most terrible [hell] has been closed."
Indeed, the path to ruin is fraught with many faults;
the auspicious path to heaven has been opened, and the path to Nirvana has been found by me.
Through reliance upon you, I have today attained the pure, stainless eye of supreme clarity;
and I have reached the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones.
And I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
In this world, he is worshipped by Daityas, humans, and gods;
he is free from birth, old age, death, and disease;
and his vision is extremely difficult to obtain even in a thousand lifetimes.
O Sage, today your sight has become fruitful for me.
Then, leaning upon his long necklace and having bowed at both feet with joy arisen,
he circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies, keeping him to his right.

Facing the world of the gods, he went to heaven. Then the son of the gods, who had previously been a yakṣa, departed for the presence of the Blessed One with such splendor— as a merchant who has gained profit, as a farmer whose crops have ripened, as a hero who has won a battle, or as a sick man freed from all disease.
Having returned to his own abode with that very same splendor,
the monks, who were dwelling devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night,
saw a magnificent radiance in the presence of the Blessed One.
Seeing this, they became doubtful and asked the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, did Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approach the Blessed One for a vision this night? The Blessed One said:
"Monks, neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of the gods, nor the four world-protectors have approached me for a vision."
Moreover, when Devadatta, intent on my murder, hurled a boulder from Vulture Peak Mountain by means of a mechanical device, it was pulverized by Vajrapāṇi with his thunderbolt while still in mid-air.
As half of it fell upon me, the yakṣa Kumbhīra seized it poorly;
he was killed by it, and having developed a serene mind toward me, he passed away.
He was reborn among the sublime gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three; he approached me this very night,
and I taught him the Dharma.
Having seen the truth, he returned to his own abode.
Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black; the ripening of entirely white actions is entirely white.
"For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.

Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to actions that are exclusively white. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Then the monks, overcome by doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, venerable sir, how the yakṣa Kumbhīra has sacrificed himself for the sake of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, he sacrificed himself for my sake."
Listen to that:
the story of a hunter (concerning a previous birth of the yakṣa Kumbhīra).
Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people.
At that time, not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, in a certain hermitage endowed with roots, flowers, fruits, and water, and resounding with the songs of various birds, there lived a seer (ṛṣi).
He was one who practiced severe austerities, subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, and was clothed in deerskins and bark garments.
In the vicinity of that hermitage, a deer-hunter made his living by repeatedly killing deer;
he would approach that seer from time to time,
and the seer would provide him with roots and fruits whenever he was weary.
"Perhaps this greedy hunter will not kill the deer living nearby";
thus, the mutual perception that they were father and son arose between them.
The hunter addressed the seer with the address of "father," and the seer likewise addressed the hunter with the address of "son.
Then, at another time, King Brahmadatta rose early in the morning and went out for the purpose of hunting deer.
Struck by that succession of arrows, the deer leapt up and entered the sage’s hermitage;
there too, struck in a vital spot by the king with an iron shaft, it died.
Overcome with anger, the sage said:
"You are a wicked king, Kali-rāja, by whom a deer that had come to me for refuge was slaughtered.
When this was said, the king, his mind possessed by the obsession of hatred, said to his ministers:
"Sirs, what punishment is there for one who reviles a consecrated Kṣatriya king?"
The ministers said,
"The punishment is execution";
the king said:
When he had thus been abandoned by me,
the ministers began to have the seer executed;
by chance, that hunter arrived in the presence of that seer.
Having arrived, he reflected:
"While I am alive, how can this seer be slain?
He then began to fight.
The seer fled;
he was slain by a great body of troops.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? At that time and on that occasion, the seer was none other than I;
at that time and on that occasion, the hunter was this very same yakṣa Kumbhīra.
Even then, he sacrificed his own life for my sake."
"Even now, he has sacrificed his own life for my sake," [thinking thus],
Jīvaka prescribed a very rare substance called *gośīrṣacandana* in order to stop the hemorrhage at the foot of the Blessed One caused by a stone fragment. (A 486a)
The foot was wounded;
blood flowed continuously and would not stop.
Jīvaka, the king of physicians and the observer of the Blessed One’s ailments, approached him three times a day.
There was a faithful multitude of people residing in Rājagṛha, as well as wealthy merchants, guild-leaders, and caravan-chiefs who had arrived from various countries and were endowed with right view;
among them, some said:
"Jīvaka, this medicine here is excellent."
Others said,
"This is excellent," but Jīvaka, the king of physicians, said:
"There is a medicine here that provides immediate relief,
but it is difficult to obtain.
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"Jīvaka, what is that?
He replied,
"Gośīrṣa sandalwood."
At that time, indeed, the acquisition of gośīrṣa sandalwood had been completely cut off;
however, a certain merchant had set aside some gośīrṣa sandalwood for an emergency, thinking:
"This King Ajātaśatru is fierce, impetuous, and harsh."
"If by chance he has need of gośīrṣa sandalwood,
he will certainly even cut off my head for its lack;
for I have been selling gośīrṣa sandalwood from time to time."
He heard that the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, had prescribed gośīrṣa sandalwood for the alleviation of the Blessed One’s ailment;
he reflected:
"This Ajātaśatru, instigated by Devadatta, has set his mind firmly against the Blessed One."
"If I were to offer gośīrṣa sandalwood to the Blessed One, it is possible that he would cause me harm";
then he reflected again: "The Blessed One is honored by gods and humans."
"If his life were to be lost for its sake, it would indeed be so;
what if I were to offer the Blessed One some gośīrṣa sandalwood?"
Taking gośīrṣa sandalwood, he approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Blessed One, I have obtained gośīrṣa sandalwood for the sake of the Blessed One;
may the Blessed One accept it out of compassion."
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Accept, Ānanda, this gośīrṣa sandalwood from this Great Being. It was accepted by the venerable Ānanda.
Then that merchant, filled with affection and joy, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One manifested a smile.

It is the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some of these go downward.
Some go upward;
those that go downward [fall into] Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṅghāta, Raurava,
Mahāraurava, Tāpana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma.
Having gone to hell, those who are in the hot hells fall down cooled,
and those who are in the cold hells fall down heated;
thereby the particular tortures of those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them:
"Sirs, have we indeed passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing their emanation, it occurs to them: "Sirs, we have certainly not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere."
"Moreover, this is a being never seen before;
it is through his majesty that our particular sufferings have been stilled.
Having thus conceived faith in the emanation, they...
Having exhausted that karma to be experienced in hell, they take rebirth among gods and humans where they become vessels for the truths;

those who go upward [pass through] the realms of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin; and the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, the Mahābrahman, the Parīttābha, and the Apramāṇābha.

Having gone to the Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," and they recite two verses:
Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket.
"For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Then those rays of light, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wishes to declare past karma, they vanish behind the Blessed One; if he wishes to declare future karma, they vanish in front of him.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear into the soles of his feet;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts, they disappear into his big toe; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans, they disappear into his knees;
if he wishes to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful wheel-turning monarch, they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

If he intends to prophesy the attainment of the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), they vanish into the palm of his right hand; if he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods, they vanish into his navel;
if he intends to prophesy the awakening of a disciple (*śrāvakabodhi*), they vanish into his mouth.
If he intends to prophesy Pratyekabodhi, they vanish into the ūrṇā;
if he intends to prophesy Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they vanish into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays of light, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the ūrṇā of the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"A multitude of rays, variegated with thousands of diverse colors, has issued forth from within your mouth."
By him the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And the Buddhas, who have transcended rebirth, abandoned wretchedness and pride, and have become the supreme cause for the world, speak these verses:
The Victors, who have conquered all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.

O steadfast one, O Lord of Jinas, O bull among sages, having yourself realized that at that very moment through your own wisdom, please [speak] with your firm and supreme words for the sake of the listeners who long [for it].
Dispel this arisen doubt with auspicious words;
for the Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors who possess the steadfastness of the salt-water ocean and the king of mountains, do not display a smile without cause.
"The multitudes of people desire to hear that for which the wise manifest a smile. Thus the Blessed One said.
"So it is, Ānanda, so it is!
Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition. Did you see that merchant, Ānanda?"

"Venerable sir, I have seen that merchant who, having inspired faith in the mind of the Tathāgata, offered gośīrṣa sandalwood. Ānanda, by virtue of that root of merit, that production of the thought of awakening, and that relinquishment of the gift, he shall become a Pratyekabuddha named Candana."
"This is his gift of merit: the clarity of mind he has toward me.
The hemorrhage did not stop, and Jīvaka prescribed the milk of a young woman.
Nevertheless, that blood continued to flow and would not stop;
Jīvaka said:
"Now, let a sprinkling with a maiden's milk be given.
The monks did not know what kind of milk a maiden's milk was;
the Venerable Ānanda said:
"Jīvaka, what is 'maiden's milk' like? He replied: "It is that of a woman who has given birth for the first time."
"In this context, 'woman' refers to a maiden; her milk is what is called 'maiden's milk.
Thus, the Venerable Ānanda employed all four assemblies for the sake of obtaining maiden's milk.
The monks began to search for the girl’s milk;
the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen— and indeed almost the entire population residing in Rājagṛha, with the exception of Devadatta and his faction—
created obstacles by every possible means for the fourfold assembly and the populace as they were searching.
Meanwhile, in Rājagṛha, a certain woman who had given birth for the first time had so little milk that she could not even satisfy her own child with it,
let alone give to another.
She heard that the Blessed One had need of a maiden’s milk.
She reflected:
"If I give him away, my son, being so young and lacking milk, will lose his life;
this would not be the only misfortune."
Furthermore, Devadatta has for a long time been an adversary and an enemy of the Blessed One;
likewise, King Ajātaśatru has been incited by him, as have Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta, who belong to Devadatta’s faction.
"These will deprive me of my life," he thought;
then he reflected further:
"Granted, there may be the loss of my own life and the loss of my son."

"But it is not fitting that the Blessed Buddha, who is honored by gods and humans, should experience the suffering of illness, on account of which the entire populace residing in Rājagṛha is utterly distressed.
What if I were to take some milk and go?
Having thus conceived a heart of serene faith toward the Blessed One, she milked the cow into a new vessel and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, I have obtained from Jīvaka that which was prescribed for the Blessed One—virgin’s milk.
May this virgin’s milk be accepted out of favor toward me."
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, this girl has noble intentions; receive milk from her."
He accepted the milk;
she bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence,
whereupon the Blessed One was struck with wonder.

It is indeed the nature of things that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some go downward and some go upward.
Those that go downward reach the Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṅghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, and Tapana hells.
Having gone to the Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma hells, they fall upon those that are hot hells having become cool,
and upon those that are cold hells having become warm.
By that means, the particular causes of suffering for those beings are stilled;
it occurs to them:
"Friends, have we passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?"
In order to generate faith in them, the Blessed One emits a magical creation;
upon seeing that creation, they think:
"Sirs, we have certainly not passed away from here."
"Nor have they been reborn elsewhere; rather, this is a being never seen before,
by whose power our particular sufferings have been stilled."
Having developed serene confidence in that emanation,
they exhaust that karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans, where they become vessels for the truths;
those who proceed further upward go to the realms of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, and the Nirmāṇarati.

Having gone to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahman, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
And they recited these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket."
"For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Then those rays of light, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wishes to explain past karma, they vanish behind the Blessed One; if he wishes to explain future karma, they vanish in front of him.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear into the soles of his feet;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts, they disappear into his big toe; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans, they disappear into his knees;
if he wishes to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful wheel-turning monarch, they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

If he wishes to prophesy the attainment of the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartirāja*), they disappear into the palm of his right hand; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the gods, they disappear into his navel;
if he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a disciple (*śrāvakabodhi*), they disappear into his mouth.
If he wishes to prophesy Pratyekabodhi, they disappear into the ūrṇā;
if he wishes to prophesy Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they disappear into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays of light circumambulated the Blessed One three times and disappeared into the ūrṇā of the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"A multitude of rays, variegated with thousands of different colors, has issued forth from within your mouth."
By whom the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And the Buddhas, who have transcended rebirth, who have abandoned wretchedness and pride, and who have become the supreme cause for the world, speak these verses:
The Victors, who have conquered all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.
At that time, O steadfast one, having personally realized it through your own wisdom,
O Śramaṇa, Lord of Jinas, please satisfy the desires of the listeners with your firm, supreme words, O Bull among Sages.
Dispel this arisen doubt with your auspicious words;
for the Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause.
"The multitudes of people desire to hear that for the sake of which the wise display a smile. Thus the Blessed One said.

“Ānanda, did you see that girl who, having conceived a serene faith in me, gave me milk? “I saw her, Venerable Sir. “Ānanda, by this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishment of the gift, that girl shall become a Pratyekabuddha named Kṣīraprada.”
"This gift of hers is the clarity of mind she has toward me," said Daśabalakāśyapa;
yet even so, that blood continued to flow.
He did not remain [alone];
for monks dwelling in various regions had arrived upon hearing that the Blessed One was afflicted by such an illness, as had other faithful brahmins and householders.
There, some pronounced medicines, while others performed medical treatment with mantras;
the Venerable Daśabalakāśyapa began to perform an invocation of truth.
“O Blessed One, your mind is impartial toward both your sons and your enemies.
By this word of truth, remain still; O blood, do not flow!
Immediately upon this invocation of truth, that blood ceased.

The monks became joyful in mind, as did the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen; indeed, almost the entire body of people residing in Rājagṛha was so, with the exception of Devadatta and Ajātaśatru, and Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta.
The Blessed One, though already knowing who was treating him and how, [proceeded to act].
He rejoiced in that manner; then, in order to plant the seeds of their roots of merit, the monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable One, how the blood flowing from the Venerable Daśabalakāśyapa was checked by the Blessed One through a prayer of truth!
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, when I was troubled by this poison, I was rendered free of poison by him."
Let that story of Dharmakāma (concerning a previous birth of Daśabalakāśyapa) be heard.
Long ago, monks, not far from a certain mountain village there was a park, well-provided with roots, tubers, flowers, fruits, and water, and resounding with the songs of various birds.
An ascetic lived there, subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, clothed in deerskins and bark garments, and a master of spells and mantras.
And in that mountain village there lived a householder.
He brought a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, took pleasure, and dallied with her.
While he was playing, taking pleasure, and dallying, in the course of time his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born.
Having performed the birth ceremonies for the newborn in detail for three weeks—twenty-one days—they established his name.
He was raised and nurtured until he became a man;
while walking,
standing, or lying down, he performs wholesome and most excellent deeds with a virtuous mind.
The body of people gave him the name Dharmakāma;
out of a desire to seek what was wholesome, he would go forth from the mountain hamlet from time to time and approach that seer,
where he performed service for him.
Because she approached those who practiced austerities,
she became known as "Tāpasī" (the Adept);
later, at another time, poison-induced symptoms arose within her.
He was treated with many applications of medicinal herbs and mantras,
yet that disease did not subside;
he was then brought by his parents into the presence of that seer.
"Great Seer, your attendant is being deprived of life by poison;
please provide medical treatment.
He then began to perform an invocation of truth.
"O boy, your mind is equal toward friends and toward enemies alike.
By this word of truth, O boy, become free from poison!
Immediately after this appeal to truth, he was rendered free from poison.
"What do you think, monks? That boy at that time and on that occasion was none other than I myself;
that seer was this very Daśabalakāśyapa.
Even then, I was restored to health by him through this prayer of truth."
Even now, I have been restored to health by this truthful supplication of his.
Devadatta, suffering, dejected, and full of remorse, thought to himself:
"In vain have I hurled a stone at the ascetic Gautama;
the ascetic Gautama has not been killed,
yet it has become known to the great multitude."

Having gone to the foot of a tree, he remained there absorbed in thought, assuming a formal cross-legged posture with affected composure; meanwhile, the monks, at various places, reproached, reviled, and censured him, saying:
"Venerable Sir, look how such is Devadatta’s cruel disposition!"
"By whom was even the Blessed One, though he had already gone forth,
assailed? A stone was thrown from above," said Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta.
"Sirs, do you speak thus without having investigated whether it be so or not? Do you not see Devadatta here at the foot of this tree?
That great soul has attained the fourth dhyāna;
how could he act in such a manner?"
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, behold! These Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta—being themselves shameless—are speaking in praise of the shameless Devadatta.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that these shameless ones have spoken in praise of those who are shameless; listen to how this was so even in the past.
[This is] the story of the jackal and the crow."
(Concerning a previous birth of Devadatta, etc.
Once upon a time, monks, the people of Rājagṛha and a certain king, having made an agreement for some reason, established two cemeteries:
men were to be cast away in one place, and women in the other.
Then, at another time, the paṇḍaka died;

he found no space in one cemetery, nor in a second. In a certain region of Rājagṛha there was a park, abundant with roots, tubers, flowers, fruits, and water, and filled with the warbling of various birds.
And in that place lived a seer named Khustaśirā,
who subsisted on fruits, roots, and water, and was clothed in deerskins and bark garments;
and in that region there were fields of *trikaṇṭaka* plants and *eraṇḍa* trees.
There, that paṇḍaka was abandoned;
a jackal, drawn by the stench of a corpse,
arrived and began to devour that paṇḍaka.
A crow was perched at the top of a castor-oil tree,
and the thought occurred to him:
"I shall describe the jackal's appearance."
"Perhaps he might give me the remains of his meal.
He then began to praise him with a verse:
"Your neck is like that of a lion, and your waist is like that of a bull."
"O King of Beasts, homage to you! May we receive what remains after your meal.
Having looked out, the jackal replied:
"Who indeed is this preeminent among the twice-born at the top of this excellent tree?"
"Having illuminated all directions, it shines like a mass of jewels. Thus the crow said:
"O fortunate one, I have come here for the purpose of seeing you."
"O King of Beasts, homage to you! May we receive what remains after your meal.
Thus spoke the jackal:
"O crow, you have the neck of a peacock; you are pleasing to behold!"
"O best of those who wander for food, come and eat as you please!
Thus addressed, he descended and was seen by that seer as he ate the corpse together with the jackal;
the seer then spoke this verse: (SBV II 177)
"Ah, after a long time I behold the meeting of two shameless ones:
they eat a corpse together in the shade of the lowest of trees! Thus was it heard by the crow.
He spoke this verse with indignation:
"If a lion and a peacock were to eat choice meat from the forest, what would be the use of one with a shorn head who lives on what is given by others?"
The seer, filled with indignation, also spoke this verse:
"Among birds, the crow is the lowest; among quadrupeds, the jackal;
among trees, the castor-oil plant; and among men, the eunuch."
"The lowly fields of thorny brambles—behold the meeting of the shameless!
Thus, the crow, becoming even more incensed, entered the sage’s fire-sanctuary and began to look about, but he saw nothing;
having smashed the water-pot, he fled.
When that seer entered the fire-sanctuary and saw that the water-pot was broken,
he reflected:
"This is the deed of that wicked crow and no one else."
Having understood this, he spoke this verse:
"Such shameless ones of cruel intent do not please you;
the fire-shelter has been defiled and the water-pot too has been broken."
"One who is unworthy of praise is not worthy of praise; indeed, nothing at all should ever be spoken by a wise person. Constant silence brings happiness.
"What do you think, monks? That seer at that time and on that occasion was none other than I myself."
At that time, on that occasion, Devadatta was the jackal,
and Kokālika was the crow;
even then, these two shameless ones spoke in praise of one another’s shamelessness.
Even now these two shameless ones speak in praise of the shameless.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, where did the enmity first arise between the Blessed One and Devadatta?"
The Blessed One spoke:
The Story of the Two Birds, Dharma and Adharma (concerning a previous birth of the Buddha and of Devadatta).
Once upon a time, monks, there were two jīvajīvaka birds living on the seashore with one body, named Dharma and Adharma. Eventually, Adharma was overcome by sleep.
Dharma was awake;
he saw the fruit of immortality being carried away and took hold of it.
He reflected:
"Should I first cause him to rise, or should I devour him?"
Thus he thought; furthermore, he reflected:
"I shall eat [it], for it will be digested within this very body."
He was not raised up by him;
he was devoured by himself; then he woke up.
In that region, an outpouring of the fruit of Dharma arose;
it was smelled by Adharma,
who said:
"Whose excrement is this? he asked.
He replied, "It is the excrement of the *amṛta* fruit."
"Where was it obtained? He replied,
"While you were sleeping, I obtained an amṛta fruit."
That was eaten by me;
you were not revived, for it would have been digested within a single body.
He said: "This was not well done;
I too shall become one who knows the proper time."
Then, at another time, Dharma fell asleep while Adharma remained awake;
he saw a poisonous fruit being carried along.
He ate it,
and both of them fainted;
Adharma, overwhelmed by the poisonous fruit, said:
"May I be reborn in each and every place where, in whatever birth, I might be your slayer, adversary, or enemy.
Dharma replied:
The Blessed One said: "In whatever place I may be reborn, in each and every birth there I shall extend my loving-kindness toward you."
"What do you think, monks? He who was that Dharma at that time, on that occasion, was none other than I.
He who was that Adharma at that time, on that occasion, was this very Devadatta. It was there that he first became hostile toward me."
And I remained toward him with a mind of loving-kindness; furthermore,
even though he became harsh toward me,
I maintained a mind of loving-kindness toward him.
Let that be heard:
the story of the poet Sūryanemi (concerning a previous birth of the Buddha and of Devadatta).
Once upon a time, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Sarjarasa reigned over a kingdom that was prosperous and teeming with many people.
He obtained a maiden from a neighboring king;
he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, that girl became pregnant in the course of time;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth at sunrise;
a boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
When his birth had been celebrated with a birth festival, the naming ceremony was established, and they deliberated, "What shall be the name of this boy?
The ministers said,
"This boy was born at the rising of the sun."
"Therefore, let the boy's name be Sūryanemi.
Thus the name Sūryanemi was established for him,
and the boy Sūryanemi was entrusted to eight nurses.
He was raised by eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean him, and two to play with him.
He was nourished by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various highly refined provisions; he grew rapidly, like a lotus in a pond.

When he had grown up, he was introduced to writing, arithmetic, calculation, and accounting; and to those various arts and crafts that belong to anointed Kṣatriya kings who have attained sovereignty, power,
and valor over their realms and dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth.

Namely, he became a master in five areas: on the neck of an elephant, on the back of a horse, in a chariot, in archery, and in the use of the bow; in retreating, in charging forward, in seizing with the goad, in seizing with the lasso, and in seizing with the javelin; in cutting, in splitting, and in piercing; in the binding of the fist, the binding of the feet, and the binding of the topknot; and in shooting from a distance, in shooting by sound, in shooting at vital points, and in shooting without missing the mark, as well as in delivering firm blows.
He was installed by his father in the position of crown prince.
King Sarjarasa’s chief queen was named Dharmā,
and his chief minister was named Goniṣāda.
And the king placed his full trust in him.
Then, on another occasion, while the king was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself with Dharmā,
Dharmā became pregnant as he was thus sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself.
She was prophesied by the fortune-tellers:
"She will give birth to a son;
he, having deprived the king of his life, will himself bind on the royal turban and exercise the sovereignty, lordship, and dominion of the kingdom."
When King Sarjarasa became ill,
he was attended with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits,
yet that disease did not subside.
The state of his body was clearly defined;
he reflected:
"After my passing, Sūryanemi will become king."
"He will certainly destroy the Dharma;
what is the appropriate course of action here?
Thus he reflected further.
"This minister Goniṣāda has been provided with enjoyments by me and has been protected;
I now entrust my duties to him."
He summoned Goniṣāda and said to him:
"My Dharma is the chief queen, and you are the chief minister."
"The state of my body is determined;
I shall certainly be parted from my life-breaths.
Out of love for me, you must act in such a way that Dharmasūryanemi is not deprived of his life."
Thus he spoke; the king replied:
"Your Majesty, even that cannot be done by you;
let Your Majesty be of little concern."
"I shall act in such a way that he is not slain.
Thus it is said: "All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
all unions end in separation; and life ends in death."
Thus King Sarjara passed away;
he was cremated with great honor and the splendor of parasols, banners, flags, and so forth;
and the Great King Sūryanemi was consecrated with the great royal inauguration.
He gave an order to the ministers:
"Have Dharmā killed! Goniṣāda said:
"Your Majesty, why is he being put to death without due consideration?
It is not known whether he will give birth to a boy or a girl."
"Therefore, if she gives birth to a boy, he himself shall be deprived of life.
King Sūryanemi replied,
"So be it."
"She must be protected by you alone";
thus she was placed in his house,
and after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A boy was born;
on that very same day, a fisherwoman gave birth,
and a girl was born to her.
As soon as he was born, he was exchanged for a fisherwoman’s child after she had been enticed with wealth;
Goniṣāda informed the king:
"Your Majesty, Dharmā has given birth."
"A daughter has been born," [they said].
The king replied, "Excellent! We are liberated."
That boy was suckled, nourished, and raised by a fisherwoman; he grew up and was taught the scripts and letters;
he then began to compose poetry.
The name "Kavi" (the Seer), "son of a fisherman," became his designation;
and Goniṣāda announced to Dharmā:
"A son has been born to you who will be a composer of poetry."
She said,
"Let me first see what kind it is"; he replied:
"Enough! What is the use of seeing him?
She replied, "Desiring a son, she longs to see him and will not desist."
Goniṣāda, perceiving her persistent insistence, prepared a stratagem and had him enter [the city] disguised as a fish.
As he was entering, the soothsayers prophesied:
"This fisherman’s son, Kavi, shall deprive the king of his life."
"He himself, having bound the turban, will exercise sovereignty";
this was heard by the king, who then gave an order to his ministers:
"Take hold [of it] so that it does not slip away";
this he heard through a succession of whispers.
Fleeing hither and thither, he entered the house of an elderly woman.
He was protected by her;
then, having smeared his limbs with yellow oil and placed him upon a couch, she had him carried out on the pretext that he was dead,
and he was cast away in the cremation ground.
Having risen, he fled;
in that place, a certain man was searching for flowers and fruits,
and he saw him fleeing.
Pursuers ran after him from behind;
they questioned that man:
"O man, have you seen any person of such stature and complexion traveling along this path?"
He said, "I have seen him; go by this path.
They followed after him.
He entered the house of a washerman in a certain mountain village and informed him of what had occurred;
then the men of the guard began to search the village.
The washerman, having wrapped him in a bundle of clothes, placed him upon a donkey and drove him out of the village;
having been led to the bathhouse, he was released;
rising up and looking in the four directions, he fled.
There too, he was seen by a certain man,
who informed the prison guards:
"Sirs, for what purpose you are inspecting Karvaṭaka— "
"That man went by this path;
go quickly! they said, and so they set out.
He also entered a leather-worker’s house in another village; he informed the man there of everything that had happened, and the man said:
"Place the sandals on the back of the face," he said;
he replied,
"I have never before made sandals of such a form."
He speaks this verse: "For those of various views and many forms have been weighed by no single scale."
"O leather-worker, fashion a forest for me; turn that which was my back here into my front.
Thus was that leather-worker instructed by him.
A shoemaker made a pair of sandals just like that;
this small village was surrounded by walls;
having put on those sandals, he escaped through a small opening.
The guards, following his footprints, searched throughout the village;
he, fleeing for his life, entered the water and was led into the Naga realm by the Nagas.
The king heard through a succession of reports that he had been led into the nāga-abode by the nāgas;
the king then gave an order to his ministers:
"Sirs, those snake-charmers who dwell within my domain—"
"All of them must be brought into my presence.
Accordingly, all the snake-charmers residing in the kingdom were brought before the king by them,
and the king gave them this command:
"Sirs, go; extract the nāga from that nāga-abode.
"So be it, Your Majesty," all the snake-charmers replied to the king and went to that nāga-abode.
In one part of that forest there was a yakṣa named Piṅgala, who fed on flesh and blood;
out of fear of him, even wild beasts abandoned that forest, let alone human beings, so it became known as the Piṅgalā Forest.

It happened thus: that nāga was so harassed by the snake-charmer through the application of the power of mantras that, being terrified, he was cast into the Piṅgalā forest and was unable to pass beyond it.
Then the nāgas held a consultation:
"It was not well done by us that he was not led beyond the Piṅgalā forest;
he too is being slain by the Yakṣa Piṅgala,
and we have rushed here for his sake."
"How should we proceed in this matter?
That nāga king replied,
"Let us inform the snake-charmers of this situation."
They informed the snake-charmers: "Sirs, he for whose sake we have been troubled has,
in effect, already been killed by us."
"As for the fact that he was abandoned in the Piṅgalā forest";
this matter was reported to the king by the snake-charmers;
the king said:
"Even if this is so, nevertheless, let him be searched for.
He then began to wander here and there in the Piṅgalā forest;
and the yakṣa Piṅgala was staying in a certain spot, surrounded by dogs.
He was seen by the dogs from afar;
he reflected:
"Has news of my death been heard by them?"
"By whom has he been made to enter here? Thinking this, he released his dogs;
fleeing from them, he climbed up a tree.
The dogs and Piṅgala were stationed beneath the tree;
Piṅgala said:
"O man, have you not heard that in the Piṅgalā forest there dwells a non-human being named Piṅgala?"
"Whoever enters there, he kills him;
your time has come; descend."
He said, "I shall remain as long as I live";
thus the yakṣa Piṅgala tied himself with a cloth-sling and remained there obstinately.
He began to shake him;
he threw a cloth over him, and the dogs perceived:
"This is that very same man who fell!
Having devoured the Piṅgala Yakṣa, they departed;
he, having slowly descended from the tree, set out, wandering here and there.
He reflected:
"My maternal uncle has gone forth among the sages;
I shall go into his presence."
And on a certain mountain belonging to that seer, there was a grove abundant in roots, flowers, fruits, and water, adorned with various groves of trees and resounding with the songs of diverse birds;
he, having approached the presence of that seer by means of a succession of hearsay,
remained there after announcing his kinship connection.
There too he was pursued by the officers of the guard;
they began to seize him,
whereupon he threw himself down from a mountain precipice.
As he was falling, he was seized by the crown-lock by a certain man;
the crown-lock was torn out,
and he fell.
They reflected:
"This man is dead; let us go. Taking his topknot, they went into the presence of the king and said:
"Your Majesty, that poet has been killed."
"This is his topknot," he said;
the king was highly pleased and shared his enjoyments with them.
Then, the deity who resided in the seer’s grove informed that seer:
"Your nephew has fallen into a state of hardship, distress, and peril."
"Did you not pay attention?
he asked.
He replied, "If I had not paid attention, he would have been deprived of his life."
That seer was a master of spells and mantras;
he knew such a spell by which a man becomes a woman and a woman becomes a man.
He caused him to learn that spell and said:
"Go now;
dwell free from fear on all sides.
He [then assumed] another suitable female disguise.
Having created [an illusion] by means of his magical knowledge, he went to Vārāṇasī and stayed in the royal park;
he was seen by the park-keepers,
who were filled with great wonder.
Having gone there very quickly, they reported to King Sūryanemi:
"Your Majesty, a woman endowed with such beauty and youth is staying in the park"; he gave the command: "Let her be brought here."
She was ushered into the royal palace with a great display of splendor;
King Sūryanemi became excessively infatuated with her.
Then, perceiving an opportunity, she deprived him of life while he was staying in private.
Then, having transformed his knowledge once more, he became a man;
thereupon, binding the turban upon himself and informing the minister Goniṣāda, he was established in the kingdom.
A deity spoke this verse:
He is not truly slain by whom the head is not cut off, for he rises again and performs action;
but he is indeed slain by that which destroys the sound [of the ego].
"Just as Kavi was the son of King Sarjara.
"What do you think, monks? He who was King Sūryanemi, the son of King Sarjara at that time and on that occasion, was none other than this Devadatta.
He who was Kavi, the fisherman's son at that time and on that occasion, was none other than I myself."
Even then he was intent on enmity toward me; even now he is intent on enmity toward me. Listen further to how he remains bound to me by this hostility.
The Story of the Two Jewelers (concerning a previous birth of the Buddha and of Devadatta):
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain mountain village there lived two jewelers.
The road between those two was divided and there was a house [there];
at that time, a certain merchant whose wealth was exhausted arrived at that small town, taking a jeweled vessel with him.
Then, having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he approached a certain jeweler and said,
"Appraise this jewel casket.
He set a very low price for it.
He said: "Why do you speak thus?
Although I have fallen away from wealth, I have not fallen away from wisdom."
"I myself know its value," he thought; so, having approached the first man, he went to the second and said:
"This is a jeweled vessel; set its price," he said;
and he set a high price for it.
Being well-pleased, he said: "Take it;
give me the price. He replied:
"I do not have such a price," he said; the other replied,
"Give me whatever you have."
He took it;
another jewel-worker heard of this,
and having become incensed, he approached him.
"I previously brought this home; I have already fixed its price. Why do you take it?"
Thus it was; mutual animosity arose between them.

"What do you think, monks? He who was that jeweler at that time and on that occasion, by whom the small value was set for the gem-vessel, was none other than this Devadatta. He who was that second jeweler at that time and on that occasion, by whom the abundant value was set, was I myself."
Even then, mutual hostility arose between us;
listen again to how this hostility arose once more.
The Story of the Elder Son of a Householder (concerning a previous birth of the Buddha and Devadatta):
"Long ago, monks, in a certain mountain village, there lived a householder."
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, took pleasure, and dallied with her.
As he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and dallying, (A 492a)
In the course of time, his wife became pregnant;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth,
and a boy was born.
His wife passed away;
he reflected:
"Who will raise this child?"
"I will bring another";
so he brought another,
and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
A son was born to her as well;
she too passed away,
and that householder reflected:
"If I bring another wife,
she too will die;
therefore, I shall provide a marriage portion for my eldest son."
He then performed the marriage ceremony for his eldest son;
many sons and daughters were born to him,
and his wife said to him:
"Noble son, who is this boy to you? He replied, "He is my younger brother."
She said: "Noble sir, you have many sons;
this is but one."
"An equal share of household enjoyment should be given to both them and him";
he replied,
"Lady, this is the way of the world."
She said, "If that is so, then have him executed.
For one who indulges in sensual pleasures, there is indeed no evil deed that is not to be committed. Thus, under the pretext of [gathering] flowers and fruit, he was led into the forest and executed.
"What do you think, monks? He who was that eldest son of the householder at that time and on that occasion was none other than Devadatta.
He who was the younger one at that time and on that occasion was I myself. Even then, he conceived malice toward me."
Even now, he has produced hostility toward me;
listen further to how hostility arose between us once again.
The Story of a Girl and an Astrologer (Concerning a Previous Birth of the Buddha and Devadatta):
Once upon a time, monks, there lived in a certain mountain village a brahmin.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, took pleasure, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and enjoying himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a girl was born, beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold.
That brahmin reflected:
"Whatever brahmin enters my house today seeking alms,
to him I shall give this maiden as alms";
meanwhile, a certain young man entered his house seeking alms.
"May it be well with you; please give me alms.
Having been thus addressed, that brahmin called out to him and said, "Young man, this is my daughter."
"I have given you a maiden as alms," he said; he replied,
"I do not accept it today."
"I shall accept [it] within a single day-muhūrta";
he departed.
Then, another young brahmin seeking alms entered his house.
"May it be well with you; please give me alms.
He was then summoned by that brahmin and told:
"Young man, this is my daughter."
"I have given you a maiden as alms," he said; he replied,
"Another young man has entered here seeking alms."
"Why was it not given to him?
[He] replied:
"Because he said that the lunar mansion was inauspicious."
He said:
"If that is so, let it be accepted.
The brahmin said:
"But for what reason do you not see the constellation? he asked. He then spoke this verse:
"Every constellation is auspicious, and all days are favorable."
When tasks have arisen, all of this is auspicious.
For men intent on calculating the constellations miss their true purpose;
indeed, purpose is the constellation for purpose—what further need is there for the stars?
Having accepted her, he departed.
Another young brahmin heard that this brahmin girl had been accepted by this young man;
he went into his presence.
He said: "Young man, for what reason did you accept that girl?
[The other] replied: "Because she was previously obtained by me. He said:
"You are intent on counting the constellations;
first examine the constellation yourself!
As for me, however, the constellation is auspicious. He became enraged.

"What do you think, monks? He who was that young brahmin at that time and on that occasion was none other than Devadatta. He who was that last young brahmin at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
Even then, hostility toward me arose within him."
Even now, this harshness has arisen in him toward me—
the extremely fierce elephant of Ajātaśatru,
named Dhanapālaka.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, there was a wicked elephant belonging to King Ajātaśatru named Dhanapālaka, who, coming out from his quarters every day, caused great harm to the multitude of people.
The body of people residing in Rājagṛha made a petition to King Ajātaśatru:

"Your Majesty, the wicked nāga Dhanapālaka, coming out from his dwelling every day, causes great harm to the multitude in the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions. Therefore, it behooves Your Majesty to give orders to the elephant-trainers so that they do not let him out every day,
and to have a proclamation made by the ringing of a bell that he shall be let out tomorrow."
The king said, "So be it; go!
and the king gave this command to his ministers:
"Let the elephant tamers be summoned," he said; they summoned the elephant tamers,
and the king spoke:

"Sirs, I have been addressed by the body of people residing in Rājagṛha: 'The wicked elephant Dhanapālaka, being led out from his quarters every day through the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, causes great harm to the populace;

therefore, it behooves Your Majesty to give orders to the elephant trainers so that they do not lead him out every day, and to cause a proclamation to be made by the ringing of bells that he shall be led out tomorrow.'"
"Therefore, you must not let him out every day;
rather, you must have a proclamation made by the ringing of a bell, saying, 'He shall be let out tomorrow.
Having given their word to King Ajātaśatru and prostrated at his feet, the elephant trainers departed.

In Rājagṛha, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments. He invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal at his home on the following day. Devadatta then attempted to kill the Buddha by means of the elephant Dhanapālaka.
Devadatta heard that a certain householder had invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal at his home the following day.
He gave a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces] to an elephant trainer and said:
"A certain householder has invited the ascetic Gautama, together with the community of disciples, for a meal at his home tomorrow."
"Therefore, you must release the noble elephant Dhanapālaka.
He replied, "Noble sir, let it be so."
"But look upon the god however it may be.
Then Devadatta approached King Ajātaśatru; having approached, he said this to King Ajātaśatru:
"You are capable of establishing me in Buddhahood;
however, you have established yourself in the kingdom by depriving your father of life.
I too shall slay the ascetic Gautama and achieve omniscience."
"Release the elephant Dhanapāla! Ajātaśatru said:
"Have you not heard?"
"The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are tamers of the untamed";
he said,
"If they are tamers of the untamed, then I myself would first be tamed by him."
Having observed him in whatever manner it was, he approached the elephant trainers and said:
"I have informed His Majesty;
therefore, you must release the noble elephant Dhanapālaka tomorrow."
Then the elephant tamers had a proclamation made by the ringing of bells in Rājagṛha:
"Listen, O citizens residing in Rājagṛha! Tomorrow the noble elephant will be released."
"Therefore, you must all protect yourselves with every effort tomorrow.
Having heard this, the householder remained lost in thought: "I am so unfortunate!"
"I have invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal at my home tomorrow;
yet the wicked nāga Dhanapālaka is to be released tomorrow.
How then am I to feed the community of monks, headed by the Buddha?"
Again he reflected:
"I shall prepare the cooked food;
having taken it right there, I will feed the Blessed One."
Having prepared pure and exquisite hard and soft foods, he rose early in the morning and went into the presence of the Blessed One, saying:
"Lord, an announcement has been made by the sounding of a bell in Rājagṛha: 'Tomorrow the noble elephant Dhanapālaka will be released;
you must protect yourselves according to your ability.'"
"Therefore, the Blessed One should not enter Rājagṛha; I shall bring food and drink right here," [the king said].
The Blessed One replied:
"Be free from anxiety, householder;
prepare food and drink;
the Tathāgata’s fear of the nāgas has vanished."
"I shall enter together with the community of disciples.
Thereupon, that householder, with a heart full of joy, went to his own home; having prepared food and drink and arranged seats and other necessities, he remained waiting for the Blessed One.
Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Rājagṛha together with five hundred bhikṣus;
the noble elephant Dhanapālaka was let loose,
and the noble elephant Dhanapālaka saw the Blessed One from afar.
Having seen him, Devadatta knit his brows, let out a roar, and rushed with full force toward the Blessed One.
Then Devadatta, together with Ajātaśatru, climbed up to the upper terrace of the palace and stood there,
thinking, "I shall watch the ascetic Gautama being slaughtered."
Then Devadatta, seeing the Blessed One, thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, spoke this verse aloud:
"O you who possess the ten powers, I see that you have been crushed by the power of the elephant;
O son of the Śākyas, together with your disciples, you shall no longer exist today!"
The Blessed One said: "Devadatta, you are base;
you utter this proclamation without taking account of me, who am endowed with the ten powers."
"Now let him behold the power of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, the Wondrous One!
Then the Blessed One manifested five maned lions wearing royal turbans upon his right palm;
smelling their scent, [the elephant] began to discharge urine and excrement and started to flee.
The Blessed One resolved that all directions were ablaze, burning, fiercely flaming, and become a single mass of fire, while he himself established his own feet as peaceful and cooled;
then the elephant-noble Dhanapālaka, running here and there, saw everything set ablaze.
Nowhere else but at the feet of the Blessed One was there coolness;
seeing the wrath of Dhanapālaka, all the monks fled, with the exception of the Venerable Ānanda.
Then Dhanapālaka, his intoxication having subsided, approached the presence of the Blessed One with slow and deliberate steps.
The Blessed One touched his head with a hand marked by the wheel, the svastika, and the nandyāvarta, produced from hundreds of manifold merits, which brings comfort to those who are afraid;
and he spoke this verse:
"O elephant, do not harm the nāga."
"O elephant, there is suffering and injury for him who strikes a noble elephant; for one slain by a noble elephant, O elephant, there is indeed a fortunate rebirth in the next world. Thus it is said.
The elephant Dhanapālaka followed the Buddha in humble obedience, died of grief, and was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
"My good sir, you were born in this inferior animal womb because of your past misconduct."
Yet now you take the lives of others and find satisfaction in obstructing the lives of others;
when you have passed away from here, what will be your destination, what your rebirth, and what your future state? For, O gentle-faced one, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
"All phenomena are without self;
Nirvana is peace.
Having developed serene confidence in my presence, this very day you shall abandon the animal realm."
Having said this, he went to where the householder’s residence was;
having arrived, he sat down on the seat that had been prepared.
Dhanapālaka also followed closely behind the Blessed One.
The Blessed One entered; he stood at the threshold of the door;
not seeing the Blessed One, he began to break down the house.
The Blessed One miraculously transformed that house into one made of crystal, so that he could see the unobstructed form of the Buddha;
having seen the Blessed One, he did not begin to break it.
The Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, having eaten and given the instruction on the merit of the gift, departed.
He remained following closely behind the Blessed One;
this matter was reported to the king by the ministers;
and Ajātaśatru addressed Devadatta as follows:
"You have caused me harm;
for it was by relying on that elephant that kings from the borders did not attack me,
yet even he has been deprived of his pride by you."
He remained silent.
The king gave an order to his ministers:
"When the Blessed One has departed, you must station the state elephant Dhanapāla at the gate, blocking it, so that he does not go out behind the Blessed One."
The ministers also gave an order to the elephant trainers: "Secure the gatekeeper elephant Dhanapālaka and station him so that he does not emerge behind the Blessed One.
Not seeing the Blessed One, he pressed his trunk against the ground with his foot and passed away, being reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
It is the natural law that when a son or daughter of the gods has recently been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?
He perceives: [I have come] from among the nāgas.
Having passed away, he was reborn among the sublime gods of the Cāturmahārājika realm because he had conceived a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed One. Then,
this thought occurred to the son of the gods who had previously been a nāga:
"It would not be fitting for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit while my probation is still unfulfilled;
what if I were to approach the Blessed One for a visit before my probation has expired?
Then, that night, the son of the gods Nāgapūrvī—wearing shimmering, stainless earrings, his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces—[approached].

Having filled his lap with divine flowers— blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and māndārava flowers— he illuminated the entire Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, with a sublime radiance; then, having scattered those flowers over the Blessed One,
he sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then, the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, element, and nature, gave such a teaching of the Dharma that upon hearing it, the divine son who was formerly a nāga shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
"Venerable Sir, this has not been done for us by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the gods."
Neither by our own circle of kinsmen and relatives,
nor by those who have passed away before us, nor by recluses and brahmins, has that which has been done for us by the Blessed One been done;
the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up.
The mountains of bones have been leaped over, the gates to the states of woe have been closed, and the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened;
we have been established among gods and humans. And he said:
"By your power, the most terrible [hell] has been closed."
The path of ruin is indeed fraught with many faults;
yet I have discovered the open gateway to the heavenly realms and the most meritorious path to Nirvana.
Through reliance upon you, I have today attained the pure, stainless eye of perfect clarity;
and I have reached the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones.
And I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.
In this world, he is worshipped by Daityas, humans, and gods;
he is free from birth, old age, death, and disease;
and his sight is extremely difficult to obtain even in a thousand lifetimes.
O Sage, today your sight has become fruitful for me.
Then, bowing down and having prostrated at both feet with his long necklace hanging low, he was filled with joy;
and having circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies, keeping him to his right—
Facing the world of the gods, he went to heaven.

Then the divine son Nāgapūrvī, like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, like a hero who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease, returned to his own abode with the very same splendor with which he had approached the presence of the Blessed One.
The monks were dwelling devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night;
they saw a sublime radiance in the presence of the Blessed One,
and having seen it, they questioned the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, did Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approach the Blessed One for a vision this night? The Blessed One said:
“Monks, it was not Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of the gods, nor even the four world-protectors who approached me for a vision;
rather, monks, it was that elephant-nāga Dhanapāla whom you [saw].”

"Venerable sir, that one who was so fierce and so impetuous when he strove for the murder of the Tathāgata—having been seen by me, he was disciplined; having developed a serene mind toward me, he passed away and was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings. He approached my presence this very night."
"I have taught him the Dharma, and having seen the Truths, he has gone to his own abode.
Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:
"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by Dhanapālaka, the ripening of which caused him to be reborn among the animals?
And what karma was performed by which he was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings and attained the vision of the Truths?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Dhanapāla himself; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
Who else shall experience the results of the actions performed and accumulated by Dhanapāla?"
"Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not [perish],
as previously stated, until they bear fruit for embodied beings— [this was said] regarding Dhanapālaka in a previous birth."
Long ago, monks, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world—
endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt near the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
And he had gone forth in that teaching as a steward;
there, he showed disregard for the minor and lesser rules of training. As the ripening of that karma, he was reborn among the animals.
Because he performed service for the Saṅgha there, as the ripening of that action, he has become a recipient of food and drink.
Because he passed away having conceived a mind of serene faith toward me, he has been reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
Because he was one who had gone forth under the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa and had studied and recited the expertise regarding the aggregates and the expertise regarding the elements...

"Skill in the sense bases, skill in dependent origination, and skill in what is possible and impossible were cultivated by him while he was a god, and thus he attained the vision of the Truths in my presence.
Therefore, monks, as before, one should apply oneself to deeds that are entirely white; in this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
The summary verse:
The swan, the distressed one, the released deer, the putrid one, the monkey, and the elephant.
O monks, having become doubtful regarding the cat, the ox, the moonstone, the elephant, and the jackal, they questioned the Blessed Buddha, the cutter of all doubts:
"Behold, venerable sir, the Blessed One has been abandoned by five hundred monks,
yet he has not been abandoned by the Venerable Ānanda.
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it was not only now; even in the past he was abandoned by these [others],
but not abandoned by Ānanda.
Let that be heard:
the story of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
his loyal captain Pūrṇamukha, and others.
(Concerning a previous birth of Ānanda, etc.
Once upon a time, monks, at the great lake Anavatapta there was a king of swans named Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
he had two sons, Pūrṇa and Pūrṇamukha.
Pūrṇa was the eldest, Pūrṇamukha was the youngest;
then there was Caṇḍapūrṇa, who was impetuous, violent, and harsh.
He constantly tormented the swans; he plucked out the wings of some and wounded others with his claws.
He causes these and hundreds of other calamities;
those swans, arriving every day, report this to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of swans,
who reflects:
"Pūrṇa is fierce, impetuous, and harsh;
if I establish him in the position of crown prince, he will destroy the flock of swans after my passing.
Therefore, a strategic plan must be devised."
Both Pūrṇa and Pūrṇamukha were told:
"He who, having surveyed the springs, lakes, and ponds, comes before me first, him I shall appoint as the lord of the swans.
Out of rivalry with one another, the two set out, each accompanied by a retinue of five hundred.
Looking here and there at springs, lakes, and ponds,
they gradually reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, a king named Brahmadatta was ruling in Vārāṇasī, and his kingdom was prosperous and teeming with many people.
Not far from that park in Vārāṇasī, there was a lotus pond named Brahmāvatī, renowned as being superior even to lakes;
in it were planted various kinds of aquatic flowers,
and on its banks, all around on all four sides, thousands of trees bearing flowers and fruits were planted.
It was covered with blue, white, and red lotuses, adorned with many groves of trees, and filled with the warbling of various kinds of birds;
seeing its splendor, Pūrṇa the swan, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, descended and began to sport, moving about as he pleased.
Pūrṇamukha, too, was addressed by his own flock:
"You too should descend and play," he said;
he replied,
"First, let me accept the kingdom."
"Then, having returned afterwards, I shall play. Having gone there with great speed, he accepted the kingdom;
then, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, he arrived at Vārāṇasī, descended into the Brahmāvatī lotus pond, and began to play.

Seeing him dwelling thus in such joy, the multitude of people fell into doubt: "Aha! This most beautiful lord of swans has arrived here from somewhere or other; having adorned the Brahmāvatī lotus pond and surpassed all aquatic birds in the splendor of his form, he inspires longing in the world."
And he dwells according to his pleasure;
having heard this, the entire populace residing in Vārāṇasī surrounded the Brahmāvatī lotus pond on all sides and remained there,
gazing at his state of dwelling in confidence and the beauty of his form.
The ministers informed the king:
"Your Majesty, a lord of swans has arrived from somewhere;
having descended into the Brahmāvatī lotus pond, surrounded by many hundreds of swans, he has surpassed all the water-dwelling birds in the beauty of his form."
"Causing the world to feel longing [for him], he remains in a state of confident ease.
The king said,
"Sirs, if that is so, let the fowlers be summoned."
They summoned him,
and the king said:
"Gentlemen, it is heard that a lord of swans, whose form is exceedingly beautiful to behold, has arrived from somewhere at the Puṣkariṇī lotus pond in Brahmāvatī."
"He must be brought to my presence by you, bound with a single unbroken noose";
thus he was bound by them with a most delicate noose,
and he spoke this verse:
"I am overwhelmed, bound, and have fallen into the power of men;
I am beyond help. Take the flock of swans and go quickly to Lake Anavatapta!
Thus, four hundred and ninety-nine fled.
Only one did not flee;
he remained there grieving for the very one who was bound.
Seeing this, those fowlers were struck with great amazement.
Out of fear of the king, they did not bind him,
nor did they kill him; taking that lord of geese with them, they went into the presence of the king.
The second one was unbound;
though fettered by the snares of affection, he went of his own accord. That lord of swans was then presented to the king.
The king asked: "Sirs, for what purpose has this second one been brought?
They replied:
"Your Majesty, he was not bound by us; rather, he came here of his own accord.
The king, overcome with great amazement, said:
"Surely this is his wife; go,
release this lord of swans together with his wife."
"And neither of these two should be killed by any of you.
The fowlers replied,
"Your Majesty, others will kill them."
"Let it be announced to the body of people";
thus the king gave the command to his ministers: "Go, sirs, and cause a proclamation by the ringing of bells to be made in the city of Vārāṇasī: 'The King himself commands thus:'"
"No one residing within my domain shall kill aquatic birds";
they had a proclamation made by the ringing of bells.
"What do you think, monks? That Pūrṇamukha, the lord of geese, at that time and on that occasion, was none other than myself."
She who was his wife at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Ānanda;
and those four hundred and ninety-nine swans were these very four hundred and ninety-nine monks.
Even then, I was abandoned by these who had become swans,
yet I was not abandoned by Ānanda, who had become a swan;
even now, I am abandoned by these.
The monk Ānanda did not abandon me;
furthermore, monks, listen to how I was abandoned by these [others], but not abandoned by the monk Ānanda. (SBV II 195)
The Story of Karadaṇḍī, the Sahasrayodhin (concerning a previous birth of Ānanda, etc.)
Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Aṭṭa reigned over a kingdom that was prosperous, flourishing, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
He had five hundred ministers, through whose power he was not overcome by neighboring petty kings. Eventually, from the southern region, a thousand-man warrior named Karadaṇḍī arrived.
He was brought into the presence of the king by one of the ministers, who said:
"Your Majesty, this man named Karadaṇḍī is a warrior capable of fighting ten thousand; he has come from the Deccan seeking Your Majesty."
"Therefore, it is fitting that Your Majesty should accept him as your own";
he was thus accepted by the king and provided with a share of enjoyments.
