Then, at another time, the neighboring kings of King Aṭṭa became possessed of accumulated strength and resources; having arrayed their fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—they marched against King Aṭṭa for battle.
King Aṭṭa also, having arrayed his fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—went forth to meet the neighboring kings for battle.
King Aṭṭa conquered the neighboring kings; they were terrified, broken, defeated, and turned back with their backs to him, each returning to his own territory.
Having regrouped once more, those five hundred ministers of King Aṭṭa were defeated by means of a stratagem: "Come, you all! they said.
"We shall share with you distinguished enjoyments";
they agreed to this.
Then, O King, the neighboring kings once again mobilized their fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—and approached King Aṭṭa for battle.
King Aṭṭa indeed mobilized his fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—and marched out from his own territory to do battle.
While the battle was underway, King Aṭṭa’s five hundred ministers turned back and began to fight with Karaṇḍin, the thousand-man warrior.
Seeing this, the king was distressed.
Karadaṇḍī, a warrior of a thousand, recited this verse:
"They abandon all your friends with whom you have long been acquainted;
but Karadaṇḍī alone shall not desert you as a friend. Thus he spoke.
By him they were all put to death.
What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king named Aṭṭa, was none other than myself.
He who was Karadaṇḍī, the warrior of a thousand, was Ānanda at that time, on that occasion.
Those five hundred ministers were these very same five hundred monks;
even then I was abandoned by them,
but not by Ānanda.
Even now I have been abandoned by these,
but not by Ānanda;
furthermore, just as I was abandoned by these, so too [was it before].
Listen to the story of the lion and his jackal friend (concerning a previous birth of Ānanda, etc.), in which he was not abandoned by Ānanda.
Once upon a time, monks, while the Bodhisattva was still situated in the stage of the undetermined, he became a lion, the king of beasts, on a certain part of a mountain.
Five hundred jackals, who fed on leftovers, remained constantly following him, dwelling in reliance upon that mountain.
After the lion had slain living creatures and drunk the choice meats and choice blood, he would depart without looking back.
Thus a great length of time passed for them;
then, on another occasion, while Siṃha, the king of beasts, was searching for prey at night, he fell into a well.
Of those five hundred jackals, all but one departed.
One remained at the edge of the well and thought:
"What means might there be by which I could lift him out?"
He began to wander here and there around the vicinity of the well,
until he saw a pond not far from the well.
Having reflected on this, he dug a tunnel in one part;
then that well was filled with water from the pond,
and the lion rose up by himself.
A deity recited this verse:
"Friends should be made, even those who are weak as well as those who are strong;
behold how the lion was rescued from an old well by a jackal. Thus it was said.
"What do you think, monks? He who was that lion at that time and on that occasion was none other than I;
the jackal at that time and on that occasion was the monk Ānanda;
and those four hundred and ninety-nine jackals were these very five hundred monks."
Even then I was abandoned by these,
but not by Ānanda; even now I am abandoned by these.

Listen further to how I was abandoned by these very ones. Once upon a time, monks, while the Bodhisattva was dwelling in the state of the indeterminate group, he became the leader of five hundred deer in a certain region.
Meanwhile, a certain hunter had set out numerous snares and traps for the purpose of killing deer;
that lord of the deer, wandering through the deer park with a retinue of five hundred, moved about with complete confidence;
as he was walking at the head of the herd, he was caught in a snare.
Seeing him bound, all the deer fled;
however, one doe remained by the side of the leader of the herd;
that lord of the deer strove to sever the snare.
He was able to do so;
seeing him moving in that manner, the doe spoke this verse:
"Exert yourself, O illustrious one! Exert yourself, O best of deer!"
"That hunter by whom this snare was set will arrive.
He too spoke a verse:
"What can I do? I am unable to split open this earth quickly."
"The firm leather straps are pulling my feet very tightly.
Then that hunter, bow and arrow in hand and clad in saffron-colored robes, approached that place.
That doe saw the hunter approaching the lord of beasts, intent on killing him.
And having seen him, she spoke these verses with great haste:
"Exert yourself, O illustrious one! Exert yourself, O best of deer!
For that hunter has arrived by whom this snare was set."
He too spoke this verse:
"What shall I do? I am unable; I would quickly cleave this earth, yet these firm leather straps pull my feet with great force. (SBV II 198)
Then that doe, with a vacant heart, spoke this verse in the presence of the deer-hunter: "O hunter, lower your bow and take up your sword;
first kill me, and only after that, the lord of the deer."
Then that deer-hunter, his mind overcome with wonder, asked: "Who is this person of yours?
She replied:
"O Lord," she said; he replied to her with a verse:
"I shall not cause you harm, nor will I kill the lord of beasts;
I shall bring about a reunion for you with your beloved husband."
She too spoke this verse: "Just as I, O hunter, rejoice with my beloved husband,
so may you, O hunter, rejoice together with all your kinsmen."
Then, filled with even greater wonder, that hunter released the deer.
What do you think, monks? He who was the lord of the deer at that time and on that occasion was none other than I. She who was the doe at that time and on that occasion was Ānanda.
Those five hundred deer minus one were these very same five hundred monks minus one;
even then I was abandoned by them,
but not by Ānanda.
"Even now I have been abandoned by these, but not by Ānanda. Then the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, venerable sir, Devadatta, putrid as he is, has been destroyed by putrid gain and honor.
The Blessed One said: "Monks, it was not only now."
Just as in the past he was likewise foul and ruined by foul gain and honor; hear that story:
"The Story of the Jackal Competing with the Elephant."
(Regarding a former birth of Devadatta:
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain region of the mountains there was a great lotus pond;
near it lived an elephant.
In another region there also lived a jackal.
Once, at a later time, the elephant emerged after drinking water from that lotus pond,
while the jackal was descending into it.
He said to the elephant, "Give me either battle or the way";
the elephant reflected: (SBV II 199)
"This ascetic is putrid and like a crow;
if I were to strike him with my foot, or destroy him with my trunk, or with my tusk, or with something impure."
Again he reflected:
"In every way, this putrid thing must be destroyed by that which is itself putrid";
having understood this, he spoke this verse:
"I will not kill you with my feet, nor with my tusks, nor with my trunk;
I shall kill you with something foul, for the foul should be killed by the foul. Thus the elephant reflected.
"I shall go aside to a secluded spot;
surely he will follow after me.
Thinking thus, he stepped off the path and set out with great haste.
The jackal reflected:
"He has been broken by me with mere words, which is why he has fled away in great haste";
and so he followed closely behind him.
Knowing that he had come near the elephant, [the elephant] discharged dung upon him with great force;
he fell down and died.
What do you think, monks? That jackal at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Devadatta; even then, he who was already putrid was struck down by one who was putrid.
Even now, this one who is putrid with rot is destroyed by gain and honor.
Again, monks, having become doubtful, they questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how Devadatta has deceived the world by means of the 'door of the Dharma'!
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is not only now;
just as in the past, too, the world was deceived by him through this very gateway of the Dharma—
listen to that.
The Story of Āgneya the Cat (concerning a previous birth of Devadatta):
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain region there lived a leader of a troop of mice with a retinue of five hundred.
There was a cat named Āgneya;
in his youth, he killed all the mice in the vicinity of the place where he lived.
At a later time, he became old; he was no longer able to catch mice by means of his prowess,
and he reflected:
"Formerly, in my youth, I was able to catch mice by means of my prowess; now I am no longer able. However, I shall eat them by employing a stratagem. Thus he spoke slowly. (SBV II 200)
He began to search for the mice very slowly;
while searching, he discovered a troop of five hundred mice,
and he practiced artificial austerities not far from the mouse hole.
He was seen by the wandering mice as he stood there with a tranquil deportment;
standing at a distance, they said,
"Uncle, what are you doing?"
He said: "In my youth, I committed much demerit;
I am practicing asceticism in order to exhaust it."
In his presence, they developed a faith based on the Dharma, thinking, "This man has desisted from that evil, unrighteous practice"; thus,
every day they circumambulated him and entered the opening.
He would seize the last among them and eat it,
until that herd began to diminish.
Then the leader of the herd reflected:
"My mice are diminishing,
yet this cat has become strong;
there must be a reason for this."
He began to examine the cat's excrement;
as soon as he saw that the excrement was covered with all its fur,
he reflected:
"Certainly, these mice are being slaughtered by him;
what if I were to seize him?
Thinking thus, he remained intent on his purpose, watching for him out of the range of his sight.
When he saw that [cat] eating the last mouse,
he approached him, kept his distance, and addressed him with a verse:
"The body of my maternal uncle is growing, while the number of mice is diminishing."
The excrement of one who subsists on roots and fruits does not become hairy.
"This Śikhin is not a true follower of the Dharma; this Śikhin is so called for the sake of gain. May it be well with you, O Agni-born one! The mice are being driven away.
Monks, what do you think? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the cat Agneya, was Devadatta.
Even then, he devoured mice under the guise of the Dharma; even now, he has deceived the world under the guise of the Dharma.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Behold, Venerable Sir, those who have come to agree with the view of the Blessed One have crossed over the wilderness of saṃsāra by way of well-being and security; whereas those whom Devadatta has caused to agree with his view have met with disaster through that wrong course.
The Blessed One said:

Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, those who accepted my view crossed over the wilderness of saṃsāra with well-being and safety, while those who did not accept my view met with calamity through their misconduct.
Let that be heard:
the story of a bull who, through evil counsel, brought other bulls into distress (concerning a previous birth of the Buddha and Devadatta).
Long ago, monks, two caravan leaders, traveling together with five hundred wagons, set out upon a trackless wilderness road.
While they were on that wilderness road, at times there was a scarcity of fodder for the oxen,
and at times there was a scarcity of drinking water.
At one point, it was no longer there;
then that caravan, together with its oxen, being exceedingly exhausted, proceeded along the difficult path with great effort and saw in a certain place a lush green meadow, well-supplied with water,
where they bathed.
And they drank an abundance of water; then those oxen, exhausted by the meager water and fodder,
having drunk their fill of fodder and water, became rested.
The lead ox among them rouses them, saying: "Sirs, we have been exhausted by meager fodder and meager water;
this region is lush with green grass and abundant in water."
"If it is your intention to remain right here by force," said the second leading bull to his herd-mates,
"gentlemen, these men are powerful and are tamers of the difficult-to-tame."
"Just as we carry [the load], so too must you carry it; do not bring about misfortune.
When this was said, the leading ox became enraged and spoke to his fellow herdsmen:
"Sirs, by whom was the back of the moon seen? You must not carry these [goods].
Thereupon, the caravan leaders began to yoke the oxen.
Those oxen, appearing distressed, were made to stand still;
the caravan leaders, having dealt them many blows and repeatedly striking them with goads, yoked them to the carts while blood was flowing from them;
others, however, began to pull silently.
Nothing at all was done by them;
a deity speaks this verse:
"Behold these cows, truly urged on falsely by the bull!"
Their flesh was torn away, they were drenched in blood, and they were utterly overwhelmed by hunger and thirst.
Behold these cows, properly urged on by the bull;
having indeed crossed the wilderness, they drink cool water.

"What do you think, monks? That leading bull by whom they were properly urged was I at that time, on that occasion. But he by whom the bulls were led astray was [Devadatta] at that time, on that occasion.
Even then, those who heard my words crossed the wilderness path in safety and well-being."
Those who heard the words of Devadatta met with calamity through that misconduct;
even now, those who have entered into agreement with my vision have crossed over the wilderness path of *saṃsāra* by means of well-being and security,
whereas those who have entered into agreement with the vision of Devadatta have met with calamity through that misconduct.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, Devadatta is a fool with a foolish retinue.
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, Devadatta was a fool with a foolish retinue.
Listen to that.
The Story of the Leader of the Monkeys (concerning a previous life of Devadatta): Once upon a time, monks, there lived a leader of a troop of monkeys in a certain forest retreat.
As he was wandering about, he saw the reflection of the moon in a well;
the leader of the herd said, "Sirs, the moon has fallen into the well!"
"Let us rescue him! Will the world become moonless? they asked, and they said:
"It is well; let us pull it out.
Having thus begun their consultation, they asked:
"How should it be pulled out from here?"
Thus they spoke; others said: "What is known in this matter?
Let us make a 'monkey-rope' and pull him out."
They made a rope of monkeys; one clung to a branch, and another clung to his tail.
Another branch was fastened to that one as well, and so on until all the branches were fastened together; they became excessively heavy,
and they began to disturb the water.
The reflection of the moon has vanished;
the branch is broken;
they have all fallen into the well.
Having fallen into calamity through misconduct,
a deity spoke this verse:
"For those fools here in this world, if their leader is a fool..."
"They all go to their destruction, like the monkeys who tried to pull out the moon.
What do you think, monks? He who was the leader of that monkey troop at that time and on that occasion was Devadatta;
even then, he was a fool with a foolish retinue.
Even now, this fool has a following of fools.
The five causes for the schism of the Saṅgha: The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:

"The deeds of the Tathāgata—those for which the accumulations have been gathered, performed, and built up; those for which the accumulations have been obtained and the conditions have matured; those that stand before him like a surging flood—are inevitable."
The Tathāgata himself has performed and accumulated these actions; who else would experience them?
For actions that have been performed and accumulated [do not perish].
They ripen in the external earth element as before, until they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings;
Devadatta must necessarily cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata.
The Saṅgha is split by five causes:

First of all, the Saṅgha is not split as long as a Buddha has not appeared in the world; for as long as he remains in the world, the world stays oriented toward him, thinking, "Friends, a Buddha has indeed appeared in the world.
But when the Teacher has passed into parinirvāṇa, the Saṅgha is split.
If anyone were to say,
"I alone am the Teacher," he should be told:
"When the Blessed One was living, remaining, staying, and maintaining himself, where were you then?"

When a *arbuda* has not arisen, the Saṃgha is not split—whether it be a *dṛṣṭyarbuda* (a tumor of views) or a *śīlārbuda* (a tumor of conduct). As long as the pair of disciples (*śrāvakayuga*) has not been designated, the Saṃgha is not split.
Why is that? Because once the Saṃgha is split, it necessarily reunites through the pair of disciples.
When the boundary (*sīmā*) has not been fixed, the Saṃgha is not split.

For what reason? Because the Saṅgha is split within the boundary, not outside the boundary. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: [The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Last Instructions] *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra*, Chapter on the Buddha’s Final Exhortation: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly: 'O sons of the Buddha, you should know that the Tathāgata has already attained parinirvāṇa. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s body is eternal and unchanging; it is not subject to birth or death, nor does it undergo transformation. It is because sentient beings are deluded and do not understand that they perceive the Tathāgata as having entered nirvāṇa. O sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgata’s true nature is like empty space—eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging. It is only for the sake of saving sentient beings that he manifests the appearance of entering nirvāṇa. In my community of monks, which was free from boils, two boils have arisen: a boil of moral conduct and a boil of views.
The boil of moral conduct was produced by Sudatta, the son of Kalantaka;
the boil of views by the monk Ariṣṭa.
"Devadatta must certainly split the Saṅgha;
what if I were to enter the rains retreat at Rājagṛha?
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"If I go to Rājagṛha together with the persons who are in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), Devadatta will not be able to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
What if I were to go together with virtuous ordinary persons (pṛthagjana-kalyāṇaka)?

Having understood this, the Venerable Rāhula, acting as his attendant, accompanied him along with five hundred monks; and after staying in Śrāvastī for as long as he pleased, he set out on a journey toward Rājagṛha.
Wandering on his journey in due order, he arrived at Rājagṛha. (SBV II 204) [This section concerns] the famine in Rājagṛha,
the schism in the Saṅgha, and the new rules imparted by Devadatta.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, had entered the rains retreat at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground. At that time, there was a famine; it was a time of hardship and distress, and alms were difficult for a beggar to obtain.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I wish to remain in seclusion for these three months;
no monk should approach me, except for one who brings almsfood."
"That very [day] shall be the Poṣadha.
A formal agreement was made by the community of monks: "None of us shall approach the Blessed One for a visit during these three months, with the exception of one who brings almsfood;
that very [day] shall be the Poṣadha."
At that time, the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had entered the rains retreat in Dakṣiṇāgiri.
Devadatta had provided for the community of monks throughout the three-month period with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
At the end of two or three months, he addressed the monks:
"Venerable sirs, the ascetic Gautama teaches the Dharma to his disciples in this way:
'By being a forest-dweller, a monk is purified, liberated, and delivered; he transcends pleasure and pain, and attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain';
[and likewise] by being an alms-food eater and a wearer of rag-robes."
"By means of wearing only three robes and by dwelling in the open air, one is purified, liberated, and delivered; one transcends pleasure and pain and attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain.
O Venerable Ones, whoever does not find these five points of the vow pleasing, acceptable, or clear, let him stay far away from the ascetic Gautama, let him stay at a great distance;
let him take the voting stick."
Five hundred monks took up the voting tickets;
Devadatta rose from his seat and departed,
followed closely behind by those five hundred monks.
The Venerable Rāhula was standing at the door; he saw those [footprints] following closely behind Devadatta, and he said:
“Venerable ones, for what reason do you follow closely behind this man of evil intent, having abandoned the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha?
They replied:
“Venerable Rāhula, in such a time of famine, hardship, and wilderness, the Blessed One remains out of sight; we—”
It was through the power of Devadatta that they were not deprived of their lives;
for if Devadatta had not provided for the community of monks for three months,
not a single monk would have survived.
When the Tathāgata Devadatta split the community of disciples, a great earthquake occurred;
meteors fell and the quarters of the sky blazed.
The divine drums resound;
those who have not entered the discipline do not enter the discipline;
they do not attain the fruit.
They do not attain detachment;
they do not exhaust the outflows;
they do not give instruction.
They do not recite; they do not study;

those who uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, as well as the forest-dwellers, do not apply themselves to the contemplation of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, and the forest life.
They do not plant the seed for the awakening of a śrāvaka; nor for the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; nor for unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
The world, including its gods and humans, remains in a state of turmoil;
throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, the Wheel of Dharma stands still and does not turn within the mental continuums of sentient beings.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana visit the Buddha and pledge to him that they will restore the Saṅgha.
The venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana reflected:
"For what reason is this great earthquake occurring?
However, having applied their minds, the knowledge and vision of the Arhats did not function [to discern the cause].
The two of them set about reflecting and saw that Devadatta had caused a schism in the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples;
this occurred to them:
"Let us go to reunite the Blessed One’s community of disciples.

Then, after the three months of the rainy season had passed, the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having finished their robes and completed their sewing, took up their bowls and outer garments and set out on a journey toward Rājagṛha.
Wandering on their journey in due order, they arrived at Rājagṛha.
Then the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having set aside their bowls and robes and washed their feet, approached the Blessed One.
At that time, the venerable Rāhula was standing at the gate.
Then the Venerable Rāhula said this to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Upādhyāya, Devadatta has split the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples. He replied:
"Venerable one, it is for this very purpose that we have come."
"Be free from anxiety;
we shall effect a reunion," they said,
and having spoken thus, they entered the presence of the Blessed One.

Having entered, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side; as they were seated to one side, the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable Sir, let us go to reconcile the divided Saṅgha of the Śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: [The Discourse on the Four Meritorious Persons]... “The Blessed One said:”

Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana! He who reunites the broken Saṅgha of disciples of the Tathāgata produces much merit— immeasurable and incalculable— just as one who might join together the tip of a hair split a hundred times with the tip of a hair split a million times.
In the same way, he produces much merit—immeasurable and incalculable—who reunites the broken community of disciples of the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra, these four produce Brahmā-merit;
what are the four? 1)

The first person is one who establishes a stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata on a spot of earth where none has been established before; this person generates Brahma-merit and rejoices in the heavens for an eon. 2)
Furthermore, that person who establishes a monastery for the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions on a site where no monastery has previously stood—
this is the second person who generates Brahma-merit and rejoices in the heavens for an eon. 3)
Furthermore, that person who reunites the Sangha of the Tathāgata’s disciples when it has been split—
this is the third person who generates Brahma-merit and rejoices in the heavens for an eon. 4)

Furthermore, there is the person who, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— free from enmity, free from rivalry, free from ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated— abides having resolved upon, pervaded, and attained one direction;
likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, he dwells having pervaded this entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness— free from enmity, free from rivalry, free from ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated— and having resolved upon it and attained it. In the same way, he dwells having pervaded it with a mind accompanied by compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— free from enmity, free from rivalry, free from ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated— and having resolved upon it and attained it.
Likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth;

thus above, below, across, and everywhere, he dwells having resolved upon this entire world in every respect with a mind accompanied by equanimity— free from enmity, free from rivalry, free from ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, well-cultivated— pervading one direction.
Having pervaded [the world] and attained [this state], he dwells therein; this is the fourth person who generates Brahma-merit and rejoices in the heavens for an eon.

Then the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having rejoiced and delighted in what was spoken by the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence. At that time, Devadatta was teaching the Dharma in accordance with the truth among the people of Dakṣiṇāgiri, displaying the playful grace of a Buddha. He exhorted the misguided monks to return to the true doctrine.
Kokālika was seated on his right side,
and Khaṇḍadravya on the left;
Devadatta saw Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana from afar.
Having seen this, he reflected again:
"Even the great śrāvakas have been converted by me;
now I am the All-Knowing One."
He struck Kokālika and Khaṇḍadravya with his arms, saying, "Arise! Arise!
They reflected: "This very fault is ours, in that we rendered assistance to him in the schism of the Saṃgha."
"Let us rise;
if he strikes,
this powerful man will surely kill us."
The two of them rose;
the Venerable Śāriputra sat on the right side, and the Venerable Maudgalyāyana on the left.
Thereupon Devadatta addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "May it be your inspiration, Śāriputra, to deliver a discourse on the Dharma to the monks;
my back is aching, so I shall stretch it for a moment."
The venerable Śāriputra consented to Devadatta by remaining silent;
then Devadatta, having arranged his upper robe in four folds and laid down on his right side, fell into a sleep.
By the venerable Śāriputra... [the rest of the sentence continues].
He was thus empowered so that he remained with his body stretched out and writhing; there, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the monks:
"Behold, venerable ones, the condition of the Teacher!"
"Uttānaka has fallen asleep while his body was being massaged.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, stir up a sense of spiritual urgency in the assembly."

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he rose up into the air in the eastern direction and performed the four modes of conduct: he walked, stood, sat, and lay down.
He also enters the fire element;
as the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana has entered the fire element, various rays of light issue forth from his body— blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and crystal-colored—
and he even displays twin miracles.

The lower part of his body blazes, while a cool stream of water flows from the upper part of his body; the upper part of his body blazes, while a cool stream of water flows from the lower part of his body;
as it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the southern, western, and northern directions.
Having thus displayed these four kinds of miraculous feats in the four directions, he withdrew those supernatural transformations and sat down upon the very seat that had been prepared.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana inspired those monks with a sense of spiritual urgency,
and thereafter the Venerable Śāriputra taught them the Dharma in such a manner.
Having heard this, they became indifferent toward Devadatta and said:
"Venerable ones, those for whom the Teacher is dear, arise!
Let us go."
Many misguided monks were led back to the Buddha and readmitted into the Order without a word of reproach.
The Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana set out,
and the monks followed closely behind them.
Kokālika roused Devadatta, saying: "Arise, arise!
Your assembly is being carried away by the great śrāvakas!"

Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Śāriputra: "If I lead Devadatta away from the assembly while he is not looking, it is possible that he will vomit hot blood and die; therefore, he must be led away while he is actually watching."
The two of them proceeded together with the Saṅgha, moving with slow steps;
Devadatta, however, with intense agitation, ran along while rubbing his eyes.
By the Venerable Śāriputra, [the ground] was perceived as resembling the most extremely terrifying Pātāla.
A pit was constructed; Devadatta, together with Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta, began to wander all around that pit,
but he was unable to climb out.
He reflected:
"I shall not please the assembly,
and furthermore, I shall fall into calamity through this improper course."
Having understood this, he turned back;
the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana also, taking the community of monks with them, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Then those monks, filled with shame, dejected, with shoulders drooping and faces cast down, approached the presence of the Blessed One.
"How is it that we have remained associated with Devadatta, who has evil desires, having abandoned the Blessed One who is endowed with immeasurable qualities?
Then the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those monks with his own mind, addressed the monks:
"Welcome to you, monks; well-faring is your renunciation."
Well obtained by you is this acquisition of human birth;

at some time or other, there has been rebirth in a noble realm, with unimpaired faculties, without dullness, without deaf-muteness, not mute, and possessing the capacity to understand the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings.

Only at rare intervals do Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas appear in the world; only at rare intervals is the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed in the world as revealed by the Tathāgata. Therefore, monks, this is extremely difficult to obtain, indeed extremely difficult to obtain: namely, rebirth in a noble realm.
The faculties are unimpaired, one is not dull-witted, not deaf-mute, and not mute by hand; one is capable of understanding the meaning of teachings that are well-spoken or ill-spoken.

And now I have arisen in the world as a Teacher—a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

And the Dharma is taught—leading to tranquility, leading to final nirvana, leading to perfect awakening, and personally realized by the Sugata—namely: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases;

with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; and with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering;
that is to say, when this is not, that does not come to be;
from the cessation of this, this ceases.

That is to say: from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling... (SBV II 210)
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Therefore, monks, those who regard their own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both, should train themselves thus:
"May our going forth not be in vain; may our actions be fruitful, resulting in happiness and ripening in happiness."
"And for those from whom we shall receive robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
their services will become exceedingly fruitful, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great extent; in this way, monks, you should train yourselves."

When those monks were addressed by the Blessed One with words of welcome and words of praise for their successful going-forth, then whatever dullness, remorse, irritation, dejection, and regret they had experienced vanished entirely.
Thereupon, other monks, having become filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Blessed One, the ripening of which resulted in the schism of the Blessed One’s community of disciples?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is by the Tathāgata himself that these actions were performed and accumulated in previous births—as before—until: 'Indeed, for embodied beings, [actions] bear fruit.'"

The Story of an Ṛṣi Living in the Countryside (Concerning a Previous Birth of the Buddha and Devadatta): "Once upon a time, monks, in a certain hermitage endowed with roots, flowers, fruits, and water, adorned with various trees and frequented by many flocks of birds, there lived an Ṛṣi together with five [disciples]."
He was the leader of hundreds of seers.
Once, while traveling on a tour through the countryside, another seer arrived at that hermitage; however, he was not properly honored by that [first] seer.
Filled with indignation, he caused a schism in his assembly, saying:
"This wicked-minded seer knows nothing at all;
for what purpose do you remain in his presence?"
"Come! Come with me! I shall establish you in the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā).
Being thus divided, they remained steadfast through the instruction of that seer (ṛṣi).
That seer perceived:
"These seers of mine have been alienated by this evildoer";
he then began to conciliate him.
"Venerable one, do not cause a schism in the assembly;
this is not the dharma of a seer.
Even so, he still causes a schism.
Thinking, "He does not remain," that seer became dejected and remained there by means of a strategic device.
When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise;
they are compassionate toward the lowly and the miserable, frequent remote lodgings and seats, and are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
Then, a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering through the countryside, arrived at the hermitage of that seer; he saw him, who was pleasing in body and possessed of a peaceful deportment,
and upon seeing him, he became full of faith.
Having performed services for him, he made a false vow:
"Since this wicked seer has caused a schism in my assembly, may I too cause a schism in the assembly of this one who has attained mastery over all that is to be known.
Monks, what do you think? That provincial seer who caused a schism in the assembly of that seer at that time and on that occasion was none other than I myself.
He who was that resident seer Devadatta at that time and on that occasion was he.
Because I split his assembly, through the ripening of that karma, he made a false aspiration and split my Saṅgha.
Thus, monks, regarding actions that are entirely black, as previously stated—thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, behold how Devadatta, by making those who were outside his circle insiders and those who were insiders outsiders, has won over the assembly."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, he deprived me of my assembly by bringing those who were outside within and casting those who were inside out."
Let that be heard:
the story of a jackal named Śatadru.
(Concerning a previous life of Devadatta:
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain place there lived a jackal. He was exceedingly greedy and roamed about both in the forest and in the village.
Wandering on in due order, he entered the house of a blue dyer and fell into a vat of blue dye;
he was seized by a sense of revulsion.
Not far from him stood a heap of ashes;
he fell upon it and rolled from side to side;
then, with even greater loathing for his body, he fell into the water.
Having risen and set out, he was touched by the rays of the sun and turned the color of a dark-blue sapphire;
when he was seen by jackals,
they fled in all directions.
Standing at a distance, they asked: "Who are you? Or from where have you come? He replied: (SBV II 212)
"I am named Śatadru, consecrated by Śakra, the lord of the gods, to the sovereignty over four-footed creatures. The jackals reflected: "This is one of unprecedented appearance."
"Surely this must be so," the jackals informed all the quadrupeds;
the lions reflected:
"Who is this person superior to us who will become the king of four-footed creatures?
Let us go now;
let us inform our own herd-leader."
Their leader lived in a certain part of a mountain;
he was a maned lion wearing a cloth band.
They informed him of this.
He gave an order to another four-footed creature:
"Go and examine the lord of four-footed creatures to see whether he has been seen by any other four-footed creature or not.
Having gone there, he examined him and found that he was one never seen before.
Surrounded by all four-footed creatures, with the exception of lions,
he went to him and reported what he had seen;
having heard this, he approached him surrounded by a pride of lions.
Surrounded by many four-footed creatures and mounted upon the back of an elephant, he wanders about;
surrounding him, lions go along,
and after them, tigers.
Beyond those are the four-footed animals;
far outside of them are the jackals;
his mother dwells in another mountain thicket.
He sent a jackal to her, saying:
"Come, enjoy the kingdom of your son";
she replied:
"What is his retinue like? he asked. He replied:
"Lions, tigers, and elephants constitute his inner retinue."
"But we are outsiders," they said.
She replied, "Go; he is ruined."
She spoke this verse:
"I dwell happily in a bower of this mountain; at ease, I drink the cool water."
"As long as he does not hear the sound of a jackal, that elephant travels happily. Having said this, he departed. He then informed those jackals:
"This is merely a jackal, the king of quadrupeds;
I have seen his mother,
who dwells in that mountain thicket."
They said:
"If that is so, we shall find out whether he is a jackal or not;
for it is the nature of jackals that they howl upon hearing the cry of another jackal."
The hairs on his body will fall out;
jackals will begin to howl;
he reflects:
If I do not cry out,
my body hairs will surely fall off; if I were to descend from the elephant's shoulder and cry out, [the hairs would remain].
"These men will kill me;
I shall cry out right here! and even while still upon the back of the elephant, he began to cry out.
The elephant realized, "A jackal is carrying me";
he threw him down and crushed him with his feet; then a deity spoke this verse: (SBV II 213)
"Or he for whom those who are internal have been made external, or those who are external have been made internal—he likewise goes to his destruction, just as the jackal did by the elephant.
"What do you think, monks? That jackal at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Devadatta."

Even then, having excluded those who were insiders and included those who were outsiders, he met with disaster through his misconduct; even now, by excluding the insiders and including the outsiders, he has lost the assembly— Devadatta, becoming angry with Kokālika and Khaṇḍadravya.
When the assembly of Devadatta was taken away by the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, Devadatta then began to beat Kokālika and Khaṇḍadravya,
saying, "The assembly has been lost to me by you two!
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, venerable sir, how Devadatta’s assembly has been taken away by others,
and how suffering has been produced for others by him.
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it was not only now; even in the past, his wife was carried off by another,
and suffering was caused by him to others.
Let that be heard:
the story of the elephant (concerning a previous life of Devadatta).
In the past, monks, there lived a leader of an elephant herd in a certain region.
Among them, a certain female elephant was highly esteemed by another elephant; she was excessively attached to a certain young calf.
She said to that young elephant,
"Let us flee";
he replied:
"What is that means by which we may escape?
She replied,
"I know a means."
The elephant was addressed by the two of them:
"Let us bathe; let us descend into the lake. He descended.
She said,
"Let us see which of us remains submerged for the longer time. That mass of delusion then submerged himself in the water together with her.
She rose and fled with a young elephant;
after the elephant had stood there for a long time, he arose and did not see her.
He reflected:
"I shall dive in again, lest I suffer defeat";
having dived in once more, he remained there for a long time with his tusks firmly embedded, his life-breath having nearly departed;
when he emerged, he did not see that female elephant.
He began to agitate that lake here and there;
by him, many living beings there—fish, turtles, frogs, and so forth—were brought to ruin through his misconduct.
A deity spoke this verse: (SBV II 214)
"Vṛndī said, 'He is very great, yet he possesses no wisdom.
His wife was carried off by another, and others are the sharers of his suffering.
What do you think, monks? He who was that noble elephant at that time and on that occasion was Devadatta."
Even then, his wife was carried off by another;
he caused suffering to others.
This is the summary verse (uddāna).
The wave, the visible [result], and the killing by Utpalavarṇā;
the bowl, the triad, and likewise the milk; Gopikā and the act of seeking forgiveness; the bones, the stūpa, and finally the bird’s footprint.

The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, behold how the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, while awaiting the turn of Devadatta, have obtained their own turn."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, while Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were waiting for Devadatta's downfall, they obtained his downfall."
Let that be heard:
the story of a leader of thieves (concerning a previous life of Devadatta, etc.).
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain mountain village there lived a teacher of archery.
He took a wife from a family of equal status,
and he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, after some time his wife became pregnant;
when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth,
and a daughter was born.

For her, having performed an extensive birth ceremony for twenty-one days— three times seven days— a name was established in accordance with her family; she was reared, nurtured, and grew up to become a young woman.
The master of archery reflected:
"This girl must not be given by me to anyone on account of their beauty, nor their moral character, nor even their wealth;
rather, she should be given to whoever becomes proficient in my presence in five specific areas."
"This [daughter] is to be given by me to him.
And from his presence, two young men were trained in archery; among them, one became accomplished in the five branches of the science.
But the second became skilled in the art of cutting;
he was given that girl by him,
while the other, having become filled with resentment, entered into the midst of thieves.
He became the commander of five hundred thieves;
having blocked the road at a certain location, he stood there waiting.
Then that first man married her, placed her upon a chariot, and set out for his own home.
When the caravan, fearing bandits, came to a halt while moving forward,
he said: "Sirs, go on!"
"Why do you stand here? they asked.
They replied, "The road has been blocked by thieves."
He said:
"Noble ladies, go;
what will they do?"
He set out;
the caravan traders said, "Sirs, let him go."
"Let us wait;
it is possible that he will cause himself to be torn apart and cause his wife to be taken away."
The thieves climbed a tree and remained there, surveying the directions;
they saw him mounted upon the chariot and said:
"Sirs, a man mounted on a chariot is approaching"; thus the bandit chief dispatched a messenger,
saying, "Turn back the chariot."
He said:
"Sirs, grant the exemption from taxes due to a hero to Śūra.
They replied:
"We too are heroes," they said;
five thieves were sent by the general,
and they were killed by him.
In this way, twenty arrived and they too were killed;
eventually, all were killed.
Only one general remained;
taking up his sword, he stood at the front and began to discharge arrows.
He cut them with his sword;
then he discharged a quiver containing five hundred arrows,
and he cut all of them with his sword.
A single arrow remained lodged there; he would not release it.
Then the girl said:
"Release the arrow! Why do you remain standing?
he asked, and he replied:
This alone is what remains;
if this is liberated,
I am destroyed.
"And you were carried off.
Then that girl, while yawning, began to bind her braid;
as she was doing so, the bandit commander began to gaze intently at her.
Struck in a vital organ by that arrow, as he was dying, he spoke this verse:
"I was not killed by the charioteer; I was killed by the fickle, evil-minded one."
"I, who was in the midst of battle, gazed upon the face of a young woman.
What do you think, monks? At that time, on that occasion, the charioteer was Śāriputra;
at that time, on that occasion, the girl was Maudgalyāyana.
He who was that chief of thieves, Devadatta, was at that time and on that occasion;
then, while these two were searching for an opportunity against him, they found an opportunity; even now, while these two are searching for an opportunity against him, they have found an opportunity.
The Fruit of the Monastic Life in the Visible World: Ajātaśatru Visits the Buddha 1. The Buddha, the Blessed One, had entered the rains retreat at Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta’s mango grove near Rājagṛha.
Then, on that very night of the full moon in the month of Āṣāḍha, during the bright moonlight, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha [went there].

When the time for the commencement of the rains had arrived, being well-known, distinguished, and full on the night of the full moon of the month of Āṣāḍha, he went to the upper terrace of his palace and addressed his ministers:
"O village chiefs, on such a moonlit night as this, during the commencement of the rains, when it is well-known, distinguished, and full on the night of the full moon of Āṣāḍha, what should we do?"

2. Then a certain concubine said this to King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī: "O Lord, on such a night as this—bright with moonlight, during the month of Āṣāḍha at the commencement of the rains, well-known, distinguished, full, and being the day of the full moon—since Your Majesty is provided with and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure..."
"Let us play, enjoy ourselves, and amuse ourselves; I consider this to be what must be done for Your Majesty.
Then, a certain concubine spoke thus:
"O King, on such a night as this—bright with moonlight, during the month of Āṣāḍha at the commencement of the rainy season, well-known and distinguished—"
On the full moon of the Pūrṇamāsī, when the King, wandering along the processional paths of the city of Rājagṛha,
is provided with and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, and plays, enjoys himself, and amuses himself— this, I consider,
is what ought to be done for the King.
4. Prince Udāyibhadra spoke thus:

"O Lord, on such a night as this—bright with moonlight, during the month of Āṣāḍha at the commencement of the rains, well-known, distinguished, full, and on the day of the full moon—if Your Majesty were to mobilize a fourfold army, including the elephant corps..."
Having led the body of chariots, the body of cavalry, and the body of infantry into another kingdom or foreign territory, and having fought a great battle,
if one has won the battle but then retreats from the front of the battlefield while still defeated—
this, I consider, is what ought to be done by Your Majesty.
5. Then a certain elder minister spoke thus:

"O Lord, on such a night as this—bright with moonlight, during the month of Āṣāḍha at the commencement of the rains, well-known, distinguished, full, and on the day of the full moon—this Lord Pūraṇa Kāśyapa is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, and a teacher of a group."
He is esteemed as one of virtuous form by many people and is honored by a great multitude of folk; he is the leader of about five hundred Ājīvikas.
He has entered the rains retreat here in Rājagṛha;
let Your Majesty attend upon him.
"I consider this to be a duty for Your Majesty.
Then another elder minister spoke thus:
"O King, on such a moonlit night as this..."

On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, the occasion for entering the rains-retreat— well-known, well-marked, and complete— the venerable Maskarin Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana,
and likewise the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, who is a member of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, and esteemed as a holy man, [arrived].
Honored by a great multitude and a vast assembly, he has entered the rains retreat right here in this very city of Rājagṛha;
Your Majesty should attend upon him;
I consider this to be a service that Your Majesty ought to perform.
At that time, Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta was seated and present in that very assembly.
Then King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha addressed Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta:
"O Jīvaka, why are you silent?"
"Why do you not speak? He replied:
"O King, on such a night as this, under the moonlight of the month of Āṣāḍha at the commencement of the rainy season—a night so well-known and distinguished—"

On this full-moon day of the Pūrṇamāsī, this Blessed One, a god who is a community leader, a member of a group, a teacher of a group, esteemed as virtuous by many people, and honored by a great multitude, has entered the rains retreat right here in Rājagṛha, in our very mango grove; let the King attend upon him.
"I consider this to be a service for Your Majesty.
Now at that time, the mind of King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha was inclined toward the Blessed One, leaning toward the Blessed One, and tending toward the Blessed One.
Then King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, said this to Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya:
"Go, Jīvaka, have the royal elephant harnessed so that I may mount it and go this very day to visit the Blessed One.
"So be it, Your Majesty," replied Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya, having assented to King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī.

Having equipped a great state elephant and five hundred female elephants, each accompanied by five hundred attendants holding torches in their hands, he mounted them one by one and approached King Ajātaśatru of Magadha,
the son of Vaidehī; having approached him, he spoke thus to King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī:
"The great state elephant of the King is equipped;
now, O King, let the Lord do as he deems timely.
Then King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, having mounted the great state elephant, together with about five hundred...
Accompanied by hundreds of female attendants, each mounted upon a female elephant and holding lamps in their hands,

he set out from Rājagṛha toward the presence of the Blessed One, in order to see, approach, and pay homage to the Blessed One. At that time, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha was at war with the Vṛjis.

Then, immediately after King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, had departed from Rājagṛha, fear arose within him, a state of trepidation came over him, and his hair stood on end: "Could it be that Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya wishes to have me killed, or does he wish to deceive me?"
Having understood, "Does he wish to hand me over to executioners or to enemies? Jīvika, who was supported by the prince, said this to him:
"Jīvika, do you not wish to have me killed, or do you wish to have me imprisoned, or do you wish to deceive me?"
"Or do you wish to hand me over to executioners, adversaries, or enemies?

He replied: "No, Your Majesty, I do not wish to have you killed, nor do I wish to have you bound, nor do I wish to deceive you, nor do I wish to hand you over to executioners, adversaries, or enemies.
Then King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha said this to Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya:
"How large is that Blessed One’s retinue? "His retinue consists of more than twelve hundred and fifty monks.

"Aha, Jīvaka! Why is it that you do not wish to have me killed, nor wish to have me bound, nor wish to hand me over to executioners, adversaries, or enemies—such that now, with such a retinue, not even the sound of a cough is heard?"
"O King, that Blessed One desires little noise, delights in little noise, is content with little noise,
and speaks in praise of having little noise;
his assembly likewise has little noise."
"Therefore, Your Majesty, dispatch the great state elephant with all possible speed;
for the light of oil-lamps is now seen in the arena.
Then King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, dispatched the great state elephant with all possible speed.
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground was passable for a vehicle, he alighted from it and entered the grove on foot.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated in the midst of the community of monks, like a lake—clear, serene, and undisturbed.
Then King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha, having traversed the circular courtyard, addressed Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya:
"Jīvaka, where is that Blessed One? "Your Majesty, that Blessed One is seated in the midst of the community of monks, like a lake that is clear, serene, and undisturbed.
Then King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, may Prince Udāyibhadra be endowed with that same kind of mental self-control and tranquility as the Blessed One and the community of monks are endowed with.
"Excellent, excellent, Great King! I shall explain it to you."
"Great King, [this is] your own affection;
Great King, sit down upon your own seat.
Ajātaśatru asks the Buddha whether it is possible to point out any visible benefit to be derived from asceticism.
12. Then King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, we would ask the Blessed One about a certain matter, if he would grant us the opportunity for an answer to our question."

"Ask, Great King, whatever you desire. "Venerable Sir, these are those engaged in various crafts and occupations; namely: garland-makers, reed-workers, mat-makers, grass-cutters, charioteers, elephant-riders, horse-riders, chariot-warriors, and swordsmen."
Archers, attendants, servants, those who live on alms, fierce men, heroes, leapers, great wrestlers, princes, courtiers, hairdressers, and bath-attendants—
they each perform their duties through their respective crafts and occupations.
They give gifts,
perform meritorious deeds, and support their dependents; endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves.
"Is it possible to designate such a visible fruit of the ascetic life?
Do you recall, Great King, having previously asked other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas such a question?
"I do recall it, Venerable Sir."
Ajātaśatru recounts how he put this very same question to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others, and how each of them explained it to him according to his own particular doctrine.
14. "Venerable sir, there was one occasion when I approached Pūraṇa Kāśyapa; having approached him, I spoke thus to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa:"

"Venerable Kāśyapa, these people in the world are craftsmen and practitioners of various arts and trades; namely: garland-makers, reed-workers, weavers, grass-harvesters, charioteers, elephant-riders, horse-riders, chariot-warriors, swordsmen, archers, attendants, servants, alms-gatherers, the Ugras, the Śūras, the Praskandins, and the Mahānagnas."
The princes were attendants, ritual specialists, and bath-attendants;
they performed their duties according to their respective crafts and occupations and gave gifts.
They perform meritorious deeds and support their dependents;
endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves.
"It is indeed possible to designate a visible fruit of the ascetic life for those of such a nature.
He then said: "Great King, I hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine:
there is no gift, there is no [offering]."
"There is no sacrifice, there is no oblation, there is no good conduct; there is no fruit or ripening of deeds, whether good or evil.

There is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father; there are no spontaneously born beings. There are no arhats in the world who have attained rightly, who have practiced rightly, and who, having realized and personally witnessed this world and the other world through their own higher knowledge in this very life, declare them."
"Birth is exhausted for me, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, and I know there is no further state of existence beyond this.

[They hold that] while the living being lives here, it is cut off, perishes, and ceases to exist after death; the person's physical aggregation, composed of the four great elements, is destroyed. At the moment of death, its earth-element returns to the earth-body.
In water, the water-body; in fire, the fire-body;
in wind, the wind-body.
The sense organs dissolve back into space;
men, with a bier as the fifth, carry a man to the cremation ground, and after the burning, he is no longer perceived;
the offerings turn to ashes.
"The bones remain pigeon-colored";
this is the gift conceived by Dṛpta,
while the acceptance is conceived by Paṇḍita.

In this regard, all those who maintain the doctrine of existence (astivādin) speak what is empty, vain, and false; both the fool and the wise alike, after passing away, are cut off and perish, and do not exist beyond death. Venerable sir, it is just as if one, when asked about mangoes, were to explain them by means of breadfruit.

"Or, if asked about *lakucas*, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa would explain them as mangoes. When I asked him about the visible fruit of the ascetic life (*sāndṛṣṭika-śrāmaṇyaphala*), he explained it as non-existence.
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me: 'It would not be fitting for a discerning man such as myself to personally disparage a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa of good repute who dwells in my own territory.'"
"Venerable sir, I neither approved nor rejected what Pūraṇa Kāśyapa said; without approving or rejecting it, I rose from my seat and departed.
[This refers to the theory of] Maskarī Gośāliputra.
17. I went to where Maskarī Gośāliputra was; having approached him, I said this to Maskarī Gośāliputra:
"Venerable Maskarī, these various people in the world are engaged in the work of various arts and crafts."

Namely: garland-makers, reed-workers, basket-makers, grass-cutters, charioteers, elephant-riders, horse-riders, chariot-warriors, swordsmen, archers, attendants, servants, alms-collectors, fierce men, heroes, leapers, great wrestlers, princes, courtiers, barbers, and bath-attendants.
They perform their duties through their respective crafts and occupations,
give gifts,
and cultivate merit.
They support their dependents;
provided and fully endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves.
It is indeed possible to designate such a visible fruit of the ascetic life for those of this kind.
18. He spoke thus: "Great King, I hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine: there is no cause and no condition for the defilement of sentient beings."
Beings are defiled without cause and without condition;
there is no cause and no condition by which beings are purified;
beings are purified without cause and without condition.
There is no cause, there is no condition; the ignorance and lack of vision of sentient beings arise without cause and without condition;
there is no cause, there is no condition.
Do the knowledge and vision of sentient beings arise without cause and without condition?
There is no power, no vigor, no power and vigor, no human effort, no exertion, and no human effort and exertion.

There is no action performed by oneself, nor action performed by another; all beings, being devoid of self-agency or agency by another, are without power, weak, helpless, lacking in vigor, and lacking in prowess. They experience pleasure and pain as they are transformed by their fixed destiny and inherent nature—namely, within the six classes of birth.
It is just as if a man, when asked about mangoes, were to explain them in terms of breadfruit.

Just as one asked about *lakuca* fruits might instead explain *āmra* fruits, even so, when I questioned Maskarī Gośāliputra regarding the visible fruit of the ascetic life (*sāndṛṣṭika-śrāmaṇyaphala*), he explained it in terms of causelessness (*ahetutā*).
Then this thought occurred to me:
"How could a discerning man such as I now disparage before his face a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is esteemed for his virtuous appearance and dwells among the people?"
Thus, I neither approved nor rejected the words spoken by the wandering ascetic Gośāliputra;
having neither approved nor rejected them, I rose from my seat and departed.
[This concludes] Sañjayī Vairaṭṭīputra’s theory.
20. So I approached Sañjayī Vairaṭṭīputra; having approached him, I said this to Sañjayī Vairaṭṭīputra:
"Venerable Sañjayī, these people in the world are practitioners of various crafts and occupations."

They were as follows: garland-makers, reed-workers, mat-makers, grass-cutters, charioteers, elephant-riders, horsemen, chariot-fighters, swordsmen, archers, attendants, servants, alms-collectors, fierce men, heroes, leapers, great wrestlers, princes, courtiers, barbers, and bath-attendants.
They perform their duties through their respective crafts and occupations,
give gifts,
and cultivate merit.
They support their dependents;
provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves.
It is indeed possible to designate such a visible fruit of the ascetic life for those of such a nature.
21. He spoke thus: "Great King, I hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine:

for one who acts or causes to act, who cuts or causes to cut, who cooks or causes to cook, who harms or causes to harm, who injures living beings, who takes what is not given, and who engages in sexual misconduct while being fully conscious—"
For one who speaks falsehoods, drinks intoxicants, breaks into dwellings, unties knots, commits robbery, stands as a highwayman, or carries out the plundering of a village;

Whether it be the destruction of a city or the destruction of a countryside by means of a wheel with edges as sharp as razors— one who cuts, pierces, crushes, and utterly destroys all living beings upon this great earth,
having cut, pierced, crushed, and utterly destroyed them all, making them into a single heap of flesh, a mass of flesh, a pile of flesh;

For one who trains himself thus, there is no evil on that account, nor is there any arrival of evil on that account. One might come along cutting and breaking through the south bank of the river Gaṅgā, or one might come along giving and sacrificing on the north bank of the river Gaṅgā;
yet there is no merit or evil on that account.
"There is no acquisition of merit or demerit resulting from this;
namely, that one who acts with generosity, self-control, restraint, beneficial conduct, and impartiality does not actually produce merit.
"Venerable sir, it is just as if a man, when asked about mangoes, were to explain them by means of *lakucha* fruits."
Just as one who is asked about *lakuca* fruits might explain them as mangoes, so it was with him;
when I asked Sañjayī Vairaṭṭīputra a question regarding the visible fruit of the ascetic life, he explained it in terms of non-action.
This occurred to me:
"How could a wise man like me now disparage a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa residing in this region, who is esteemed as virtuous?
Thus, I neither approved nor rejected what Sañjayin Vairaṭṭīputra had said; without approving or rejecting it, I rose from my seat and departed.
23. So I went to where Ajita Keśakambala was; having approached him, I said this to Ajita Keśakambala:

"Venerable Ajita, these are those in the world who occupy various crafts and occupations; namely: garland-makers, reed-workers, basket-makers, grass-cutters, charioteers, elephant-riders, horse-riders, chariot-warriors, swordsmen, archers, attendants, servants, alms-gatherers, the Ugras, the Śūras, the Praskandins, and the Mahānagnas."
The princes were attendants, barbers, and bath-attendants;
they performed their duties according to their respective crafts and occupations and gave gifts.
They perform meritorious deeds and support their dependents;
endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves.
"It is indeed possible to designate such a visible fruit of the ascetic life.
When this was said, Ajita Keśakambala spoke thus to me:
"Great King, I hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine:"
There are these seven bodies which are uncreated, not made by a creator, unproduced, not fashioned by a fashioner, indestructible, immovable, and situated like a stalk of grass.

Which are the seven? Namely: the earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the wind-body, pleasure, pain, and the living soul as the seventh. These are the seven bodies which are uncreated, not made by a creator, unproduced, not fashioned by a fashioner, and indestructible.
Immovable like a stalk of grass, they remain as they are;
they do not stir, nor do they undergo transformation.
They do not harm one another for the sake of merit or for the sake of evil; nor for the sake of both merit and evil; nor for the sake of pleasure or for the sake of pain.
Whether for pleasure or pain;

even that man who cuts off another man's head does not harm anything at all in the world, whether moving or stationary, for the weapon passes through the interval between the seven elements (kāyas), and no living being (jīva) is killed therein.
In that regard, there is no one at all who kills or causes to kill, who cuts or causes to cut, nor anyone who remembers or causes to remember.
Whether one has awakened them or caused them to be awakened;
whether one has informed them or caused them to be informed:
these are the fourteen thousand principal origins, sixty thousand great modes of practice, and six hundred and five.

And three types of karma, two types of karma, one type of karma and half a type of karma; sixty-two types of karma, sixty-two intermediate beginnings, seven designations, one hundred and twenty hells,
one hundred and thirty faculties, thirty-six dust-elements, forty-nine thousand families of nāgas, and forty-nine [thousand].

Forty-nine thousand families of Suparṇins, forty-nine thousand families of Ājīvikas, forty-nine thousand families of Acelakas, forty-nine thousand families of Nirgranthas; seven kalpas of perception, seven kalpas of non-perception; seven [classes of] gods, seven Piśācas, seven Ādityas, seven humans, and seven lakes.

Seven hundred lakes, seven lower realms, seven hundred lower realms, seven dreams, seven hundred dreams, seven awakenings, seven hundred awakenings, seven precipices, seven hundred precipices, six noble lineages, ten increases, and eight stages of the great person.
These eighty-four thousand great aeons, which the fool and the wise alike must traverse and wander through before making an end of suffering;
it is just as when a small ball of thread is thrown into the air, it unwinds until it reaches the ground—
exactly so do the fool and the wise alike traverse these eighty-four thousand great aeons.
Having transmigrated, they bring an end to suffering;
in this regard, there is no ascetic or brahmin who could say:
"By means of this morality, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall ripen unripened karma, or having touched ripened karma, I shall vomit it out."
This happiness and suffering are constant;
neither increase nor decrease can be discerned;
thus, or perhaps not, has saṃsāra been weighed.

"25. 'Just as, venerable sir, a man asked about mangoes might explain jackfruits, or asked about jackfruits might explain mangoes, even so Ajita Keśakambala, when asked about the visible fruit of the ascetic life, explained the purification of cyclic existence.
Then this thought occurred to me:'"
"How could a wise man like me now disparage in the presence of a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, esteemed as virtuous, who dwells within my own realm?
Thus, I neither approved nor rejected what Ajita Keśakambala had said;
having neither approved nor rejected it, I rose from my seat and departed.
26. So I went to where the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra was; having approached him, I said this to the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra:

"Venerable sir, these sons of the kinsmen are engaged in various worldly crafts and occupations; namely, garland-makers, reed-workers, basket-makers, grass-cutters, charioteers, elephant-riders, horse-riders, and chariot-warriors."
Sword-bearers, bowmen, attendants, servants, those who eat from shared morsels, fierce ones, heroes, leapers, great wrestlers, princes, courtiers, barbers, and bath-attendants—
each performed their duties according to their respective crafts and occupations.
They give gifts, perform meritorious deeds, and support their dependents.
Provided with and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves;
it is indeed possible to designate such a visible fruit of the ascetic life for those of such a kind.
He spoke thus:

"I am, Great King, one who holds such a view and speaks thus: whatever this person experiences, all that is caused by the past; it is the exhaustion of former karmas through asceticism, and the total eradication of new karmas through non-performance."
Thus, there is no outflow in the future; from the absence of outflow comes the exhaustion of karma;
from the exhaustion of karma comes the exhaustion of suffering.
"From the destruction of suffering, the making of an end to suffering occurs.

"Venerable sir, it is just as if a man, when asked about mangoes, were to explain jackfruit, or when asked about jackfruit, were to explain mangoes; even so, venerable sir, when I asked the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra about the fruit of the ascetic life visible in this very world, he explained it to me only in terms of causes produced in the past."
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
"It would not be fitting for me to personally disparage a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is esteemed as virtuous and dwells within my own domain.
Thus, I neither approved nor rejected what was spoken by the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
Without expressing approval or disapproval, he rose from his seat and departed.
I then approached where Kakuda Kātyāyana was.
Having approached Kakuda Kātyāyana, I said this to him:

"Venerable Kātyāyana, these people in the world occupy various positions of craft and occupation; namely, garland-makers, reed-workers, mat-makers, grass-cutters, charioteers, elephant-riders, horse-riders, and chariot-warriors."
Swordsmen, archers, attendants, servants, those who eat from morsels, fierce men, heroes, leapers, great wrestlers,
princes, courtiers, ritualists, and bath-attendants—
each performed their duties according to their respective crafts and occupations.
They give gifts, perform meritorious deeds, and support their dependents.
"Endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves;
it is indeed possible to designate such a visible fruit of the ascetic life for those of such a kind.
When this was said, Kakuda Kātyāyana spoke this to me:
"I am such-and-such a person, Great King, holding this view and speaking thus:
if someone were to approach me and ask, 'Is there a world beyond?', and he should think, 'There is a world beyond,' then to him I would answer his question: 'There is a world beyond.'"

If asked, I might explain: "There is no other world," or "There both is and is not another world," or "There neither is nor is not another world," or "It is thus," or "It is not thus," or "It is otherwise," or "It is neither so nor not so," or "It is not that it is not so," or "It is not that it is not so"— that such [views] regarding the other world might exist.

"Whether it be 'no' or 'not' or 'is it not? or 'is it not?', regarding the question of whether there is a world beyond, when asked, I would not explain it as 'no,' 'not,' 'is it not? or 'is it not? "Venerable sir, I reflect thus:
Of all those who have gone forth and dwell here in Rājagṛha, this Kakuda Kātyāyana is the most foolish, the most dull-witted, and the most like a block of wood."
The thought occurred to me:
"It would not be fitting for me to personally discourage a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is esteemed as virtuous and a resident of this realm.
Therefore, I neither approved nor rejected what Kakuda Kātyāyana had said.
Without expressing approval or disapproval, he rose from his seat and departed.
Then Ajātaśatru addressed this question to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, I ask the Blessed One about this matter: regarding these various worldly craftsmen and those engaged in various occupations..."

Namely: garland-makers, basket-weavers, mat-makers, grass-cutters, charioteers, elephant-riders, horse-riders, chariot-warriors, swordsmen, archers, attendants, servants, alms-collectors, fierce men, heroes, leapers, great wrestlers, princes, courtiers, barbers, and bath-attendants.
They perform their duties through their respective crafts and occupations,
give gifts,
and cultivate merit.
They support their dependents;
endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves.
Is it possible to designate such a visible fruit of the ascetic life for those of such a kind?
The Buddha’s reply: 33. "In that case, Great King, I shall question you; answer as you see fit."
It is just as if, O Great King, you had a servant here— a messenger, one to be commanded, a dependent who goes wherever he is told to go—

and he were to see you situated upon the upper terrace of your palace, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, sporting, delighting, and enjoying yourself with music performed by women alone.
Having seen this, it would occur to him:
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, is a person;
I too am a person; there is no difference between King Ajātaśatru of Magadha and me.

The son of Vaidehī, having previously performed meritorious deeds and accumulated them, now, while situated upon the upper terrace of his palace, plays, enjoys himself, and amuses himself with music performed by women.
"What if I were to live having undertaken some wholesome quality (kuśala-dharma)?
Which wholesome quality, indeed, should I undertake and live by?"
