"What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with perfect faith go forth from the home life into homelessness? Having reflected thus, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes,
and with perfect faith went forth from the home life into homelessness.
For as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from taking life;
having abandoned taking what is not given, unchastity, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, he should abstain from wrong view.
Then your servants, wandering about among the people of the countryside, might see him.
And upon seeing him, it would occur to them:

"This is that slave, servant, messenger, and dependent of King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha, who was to go wherever he pleased; yet, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he has gone forth with perfect faith."
Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, he abandons taking life for as long as he lives and abstains from taking life;
having abandoned taking what is not given, unchastity, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, he abstains from wrong view.
"What if we were to go to the king and inform him?

Having approached him, they would say: "May your majesty know this: that servant, messenger, subordinate, and dependent of yours, who used to go wherever he pleased, has now shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and correctly..."
Thus, out of faith, he went forth from the home life into homelessness;
for as long as life lasted, having abandoned the taking of life, he abstained from taking life.
"Having abandoned taking what is not given, unchastity, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, one possesses right view.
What do you think, Great King? Would you say this: "Go, sirs"?
"Bring that man back;
he shall once again be my slave, servant, attendant, and dependent, one who goes wherever he is led at will. "No, Venerable Sir."
I would not approach him for the sake of seeing him otherwise;
whatever salutation, prostration, rising to meet him, joining of palms, or respectful service I previously performed for him, I myself would perform for him;
and for as long as I live, I would offer him invitations consisting of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
"What do you think, Great King? Is it not the case that, this being so, I have thereby demonstrated the visible fruit of asceticism?
It is true, Venerable Sir."
Thus has the Blessed One demonstrated the visible fruit of the ascetic life:

"Suppose, Great King, there were a householder who was a farmer, a provider, a sustainer, and one who increased the royal treasury; and he were to see you seated upon the upper terrace of your palace, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, sporting, delighting, and enjoying yourself with music performed by women."
And having seen him, it would further occur to him:
"This King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, is a human being;
I too am a human being."

"It is not otherwise: because he has previously performed and accumulated meritorious deeds, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehiputra of Magadha now, having ascended to the upper terrace of his palace, sports, enjoys himself, and amuses himself with instrumental music performed by women alone.
What if I were to live having undertaken some wholesome quality?"
"What wholesome dharma, then, should I undertake and abide by?

What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with right faith go forth from the home to the homeless life? Having reflected thus, he shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes.
Having properly clothed himself with robes out of faith, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness;
for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from taking life;
and having abandoned taking what is not given, unchastity, false speech, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, he should abstain from wrong view.
Then your men from the city and the countryside, while wandering about, might see him;
and having seen him, it would occur to them:
"This is that very farmer, the householder, the provider and sustainer for King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha."
Increasing the royal treasury, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron-colored robes, and with perfect faith went forth from the home to the homeless life;
for as long as life lasted, having abandoned the taking of life, he abstained from taking life.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, unchastity, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, he abstains from wrong view and possesses right view.
"What if we were to go to the king and inform him?
Having approached you, they would report: "May Your Majesty know that there is a certain farmer, a householder, belonging to Your Majesty."
He was a provider and a sustainer who increased the royal treasury; having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he went forth from the home to the homeless life with perfect faith.
For as long as life lasted, he abandoned the taking of life and abstained from taking life.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, unchastity, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, he abstains from wrong view and possesses right view.
What do you think, Great King? Would you say this: "Go, sirs"?
"Bring that man here;
he shall once again be my farmer, my provider, and my sustainer."
"He increases the royal treasury," [he said].
"No, Venerable Sir;
rather, I myself would go to see him."
And as for those acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining of palms, and respectful conduct that he previously performed toward me, I myself would perform them for him;
and for as long as life lasts, I would offer him invitations consisting of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
What do you think, Great King—is it not the case that, this being so, I have demonstrated a visible fruit of the ascetic life?
"It is true, Bhadanta;
such being the case, the visible fruit of the ascetic life has been demonstrated by the Blessed One.

37. Here, Great King, a Teacher arises in the world, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a Teacher."
The Buddha, the Blessed One, is the teacher of gods and humans;
he teaches the Dharma, which is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; absolute, complete, pure, and radiant.
He teaches the holy life;
a householder or a householder’s son hears that Dharma.
Having heard that Dharma, he seeks purity from the Teacher in three respects, namely: in the quality of greed, in the quality of hatred, and in the quality of delusion.
Could it be that this venerable one still possesses that greed which is not abandoned, not fully understood, not ceased, and not eliminated,
such that being overcome by that greed and with his mind possessed by it, he might— while being ignorant— say "I am knowing," and while being without vision—
say "I am seeing"?
Or would he cause others to act in such a way that it would lead to their long-term misfortune, harm, and suffering? Or rather, does this venerable one not possess that greed which is unabandoned,
unrecognized, unceased, and not cast out— that greed by which, being overwhelmed and possessed in mind, though actually ignorant, he might say "I know," and though not seeing, [say] "I see"?
While being thus, one might say, "I am a seer," or might instruct others in such a way that it would lead to their long-term misfortune, harm, and suffering;
of him, this occurs:

Venerable sir, there exists no such greed in you that is unabandoned, unrecognized, unextinguished, or not cast out, by which greed— being overcome and possessed in mind— you might, while being ignorant,
claim "I am knowing," or while being without vision, claim "I am seeing";
or that you might instruct others in such a way that it would lead to their long-term misfortune, harm, and suffering.
For what reason?
Because those bodily formations, vocal formations, and mental formations of this venerable one are free from greed.
And this very Dharma he speaks, either in brief or in detail;

this Dharma of his is peaceful, sublime, profound, and of profound appearance; it is difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond the sphere of logic, not accessible to reasoning, subtle, refined, and to be realized by the wise and the learned.
And it was not easy for that venerable one to understand this, as he was entirely greedy;
yet this venerable one is not greedy; this venerable one is not greedy.
And when he perceives purity in this first quality of greed,
he then searches for it further in the second quality of hatred and the third quality of delusion.

Could it be that this Venerable One’s delusion has not been abandoned, not fully understood, not ceased, and not eliminated, such that being overwhelmed by that delusion and his mind possessed by it, he might— while being ignorant, claim "I am knowing," or while being sightless, claim "I am seeing";
or he might instruct others in such a way that it would lead to their harm for a long time?
Is it for his detriment and suffering? Or rather, does that delusion not exist for this venerable one— which is unabandoned, unrecognized, unceased, and not cast out—
by which delusion he is overwhelmed and possessed in mind, such that being ignorant, he would say "I know," and being without vision, [he would say] "I see"?
One might say, "I am a seer," or one might instruct others in such a way that it would lead to their misfortune, disadvantage, and suffering for a long time;
of such a person, this occurs:

This Venerable One has no such delusion that is unabandoned, unrecognized, unextinguished, or not cast out, by which delusion— overpowered and possessed in mind— he might, while being ignorant, say "I am knowing," or while being sightless, say "I am seeing";
or he might instruct others in such a way that it would lead to their long-term misfortune, harm, and suffering.
For what reason?
Because these bodily formations, vocal formations, and mental formations of this venerable one are those of one who is undeluded;
and he speaks this Dharma, either in brief or in detail.

His Dharma is peaceful, sublime, profound, and of profound appearance; it is difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond the sphere of logic, and not within the reach of reasoning; it is to be realized by the wise who are subtle, skillful, and learned.
And it is not easy for this venerable one to comprehend it, as he is thus utterly deluded.
"This venerable one is undeluded;
this venerable one is not deluded," when he perceives his purification in this third factor of delusion.
Then, he directs his faith toward that which possesses form;
having conceived faith, he trains himself thus:
"Dwelling in a household is a confinement, a dwelling place of dust."
And going forth is an open space;
this is not easy for one living as a householder in a home to practice throughout their entire life with absolute purity and complete integrity.
It is complete, pure, and utterly cleansed;
it is for the sake of practicing the holy life.
What if I were now to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with right faith go forth from the home to the homeless state?
Having reflected upon this, he abandons a great or small mass of wealth,
abandons a great or small circle of kinsmen, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron-colored robes,
and with right faith goes forth from the home to the homeless life. Having thus gone forth, he dwells as one possessed of virtue.

Restrained by the Prātimokṣa vow, perfected in conduct and sphere of activity, seeing danger even in the slightest faults, he encourages others [to do the same] and trains himself in the precepts of training;
having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from the taking of life.

Having laid aside the rod and laid aside weapons, modest and compassionate toward all beings, creatures, and living things—down to even an ant or a termite—he abstains from taking life. 38. Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, delights in what is given, and expects only what is given, relinquished, and released. Avoiding himself being a thief, greedy, impure, or unclean, he remains blameless, abstaining from taking what is not given.
He exists; having abandoned unchaste conduct, he abstains from unchaste conduct;
he is a practitioner of celibacy, refraining from misconduct, pure, clean, and free from the stench of impurity.
He abstains from sexual intercourse, is free from vulgar conduct, and refrains from unchastity.
Having abandoned false speech, he refrains from false speech;
he is a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, steadfast, and one who does not deceive the world—he thus refrains from false speech.
Having heard from these, he does not report it to those for the sake of creating a division among them;
nor, having heard from those, does he report it to these for the sake of creating a division among them.
He is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united; delighting in concord and rejoicing in concord, he utters speech that brings about concord.
He abstains from malicious speech;
having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech;
as for that speech which is harmful—

Having abandoned speech that is harsh, bitter to others, offensive to others, disliked by many people, unloved by many people, unpleasant to many people, disagreeable to many people, unconcentrated, and conducive to a lack of concentration— having abandoned such speech as this— one utters that speech which is gentle, pleasing to the ear, heart-pleasing, affectionate, polite, elegant, clear, intelligible, independent, not disagreeable, and not exhausting.
He speaks words such as these: "They are desired by many, beloved by many, dear to many, and pleasing to many; they are concentrated and conducive to concentration."

He abstains from harsh speech; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is factual, speaks what is meaningful, speaks according to the Dharma, and speaks what is well-considered.
He utters speech that is well-considered—timely, not incoherent, coherent, instructive, righteous, and endowed with purpose.
He abstains from frivolous speech (saṃbhinnapralāpa).
Having abandoned killing, binding, mutilating, beating, and seizing, he abstains from killing, binding, mutilating, beating, and seizing.
Having abandoned sleeping in a house with women present, he abstains from sleeping in a house with women present.

Having abandoned the acquisition of fields, houses, and shops, he abstains from the acquisition of fields, houses, and shops; having abandoned the acceptance of elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, and pigs, he abstains from the acceptance of elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, and pigs; having abandoned the acceptance of female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, he abstains from the acceptance of female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.

Having abandoned the acceptance of women, men, boys, and girls, he abstains from the acceptance of women, men, boys, and girls; having abandoned the acceptance of gold and silver, he abstains from the acceptance of gold and silver; having abandoned the acceptance of raw grain, he abstains from the acceptance of raw grain.
He eats but one meal a day; he abstains from food at night;
he has desisted from eating at improper times, moving only at the proper time and devoted to the practice of moving at the proper time.
He is content and fully satisfied with robes that merely suffice for the body;
he is content and fully satisfied with almsfood that merely fills the belly.
Wherever he went, he went with his bowl and robes;
just as a winged bird flies wherever it flies with its wings and feathers, even so was he content with the robe that served for the protection of the body.

Content with alms-food that merely fills his belly, he is content; wherever he goes, he goes equipped with his bowl and robes. 41. Just as, Great King, certain recluses and brahmins, while enjoying gifts given out of faith, dwell devoted to the practice of injuring various groups of seeds and various groups of living beings—namely, those from roots, from stems, from tips, from joints, and fifthly, from seeds—so too, from such a practice of injuring various groups of seeds and various groups of living beings, [the recluse abstains].
He abstains from these.

42. For instance, Your Majesty, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who, while enjoying gifts given out of faith, live devoted to the practice of amassing various kinds of stores; namely, stores of food, stores of drink, stores of clothing, stores of perfumes, and stores of garlands.
He abstains from the practice of engaging in various kinds of preparations for storage, such as keeping vessels nearby, flowers nearby, or fruits nearby.
43. Furthermore, Great King, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who, while consuming what is given in faith, live devoted to the practice of preparing high beds and grand couches;
that is to say, on chairs, divans, cushions, woolen rugs, stuffed mattresses, large coverlets, and embroidered spreads.
From such things as mattresses made of hair-cloth, elephant blankets, horse blankets, single-layered wool, thick wool, wool from the lower belly, shoulder wool, Kāliṅga coverlets, spread rugs,
and spread rugs with upper covers and cloths, along with red pillows at both ends— a monk abstains from the practice of undertaking high beds and grand couches.

44. Furthermore, Great King, there are certain recluses and brahmins who, while enjoying gifts given out of faith, dwell devoted to the practice of various forms of adornment and grooming; namely: massaging, bathing, rubbing with fragrant oils, wearing garlands, scents, and ointments, maintaining a fair complexion, manicuring the nails, cleaning the teeth, applying cosmetics to the face, using a mirror for the face, binding the topknot, using a staff, a stick, an umbrella, a sword, and a yak-tail fan.
Even such things as variegated sandals and new, unwashed garments with long fringes, which are of a kind that must be worn—a śramaṇa abstains from such engagement in various forms of adornment.
45. Furthermore, Great King, some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed the gifts of the faithful, dwell devoted to the practice of various spectacles.

Namely: elephant-fighting, horse-fighting, chariot-fighting, infantry-fighting, staff-fighting, fist-fighting, bull-fighting, buffalo-fighting, goat-fighting, ram-fighting, cock-fighting, quail-fighting, partridge-fighting,
cock-quail-partridge fighting, women’s fighting, men’s fighting, boys’ fighting, girls’ fighting, and at the watchtower in the city of Śobhitā during the festival.

At the top of a banner, at the head of an army, when troops are arrayed and visible, or when they wish to see a great assembly—out of such circumstances as these, the ascetic is one who abstains from the pursuit of engaging in various kinds of spectacles.
46. Furthermore, Great King, there are some ascetics and brahmins who, having consumed gifts given out of faith, dwell devoted to the pursuit of engaging in listening to various sounds.

Namely: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of conchs, the sound of drums, the sound of kettledrums, the sound of war-drums, the sound of kettles, the sound of dancing, the sound of singing, the sound of musical instruments, the sound of recitation, the sound of snapping fingers, the sound of hand-clapping, the sound of the *kumbha* and *tūṇīra* drums,
the *kavatī* and *kāveya* chants, variegated syllables, variegated words and phonemes, the proclamations of the Lokāyata, or in narrative tales.
He abstains from the pursuit of engaging with various sounds, such as when some people say, "We wish to hear [this]," or even other such things.

47. For instance, Great King, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who, having consumed gifts given out of faith, dwell devoted to the pursuit of engaging in various games of dice, deception, and gambling; namely, on an eight-row board, a ten-row board, at drawing lots, at *pare*, *ghaṭikā*, *cale*, *muṣkala*, and at following the movements of crooked dice.
Or, as some employ [divination] with a stick in their hand—by such means as these, a śramaṇa abstains from the practice of deceitful gambling enterprises.
48. Furthermore, Great King, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, having consumed what is given in faith, dwell devoted to the practice of engaging in various kinds of talk;
namely, talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks, and talk of clothing.

In talk of streets, talk of courtesans, tales of maidens, tales of the ocean, tales of the world, and tales of provincial ministers—a monk abstains from such engagement with the undertaking of various kinds of talk.
49. For instance, Your Majesty, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who, having consumed what is given in faith, dwell devoted to the undertaking of various disputatious talks.
For example: "You do not understand this Dharma and Vinaya; I understand this Dharma and Vinaya;
as I understand this Dharma and Vinaya day by day."
Just as you do not understand this Dharma and Vinaya day by day—
what is appropriate for me and what is inappropriate for you.
"This is consistent for me; that is inconsistent for you.
"What should have been said first, you said last."
What should have been said later, you said first;
you grasped too hastily; you have raised a point for the sake of debate that was already established against you.
"Abandon this dispute for the sake of releasing yourself from the dispute; you are caught, so explain yourself;
if you know a superior answer, speak when asked"—from such undertakings of engaging in various contentious discourses, the ascetic abstains.

50. "Furthermore, Great King, there are certain recluses and brahmins who, having consumed gifts given out of faith, maintain their livelihood through the wrong mode of life consisting in sending and dispatching messengers. They say to kings, royal ministers, brahmins, merchants, country folk, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders: 'Summon such-and-such a person here; send such-and-such a person there; send such-and-such a person here; summon such-and-such a person there. It is from such [practices] as these..."
The ascetic abstains from wrong livelihood consisting in acting as a messenger or sending messages.

51. For instance, Your Majesty, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who, while consuming what is given in faith, are deceivers, flatterers, soothsayers, and extortionists, seeking to obtain gain by means of gain.
They maintain their livelihood by means of gain through hypocrisy, flattery, hinting, and coercion, desiring to acquire further gain from that very gain.
In this way, a śramaṇa abstains from such various forms of hypocrisy, flattery, hinting, and coercion, which consist in the desire to acquire gain from gain.

52. Furthermore, Great King, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, having consumed what was given out of faith, maintain their livelihood through the wrong livelihood of animal sciences and sorcery.

For example, some employ [these arts] in the interpretation of portents, the marks of wounds, the marks of dreams, burns by fire, touch by water, gnawing by mice, possession, the analysis of voices, the cries of all beings, the science of limbs, the science of architecture, the science of parrots, and the science of omens;
a monk refrains from such wrong livelihood consisting of the sciences of lower animals.

53. "Furthermore, Great King, there are certain recluses and brahmins who, having consumed what is given in faith, maintain their livelihood through the wrong way of life consisting of 'animal-knowledge' (tiryag-vidyā).

That is to say: in the conjunction of the constellations, in the rising of the moments (muhūrta), in the examination of corpses, in the art of leaf-divination, in rites for pacification, in rites for spirits, in rites for prosperity, in rites of aspiration, in writing, and in calculation and the laying down of numbers."

Some apply themselves to arithmetic, to the art of finger-calculation (*mudrā*), and to the sciences of divination; in this way, a śramaṇa abstains from such wrong livelihood consisting of the science of omens.
54. For instance, Your Majesty, some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed what was given in faith, make their living by means of the wrong livelihood of the science of omens.

For example, in medical treatment—whether in the administration of root medicines, collyriums, or elixirs; in the treatment of women, men, boys, or girls; or in the application of medicinal herbs—a śramaṇa abstains from such wrong livelihood consisting of the "sciences of beasts."

55. "Furthermore, Great King, there are certain recluses and brahmins who, having consumed what is given in faith, maintain their livelihood through the wrong way of life consisting of animal sciences (*tiryagvidyā*). That is to say: the science of gems, the science of staffs, the science of swords, the science of arrows, the science of weapons, the science of elephants, the science of horses, the science of bulls, the science of buffaloes, the science of goats, the science of rams, the science of sheep, and the science of cocks."

In the characteristics of quails, in the characteristics [of animals], in the characteristics of women, in the characteristics of men, in the characteristics of boys, in the characteristics of girls, in the characteristics of short life, in the characteristics of long life, in the characteristics of small fortune, in the characteristics of great fortune, in the characteristics of little merit, in the characteristics of great merit, in the characteristics of little power, in the characteristics of great power, in the characteristics of the noble, and in the characteristics of the servant— thus.
In this way, a śramaṇa abstains from such wrong livelihood consisting of animalistic sciences (tiryagvidyā).

56. For instance, Your Majesty, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming what has been given out of faith, make their living through wrong livelihood consisting of animalistic sciences; namely, by means of incantations for driving away, incantations for summoning, emetics, purgatives, and nasal treatments.

Some practitioners employ the Vetāla and Ardha-vetāla rites for inhaling smoke, for sudation therapy, or when there is an accumulation of undigested matter (*āma*), accumulated waste (*pakva*), or abscesses; or they use them on the *cakra*, the *vāyasamaṇḍala*, the joining of the jaws, or for cutting the tongue.
A renunciant refrains from such wrong livelihood consisting of the "animal-knowledge" (*tiryag-vidyā*) of these ascetics.
57. For instance, Great King, some ascetics and brahmins, having consumed gifts given out of faith, [live] by the wrong livelihood of animal-knowledge.
They make their living by means such as: carrying away, bringing together, marrying off, bewildering, completely deluding, causing displacement, killing, producing happiness, producing suffering,
and performing burnt offerings with *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, rice grains, wealth, grain, mung beans, black gram, or various substances.

Some cause the fire-oblation (*agni-homa*), the worship of the sun (*ādityopasthāna*), the worship of the constellations (*nakṣatropasthāna*), the worship of deities (*devatopasthāna*), or even the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*) to be performed;
in this way, too, the ascetic is one who abstains from the wrong livelihood of the "animal-knowledge" (*tiryag-vidyā*).
58. For instance, Your Majesty, some ascetics and brahmins, having consumed what has been given out of faith, maintain their livelihood through the wrong livelihood of animal-knowledge.

For example, thinking, "There will be danger," "there will be security," "there will be famine," "there will be abundance," "there will be drought," "there will be good rain," "there will be pestilence," or "there will be no pestilence"—
a śramaṇa abstains from such wrong livelihood consisting of the science of omens.

59. "Furthermore, Great King, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who, having consumed what is given in faith, maintain their livelihood through the wrong way of life consisting of animal sciences (*tiryagvidyā*).

For example: 'Victory will belong to the internal kings and defeat to the external ones'; 'Victory will belong to the external kings and defeat to the internal ones'; 'The internal kings will retreat'."
"‘The departure of outsiders will be the retreat of outsiders, and the departure of insiders’—from such a wrong livelihood consisting of the sorcery of heretics, the ascetic refrains.
60. Furthermore, Great King, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who, having consumed what is given in faith, make their living by the wrong livelihood of the sorcery of heretics."
Just as the sun and moon travel by the proper path, so too do the sun and moon travel by the wrong path. In such a manner, the sun, moon, and planets follow the proper path;

likewise, meteors fall, the quarters blaze, and divine drums resound in the sky when the sun, moon, planets, meteors, and blazing quarters follow the wrong path. Or rather, it is the rising, setting, defilement, purification, establishment, and purity of these two—the sun and moon—who possess such great supernatural power and such great majesty.
It is not discerned whether this is the right path or the wrong path; thus, a śramaṇa abstains from such a wrong livelihood consisting of the sciences of the beasts.

61. For instance, Your Majesty, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, having consumed what was given in faith, maintain their livelihood through the wrong livelihood of the sciences of the beasts; that is to say, they claim:
"The sun and the moon travel along the right path with such-and-such a ripening, and the sun and the moon travel along the wrong path with such-and-such a ripening."

As they were going along, such were the portents on the road: eclipses of the sun, eclipses of the moon, falling meteors, and the burning of the quarters of the sky; in the atmosphere, the celestial drums resounded loudly. Such were the portents on the wrong path: eclipses of the sun, eclipses of the moon, falling meteors, the burning of the quarters of the sky, and in the atmosphere, the celestial drums resounded loudly.

Furthermore, even regarding these two, the sun and the moon—so majestic in power and so great in majesty—their rising and setting, their defilement and purification, and their established order and purity cannot be discerned, whether by way of the proper path or even by a wrong path. It is from such a form of animalistic science and wrong livelihood that the ascetic abstains.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of ethical discipline, he experiences within himself a blameless happiness.
He has the doors of his sense-faculties guarded; he possesses constant mindfulness and a mind protected by mindfulness, dwelling in the practice of remaining [in the present].

Having seen forms with the eye, he does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics; because, if he were to dwell unrestrained with the faculty of the eye, covetousness and dejection— evil, unwholesome states that flow into the mind from such a basis— would leak into it.
He practices for their restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye;
he attains restraint through the faculty of the eye.

Having cognized sounds with the ear-faculty, odors with the nose-faculty, tastes with the tongue, tangibles with the body, and mental phenomena with the mind-faculty, he does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics.
For if one dwells unrestrained in the faculty of the mind, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states that flow into the mind from such a basis—would leak into it.
He practices for the sake of restraint regarding these.
He guards the faculty of the mind;
he practices restraint with the faculty of the mind.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of ethical discipline and through this guarding of the doors of the faculties, he experiences within himself a blameless happiness.
He dwells with clear comprehension in going forth and returning;

he dwells with clear comprehension in looking ahead and looking aside, in bending and stretching his limbs, in carrying his outer robe, bowl, and inner robes, in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, remaining silent, and in dispelling drowsiness and fatigue.

Endowed with this noble aggregate of ethical discipline, with this guardedness of the doors of the sense faculties, and endowed with this supreme mindfulness and clear comprehension, he dwells in remote lodgings— forests— inwardly experiencing the happiness of freedom from affliction.

Endowed with this noble aggregate of ethical discipline, with this guardedness of the doors of the sense faculties, and endowed with this supreme mindfulness and clear comprehension, he occupies remote dwellings in the wilderness.
There are the roots of trees and empty dwellings;
having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind frequently free from covetousness.
He purifies the mind of covetousness;
having abandoned ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt regarding the world, he becomes one who has crossed over uncertainty;
having crossed over doubt and uncertainty, he purifies the mind of doubt concerning wholesome qualities.

64. It is just as if, O Great King, a man were to take a loan and apply himself to various occupations, and those occupations of his should succeed; he would thereby repay that debt, and he would possess enough wealth for the mere maintenance of his wife.
It occurs to him:
"Having taken a loan, I engaged in various undertakings;
those undertakings of mine have been successful."
They have not failed;
therefore, I have cleared that debt,
and I possess enough wealth for the maintenance of my wife.
On that account, he would experience gladness.
For example, suppose there were a man who was afflicted, suffering, diseased, and weak;
for him, the food he ate did not nourish his body.
The drink he drank pains his belly;
yet at a later time he may become happy, free from disease, and strong;
then the food he eats covers his body.
The drink he drank did not distress his stomach;
it occurred to him:
"Previously, I was afflicted."
Suffering (sick, weak;
my food has been eaten [but] does not clothe the body);
a drink.
The yellow [bile] does not afflict his belly;
on that account, he would attain joy, just as a man... (66) ...[would feel].

He would be a slave, a servant, one to be commanded, a dependent, one who must follow another's will and cannot go where he desires; yet at a later time, he would no longer be a slave, a servant, one to be commanded, a dependent, or one who must follow another's will and cannot go where he desires.
It would then occur to him:
Formerly, I was a slave, a servant, subject to commands, dependent, and led wherever I wished to go;
but now, I am no longer a slave.
A servant who is not unfree, yet not one who goes wherever he pleases.
On that account, he would experience joy,
just as a man bound in a prison, his arms tightly fettered behind his back.
And having been released from that, he would arrive safely, securely, and without harm;
it would then occur to him:
"He who was previously bound in the prison..."
"I was bound with my arms tightly tied behind my back, yet I was released from that by means of well-being, safety, and security;
on account of this, he would experience joy—
just as a man who has been in danger becomes happy."
Having brought about famine, he brings about abundance; it might occur to him: "I am happy, having emerged from a state of peril."
For one who previously experienced famine but now experiences abundance,
on that account he would attain happiness and attain gladness.
"In the same way, O Great King,
one perceives these five obscurations— namely, debt, disease, slavery, imprisonment, and the wilderness— as having been abandoned."
Having abandoned these five hindrances— which defile the mind, weaken wisdom, belong to the side of affliction, and do not lead to Nirvana— he, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil,
unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with joy and happiness.
He drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion;
there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by it.
It becomes impossible to pervade [the body] with that which is born of seclusion— namely, joy and happiness.
For example, it is like a skilled washerman or a washerman’s apprentice who, having scattered cleansing powder, [sprinkles it] with water.
Sprinkling it again and again, one should cause it to flow;
and his bath-paste— moist, permeated with oil, enveloped in oil, and manifest both internally and externally— neither drips nor flows out.
In the same way, he drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion;
there is nothing throughout his entire body that is not suffused or unsuffusable by that joy and happiness born of seclusion.
What do you think? (ma-)
"O King, this being so, the Blessed One has indeed demonstrated a visible fruit of the ascetic life:

through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, with internal clarity and the unification of the mind, one enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness."
Having attained this, he dwells therein; he drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the joy and happiness born of concentration,
so that there is nothing in him entirely untouched by it.
The body becomes unpermeated and incapable of being permeated by the joy and bliss born of concentration,
just as, for example, there might be a pool of water on a mountain peak above.
No water flows into it from the east, nor from the south, nor from the west, nor from the north;
nor does a rain god there, from time to time, properly bestow showers of rain.
Except for that very lake of water, [there would be] a great [drought].
Just as a water-sprinkler or a water-nozzle would drench, soak, fill, and saturate that entire pool of water with cool water, leaving nothing whatsoever untouched on all sides; (SBV II 244) so too...
Just as a pool of water becomes unobscured and unfilled by cool water,
even so he drenches, saturates, fills, and pervades this very body with the joy and happiness born of concentration.
"There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded or unsuffused with the joy and happiness born of concentration.
What do you think, Great King— is it not the case that, this being so, I have demonstrated to you the visible fruit of the ascetic life?"
"It is true, Venerable Sir.
This being so, the Blessed One has demonstrated the visible fruit of recluseship:
through the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body."
He experiences that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous"; having attained and dwelled in the third dhyāna, which is free from joy,
he drenches, permeates, gladdens, and suffuses this very body with the joyless happiness.
There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded or not suffused by a joy and happiness devoid of rapture—
just as in the case of blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, or white lotuses.
Born in water and grown in water, they remain there; from their tips to their roots, nothing remains unsuffused or unsaturated by the cool water.
In the same way, he drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the pleasure that is free from rapture (*niṣprītika-sukha*);
there is nothing throughout his entire body that is not pervaded or cannot be pervaded by that pleasure which is free from rapture.
"What do you think, Great King? Is it not the case that, this being so, I have demonstrated the visible fruit of asceticism?
"Truly, Venerable Sir, this being so, the Blessed One has demonstrated the visible fruit of asceticism."

75. Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness; having entered it, he pervades and suffuses this very body with a mind that is pure and cleansed.
He dwells; there is nothing at all of his entire body that is not pervaded or not suffused by his pure and cleansed mind.
Just as a householder or a householder’s son [might do], even so he dwells having attained and suffused this very body with a pure and cleansed mind, having resolved upon it.
"There is nothing whatsoever of his entire body that is not pervaded or cannot be pervaded—namely, by a mind that is pure and cleansed.
What do you think, Great King? Is it not so, then, that I have demonstrated a visible fruit of the ascetic life?
"It is true, Venerable Sir; it is so. A visible fruit of the ascetic life has been demonstrated by the Blessed One."

77. At the time, Great King, when a noble disciple, through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna— which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness—
At that time, his mind is neither elated nor depressed; it is not bent forward, but remains steady, having attained imperturbability—
just like a peaked roof chamber.

Or, in a gabled hall, the flame of its oil-lamp does not rise, nor does it sink; it remains level, having attained imperturbability. In the same way, at whatever time a noble disciple, through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of joy and dejection, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna—which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness—[his mind remains level, having attained imperturbability].
Having attained and dwelling in meditative absorption, at that time his mind is neither elated nor depressed, not leaning forward, but steady and attained to imperturbability.
It occurs to him:
"This body of mine is material and gross."
(Consisting of the four great elements);
consciousness is established here, included herein;
what if I were to withdraw the mind from this body and manifest another body—material, mind-made, complete, with unimpaired faculties?
Having withdrawn the mind from that body, he creates another body— material, mind-made, complete, and with unimpaired faculties.
It is just as if there were a beautiful, well-born, clear, limpid, and unclouded beryl gem of eight facets, strung upon a five-colored thread—blue, yellow, red, white, and madder-red;
a man with good eyesight, seeing it, would know: "This is the gem, this is the thread; the gem is strung upon the thread."
In the same way, having withdrawn his mind from that body, he creates another body— material, mind-made, complete, with unimpaired faculties—
just as a man might pull a reed from its sheath.
Just as a man with sight, having seen it, would know:

"This is muñja grass, this is iṣikā reed; I have pulled the iṣikā from the muñja," even so does he, having withdrawn the mind from that body, manifest another body—material, mind-made, complete, and with unimpaired faculties.

Just as men might pull a snake out of a basket, and a man with sight, having seen it, would know: "This is the basket, this is the snake; he has pulled the snake out of the basket"—even so, having withdrawn his mind from that body, he manifests another body, material, mind-made, complete, with all its faculties unimpaired.

Just as a man might draw a sword from its scabbard, and a man with sight, having seen it, would know: "This is the scabbard, this is the sword; he has drawn the sword from the scabbard"—even so [he draws the mind from that body].
Having emerged from that, he creates another body— material, mind-made, complete, with all its faculties unimpaired.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary afflictions, supple, wieldy, stable, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the sphere of psychic power.
He experiences various kinds of supernormal powers (ṛddhi), such as: having been one, he becomes many;
having been many, he becomes one.
He experiences manifestation and disappearance through his knowledge and vision;
he passes through walls, through mountains, and through ramparts with his body without obstruction, just as if through space;
he performs diving and surfacing in the earth, just as if in water.
He walks upon water without breaking the surface, just as on solid ground;
he travels through the air cross-legged, just like a winged bird;
and with his hand he touches and strokes even these two, the sun and the moon, so mighty and so powerful, reaching as far as the Brahma-world.
He exercises mastery over the body;
just as a skilled smith or a smith’s apprentice, having recognized well-refined gold,
desires to fashion whatever ornament he wishes to produce— whether it be a flat band or a circular earring.
Whether it be a neck-ornament, or a hand-ornament, or a foot-ornament, or a finger-ring, or a garland of gold, he brings each of these very quickly to that respective place;

even so, when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary defilements, upright, pliable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he realizes the knowledge of the sphere of supernormal power.
He directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledge and experiences the various spheres of psychic power.
That is to say: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one;
he experiences manifestation and disappearance through his knowledge and vision.
He passes through walls, through mountains, and through ramparts with his body without obstruction, just as if through space;
he performs the act of diving and resurfacing in the earth just as in water;
and he walks upon water without breaking the current, just as on the earth.
He travels through the sky cross-legged, just like a winged bird; moreover,
he touches and strokes with his hand these very sun and moon, so powerful and majestic, and exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world,
just as a skilled potter or a potter’s apprentice, having prepared a well-worked lump of clay...
Whatever kind of vessel-transformation he desires to bring forth, that very vessel-transformation he brings forth with extreme ease;
even so, when his mind is thus concentrated and purified...

When his mind is free from blemish, devoid of secondary afflictions, upright, pliable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledge that consists in the realization of the sphere of psychic power (*ṛddhiviṣaya*).
In this very way, he experiences various kinds of psychic power:
namely, having been one, he becomes many.
Having been many, he becomes one;
he experiences manifestation and disappearance through his knowledge and vision;
he passes through walls, through mountains, and through ramparts with his body without being obstructed, just as if through space.
He performs the act of emerging from and sinking into the earth as if in water;
he walks upon water without breaking the surface as if on earth;
he travels through the air cross-legged like a winged bird.
Indeed, he touches and strokes with his hand these very sun and moon, so mighty in supernatural power and so great in majesty, and exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world;
just as a skilled ivory-worker, or an apprentice of an ivory-worker, [takes] an ivory [object] that has been well-prepared and fashions it however he desires.
He brings about that very transformation of form, and he brings about each such transformation of form very quickly;

even so, when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, stainless, free from secondary defilements, upright, pliable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, [he applies it] to the realization of the knowledge of the sphere of psychic power.
He directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledges;
he experiences various kinds of miraculous power, such as: having been one, he becomes many.
Having become many, he becomes one again;
he experiences manifestation and disappearance through his knowledge and vision;
[he passes] through walls and through mountains.
He passes through walls without being obstructed by his body, just as if moving through space.
He performs the act of emerging from and sinking into the earth as if in water;
he walks upon water without breaking the surface as if on earth;
he travels through the air cross-legged like a winged bird.
Moreover, these very sun and moon, so powerful and so majestic,
he touches and strokes with his hand, and exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
What do you think?
"Great King, if that is so, has the visible fruit of recluseship not been demonstrated by me?
"It is true, Venerable Sir; if that is so, the visible fruit of recluseship has been demonstrated by the Blessed One. (SBV II 248)

81. When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the superknowledge of the realization of the divine ear. With the divine ear, which is purified and surpasses that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds: those of humans and...
Even those that are non-human;
whether they be far away or near.
It is just as if a man carrying a conch-shell, having climbed a great rocky mountain, were to blow the conch at midnight; his sound, unimpeded, would spread through the various directions.

In the same way, when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary afflictions, upright, pliable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the divine ear. With the divine ear, which is purified and surpasses that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds— those of humans and those of non-humans— whether they are far or near.
"What do you think, Great King? Is it not so that, this being the case, I have demonstrated a visible fruit of the ascetic life?
"Venerable Sir, it is true; this being the case, the Blessed One has demonstrated a visible fruit of the ascetic life.
82. When his mind was thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary defilements, and made upright...
When his mind is serviceable, steady, and has attained imperturbability, he directs it toward the higher knowledge that realizes the knowledge of the mental states of others;
he understands, as it truly is, the thoughts and reflections in the minds of other beings and other persons.
He understands, as it truly is, a mind affected by passion as "a mind affected by passion."

He understands as it truly is a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust"; he understands a mind with hatred as "with hatred," a mind free from hatred as "free from hatred," a mind with delusion as "with delusion," a mind free from delusion as "free from delusion," a contracted mind as "contracted," a distracted mind as "distracted," a sunken mind as "sunken," an exerted mind as "exerted," an agitated mind as "agitated," an unagitated mind as "unagitated," an unpacified mind as "unpacified," a pacified mind as "pacified," a concentrated mind as "concentrated," an unconcentrated mind as "unconcentrated," an uncultivated mind as "uncultivated," a well-cultivated mind as "well-cultivated," and an unliberated mind as "unliberated."
Or he understands, as it truly is, an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind"; or he understands, as it truly is, a well-liberated mind as "a well-liberated mind.
It is just as a man with sight, having taken up a perfectly pure mirror-disk, examines the reflection appearing before him.

In the same way, when his mind is thus concentrated— purified, cleansed, free from blemish, devoid of secondary afflictions, upright, pliant, stable, and attained to imperturbability— he directs his mind toward the higher knowledge that realizes the penetration of others' minds; he understands, as it truly is, the thoughts and reflections in the minds of other beings and other individuals.
He understands, as it truly is, a mind with lust as "a mind with lust";
he understands, as it truly is, a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust."

He understands as it really is a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred," a mind free from hatred as "free from hatred," a mind free from delusion as "free from delusion," a contracted mind as "contracted," a distracted mind as "distracted," a sunken mind as "sunken," an exerted mind as "exerted," an agitated mind as "agitated," an unagitated mind as "unagitated," an unpeaceful mind as "unpeaceful," a peaceful mind as "peaceful," a concentrated mind as "concentrated," an unconcentrated mind as "unconcentrated," a well-cultivated mind as "well-cultivated," an uncultivated mind as "uncultivated," and an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind."
Or, when the mind is well-liberated, he understands as it really is: "The mind is well-liberated.
What do you think, Great King—is it not the case that, this being so, I have demonstrated a visible fruit of the ascetic life?
"It is true, Venerable Sir; this being so, the Blessed One has demonstrated a visible fruit of the ascetic life:

when his mind is thus concentrated—purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary afflictions, upright, pliable, steady, and attained to imperturbability—he directs his mind toward the higher knowledge that realizes the recollection of past lives."
He directs his mind and recollects his manifold former existences;
that is to say, one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten,
twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, and many hundreds of thousands of births.

He recollects even many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, and many hundreds of thousands of births; he recollects an eon of dissolution, an eon of evolution, and an eon of both dissolution and evolution; he recollects many eons of dissolution, many eons of evolution, and many eons of both dissolution and evolution.
"Those beings were named such-and-such, where I was born with such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such a long life, and such a duration of stay;
having passed away from that place, I was reborn there."
Having passed away from there, he was reborn there; having passed away from there as well, he was reborn here—
thus he recollects his manifold previous existences with their modes and details.
It is just as if a man were to go from one village to another,
and from that village also to yet another village, and from there he might return here.
It might occur to him: "I have come from that village to this village; from there, too, I have come here."

In the same way, when his mind is concentrated, completely purified, cleansed, free from blemish, devoid of secondary afflictions, upright, pliable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the higher knowledge that consists in the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives; that is to say, one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine...

Ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; even many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, many hundreds of thousands of births; even an eon of dissolution, an eon of evolution, an eon of both dissolution and evolution, and even many eons of dissolution, many [eons of evolution].
He recollects many eons of evolution, and even many eons of both dissolution and evolution:

"Those beings were named such-and-such, where I myself was named thus, of such a birth, of such a clan, having such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a long life, remaining for such a long time;
passing away from that state, I was reborn there."
"Having passed away from there, he was reborn there;
having passed away from there as well, he was reborn here"—
thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
"What do you think, Great King? Is it not the case that, this being so, I have demonstrated the visible fruit of asceticism?
Truly, Venerable Sir, this being so, the Blessed One has demonstrated the visible fruit of asceticism."

84. When his mind was thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary afflictions, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directed his mind toward the higher knowledge that realizes the recollection of death and rebirth; with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he beheld sentient beings.

He understands, as it truly is, beings passing away and being reborn— whether beautiful or ugly, lowly or exalted, going to a good destination or a bad destination— according to their application of karma:
"These worthy beings, possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech and mind, revilers of the noble ones, holders of wrong views..."

Due to the cause of undertaking actions and dharmas based on wrong view, with that as their cause and that as their condition, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell.

On the other hand, these venerable beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view— due to the cause of undertaking actions and dharmas based on right view, with that as their cause...
With that as their condition, upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.
It is just as if a man with sight, sitting at a crossroads, were to see a great multitude of people coming, going, standing, or sitting, and observe their various activities;
so too, when his mind is thus concentrated—purified, cleansed, free from blemish, devoid of secondary afflictions, upright, and pliable—[he perceives].

Abiding in the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth, which has attained imperturbability, he directs his mind and, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, sees beings passing away and being reborn—
whether beautiful or ugly, lowly or exalted— and those going to a good destination or a bad destination.
Furthermore, he understands beings as they truly are according to their application of karma:

"These worthy beings, being possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech and mind, revilers of the noble ones, and holders of wrong views— on account of their undertaking actions and dharmas based on wrong view, with that as cause and that as condition,"
After the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell;
whereas these other beings, friends, being endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and mind,
not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on right view, for that reason...
With that as their condition, upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.
(What do you think, Great King? Is it not the case that, this being so, I have demonstrated the visible fruit of asceticism?
"It is true, Venerable Sir; this being so, the Blessed One has demonstrated the visible fruit of asceticism.")

85. When his mind is thus concentrated—purified, cleansed, free from blemish, rid of secondary defilements, upright, pliable, steady, and attained to imperturbability—he directs his mind toward the higher knowledge for the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows. He understands, as it truly is, "This is the noble truth of suffering."
"This is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering,
and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering"— thus he understands it as it truly is.
For him who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire.
The mind is liberated from the outflow of existence and the outflow of ignorance; for one who is liberated, there arises the knowledge and vision of liberation:
"Birth is exhausted for me, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, I know there is no further state of existence beyond this. (SBV II 251)
It is just as if there were a deep pool of water, clear, serene, and undisturbed, not far from a village or a town;
and a man with good eyesight, sitting on its bank, would see pebbles or gravel, or fish, or turtles, or shells, or snails.

In the very same way, when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary defilements, upright, pliable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he applies it to the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).
He directs his mind toward the higher knowledges;
he understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of suffering";
he understands, as it truly is, that "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire;
the mind is liberated from the influx of existence and the influx of ignorance. Being thus liberated, [the knowledge arises: “...[it is destroyed]” (MSV IV 222).

Liberated indeed is his knowledge and vision; he knows: "Birth is exhausted for me, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no further state of existence beyond this.
What do you think, Great King—is it not thus that I have demonstrated the fruit of recluseship visible in this very life?
"It is true, Venerable Sir; such being the case, the Blessed One has demonstrated a visible fruit of the ascetic life.
Thus, King Ajātaśatru, having repented for the murder of his father, was finally won over to the Buddha's teaching.

When this had been said, Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha and son of Vaidehī, wept, shedding tears. Then King Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha and son of Vaidehī, wiping away his tears with the corner of his robe, prostrated himself at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"I have transgressed, Blessed One; I have transgressed, Sugata! As I was foolish, as I was unskilled, as I was ignorant, and as I was unwholesome—being accompanied by evil friends and fallen under the power of evil friends—" [MSV IV]

"Enveloped by evil friends, O Venerable One, I deprived my father, a righteous king who lived according to the Dharma, of his life. Since I recognize this transgression, see this transgression, and acknowledge this transgression, please accept my confession out of compassion. It is true, Great King, that you have recognized your transgression as a transgression—just as a child, as one who is deluded, as one who is unrefined, and as one who is unskilled, because you were accompanied by evil friends, fallen under the power of evil friends."
Enveloped by evil friends, you deprived your father, a righteous king who lived according to the Dharma, of his life; yet,
O Great King, you recognize this as a transgression.
You recognize a transgression, and having seen it, you confess it; and for the future, you undertake restraint.
Only an increase, not a decline, of your wholesome qualities is to be expected.

Why is that? Great King, whoever recognizes a transgression, sees the transgression, confesses it upon seeing it, and undertakes restraint for the future—for such a person, only an increase is to be expected.

There is no decline in wholesome qualities; even so, Great King, since you recognize your transgression, see your transgression, confess it upon seeing it, and undertake restraint for the future, only an increase in your wholesome qualities is to be expected,
not their decline.
Then King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha, having invited the Blessed One, spoke thus to the Blessed One regarding the sin committed by his royal guest:
“May the Blessed One accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow at my home, together with the community of monks.
The Blessed One accepted King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra’s request by remaining silent.
Then, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, [departed].
Having rejoiced and approved of what the Blessed One had spoken, he bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.

Then, the Blessed One, perceiving that King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha had not long since departed, addressed the monks: "Monks, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha has been wounded and struck down by that evil companion with whom he associates and under whose influence he has fallen."

Enveloped by evil companions, he deprived his father— the righteous king, the king of Dharma, the great king established in Dharma— of life. Monks, had King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha not deprived his father— the righteous king, the king of Dharma,
the great king established in Dharma— of life, it is possible that in this [place]...
If he had sat down on that very seat, he would have realized the Four Noble Truths.
Thus, monks, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha was wounded and thus struck down.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall not let our minds become corrupted even toward a burnt pillar, much less toward a body endowed with consciousness."
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.

Then King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha, having prepared pure and excellent solid and soft foods that very night, rose early in the morning, arranged seats, set out a water-jar, and sent a messenger to the Blessed One.
He announced the time:
"It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready; may the Blessed One now do as he deems appropriate.

Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, went to where King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha was.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared right in front of the community of monks.

Then King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.

In many ways, having personally satisfied and served the Blessed One with pure and exquisite foods, both hard and soft, he perceived that the Blessed One had finished eating, had washed his hands, and had set aside his bowl; then, taking a lower seat, he sat down before the Blessed One,
and the Buddha conversed with Ajātaśatru.
He becomes increasingly attached to him.
Then the Blessed One expressed his approval of that gift of Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra, the King of Magadha, with this verse of rejoicing:
"The Agnihotra is the chief of sacrifices; the Sāvitrī is the chief of Vedic meters."
The king is the mouth of men; the ocean is the mouth of rivers.
The moon is the face of the stars; the sun is the face of those that give heat.
As far as the movement of the world extends—above, across, and below—the Perfectly Awakened One is the most worthy of worship among all the worlds, including the realms of the gods.
Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Ajātaśatru of Magadha with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.

When the Blessed One had established King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, in rootless faith, at that time, while the king was seated upon the roof of his palace and had dismounted from the back of an elephant, [he saw the Blessed One].
Or when he saw him, he released himself;
later, at another time, when he was mounted upon the neck of an elephant, he saw the Blessed One and released himself.
The Blessed One sustained him with his supernatural power and addressed his attendants and the household folk:
"Sirs, you should know this:"
"From this day forward, I am a disciple of the Blessed One and have gone for refuge to the Blessed One.
From this day forward, the door is open to the Blessed One’s disciples—the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—while the door is closed to Devadatta and his disciples.
Devadatta was no longer admitted into the palace.
He struck the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, who died shortly thereafter.
At another time, Devadatta began to enter the house of King Ajātaśatru and was addressed by the doorkeeper:
"Stay! You shall not enter.
For what reason? Because a command has been issued by the gods:
"From this day forward, I am a disciple of the Blessed One and have gone for refuge to the Blessed One.
From this day forward, the door is open to the Blessed One’s disciples—the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen;
but it is closed to Devadatta, to Devadatta’s male disciples, and to Devadatta’s female disciples."
He remained standing, held back at the gate;
and the nun Utpalavarṇā, having taken her alms-food, was departing from the royal palace;
then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
"This is the deed of this shaven-headed female ascetic:
she has sowed dissension between King Ajātaśatru and his harem, princes, and ministers, by which I have come to such a state. Having realized this, he said to Utpalavarṇā:
"What offense have I committed against you, that you have driven away my family of alms-seekers?"
He began to have her executed;
as she was being executed, she spoke with words of piteous and wretched lamentation: "Noble sir, may there be peace! What shall I do alone?"
"You yourself have gone forth from the Śākya clan once again under the Blessed One;
I do not act in such a way, so please forgive me.
Even as he was speaking thus, Devadatta struck her on the head with the palm of his hand.

Stricken by the pangs of death, she sustained the formative forces of life (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and relinquished the formative forces of longevity (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*); summoning her strength, she went to the rainy-season quarters of the nuns (*bhikṣuṇīvarṣaka*).
Seeing her in such a state, the nuns said, "O Noble Lady, what is this?"
She said:
"Sisters, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
All phenomena are without self;
nirvana is peace;
you must practice heedfulness regarding wholesome qualities.
Devadatta committed the third immediate transgression [by saying],
"I shall enter final nirvāṇa."
Then, having performed various miracles before the community of nuns, that nun passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder.
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how Devadatta has caused the nun Utpalavarṇā—who was lamenting most piteously—to be slain by a blow from a club."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was not only now; even in the past, while she was lamenting most piteously, I killed her and ate her flesh.
Listen to that."
The Story of the Old Sheep (concerning a previous birth of Devadatta):
Once upon a time, monks, a householder lived in a certain mountain village.
He had a flock of sheep;
the shepherd went out from the village to tend them.
Having tended them, at the time when the sun was setting, he began to lead them back into the mountain hamlet.
There, a certain old female jackal was trailing behind;
a wolf was pursuing her, and when he seized her, she said:
"Is it well with you, maternal uncle? Are you at ease, maternal uncle?
Do you find happiness dwelling alone in this forest, maternal uncle?
He replied:
"Having crushed my tail and torn out my hair, where will you escape now, you ewe who calls me 'uncle'? To this,
the ewe replied:
"The tail was behind you, yet I arrived ahead of you;
by what means, then, was the tail crushed by me? Thus he spoke, and the wolf replied further:
"These four continents, together with their oceans and mountains—all of them are my tail; so how have you come here? Thus [he spoke].
The ewe replied:
"O good sir, I had already heard from your kinsmen that your tail reaches everywhere; thus I have come through the air.
The wolf said:
"O Ajareḍikā, by you flying through the sky,
that herd of deer which had come to me as food has been terrified! Thus she lamented, and while she was so crying out, the one of evil deeds sprang up.
The ewe's head was severed, and having killed her, its flesh was eaten.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? That wolf at that time and on that occasion was none other than Devadatta;
and she who was Ajareḍikā was this very person."
At that time, on that occasion, she was Utpalavarṇā;
even then, she was killed while lamenting most piteously,
and now too, she is killed while lamenting most piteously.
Devadatta was won over by the nihilistic doctrine of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa;
then this thought occurred to Devadatta:
"I have exerted myself many times against the Blessed One, and I have committed the three deeds of immediate retribution."
A stone was thrown at the Blessed One, causing him to bleed;
this is the first *ānantarya* (immediate) offense;
the Saṃgha was split.
This is the second;
that Utpalavarṇā was deprived of life,
this is the third;
Having realized that he had not attained omniscience,
nor achieved any other success in his purpose,
and that he was now destined for rebirth in the hells, he placed his cheek upon his hand and remained lost in thought.
When Pūraṇa arrived at that place, he said:
"Devadatta, what [is this]?"
"Placing your hand upon your cheek, you remain absorbed in thought," he said;
he replied,
"How could I not remain absorbed in thought?"

"By me, out of an obsession with hatred, many assaults were committed against the Blessed One; three acts of immediate retribution were performed; and it will be necessary for me to dwell for a long time in the great Avīci hell."
He said: "I have understood that you alone among the Śākyas are wise;
you too are a fool."
"How could there be a future world for one who has committed such an act as this? We too would remain intent on anxiety for your sake.
Then, in order to inspire confidence in him, he broke a water-pot before him, saying: "Let the world, including the gods, mend this!"
By all means, do not be despondent;
there is no agent or maker here.
Nevertheless, go to the city of Kapilavastu.
"Go and rule the kingdom; we shall become your disciples before you.
Thereupon, Devadatta acquired a false view consisting of the disparagement of the noble ones (*āryāpavādikā mithyādṛṣṭi*), by which all his roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) were completely severed.
The Blessed One rebuked Devadatta there, addressing the monks: "Monks, the roots of merit have been severed by Devadatta."

"Monks, as long as I did not perceive even a single white quality in Devadatta, I did not declare of him: 'Devadatta is destined for the states of woe, for hell, to remain there for an eon, and is beyond remedy.
It was just like a heap of excrement not far from a village or a town, rising more than a man's height."
In that place, a certain man might be submerged, including his head, hands, and feet;
then another man might appear who, for a long time, desires his welfare, his benefit, his happiness, his comfort, and his security.
He would approach, surrounding that heap of excrement on all sides, thinking: "Perhaps I may find some spot on this man not smeared with excrement, where I can grasp him and pull him out."
As he approached, surrounding him on all sides, he could not find even a single spot on that man’s body smeared with excrement, not even as much as the palm of a hand;

and in this very same way, monks, as long as I did not perceive even a single white quality in Devadatta, I did not declare of Devadatta: "Devadatta is bound for the states of woe, bound for hell, destined to remain there for an eon, and incurable."
And because I did not perceive even so much as the tip of a hair’s breadth of white virtue in Devadatta, I therefore declared: "Devadatta is destined for the states of woe, for hell;
he is fixed for an eon and is incurable.
Monks, endowed with three unwholesome qualities, Devadatta is destined for the states of woe, for hell; he is fixed for an eon and is incurable.
By which three?
1) First, monks, Devadatta was one who had evil desires and was under the sway of an evil desire;
that Devadatta was first of all one who had evil desires and was under the sway of an evil desire.
"Endowed with this first unwholesome quality, Devadatta is destined for the states of woe, for hell, remaining there for an eon, and is beyond remedy.
2) Furthermore, monks, Devadatta had evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates;

because Devadatta previously had evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates, being endowed with this second unwholesome quality, Devadatta is destined for the states of woe, for hell, remaining there for an eon."
3) Furthermore,
Devadatta, having attained a distinction that was merely slight and inferior, fell into despondency midway while there remained further work to be done; he is curable.
Since Devadatta fell into despondency midway— despite there being more to be done— due to an attainment of distinction that was merely slight and trifling,
Devadatta, being possessed of this third unwholesome quality, is destined for the states of woe, for hell, remaining there for an eon, and is incurable.
May no one with evil desires ever be reborn in this world!
Therefore, by this very example, you should know what the destination is for those who desire evil.
He was renowned as a wise man, esteemed for his cultivated self, and resplendent with glory; he was known by the name Devadatta.
