Having encountered the Tathāgata here while still addicted to negligence,
he was nonetheless prophesied by the All-Knowing Buddha as one who would remain for an eon.
[Yet he remained] miserly, evil-intentioned, possessed of wrong views, and disrespectful.
He has reached the Avīci hell, which is known to have four gates.
For whoever would act with malice toward one who is innocent, who performs no evil deed—
that very sin touches him both in this world and in the next.
He who would dare to pollute the ocean with a jar of poison would not succeed in defiling it, for that great body of water is formidable.
In the same way, whoever harms the Tathāgata with words— against him,
one who possesses right vision and a tranquil mind, no dispute can take root.
A wise person should make such a person his friend and indeed serve him;
for one who serves such a person, there will be prosperity and not evil.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
the monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The new rules of Devadatta.

Then Devadatta, having acquired the false view that reviles the noble ones, with his roots of merit completely severed, reached the certainty that "there is no other world," and he taught the Dharma to the disciples in five points:
"The ascetic Gautama [prohibits] curd and milk..."
He partakes [of it];
from this day forward, we must not partake of it,
for the following reason:
On account of this, the calves are wasting away;
the ascetic Gautama consumes meat;
we must not consume it.
For this reason; for this cause, living beings are slaughtered;
the ascetic Gautama consumes salt.
"We must not consume it,
considering that it has arisen from dust;
the ascetic Gautama wears garments with frayed hems."
We must wear garments with long fringes;
for this reason,
on account of that, the manual labor of the weavers will be destroyed.
The ascetic Gautama dwells in the forest;
we must dwell in the village;
for what reason?
"For this reason, the gifts of humans are not being enjoyed. This is the intermediate summary verse:
"Milk, meat, salt, clothing, and [the rule] concerning the forest-dweller."
Devadatta was cast into a pond.
Then, while the Blessed One was wandering on a tour through the countryside, he arrived at Śrāvastī;
Devadatta reflected:
"Many times have I done harm to the ascetic Gautama, yet I have not been able to kill the ascetic Gautama;
I shall go now and cause him to suffer the loss of his wife."
He went to Kapilavastu;
having gone there, he sent word to Yaśodharā:
"The ascetic Gautama has gone forth."
"I have come for your sake;
therefore, you should enjoy yourself with me.
Thus [spoke] that Gopikā.
It was thus declared;
she said:
"Give him this message:"
"The Bodhisattva tolerates our grasping of his hand; if you too will tolerate it, come!
Out of shamelessness, he entered the inner apartments.
As he was ascending the stairs, he saw Gopikā;
he began to join his palms in mock salutation toward her,
for she possessed the strength of a great athlete.
With her left hand she pressed upon his fingers;
blood flowed out.
Then she threw him into the Bodhisattva’s pleasure pond; he let out a roar, and hearing it, the Śākyas ran forward.
"Devadatta has entered the Bodhisattva’s inner apartments and is violating his wives! They saw him fall into the pleasure pond and began to converse among themselves.
"Let us put him to death," they said;
they spoke further:
"When he is killed, [his lineage] will be destroyed."
"The Blessed One has indeed prophesied that Devadatta is destined for the states of woe, for hell, to remain there for an eon, and is incurable.
Having been abandoned by them, he fled through a crack in the wall.
His garment split and became two pieces;
he reflected:
"Excellent! In this manner, my disciples should clothe themselves in undergarments."
Devadatta, having failed in his attempts to become king of the Śākyas,
filled the undersides of his fingernails with a lethal poison, intending to scratch the Buddha’s feet.
Having died and fallen into hell, at another time he assembled the Śākyas and said:
"Establish me in the kingdom."
They said:
"The Bodhisattva’s harem is staying here; you take it for yourself first."
"After that, you shall exercise sovereignty.
Having been addressed thus, Devadatta, free from fear regarding the Śākyas, descended from the palace roof;
approaching Yaśodharā and joining his palms in reverence, he said:
"I am at your command;
grant me your favor, O Chief Queen,
and let me rule the kingdom in Kapilavastu."
Yaśodharā was more powerful than Praskandin;
then, rising from her auspicious couch and grasping both his hands, she threw him down upon his knees, and blood began to flow from his hands. (SBV II 261)
Stricken by painful sensations, he was addressed by Yaśodharā:
"You are shameless and a fool!
You who are not even able to endure my taking your hand now solicit me."
"Either a universal monarch shall be our master, or a Bodhisattva";
then, having been thus insulted by her, he departed from the inner apartments.
The Śākyas said to him, "Go and ask the Blessed One for forgiveness; if the Blessed One forgives you, you may rule the kingdom hereafter.
Having filled his claws with the most virulent poison of the *vatsanābha* variety, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.

"If the ascetic Gautama forgives me, that would be well; but if he does not forgive me, I shall fall at his feet right there and fill his feet with nail-poison. Having thought this, he fell at the Blessed One's feet and said this to the Blessed One:
"Forgive me, Blessed One!"
The Blessed One reflected:
"With what kind of mind has he approached me?
He saw that it was with a mind intent on killing.
Then the Blessed One, having fashioned his two feet from crystal from the soles of the feet up to the kneecaps, remained silent;
he [the nāga] began to pierce the Blessed One’s feet with his claws,
but his claws broke.
Being thus addressed, he replied: "I go to you for refuge,
because it was said by you:"
"Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to a miserable rebirth";
[if you say] "If I am to go to a miserable rebirth, then this [refuge] of yours is false," [we reply that] actions that are accumulated and fully ripened do not depend upon the falling of the body.
While still alive, he was embraced by the flames of the Avīci hell and began to cry out: "I am being burned, Ānanda! I am being burned, Ānanda!
Then the Venerable Ānanda—compassionate, whose nature is loving-kindness, and who is affectionate toward his own kin—said:
"Come, Devadatta, go for refuge to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Buddha.
Overcome by painful sensations and seeing the fruits of his own actions manifest before him, he conceived that thought from the depths of his heart.
The words were spoken:
"Even though I am not yet established [in the path], I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One. Having said this, he fell with his own body into the great Avīci hell.
The Buddha prophesies that at the end of a kalpa,
Devadatta shall become a pratyekabuddha.
There, the Blessed One, named Asthimān, addressed the monks:
"Monks, Devadatta has completely severed his roots of merit."
Having remained for an eon in the great Avīci hell, he will realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
he will become a pratyekabuddha named Asthimān.
As soon as he has attained full awakening, he will set aside his alms-food to one side and, while rubbing his hands together, he will reflect:
Reflecting thus, "For what purpose have I wandered in saṃsāra for so long a time? he will come to know:
"In birth after birth, I have exerted myself toward the Blessed One, even when he was a bodhisattva and had already attained mastery over all that is to be known."
"And that was for the sake of gain and honor.

Without even consuming that single portion of alms-food, he rose up into the air above and, having performed the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning, he passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana descended to hell to visit and console Devadatta.
It was the custom of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to go on occasional visits to the hells.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One has prophesied that Devadatta will attain the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha."
"Come, let us go to the great hell Avīci and comfort Devadatta.
Then the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to the great hell Avīci.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Focus your attention, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, upon the beings in the hells.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he began to rain down torrents as thick as pestles.
That water is consumed from within by the flames of the Avīci hell;
likewise, when it begins to rain with showers as thick as axles and as large as chariot-poles,
that water too is consumed from within.
Then the venerable Śāriputra entered the concentration of resolute intention (*ādhimokṣika-samādhi*);
that entire hell was flooded with water.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said,
"Let whoever is Devadatta come forward";
thereupon, many thousands of Devadattas arrived.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said,
"Let Devadatta, who was the Blessed One’s brother, come here.
Then Devadatta approached where the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were.
Having approached, he prostrated at the feet of the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana; they said to him:
"Is there any distinction among your causes?"
Thus he said:
"Let that which is established as common to the beings in the Avīci hell remain mine alone;
but hear now those [merits] which pertain to individuals. (MSV IV 238)
Iron mountains come,
ablaze, aflame, fully ignited, and turned into a single mass of fire;
they grind me like sesame seeds.
Their limbs and minor members are split apart with saws having teeth on both sides;
their heads are repeatedly crushed with iron mallets that are blazing, glowing, fiercely burning, and become a single mass of flame;
and elephants approach from the four directions.
"They are grinding me like flour," said the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
"O Devadatta, as for what you say:"
"Iron mountains are coming—blazing, aflame, fiercely burning, and turned into a single mass of fire;
they will grind me like sesame seeds.
For it was by you that a rock was hurled from Vulture Peak Mountain for the purpose of killing the Blessed One; this is the fruit of that action.
As for what you say—
that one's limbs and members are split apart by saws with teeth on both sides, which are blazing, aflame, fully kindled, and become a single mass of fire—
it is because you have caused a schism in the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples.
This is the fruit of that karma of which you speak:
that his head is repeatedly crushed with iron mallets— blazing, aflame, fiercely burning, and become a single mass of fire.
For indeed, by you the nun Utpalavarṇā, who was an arhat, was killed with a blow from a bedpost;
this is the fruit of that action of which you speak:
"Elephants are coming from the four directions;
they will grind me to powder like flour.
For it was indeed by you that the noble elephant Dhanapālaka was released for the purpose of killing the Blessed One.
"This is the fruit of that karma;
moreover, you have been prophesied by the Blessed One.
"Why so, Venerable Śāriputra?"
"Monks, Devadatta has withdrawn his roots of merit;
after remaining in the great Avīci hell for an eon, he will become a Pratyekabuddha possessed of bones."
He said,
"Venerable Śāriputra, if that is so, I am willing to remain on one side in the great Avīci hell.
Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana visited the followers of Devadatta in hell.
Kokālika and others, and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
Then the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached where Kokālika and the others were;
meanwhile, Kokālika’s tongue was being held down by a hundred ploughs.
Then Brahmā, the Lord of the Assembly, spoke to Kokālika:
"Having inspired faith in the two monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—who are gentle, affectionate toward their fellow celibates, and virtuous—one should direct one's mind toward them.
When this was said, Kokālika, seeing the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, remarked:
"Even here these two have arrived, seeking evil!"
Immediately after Kokālika had uttered those words, his tongue began to be torn out by a plowshare.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, realizing that these things were beyond remedy, departed and went to where Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was.
Then Pūraṇa Kāśyapa fell at the feet of the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana and said:
"Noble Śāriputra, by my false teaching of the Dharma, a great multitude of people was deceived.
As the ripening of that karma, five hundred plows drag across my tongue."
"In whatever manner the disciples construct the stūpa, in that very manner I experience increasingly intense pain;
therefore, you ought to inform them of my condition and dissuade them, saying:
'Do not construct that stūpa.'"
Having agreed, saying "So be it," the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana traveled through the hells and returned to Jambūdvīpa by means of their supernatural power;
they then related in detail to the Blessed One and the monks the condition of Devadatta, Kokālika, Pūraṇa, and others who had been reborn in the hells.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, behold how Devadatta, having rendered the word of the Blessed One as if it were no word, has fallen into the great Avīci hell. The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that he, having disregarded my word, met with disaster through misconduct; listen to how it was so in the past as well.
[This is] the story of the bull and the donkey."
(Concerning a previous life of the Buddha and Devadatta:
Once upon a time, monks, when the Bodhisattva was situated in the stage of the undetermined, he was reborn among cattle as a bull.
At night, having gone out from the city, he would graze in the king’s field of mung beans.
He remained in the city during the day; meanwhile, a donkey approached him and said:
"Uncle, you have grown fat with flesh and blood."
"And yet, I have never seen you grazing.
He replied,
"Sister's son, I graze at night in the king's bean field."
He said: "Uncle, I too shall travel with you. He replied:
"Nephew, you are talkative; you will bring about misfortune.
He replied, "Uncle, I am going; I will not do it."
Having broken through the enclosure, they both fell into the king’s field of mung beans;
the donkey remained silent until he was fully satiated,
after which he said:
"Uncle, I shall sing first," said the bull; Vṛṣa replied,
"Wait for a moment until I have gone out."
"Afterwards, you shall do as you please";
having said this, he fled,
and the donkey began to bray.
Having heard this, the king's men seized him, saying: "Sirs, this donkey has eaten all of this royal field of mung beans."
"Let us inflict punishment upon him";
having said this, they cut off his ears, tied a mortar to his neck, and released him.
Wandering here and there, he was seen by a bull.
He replied to him with a verse:
"Well sung! Very well sung! You have obtained the fruit of singing, since by your song you have been born without ears."
"For thus it happens to one who does not guard his speech:
he now wanders about, deprived of ears and adorned with a mortar," he said.
And he replied with a verse:
"Be silent, Khaṇḍadanta; be silent, Jaradgava!
Even you, they seek here with three men bearing staffs in their hands.
Thus [said] the Blessed One.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that bull at that time and on that occasion was none other than I;
he who was that donkey at that time and on that occasion was this very Devadatta.
Even then, having treated my word as no word, he met with disaster through his misconduct;
hear again how, once more treating my word as no word, he met with disaster.
The Story of the Bull and the Jackal (concerning a previous life of the Buddha and Devadatta):
Once upon a time, monks, a householder lived in a certain mountain village.
He had a bull endowed with auspicious marks;
having fed the ascetics, brahmins, kinsmen, the helpless, the wretched, and beggars, he released it to roam as it pleased.
At a later time, while wandering here and there, it became stuck and remained submerged in a muddy quagmire.
At the time of sunset, he heard [of this];
seeking him out, he went into his presence, and he reflected:
"I am not able to pull you out now;
I shall pull you out tomorrow at dawn," he said.
The bull replied:
"Place a snare before me and go;
if a jackal comes, I shall cast the snare over its horns.
Having placed the snare before him, he departed.
When night fell, a jackal arrived; he said,
"Who is this digging up the lotus stalks and white lotuses?"
The bull said,
"I remain submerged";
the jackal reflected:
"A prey has presented itself to me!
he thought, and he began to charge at him.
The bull said:
"Go away from this place, lest you fall into calamity through such misconduct";
yet even though he was thus being dissuaded, he continued to charge forward.
Then that bull spoke this verse:
"I do not dig up the lotus roots, nor do I [pluck] the white lotuses.
If you desire to eat them, follow behind me and eat.
Thinking, "I shall eat," the jackal followed behind him.
The bull threw the noose onto its horns;
the jackal was bound by the neck and hung suspended in the air.
The bull spoke this verse:
"Are you a dancer or an actor, or perhaps a handsome youth? Display your craft in the village; in the forest there is no patron. (SBV II 267)
The jackal also spoke this verse:
"I am neither an actor nor a dancer, nor am I the boy Śobhita;
Śakra has granted me a ladder, and I am going to the Brahma-world. (MSV IV 243)
Again the bull spoke this verse:
"Śakra does not give a guild; how then could the Brahma-world be yours?
You are bound by a snare of deception; I see no life for you. Thus he spoke.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that bull at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself;
he who was that jackal at that time and on that occasion was this very Devadatta.
"Even then, having disregarded my words, he met with calamity through this misconduct; even now, having disregarded my words, he has met with calamity through this misconduct.
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable sir, Devadatta, not heeding the word of the Blessed One, has become one whose destination is the Avīci hell.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, not heeding my words as I cried out to him, he became one whose destination was the Avīci hell."
Let that be heard:
The Story of King Caitika and the Two Sons of the Purohita (concerning a previous life of the Buddha and Devadatta).
Long ago, monks, in a certain royal capital, a king named Caitika reigned over a kingdom that was prosperous and teeming with many people.
By the power of his merit, deities held up a throne in the air.
That king had two sons by his domestic priest: an elder and a younger.
Among them, the elder delighted in renunciation, while the younger delighted in the office of a domestic priest.
The elder saw his father performing the duties of a priest through both righteous and unrighteous means.
He reflected:
"After my father's passing, I shall become the domestic priest;
what if I too were to go forth?"
Having obtained his father's permission, he went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
Later, at another time, the domestic chaplain passed away,
and the younger son was established in the position of chaplain.
He began to perform the office of domestic priest through unrighteous means;
the populace was oppressed.
Eventually, a certain man, wandering here and there, [encountered] him... (MSV IV 244)
He approached the elder who had gone forth into the religious life;
he was seen by him.
"From where do you come? He replied:
"From that royal capital."
He began to inquire after news;
he replied: "The king's domestic priest has passed away."
His youngest son was established in the office of domestic priest; he performed the duties of the priesthood unrighteously,
and thus the body of people was oppressed.
He said:
"Wait for a short while;
I myself will go there and restrain those who act harmfully and establish them in what is beneficial, so that they do not oppress the people."
That man went and reported this matter to his kinsmen;
it was heard by that youngest brother through the oral tradition,
and he reported it to the king:
"Your Majesty, that elder brother of mine will arrive. The king said, "Excellent! He himself shall become the domestic priest."
He said:
"Your Majesty, for so long a time I have served you in vain.
The king replied:
"This is the eldest custom of the world;
however, let there be your office as domestic priest in one particular manner.
If, when he has arrived, you say this:
"I am the eldest," he said; the other replied,
"So be it."
"I shall speak.
When he arrived,
the assembly, together with the king, rose upon seeing him.
But he did not rise; he was told by him:
"You are my younger brother, why do you not rise? He replied:
"You alone are the younger, while I am the elder; if you have no confidence [in me], we shall ask the elders in the royal court and the King.
Thus the King was questioned by the elder brother.
"Tell us, O King, who between us two is the elder?
The king, being fully aware of the truth, spoke a deliberate falsehood:
"This one is the elder; you are the younger."
Immediately after he had uttered those words, the deities vacated his seat;
he fell to the ground, and a foul stench issued from his mouth.
The eldest son of the family priest recited this verse:
"For the deities depart from one who speaks falsehood;
his mouth becomes foul-smelling, and he falls away from heaven."
"Speak the truth, O King; let it be as it was before. If you speak falsely, Caitika, you will clearly go to the lower realms."
He becomes tongueless like a water-dwelling fish,
he who, when questioned, demonstrates what is non-Dharma as Dharma.
"Speak the truth, O King; you shall become as you were before. If you speak falsely, Caitika, you will clearly go to the lower realms."
A non-man is born there, and a man is not born there, by one who,
when questioned, points out what is unrighteous as being righteous.
"Speak the truth, O King; you shall become as you were before. If you speak falsely, Caitika, you will clearly go to the lower realms."
The god rains out of season and does not rain at the proper time there for one who,
when questioned, demonstrates what is unrighteous as being righteous.
"Speak the truth, O King; you shall become as you were before. If you speak falsely, O Caitika, you will clearly go to the lower realms."
That person possesses two tongues, just like a serpent, who, when questioned, points out what is unrighteous as being righteous.
O King, speak the truth; you shall become as you were before.
If you speak falsely, O Caitika, you will clearly go to the lower realms.
Thus, having performed such a most dreadful deed, King Caitika reached the Avīci hell, a place of torment, on account of his evil karma.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that eldest son of the domestic priest at that time and on that occasion was none other than I;
he who was King Caitika at that time and on that occasion was none other than Devadatta.
"Even then, not hearing my words as I cried out, he fell into the Avīci hell; even now, not hearing my words as I cry out, he has fallen into the Avīci hell.
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, Devadatta, though being told what was for his benefit, did not listen to the words and has ended up destined for the Avīci hell.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, though being told what was for his benefit, he did not listen to my words and met with disaster through his own misconduct."
Let that be heard:
The Story of the Master Mechanic and His Pupil (concerning a previous life of the Buddha and Devadatta).
Long ago, monks, in a certain mountain village there lived a master of mechanical arts. He brought home a wife from a family of equal status; he played, took pleasure, and dallied with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, in the course of time his wife became pregnant;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth, and a boy was born.
For him, after a birth festival had been performed in detail for twenty-one days— three times seven days— a name was established that accorded with his family;
he was raised and grew until he became a man.
His father passed away,
and he began to learn the art of mechanical engineering from a certain master of mechanical arts in a particular mountain village.
He requested a girl from a householder in a certain market town,
and the man said:
"If you come on such-and-such a day, I will give her to you."
"It is not otherwise," he said;
he then informed the master of mechanical arts that there was a householder in that particular village.
I requested a girl from him,
and he said:
"If you come on such-and-such a day, I will give her to you."
"Not otherwise," [he said];
the master of mechanical arts replied,
"Son, if it is so, let us go."
"I myself shall receive it.
Having mounted a wooden peacock together with him, on the very day the deadline had been set, he arrived at the mountain village;
seeing this, he was struck with great wonder.
Then, having taken the girl back and once again mounted that mechanical device, he returned to his own home; having secured the device, he handed it over to his mother and said:
"This son of yours knows the method for operating the machine, but not the method for reversing it."
"You must not give him the machine," [the mother said].
He said to his mother again and again, "Mother, give me the machine; I shall win over the great multitude of people."
She said:
"Son, your teacher says:
'He knows the application for setting [the wheel] in motion, but not for stopping it.'"
"Do not give it away, for he will fall into calamity because of his pride;
therefore, I do not give it. He replied:
"Mother, I know both how to proceed and how to desist; however, this teacher does not give [the instruction] out of stinginess;
women are of light mind."
Enticed by her, he gave it;
having wound the machine and mounted it, he set out,
and a great multitude of people became filled with faith.
Then he was seen by the master of mechanical arts,
who said: "He has gone away so as never to return."
The more he hurriedly pursued him, the further away he went;
until finally, he reached the great ocean.
The god rains constantly upon the great ocean;
my bonds are soaked; through this misconduct, I have fallen into calamity.
A deity speaks this verse:

"For he who does not accept the words of one who desires his welfare and is compassionate for his benefit, according to the instruction given—he is carried away by a wooden bird; being without a leader, he hears no one here. Thus it is said.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks?
That master of mechanical arts at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself."
He who was his pupil at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Devadatta.

Even then, not listening to my words, he met with calamity through his own misconduct; and even now, though being told what is for his benefit by me, not listening to my words, he has met with calamity through his own misconduct.
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, it is said 'schism in the Saṅgha,' and it is said 'harmony in the Saṅgha.'"
In that regard, what is schism and what is concord in the Saṅgha? Upāli,

when monks who perceive as non-Dharma what is Dharma, and perceive as Dharma what is non-Dharma, perform formal acts while being divided yet perceiving themselves as undivided— this is called a schism in the Saṅgha.
But when those who perceive what is Dharma as Dharma perform formal acts (karma) in a complete assembly with the perception that it is complete,
this is called "concord of the Saṅgha" (saṃghasāmagrī);
where even a single monk is not present, there the Saṅgha is not split.
Where there are two, three, or up to eight [monks], the Saṃgha is not split there;
where there are nine monks or more, the Saṃgha is split there by two causes:
by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) and by the taking of voting tickets (*śalākā-grahaṇa*).
How is it by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*)?
It is as follows: Devadatta informs, makes known, instructs, and causes the monks to accept:
"Venerable ones, by five bases of conduct (*vratapada*), a monk is purified, liberated, delivered, and transcends pleasure and pain."
And he attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain.
By which five [factors]?
Venerable ones, by being a forest-dweller, a monk is purified, liberated, goes forth, and transcends pleasure and pain.
And he attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain.

Venerable sirs, by being a tree-root dweller, by being an alms-food eater, by being a wearer of the three robes, and by being a wearer of rag-robes, a monk is purified, liberated, and delivered; he transcends pleasure and pain, and he attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain.
"Venerable sirs, those among you who do not approve of being purified, released, and emerged by means of these five points of training, let them remain far from the ascetic Gautama,
let them remain apart, let them remain distant and remote"— this is the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus, by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), how is there the taking of voting tickets (*śalākā*)?
It is as follows: Devadatta informs the monks, makes them understand, instructs them, and causes them to grasp [the matter]:
"Venerable ones, by means of five bases of the vow,
a monk is purified, liberated, and emerges; he transcends pleasure and pain,
and attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain."
By which five?
Venerable sirs, by being a forest-dweller, a monk is purified, liberated, and emerges; he transcends pleasure and pain, and attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain.

"Venerable ones, by means of dwelling at the foot of trees, by means of eating only alms-food, by means of wearing the three robes, and by means of wearing rag-robes, a monk is purified, liberated, and delivered;
he transcends pleasure and pain and attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain.
Venerable ones, for those among you who do not approve [of this]..."
By means of these five points of discipline, may you be purified, liberated, and emerged from that ascetic Gautama; may you be far from him, separated from him, and at a great distance from him.
"Let them take the voting sticks";
then Devadatta, with himself as the fifth, takes a voting stick.
Thus, by means of taking the voting sticks—

The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, is the Saṅgha split by one who has been suspended (utkṣiptaka), or by one who follows the suspended, or by one who follows the follower of the suspended? Is it not [split] by the suspender (utkṣepaka), nor by one who follows the suspender, nor by one who follows the follower of the suspender, nor by one who follows the follower of the suspender?"

Venerable sir, the Saṅgha might be split not by one who has been suspended, nor by one who follows the suspended, nor by one who follows the follower of the suspended, nor by the suspender, nor by one who follows the suspender, nor by one who follows the follower of the suspender; rather, Venerable sir, the Saṅgha might be split by one who follows the follower of the suspended, not by one who has been suspended, nor by one who follows the suspended, nor by the suspender, nor by one who follows the suspender, nor by one who follows the follower of the suspender.
"Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha might indeed be split by means of one who has been suspended (*utkṣepaka*), but not by one who follows the suspended (*utkṣiptaka-anuvartaka*),
nor by one who follows the follower of the suspended (*utkṣiptaka-anuvartaka-anuvartaka*).
Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha might indeed be split by one who follows the suspended, but not by one who follows the follower of the suspended."
Not by one who follows a suspended monk, nor by one who follows one who follows a suspended monk, nor by a suspended monk himself, nor by one who follows one who follows a suspended monk.
"Venerable sir, the Saṅgha might indeed be split by one who follows the follower of the follower of the one who has suspended [a monk] (utkṣepaka-anuvartaka-anuvartaka);

it would not be split by the one who has been suspended (utkṣiptaka), nor by the follower of the suspended one, nor by the follower of the follower of the suspended one, nor by the one who suspends, nor by the follower of the one who suspends.
Upāli, the Saṅgha would be split by all of these, with the single exception of the one who has been suspended."
The intermediate summary verse: Schism in the Saṃgha and concord; a single Saṃgha is not split.
Among nine [cases], the last is a schism; there are three [types of] *utkṣepa* and six groups.
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, it was said by the Blessed One that one who causes a schism in a harmonious community of disciples produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell and is touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense."
"To what extent, Venerable Sir, does a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produce an offense leading to the Avīci hell and become touched by the karma of an immediate offense?

1) Upāli, when a monk, perceiving as non-Dharma that which is Dharma, and perceiving as non-Dharma the act of schism, informs the monks, persuades them, instructs them, and causes them to accept it, striving for the division of the Saṅgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell and becomes touched by the karma of an immediate offense."

2) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk, perceiving what is non-Dharma as non-Dharma, yet perceiving a schism as Dharma, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [his view] so as to bring about a schism in the Saṃgha—
by this much, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Saṃgha of the disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell and is touched by the karma of an immediate offense (*ānantarya*).

3) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk who perceives what is contrary to the Dharma as contrary to the Dharma, being of a divided mind regarding a schism, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [his view] among the monks, striving for the sake of a schism in the Saṃgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell (though not yet having committed it).
One is touched by the offense of immediate retribution through such an action.

Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk—perceiving what is not Dharma as Dharma, while perceiving schism as non-Dharma—informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [the schismatic view], striving for the division of the Saṅgha;
to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Saṅgha of disciples, produces an offense of the Avīci hell and is touched by the offense of immediate retribution.

5) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk who perceives as Dharma what is not Dharma, and who perceives as Dharma [an act] that causes schism, informs other monks, persuades them, instructs them, and causes them to accept it, striving for the sake of the schism of the Saṅgha—
to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Saṅgha of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

6) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk who perceives as Dharma what is not Dharma, being in doubt regarding a schism, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [his view] among the monks, striving for the sake of a schism in the Saṅgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Saṅgha of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

7) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk, perceiving what is Dharma as non-Dharma and perceiving schism as non-Dharma, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes [other monks] to accept [his view], striving for the sake of schism in the Saṃgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk,
having split the harmonious Saṃgha of disciples, produces an offense of immediate retribution and is touched by the karma of an immediate offense.

8) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk who perceives as non-Dharma what is Dharma, and who perceives as Dharma the cause of schism, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes other monks to accept [his view], striving for the sake of the schism of the Saṃgha—
to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Saṃgha of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

9) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk who perceives as non-Dharma what is Dharma, being in a state of doubt regarding a schism, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [his view], striving for the sake of a schism in the Saṅgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

10) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk, perceiving as Dharma that which is Dharma, yet perceiving as non-Dharma the cause of schism, informs the monks, persuades them, instructs them, and causes them to accept [his view], striving for the sake of the schism of the Saṅgha—to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Saṅgha of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell and is touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense. 11) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk, perceiving as Dharma that which is Dharma, perceives as Dharma the cause of schism... (SBV II 275)
He informs the monks, persuades them, instructs them, and causes them to accept [his views], striving for the schism of the Saṃgha;
to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Śrāvaka-Saṃgha, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

12) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk, perceiving what is Dharma as Dharma, but being in doubt regarding the schism, informs the monks, persuades them, instructs them, and causes them to accept [his views], striving for the schism of the Saṃgha; [to this extent...]

To this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

But when, Upāli, a monk who is in doubt regarding what is contrary to the Dharma, perceiving it as contrary to the Dharma, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [the schism], and exerts himself for the sake of splitting the Saṃgha;
to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell and is touched by the karma of an immediate offense.

14) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk who is in doubt regarding what is non-Dharma perceives it as Dharma during a schism, and informs, persuades, instructs, and causes other monks to accept [his view],

striving for the division of the Saṃgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

15) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk, being in doubt regarding what is non-Dharma and in doubt regarding a schism, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [the view] among the monks,

striving for the division of the Saṃgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

16) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk who is in doubt regarding the Dharma perceives it as non-Dharma during a schism, and he informs, persuades, instructs, and causes other monks to accept [his view], striving for the sake of the schism of the Saṃgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Saṃgha of the disciples,
produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell and is touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.

17) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk who is in doubt regarding the Dharma perceives it as the Dharma during a schism, and he informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [his view], exerting himself for the sake of dividing the Saṃgha—
to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious Saṃgha of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.
18) Furthermore, Upāli, when a monk, being in doubt regarding the Dharma and in doubt regarding a schism, informs, persuades, instructs, and causes others to accept [the views] of other monks,

striving for the division of the Saṃgha— to this extent, Upāli, a monk, having split the harmonious community of disciples, produces an offense leading to the Avīci hell, yet he is not touched by the karma of an immediate (ānantarya) offense.
Thus, these are the eighteen [cases].
Among these, six are touched by the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*); regarding those [six], one who perceives schism as non-dharma is touched by the offense of immediate retribution,
while the remaining ones are not touched by the offense of immediate retribution.
The section on schism in the Saṃgha within the Vinaya is completed.
The scriptural collection on the foundations of discipline.
